speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We are halfway through the current term of Government and we have made progress here.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But we still have a lot more to do.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Citizens have expectations of the Government to demonstrate leadership in formulating policies that always put the country on a better footing and care for her people.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: At the same time, they also want their voices to be heard and for the Government to stay connected and remain relevant to the ground.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Thus, I want to speak up for different groups of Singaporeans and share my thoughts on how we can do better as an economy, as a society and as one people, one nation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Looking at it from the viewpoint of our students and parents, I want to share three suggestions here.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Students have different pace of learning and each child blossoms at varying stages of their lives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For special needs children in mainstream schools, their challenge is to cope with the same number of subjects, using the same course materials and adapting to the pace of regular learning.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For some, they, indeed, struggle with something as basic as taking an additional language or subject.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Parents have shared with me that their children with such needs usually are not given exemption from the subjects until the children have proven to consistently fail.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This can be very demoralising for the child who has dyslexia, autism or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It also deters the child in wanting to learn more or do well in other subjects.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Yes, it may be a sweeping statement to say all special needs children are late bloomers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But I am certain no one will deny that these children deserve the opportunity to have a longer runway to learn and explore their potential at a pace that is suitable for them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Today, there is no shortage of daily evidences that reflect a lack of good community values and decreasing tolerance amongst people.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: From road bullies, errant users of shared bikes and personal mobility devices, high-rise litterers and so on.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: These people have little sense of how their actions impact others and the environment.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Values, to me, are fundamental guiding principles in an individual.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Our students can ace through exams; but such achievements do not empower or make them a more purposeful individual.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: VIA is unlikely to sustain at the current rate unless it is given emphasis in mainstream school admission criteria and not limited to those under Direct School Admission.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I believe that by knowing how to pay it forward and our relentless search for a higher purpose, we can nurture citizens with the spirit of care and giving to others.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Let us start to embrace and encourage this sense of responsibility amongst our young by blurring the lines of socio-economic background through valuing their actions towards our community and country.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: How should we train our students not to be regimental experts in subject matters but to demonstrate soft skills, the ability to apply and be creative?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I feel that the future skills we need to develop in SkillsFuture of our next generation are their ability to switch between industries and adjust within changing project needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Staying relevant and planning for one’s career and life must become instinctive in them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We must build their soft skills from young.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And to me, this can also help to shape their personalities and resolve when facing challenging situations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Take, for example, the role of an Industrial System Designer or Industrial System Integrator.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They have skills that are relevant to multiple industries.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While their knowledge of systems, designs, mechanics are fundamental, more critical are their management skills in integrating projects and people.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Today, we see growing trends of jobs moving towards the gig economy and remote workers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The pace of change is unpredictable and disruptive.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Increasingly, jobs are fulfilled by satellite workgroups and regional talents.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The competition for workers and jobs is no longer confined by a country’s boundary.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The number of workers is no longer the defining trait of a business or an economy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Instead, it is the quality of workers that matters.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: How well do our workers contribute to their tasks, how do they sight opportunities, can they collaborate?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The nugget is: “Can they stand out from the crowd?” Growth, we have certainly achieved in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: From a fishing village to a modern metropolis; from no industries to many multinational companies and homegrown brands.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But will this growth endure the test of time?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To me, I think we need to ensure we continue to have a role to play on the regional and global stage and, for this, the Government has to try some non-traditional approaches.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In this regard, I suggest two areas of enhancement to aid job matching and to build our home brands.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Having a job data bank like in the past is insufficient.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We need proficient actors in the industry to scout the value and talent within our workers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As traditional hiring processes fall out of favour, it is creating a vacuum and the mismatch in skills and jobs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And I see this as an opportunity for us.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We should encourage more of such partnerships and raise the bar of our work culture through different professional groups.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With the consolidation of mature industries, a vibrant startup scene and the presence of many smaller companies, the mergers and acquisitions potential also becomes livelier.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This will inevitably impact the pool of workers and freelancers during management changes and a lack of HR support is unhealthy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We need to take proactive steps to ensure progressive job mobility in order to achieve more effective social mobility.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Two, create ecosystems and build our Singapore brand.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To do so, we must build upon the illustrious track record of Singapore’s quality and brand reputation internationally.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Take it one step further, lead and create consortiums made up of more Singapore SMEs to create an industry of our own on the international stage.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This can be a paradigm shift of what the Government used to do.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We pick the potentials and help build such ecosystems.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: From developing global trade partnerships, exporting skilled workers, processes and systems, developing R&D expertise and know-how; to creation of new industries and co-sharing of resources within industries.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Ecosystems that have cross-industry demand and opportunities will give time and opportunity for our students and workers to deepen their skills and develop them into the trade craftsmen of the future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Affordability, choice, capital value, retirement – these are common words associated with the topic on housing.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On one hand, we want the Government to do more and support through policy measures.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Bearing in mind that these efforts must be taken with a multi-prong approach, I propose a few areas for consideration.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: One, change the valuation method for aged flats.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The challenge the market is facing is two-fold.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The sellers are having difficulties selling their flat with more options available in the market and a decreasing lease.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The buyers, on the other hand, find the aged flats priced out of their attainable reach.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Two, select precincts from different mature towns for lease top-up by private developers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Given the lack of new land plots in mature estates, it is difficult to effect SERS, especially when the flats are built over almost the same time span.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As HDB flats are typically built precinct by precinct, so, rather than selling new land plots for private property, allow the private developers to top up the land lease of HDB flats for future development.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Likewise, the Government can convert plots of private condo land for HDB housing in future when its lease is up.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This creates a better mix of private and public housing in the long run and allow families to have various home options in different towns at different stages of their life.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Three, allow direct rental of interim housing from HDB for the non low-income group.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For those who do not qualify as low-income group but have needs for interim housing, allow them to rent directly from HDB, only for those selected aged flats with leases of less than 45 years and, of course, subject to a capped period.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: These include families which have needs for interim housing as they transit, young working adults with little need for a permanent place due to their job nature, the single parents who need immediate shelter after their matrimonial flat is sold off and so on and so forth.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Give them the flexibility and space to manage or rebuild their lives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The next group I wish to speak for is the women.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I, too, have spoken on this Motion and am happy that some of my suggestions have been addressed or are being worked on by the Ministries.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I hope further consideration can be given to the following.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The current subsidies given to non-working mothers for infant care, childcare or kindergarten are lower compared to those of working mothers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Two, convert unused medical leave to eldercare leave.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Family remains an important first line of support for our ageing population.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Employers should feel encouraged and incentivised, particularly when the unused medical leave reflect that their employees are in good health and with little work absenteeism.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This effort is truly about giving a choice to the employees they value.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With the growing need for part-time work and care services, we should harness the strength of local entrepreneurs and the talent pool of women available in our country.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I have previously suggested establishing startup spaces in neighbourhoods to enable women to work closer to home or on a part-time basis.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Provide spaces in our town hubs to house such entrepreneurial businesses and shared platforms for them to create a service industry of its own – basic services like meal catering, minding of old folks and children at home, home cleaning, laundry and so on can be catered on a demand basis.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With proximity and a reliable supply of services, it can help ease the burden of working mothers and reduce the cost when it comes to after-school care.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Fourth, rooting for women’s education and leadership in Science, Technology, Engineering and Math (STEM).

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In today’s digital world, it is quite appalling that despite our drive for equality, people can hardly associate women with science and technology.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is not a numbers game of ramping figures to parity.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is the dawn of time; a call for change.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: An impetus to bring new perspectives from women on product design, services and emotive connections which are seldom considered previously.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With widespread technology so closely entwined in our lives, we need to embrace these technologies to achieve the much-needed productivity and innovation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Many of these tools can bring positive outcome for women in helping them balance their many roles in society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Education and careers in STEM should be encouraged amongst females.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In Singapore, we are fortunate that every child, male or female, has an equal opportunity to receive education from young.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But more can be done to enthuse females to continue pursuing roles in non-traditional industries or in male-dominated industries.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The current social gap lies in the perception that men are more suited for such jobs because they involve more problem solving and a level of technicality that historically men are seen to fit better.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But the truth is that despite the differences in the minds and behaviours of both genders, it is through pooling such differences that we can create stronger and more cohesive teams.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Such acceptance and changes in the long run will lead to more creative thinking and innovation, thus, leading to more fulfilled and satisfied employees and society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: (In Mandarin):   Next, I would like to talk about another very important group and one that is growing in our society: our seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Barely three months ago in this House, we discussed at length on the Motion of Support for Our Senior Citizens.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Given the significance and challenges that may be faced by these seniors, more enhancements were deliberated in Budget 2018.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat also announced three structural changes in his Budget Statement to better integrate health and social support services for seniors in the community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: All these are done in the hope that our seniors can age healthily and confidently in place.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Based on the current situation, our priority is to help those seniors who are isolated and need assistance the most.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Because these seniors live alone and have no family support, most of our efforts are now focused on planning and caring for them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, to ensure the other seniors are socially engaged and keeping fit, I would like to take this opportunity to call out to this generation of soon-to-be seniors to partner us in planning for the future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The adage "health is better than wealth" is well-known to many.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is ironic that we seem to understand and treasure this more as we age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As such, we must exercise often to stay fit.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: So, let us take the first active step together.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For those who actively exercise and do not have medical claims, offer them annual premium discounts.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As premiums will go up as people age, this incentive can motivate seniors to keep well, physically and psychologically.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In the long run, this will help relieve the psychological, physical and financial pressure for them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Second, to encourage the seniors to help one another in the community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We constantly look for volunteers who can provide care and assistance to needy seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To me, this initiative is one approach that increases social cohesion.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Everyone has a role to play to build a community in which people respect each other.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I urge retirees and seniors to give back to society and help make Singapore an inclusive society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Singaporeans who are keen to be more socially-engaged, please do step forward and help us build a more gracious nation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Youths and young working adults have many commitments today.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For some, to spend quality time with their parents and grandparents has become a luxury.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Even so, youths and working adults choose to spend a lot of time on social media.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This has become a trend of the modern society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Yet, as digitalisation is becoming a norm in our daily lives, why do we not pool our wisdom to enrich the digital space and create a platform for inter-generational bonding?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: If each of us can offer half an hour of our time regularly in helping the seniors in our own family to learn and navigate the digital world, inter-generational communication would grow exponentially.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The seniors will feel safer to be taught in a known environment and from people they trust.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We can all play a part to create innovative inter-generational programmes that are unique to our own family and pass on the heritage and values that will make our seniors proud of us.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: (In English): Finally, let me touch on an area that concerns all Singaporeans – the cost of living.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is natural for anyone to have concerns over necessities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: After all, these have direct impact on our lives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But with progression, it is inevitable to have an emerging middle class with rising aspirations and growing needs that go beyond necessities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: How can the Government, in reality, provide subsidies and grants for the masses without breaking the bank?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I believe this will be a difficult path to pursue.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: If we are to eschew the populist approach, the obvious answer is “We can’t subsidise for all”.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: So, I think we are at a point where we have to differentiate the "needs" from "wants", and how best to support different groups of Singaporeans.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is hard to imagine today for one to live without power, water or food in a developed country.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: These are, indeed, necessities that must be kept within affordable means for any household.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: There is a need for the Government to keep the cost low and give direct subsidies for these items.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But I think more can be done with a stronger focus on how to channel donations towards beneficiaries and social programmes that support giving necessities to those not living in public rental flats.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I am confident, if we continue to work together, the Government and people in close partnership, we will be able to seize the opportunities and effectively address the challenges – be it income inequality or social mobility – to build an even better tomorrow for ourselves, our children and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Many would also have heard of Chloe Chua, the 11-year-old violinist who won first prize at the prestigious Menuhin Competition.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I am sure there are many more awards that other Singaporeans have received and continue to work towards.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: If we ever falter and question whether Singapore can make it in future, I would say that we do not lack local talents, but we lack faith – faith in the next generation and belief that they can do better than us in their own right and style.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Their perspectives of the world also help unearth limitless possibilities that convey a fresh impetus to the development of our nation." I fully agree with her.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As a country, we can achieve much more when we put steadfast will and efforts together as one.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Let us show faith and find common grounds as one people.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Let us begin our new chapter, lift the dreams of our next generation and give them the opportunities and possibilities to make Singapore a great country, one filled with strength and hope for all.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Together, we can and will continue to build a more just, a more inclusive, a more meaningful society for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I will speak on one of the key themes outlined in the Addendum to the President’s Address for the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI), which is entitled “Staying Connected with the World as our Hinterland”.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are among the top 15 largest exporter and largest importer in the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are among the largest foreign investors in some of the major economies, including the US, China and ASEAN, despite our smaller GDP relative to those economies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore is well-regarded as a key global financial hub and a major risk management centre in Asia.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: All these and the other attributes of us being an open and internationalised economy have contributed to the growth and vibrancy of the Singapore economy in the last five decades.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It created good salaried jobs for Singaporeans, good business opportunities for our companies as well as, importantly, generated financial resources for the Government to fund its expenditures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Notwithstanding what we have achieved, which is no mean feat, staying still has never been an option for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Like every aspect and at every stage of our nation-building journey and, as what the President has said in her Address, we will always ask, “What is next for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can the Singapore of tomorrow do better than the Singapore of today?" In the case of developing our economy, much of the “what next” is already outlined in the CFE recommendations, which blueprint the transformation strategy to build our future economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is a comprehensive set of actionable initiatives there.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Among them, an important workstream is to further internationalise the economy, which is the focus of my speech.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is only so much more growth you can squeeze out of our small domestic economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just counting on our domestic market would not be enough to create more and better jobs for aspiring Singaporeans and more business opportunities for growth-seeking companies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, we need to expand our economic frontiers and, in so doing, look to also further diversify our portfolio and open up new dimensions of growth.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Growing our trade flows and investments continues to be a viable strategy for Singapore, given our still compelling propositions and the opportunities that are out there within our reach.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The escalating trade tensions between global economic powers are areas of concerns but that should not dampen our spirit.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is a strong signal that there are enough like-minded countries who believe that stronger economic linkages are mutually beneficial.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should ride on the momentum to expeditiously conclude the RCEP, which includes key players like China, India, Korea and all of the ASEAN countries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That will demonstrate to the world a strong commitment to free trade from Asia and a further indication that the centre of gravity of the world economy is shifting to Asia.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the same time, we should continue to work on bilateral linkages.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is great value in seeking more bilateral FTAs, such as the one we have just signed with Sri Lanka this year, which offers tangible benefits to Singapore companies doing business with Sri Lanka.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should also develop new government-to-government (G-to-G) business platforms with regional economies that come with complementary propositions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such business platforms, which may be at local levels, are useful in-market networks for Singapore businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These additional linkages, designed with balanced two-way business reciprocity, would help mitigate our overall trade-related exposures, strengthen our economic resilience and also sustain healthier on-going trade and investment relations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Understandably, as companies venture into newer and less familiar emerging markets, it does come with more risks and challenges for the companies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, the economic agencies and the TACs can do more to help companies to moderate the steep learning curve.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It can help companies that are entering into new markets by providing the regions’ specific insights and research, assist with grants and support programmes and, of increasing importance, to facilitate effective networking in overseas markets among Singaporean companies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The sense among companies that I have encountered is that we have yet to finesse the way to “hunt in packs” when venturing overseas.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I understand that, so far, the partnerships and collaborations among companies that venture overseas are sporadic, informal and not well-curated at times.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The sectoral-focused ITMs are important ecosystem set-ups to uplift capabilities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But it may be too vertically aligned to help enable cross-sectoral collaborations when companies venture overseas.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, an overlay of horizontal linkages across different sectoral ITMs can better bring out the synergistic value between companies and, hopefully, help to bear more fruits.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The merged Enterprise SG is now the main workhorse but we can leverage on the bigger TACs which have an overseas presence, as well as the large-size leading Singapore conglomerates which could act like queen bees to bring the smaller companies along and collaborate.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore has been successful in developing regional hubs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we know that many economies are also having similar aspirations and many do want to model after the Singapore experience.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With enough capital and enough political determination, there is no stopping these countries in the region from building and replicating physical hubs, such as ports, airports or new specific-themed hubs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, just competing on building more state-of-the-art physical infrastructure alone is not enough to maintain our superiority in global connectivity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to work on soft attributes, as the new MTI Addendum has charted.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And through both the excellent physical and digital connectivity, we can add value to the flows of capital, goods and services, whether they may be conducted in or through Singapore or elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a refreshing mindset to look at how we can extract greater value from the network, where connectivity begets further connectivity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If executed well, this would position Singapore as a key node in Asia and open up new streams of opportunities for Singapore companies and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are already bilateral digital initiatives being pursued, such as the Blk 71 Launchpads in Indonesia, Suzhou and San Francisco.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And with more of such linkages, it would proliferate further ideas and business flows.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Upping the game in digital capabilities is already a major thrust in the future economy strategy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Both at the enterprises and individual skills level, the Government is already driving adoption of digital technology, as well as helping the workforce with the requisite skills through ITMs and other initiatives.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Consumers today are prepared to pay for customisation, instantaneous response and a competitive premium for efficiency and quality.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Singapore platform must have capabilities to harness the value of data and to be a trusted hub for data and AI, which are increasingly part of the connectivity value chain.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to design a facilitative regulatory framework for a data-driven economy to thrive.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The innovation and entrepreneurial connectivity is also another dimension to add new intrinsic value into the Singapore network.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We do have an increasingly vibrant startup scene.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore is well-suited to be part of the global innovation value chain because of the integrity of our system.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Innovators can be assured that their IPs or their data will be protected and we must resolutely safeguard this advantage.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our highly trusted legal system and its enforceability are among the key cornerstones for Singapore to be the reputable global financial centre that it is today.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And this is one connectivity that we must continually strengthen and ensure that we stay ahead.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A vibrant financial sector is integral to Singapore being a globally connected city and a competitive economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As Asia continues its strong growth trajectory, demand for financial services in the region will grow exponentially, whether it is trade finance, enterprise finance, infrastructure finance, capital markets, wealth management or risk management.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Talent remains the key and we have to expand and deepen the talent pool, perhaps even bringing back early-retired financial professionals to help top-up our pool of expertise.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is high demand for talents in many areas.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, given the booming infrastructural needs in the region, best-in-class regional specialists are needed to structure complex cross-border financing and to anchor its value in Singapore; or in the insurance sector, with more global and regional insurance companies setting up presence in Singapore, they are in need of solution specialists to address emerging risks in the region.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Recently, I read in the news that Citibank has set up a China desk in Singapore to advise and service their Chinese clients that are investing into ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I suppose they do that because they see Singapore as having the needed professionals with the expertise and familiarity in the regional economies and, at the same time, is equipped to also serve their Chinese clients that are internationalising into the region.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, the talent in Singapore becomes the connector between the Chinese companies in China and the regional opportunities in, say, ASEAN, through the Singapore platform.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would be a significant niche for ourselves that is not easily replicable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There will be more demand of such talents going forward, with an economically busy Asia and with mega initiatives, such as the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) taking off with more large-scale projects in the region.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need a bigger pool of talents with deep knowledge of the regional markets, able to deal with the local market's complexity and its risk, understand the different jurisdictions, business practices, cultures and even languages and ability to develop professional and workable relationships with these entities, among others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The financial sector ITMs can continuously monitor the state of talent flows and also track whether we have fared well in expanding the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the last decade, the Chinese yuan or RMB has been progressively internationalised.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: RMB is gaining credentials to be another reserve currency of the world and we will see more international transactions settled in RMB in the decades ahead.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to seek more access so that we can participate into China’s inbound and outbound capital flows that are destined to grow further and to position ourselves as one of the key trading and settlement centres for RMB as it becomes more internationalised.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: MNCs can also serve as a connector for Singapore to the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The MTI Addendum stated it very well that MNCs bring along with them ideas, innovative capabilities and create new values for Asian markets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In working with local suppliers, it helps to transfer knowledge and deepen capabilities of our enterprises and keeps us abreast of developments and trends in the global marketplace.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When MNCs hub their regional critical functions here, whether it is marketing, operations, finance or R&D, it helps to add yet another layer of business linkage where local and other international enterprises can be networked into.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We can foster greater partnership between local companies, MNCs and Asian conglomerates to venture into other regional locations and, together, leverage on one another's strengths, as well as share the risks.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is on this basis that we build our value as a vibrant economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the economic front, we have never shied away from making bold decisions or taking bold actions, whether it is investing huge capital into building worldclass infrastructures like airports and seaports, or reclaiming Jurong Island to develop it into a petrochemical complex.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: More recently, we invested significantly to build R&D capabilities and also took bold actions to reduce our dependence on foreign labour.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The game plans are there and we are well-resourced to carry out those plans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What we need next is to excite the businesses to see these opportunities, seek to upgrade their capabilities through the ITMs or others and build a solid bench strength of talents to seek the new frontiers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We lack the conventional hinterland for access to resources and markets.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, we worked hard to grow our economic lifelines, connecting ourselves to the world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And in building a collective future for ourselves, we strived hard to unite our people from different races, languages and religions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There is, indeed, much that we can be proud of.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: However, we must never be complacent about our shared future.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In these times of rapid geopolitical shifts, technological disruption and transition, many Singaporeans are concerned, and understandably so.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Many ask very simple questions: can Singapore continue to thrive?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Will there be opportunities for future generations to similarly realise their potential?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Will we remain united despite the many forces that threaten to pull us apart?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These are important questions and I am heartened that Singaporeans are concerned with these important issues.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: While we must be alert and alive to the challenges, we need not be afraid.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Challenges there will always be; so, too, will opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our challenges do not define us; our responses will.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And just like the generations before us, we, too, can be "pioneers of our generation".

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Pioneers who will build and leave behind a stronger foundation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Pioneers who define success not just by how well we do for ourselves, but also enabling the next generation to do even better than us.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, how we must stay relevant to secure our place in the world in an uncertain geopolitical and rapidly evolving economic environment.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, what we, as "pioneers of our generation", must do to create a brighter future for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Third, why we must continue to keep our systems refreshed and special to keep our country successful.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The relative shift of geopolitical and economic weight between the West and the East, as epitomised by the US and China, will define the global security and economic environment for many years to come.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Many ask: which side should we be on?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is not the right way to frame the issue.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As a small country with an open economy, we believe in a rules-based, connected and interdependent world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Small states, more than any others, must be principled.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our task and priority is to ensure that we remain relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To do this, we need to have a deep understanding of the different interests, institutions and individuals shaping global developments.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: All of us – Government, businesses and private individuals – must understand the world and, collectively, remain alert to the forces impacting us and for us to navigate them carefully.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: China is a fast-evolving giant and China is not monolithic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Its interests vary and differ across its security, economic and social dimensions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There are also different provinces and different layers of government, each with its own perspectives and priorities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, to be relevant to China, we cannot rely on old mindsets and solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They are looking to develop their own solutions to their own unique challenges; sometimes by themselves, sometimes with partners.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, given the different interests and perspectives, knowing only the central government will be necessary but insufficient.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To do business with China, we must understand the different provinces and personalities as well.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: However, this does not mean that we become more Chinese or do we replicate the western model for them.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Instead, we must contribute to the partnership as Singapore – a multiracial and multicultural society, capable of developing unique solutions to our shared challenges, having learnt from both the East and West.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There are many successful Singaporeans making waves in China because they bring this unique value.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I had, earlier today, shared a video on my Facebook that illustrates this.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The short film shows how enterprising and spirited Singaporeans can be and how we can be relevant to China at different levels.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: How we relate to China must also be how we relate to the rest of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: What is clear is that no one deals with Singapore for our domestic markets or resources alone.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Instead, they leverage upon us as a platform to reach the region and the world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To remain effective and attractive, we must develop people with a deep understanding of the region and the world, so that we can create value when others come and do business with us.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our education and training models must similarly evolve in tandem to support this.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Beyond the technical skills which we already excel in, Singaporeans must also be equipped with the mindsets and skillsets to operate and compete globally.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This must be our competitive advantage and we can do more.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I am encouraged by the ongoing efforts that give our people this very global exposure that we desire.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: SMU believes that this will give its students a strong competitive edge and open doors to international networks and opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must also help Singaporeans – individuals, companies and businesses – access and penetrate the global markets better.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We need to ask ourselves: can we redefine the role of the overseas Singapore chapters and chambers to build the necessary networks?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These networks should be formed to achieve three outcomes: to connect Singapore to the world, to connect the world to Singapore and to connect fellow Singaporeans to compete in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our ability to network also depends on Singaporeans' ability to understand and work across cultures and nationalities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Besides enabling Singaporeans to gain overseas exposure, we must also be able to work with talented people from elsewhere locally.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must have the diversity of talent, both local and global.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Foreign professionals with knowledge, skillsets and competencies working shoulder-to-shoulder with skilled Singaporean talent, cross-pollinating ideas and bringing out the best in each other.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And, together, we will write the next chapter of the Singapore story.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To secure our place in the world, we must also better connect to the world as our hinterland, gaining access to resources and markets, and we need to step up in three areas.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, we need to widen our portfolio of markets to diversify our risks of relying on any single particular market.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are continuously exploring new markets and support bilateral and multilateral trade efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, we need to go beyond the conventional dimensions of air, land and sea connectivity, as expressed by Member Mr Liang Eng Hwa, by ensuring that we are connected to the world in the dimensions of data, finance, talent and technology.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have much work to build on to entrench ourselves as a global node for data, finance, technology and connectivity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We need to move fast before others leapfrog and overtake us.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Having a headstart does not mean that we will always be ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We can capitalise on finance and data flows by building on our reputation as a trusted financial and data hub.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These "non-physical" dimensions of connectivity are increasingly essential to reinforce the physical dimensions of connectivity that we already have a headstart on.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If we can strengthen and complement our connectivity across all dimensions, we can continue to transcend our physical challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Third, as global production and supply chains shift, we, too, must stay agile to connect to the new shifts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We need to move from getting others to trade with us, to trade through us, to also include for others to trade on our Singapore platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Since the 1980s, we knew that we could not possibly compete with other mega ports in the world in terms of size, no matter how much we try to expand our port or reclaim the entire southern coastline from Changi to Jurong.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Hence, PSA updated its strategy to become a global port and supply chain operator, to compete at the system and network level, rather than at the port level.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Today, PSA is working with partners to use the PSA platform, regardless of where the trade flows may be.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is like having an "Intel" chip on an operating system inside the global trade flow operations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To achieve sustained and quality economic growth, we must not only be able to attract activities here, we must also venture out.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is not just about giving Singaporeans the best opportunities here in Singapore, but it is also about helping Singaporeans to seize the opportunities beyond Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To be pioneers of our generation, we must be clear-eyed about our challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There are at least six areas that we need to focus on: having an innovative economy, building an inclusive society, ensuring social mobility, building our future Singapore, building our national identity and building trust.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As any society matures, it is usual for it to become more conservative – choosing to uphold the existing system, rather than breaking new grounds.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We cannot allow this to happen in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We need to keep up our vitality and verve.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is one thing to be the best-in-class for ports and airports.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But it is another to be even better, ready for tomorrow's needs, ahead of time.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is one thing to beat someone else in a competition, it is another to beat our own standards, even when we are at the top, so that Singaporeans can have even brighter prospects in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We need to ensure that the pioneering spirit lives on by embracing change and innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat will speak more about this.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Every generation aspires to do better than the previous.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is positive and this is what drives us to improve.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are aware that Singaporeans, particularly those who fall into the middle-income, middle-age category, are feeling the stresses and strains of technological and business disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As leaders, it is our responsibility to ensure that everyone progresses together.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In keeping faith with the Government, Singaporeans want us to understand their fears, concerns and aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must do better for the weak and vulnerable in society.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But beyond providing immediate relief, we must also enable them to do better for themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Minister Ng Chee Meng and the Labour Members of Parliament will elaborate more on the Labour Movement’s efforts, while Minister Masagos Zulkifli and others will speak about how we can foster a caring and inclusive society that is truly meritocratic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is often the result of "social clustering" of people from similar backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Social inequality is also partly caused by our human natural instincts to pass on wealth and privileges to our next generation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If left unchecked, our people may lose faith in our system of meritocracy and this can hurt our social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Can we mitigate the forces that widen social inequality?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: How can we better distribute the fruits of growth to a broad majority to prevent stratification as a society?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have seen the fallout from others who did not do so.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Hence, upholding social mobility is something that we must take seriously.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung and various Members will address some of these challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Fourth, as pioneers of our generation, it is also our responsibility to continue building and planning ahead for the next generation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As we progress towards SG100, we need to start planning not just for the next 50 years but also beyond.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Many of our decisions today will determine whether the next generation can have an even better living environment than ours.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, how do we refresh our HDB flats and estates?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: How do we prepare our transport, utilities, data infrastructures for the next lap?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Minister Lawrence Wong and Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will speak about these challenges and our responses.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But the bottom line is this: we must never think that we are ever finished with building Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must never think that we are ever done building Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Fifth, beyond economic and social development, our most critical piece of work is to rally our nation together.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our people must not merely be economic sojourners.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They must have the natural instincts to defend what is ours, to build upon what we have and stay put even when the chips are down.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: A nation is not just about economic benefits.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is also about the sense of community and contribution.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: A true nation is one where its people will stay and fight for its future and build it all up even when the chips are down.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is the spirit of the 1965 generation and this is what we want to imbue in every generation of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: How we communicate and work as a team will establish the foundation for our identity as Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Minister Indranee Rajah will speak on this important topic of our Singapore identity and Minister Heng Swee Keat will also discuss how we intend to engage and partner fellow Singaporeans for the next lap.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Last but not least, for Singaporeans to identify with one another and with this country, there must be trust between people and Government as well as amongst Singaporeans ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To foster trust, leaders must lead by example, develop strong connections across different segments of our population, communicate with them effectively to mobilise them.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In fact, this has intensified in this digital age.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must work harder to let our people see and understand an issue for what it is; helping our people to become better informed of the challenges, options and rationale behind our choices.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Only in this way can we all become more discerning, stay vigilant and own our choices and solutions together.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: With higher education, Singaporeans’ aspirations and expectations also evolve.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They want to be heard, considered and respected.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, we have to keep channels open for everyone to share their views and work on strengthening our engagement.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If we can do this well, we will remain cohesive as a nation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If we can have a common vision, a common set of goals and putting our national priorities above all, we will emerge stronger than ever.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Singapore has come this far because of trust, teamwork as well as our ability and guts to develop our own systems to meet our unique needs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As a small city-state with a multiracial society, situated in a volatile region, without a conventional hinterland and with no one else to depend on for our defence, our circumstances are, indeed, unique.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And while we study other systems and adapt them where suitable, we must not copy blindly or become "intellectually colonised".

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must remain prepared to develop systems that work best for us.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Today, we are also fostering stronger collaboration and synergies and tapping on different networks in society for their views and expertise.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It must also include our Trade Associations and Chambers, our enterprises and the Labour Movement.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Next, beyond having good and nimble systems, we must have good people.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have seen examples of both democratic and socialist systems failing; often, by people with the wrong motivations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To bring forth good people to serve is a never-ending challenge.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is difficult enough to bring forth good people who would sacrifice their personal and family interests for the country.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is especially so when the country is already successful, peaceful and prosperous.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We need to find the strongest set of individuals not just to solve today's current problems, but also to prevent future problems from arising in the first place.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This means that we need diverse skillsets and perspectives, so that we can combine them as necessary and tackle challenges together, when circumstances change.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This applies to the political leadership team, as much as it applies to the Public Service and business community.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Agreeing to put Singapore first and foremost is the prerequisite.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Having found the strongest set of individuals is still not enough; what we must then do is to mould them into the strongest team possible.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Countries with more resources may afford to have less cohesive leadership teams and still survive.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But, for Singapore, we must ensure that we have the strongest leadership team possible, for others to take us seriously and be willing to work with us.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For Singapore, this teamwork does not just exist within one generation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This provides continuity in our interaction with others and for us to compete at the highest global level with consistency in vision and execution with purpose.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: All these leadership traits – commitment, teamwork, courage to evolve, a sense of mission – are what we will need to keep our systems special.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Allow me to continue in Mandarin, Mr Speaker, Sir.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, although Mr Low Thia Khiang is a Member of the Opposition, he is, nevertheless, a fellow Singaporean and very much a part of Team Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: While we may not always agree with his perspectives or methods, we, nevertheless, appreciate his efforts to work together to build a better Singapore, as the leader of the Workers' Party.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Although Mr Low may have different perspectives, but, from his speeches, we can detect his pride in Singapore and his determination to defend our sovereignty.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Here, we would like to thank Mr Low Thia Khiang.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We look forward to similarly working with Mr Pritam Singh and the Workers' Party to put Singapore's and Singaporeans' interests first, always.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is about serving our country and people.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To win votes by stoking anger and unhappiness may be a common practice in politics elsewhere, but this is negative politics and is not constructive.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To win the hearts and votes of our people, we must work hard to develop sound policies for our common future.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I hope that all of us will continue to define our politics in constructive ways.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: All along, my belief is that we want political leaders, not just politicians, to lead Singapore; leaders who weigh options carefully before acting decisively and never opt for just the most expedient idea or solution for personal interests or short-term gains.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It also means not shying away from making difficult or unpopular decisions, but being guided by that resolve to always do what is in the best interests of Singapore and Singaporeans, never shirking responsibilities towards our current and future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Always putting our country and people first, our political leaders must treat people with sincerity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They know that our achievement today is built on the foundation of what our previous generations have left behind.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Therefore, the responsibility of every generation is to leave behind a better Singapore for future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They also know that the success of each generation is defined by the success of the next generation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, let me conclude in English.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In the next lap of our country's history, we will have our fair share of challenges and opportunities for our generation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But we can be confident that we will build an even brighter future for ourselves and our future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As pioneers of our generation, we must continue to break new grounds, build on our fundamentals that have brought us this far, so that we can continue to enable the next generation to succeed even more than us.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We can, and we will, together, write the next chapter of our Singapore story that is meaningful, engaging and real for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our 1965 generation has achieved that with much less.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Unlimited by our geography, unlimited by our size, unlimited by our resources.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our nation is going through a period of transition – from one generation of leaders to the next, drawing upon the wisdom and experience of the past while needing to forge new paths in this ever-changing world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But there are some things that remain constant.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Aspiration is navigation, – the direction we are headed to.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The President has outlined key priorities for the Government's latter half of this term.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One of them is "Building a Well-connected, World-class City for Singaporeans".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Part of Singapore is the Southern Islands, seven islets: Kusu Island, Lazarus Island, Pulau Seringat, Pulau Tekukor, St John's Island and, now, the Sisters' Islands.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Land in land-scarce Singapore, but not just land.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are coral, blue waters, flora and fauna unique to the islands, rich biodiversity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Currently, only St John's Island and Kusu Island are served by regular ferries and Lazarus Island is connected to St John's Island with a pedestrian causeway.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The rest, besides Pulau Tekukor, are accessed through chartered yachts or chartered ferries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore may be resource less but we are not resourceless.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should consider how we can bring out the biodiversity potential of the Southern Islands, while increasing connectivity to the islands so that Singaporeans can enjoy this part of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My aspiration is that the Southern Islands become a network, a neighbourhood of recreational parks where there are nature, biodiversity research and connectivity between the islands and the islands with the main island.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Nature and connectivity need not be mutually exclusive.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This account, which would be able to pool together contributions from many other workers, would be able to earn a more attractive interest on the sum of money pooled.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Upon termination of the work permit or pass, the worker can choose to cash out on the savings, or, if there is a renewal of the work permit, the worker can also choose to roll over the savings.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From the money deposited from his own salary into the worker's Stewardship Fund or account, there could be possible categories of expenditures that he can draw down on, for example, payment for enrichment or training courses accredited by the Government.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is hoped that, through a Stewardship Fund, foreign workers will be able to enjoy and utilise a nest egg when they go home to their families, for whom they have come here to work.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just as we cherish the contributions that Singaporeans make, we also cherish the contributions that foreign workers have made to our city.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We also want them to come and add that extra value to our livelihoods, communities and culture.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, for as long as they are here, we should be stewards of their lives, we should be good hosts, to build up and benefit their lives as they have ours.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How this fits in with aspirations to "secure a place in the world for Singapore" is that, by doing so, the foreign workers will leave with fond memories of Singapore, that the links built will forge the path for reciprocal goodwill and friendship.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this way, we can build up an overseas family of workers who have once worked and lived in Singapore, and secure a place in the world for Singapore and for her values.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A third aspiration I wish to talk about today is the ability to make tough decisions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The President said that we need to be able to go for bold changes, not merely to be content to tweak at the margins.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To take such an approach, we need to make sure we retain the ability to make tough decisions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Being able to revisit decisions, as tough as such revisiting is, must always be on the cards.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will also make sure that we are not overly reliant on the revenue generated from casinos to meet national expenditure.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should never get into a corner where we have to rely on tax on gambling revenue to meet expenditure needs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A similar aspiration applies in the international arena.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even as we recognise the importance of "upholding international law and the role of supra-national institutions", we need to make sure we retain the ability to stand for what we believe is best for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Aspirations help to direct, to navigate, a new course for our nation's future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is teamwork that helps direct the course of the ship and maintains her seaworthiness in times of squall or in times of calm.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Over the years of being a Member of Parliament, I have seen how teamwork is key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I truly hope that there will not be over-focus on one person or persons.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would much rather that the team be looked at for the prowess and the calibre of the whole team and not the characteristics of an individual person.
