speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me to share, from my experiences, why I think this is very important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are occasions when I raise issues that are close to my heart with the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In some instances, the Prime Minister would support the ideas I had suggested.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Equally important are the times the Prime Minister has had to deal with matters from the front, leading the team and the debate publicly on difficult topics and policies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yet, often times, the responsibility does not rest with the Prime Minister alone.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean weighed in on heavy topics, such as Ministerial Salaries, and the Little India riot.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are heavy topics and displayed how important teamwork is in Parliament, in Cabinet and in the caring for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Teamwork is important and this was so for the recent debates on the Motions on terrorism and the drug menace.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Minister K Shanmugam was deep in his thinking to agree that these were important topics to debate and, hence, rendered his support at the Ministerial level, and even participated in the debate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As there were many things on his plate at that time in the lead-up to the debate, the GPC worked with Minister Desmond Lee, Mrs Josephine Teo and Mr Amrin Amin.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Topics discussed were what are the enforcement capabilities that we can deliver in terms of reducing the drug menace, how we could overcome or mend the break in trust if an attack did vest on our shores – these were some of the types of questions the GPC and Members had to ask of them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In order that the debates displayed accurately the capability of our forces and that, what we say, we do, so, the threats are deterred as best we can.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After all, that was the team's aim for the debate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, it is a team effort among many different Ministers, Ministries and, indeed, Members of this House.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is a structure that does not rest on the shoulders of one man or one woman.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is even more evident when we see in action the Singapore team travel on state visits.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Sometimes, there are about six to seven Members in the political delegation, made up of front- and back-benchers as well as the team leader.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Two years ago, I witnessed first-hand how our Prime Minister engaged with President Barack Obama on the state visit to Washington DC.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I saw how he, as the leader of the team and of the Government, was clear in his mind what our positions were and how he engaged with the Americans on many topics and fronts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But there were other team members, too, including Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, whom I saw first-hand engaging world leaders – people like Mr Joe Biden, Mr John Kerry and Ms Susan Rice – on significant issues.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Part of that same delegation were Mr S Iswaran, Mr Chan Chun Sing, Mr Ong Ye Kung, Ms Rahayu Mahzam and Ms Chia Yong Yong.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Each one had a significant role to play.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Again, the point I am making is that teamwork is key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It cannot rest on the shoulders of one man or one woman.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another illustration of how teamwork is important is through the previous debate on the President's Address in January 2016.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During the debate, Minister Heng Swee Keat was able to gather the views of many of us who shared our aspirations for our country and the constituents we serve and, during the debate, attributed many of these points to the Members present.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Again, such attribution shows how each Member of the House has something to give.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And each of us here lean on our grassroots leaders, community volunteers and, certainly, our families to serve each resident.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am sorry I have not mentioned all Members in my speech.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But this does not detract from the point that I am trying to make: that all of us here, and, indeed, every resident that we serve, have a role in the next chapter of our Singapore story.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But besides aspiration that gives us direction and, teamwork, which is the all-important glue, it is the motivation to serve that is the fuel that keeps the ship of Singapore going.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At its base, it is not just about teamwork or advancing the interest of Singapore and Singaporeans, but it is about our motivation, what makes us tick.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The reason why we are here: it is serving Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Dr Balaji Sadasivan, a man I deeply respect.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2010, unfortunately, he had come down with cancer and, being a doctor himself, knew that he did not have much time more.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I remember seeing him coming to Parliament two weeks before he passed away.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To me, Dr Balaji displayed a motivation so pure.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And other examples are the many former back-benchers and front-benchers who continue to serve with vigour and rigour: Mr S Chandra Das, Dr S Vasoo, Mr Lau Ping Sum, Mr Zainal Abidin Rasheed and many, many more.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The motivation for coming into politics is to serve; to serve as part of a team.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That responsibility of leadership is shared by everyone.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Every Member of this House shares that responsibility, including all residents we serve.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, my hope, my humble hope, is that aspirations of Singapore, with which I started my speech, and the aspirations of all Singaporeans we have the sacred duty to represent here in this Chamber, will be held in the precious crucible of teamwork and correct motivation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Thirteenth Parliament is re-opening in rosier times.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Measures which the Government put in place over the last few years are beginning to show green shoots.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Yet, the President reminded us that our long-term challenges remain broadly unchanged.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Our economy needs to restructure towards higher value-added activities and stay dynamic, we need to secure Singapore’s place in the world, we need to stay focused on upgrading skills and we need to forge a caring and inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And we must keep up our efforts to make Singapore an exceptional nation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am encouraged by the determination and resolve of the fourth-generation (4G) leadership that I sense through the President’s Address.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am excited by their appetite to undertake the "bold changes" needed to navigate the unchartered waters that lie ahead for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These attributes are necessary to take Singapore forward through our next phase of development.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In order to sustain a vibrant economy despite an ageing population, a tight labour market and the changing nature of work brought on by technological disruptions, we really need fresh perspectives, breakthrough ideas and decisive action to lead us there.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The current tight labour market is really a key constraint for business growth.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Growth in our local workforce is expected to slow further, unfortunately.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This issue of talent and jobs is closely linked to the accelerating pace of technological disruption in transforming industries, business models and jobs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The future of work is now one of the hottest topics in many industries, provoking much debate and predictions about the impact of automation technology like artificial intelligence and robotics on jobs, skills and wages.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I, for one, think we need not surrender to the nightmare scenario where we would all be replaced by robots.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The most significant disruption will come from an increasing rate of change in job destruction and job creation, including new forms of work, as well as skills churn within existing occupations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Machine learning and robotics will replace specific tasks previously performed by humans, freeing them to focus on new tasks and leading to rapidly-changing core skillsets in various occupations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Workers will have to learn new skills to work alongside increasingly capable machines.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Therefore, in order to avoid having a class of people becoming unemployed and under-employed, it is imperative that we develop effective strategies to help Singaporeans make the transition, have them retrained, reskilled and capable of performing new kinds of work.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As the Fourth Industrial Revolution takes hold in different industries and job families, it, unfortunately, will affect different segments of society differently.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Automation promises great gains for higher skilled workers who can innovate, create and apply new developments, whilst mid- to low-skilled workers will be at greatest risk of being replaced by technology.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And here, we must guard against the increasing polarisation of employability, which will exacerbate income inequality.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Job families expecting the highest employment growth – in science, technology, engineering and mathematics – currently have some of the lowest female participation rates and continue to find it much harder to recruit women.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Yet, at the same time, women are over-represented in other job families, such as office and administrative roles – the ones that are expected to experience heavy disruptions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Seniors will be more adversely affected than younger workers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Government must put in place the necessary measures to ensure equal opportunities for all and avoid inequality being exacerbated by the digital divide.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Nations the world over are struggling to deal with the social and political implications of impact on jobs and society brought on by information technology, artificial intelligence and robotics.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I applaud the Government for launching this visionary initiative as far back as 2015.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I think it is time that we step on the accelerator for SkillsFuture, if it is to go the distance that we expect, at the speed it needs to.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It needs to become the new engine of education that drives Singapore’s growth and development, in much the same way that educating and training our children and young adults have helped propel our growth over the last 50 years.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We need to move from front-loading our citizens’ education in the earlier part of their lives to helping them learn at all stages of their lives.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We need to develop lifelong learning institutions, as well as the necessary discipline and comprehensive infrastructure, to ensure that a strong culture of learning and an ecosystem of continuing education take root.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: SkillsFuture must be capable of providing the adult learning that is vital to ensure today’s entire workforce can cope with the disruptions to come and be prepared for new skills requirements in both existing and new roles.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To achieve this, SkillsFuture needs to partner academic institutions, vocational training providers, trade associations and employers to develop and incentivise customised training solutions capable of lifting skill levels of the whole workforce, industry by industry.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Trade associations and industry task forces in the respective ITMs should play an active role with training providers in defining competency-based credentialing and recognition systems, as well as creating a continuous feedback loop between labour market needs and training requirements.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They should collaborate to develop robust and scalable training interventions to benefit the whole industry cluster, lifting skill levels in the sector through systematic accreditation of workers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For some workers, it may even occur multiple times during their careers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must, therefore, strengthen the support systems for dislocated workers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The key is to ensure that they are re-employed quickly to avoid sticky unemployment or under-employment.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Based on feedback from residents who have tried finding jobs through current employment services centres, it is evident that the operating model will have to evolve to include new partnerships and mechanisms that better connect workers to jobs, and jobs to workers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There should be early warning systems for possible lay-offs and rapid response mechanisms for career counselling and job placement tightly coordinated.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Even as we work on positioning Singaporeans favorably in the global marketplace for talent, Singapore must remain a magnet for expertise that our industries need but cannot fill locally.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must deal squarely with calls for help from businesses struggling with manpower shortages.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The system should provide transparency and predictability in order to help companies plan their growth strategies in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In 1974, Mr Lee Kuan Yew said, “Our lives and our children’s future must be built on a solid infrastructure of education and skills, tuned to high performance by efficient management, always able to respond quickly to sudden changes in the world.” Just as we were called upon in the country’s early years to take our fledgling nation of poorly-skilled factory labourers to one that served up world-class manufacturing and top-flight services, so we are now called upon, once again, to shape Singapore’s "future of work".

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This will be an undertaking for all Singaporeans – Government leaders, corporations and individuals – everyone playing their part and aligned towards the same vision.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must be equal to the task, for the sake of our future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And, thirdly, the 4G leadership must fire up and mobilise the spirit and energy of young Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One thread that binds these three directives is the ability and willingness to listen to the people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This trait can be understated, especially in light of the dominance of the PAP and its electoral success over more than five decades of uninterrupted rule.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, societal norms and expectations of political leadership have evolved.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Alternative views will have to be addressed, accommodated and considered thoughtfully so as to allow us to move forward together as one Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What the Government should not do is to close the door or resign itself to the politics of majoritarianism when a sensitive or difficult subject comes along, but, instead, invest a lot more energy to engage and explain, for our people have more than their fair share of good ideas.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the approach of the 4G leaders is to ignore, silence or ridicule alternative ideas, they will fail to galvanise and spur all Singaporeans to greater heights; or worse, they may even engender a divided society, rendering the message of inclusivity hollow and without substance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would be an untenable outcome for the continued success of a small country like Singapore that needs to pursue innovation and excellence and to conceive new ways of doing things to greater vigour than ever before.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will focus my speech on the cost of living, a topic which the Workers' Party believes deserves closer scrutiny by the Government for the remainder of the term and beyond.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The remaining Workers' Party Members of Parliament will address other issues, as covered in the Addenda to the President's Address.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More than a year ago, in the wake of the announcement of a hike in water tariffs, Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean sought to assure the public that the price of coffee should not go up in the aftermath of the water hikes because the cost of water in a cup of coffee is "much, much less than one cent" and that the public should not be scared of untrue stories about the coffee prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While this is true in a mathematical sense, just a few days ago, a Zaobao report confirmed that one of the largest coffee shop chains had increased the price of coffee, citing rising overheads.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The PAP Government's philosophy has always been to target assistance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For those who govern, the fear of overly generous welfare payouts for the able-bodied comes with a warning.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The message that can be inadvertently sent is that a person is not able to look after himself, hence, needing support and severely undermining the work ethic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But parallel expectations and considerations apply equally for the Government, too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But as many callers to a local radio station commented not too long ago, the costs of running and improving the transport system cannot just be seen through the eyes of fare revenue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many correctly questioned whether there ought to be some scope for other segments of SMRT's business to subsidise train operations, too, such as advertising and revenue from other investments to lessen the effect of any fare increases on the general population.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, on the 30% water hike, how do future capital investments in water supply and transmission cohere with the large capital reserves of the national water agency which have increased consistently from around $3 billion in 2007 to more than $5 billion in 2016?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Getting into the details of such matters would represent a unique partnership with the people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would represent bold leadership, but such an approach would also come with an upshot.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Price hikes are likely to be better understood and contextualised to the benefit of the policy discourse in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While 39% felt this was an ideal outcome, only 18% were able to actualise it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If, indeed, the cost of living is a major impediment to having more children, what can we do to address this issue?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How will we create a strong sense of nationhood when our Singapore Core and the values internalised over 50 years of nation building are progressively hollowing themselves out with the population not replacing itself?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Immigrants will grow old, too, and we cannot be encouraging even more immigrants to set up home on our shores without a robust strategy to raise TFR.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Not to do so would severely impact the quality of life in Singapore for our future generations in view of our limited size.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The problem is a structural one; and structural changes are necessary and bold thinking is required to break with the orthodoxy of the past.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is there scope to make HDB flats more affordable by pegging prices to income levels?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And can flexible work arrangements become a compulsory option for new parents from employers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What can we do to make the education system a reason for parents not to panic about having children?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is there scope to introduce more child-support tax credits for low- and medium income parents which can be scaled back progressively as household income increases?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is without having to even call on the President to unlock the reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is only taking into account the accumulated surplus of out of two of the five years of this Government’s term.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With $15.7 billion in hand today and, given the putatively stable formula for NIRC withdrawals in spite of market fluctuations, the picture for the immediate future does not appear to be one of a Government needing money to stay afloat and needing to tax the population as a result, raising the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We are told more money is needed for healthcare and other areas in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is not unexpected, given our demographic transition with our elderly population expected to grow to 900,000 by 2030.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But what are the Government’s current estimates and the underlying basis for its projections of higher expenditure coming on stream in future?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This information needs to be shared so that the public is clear-eyed about the sufficiency of the budget at the Government’s disposal to help Singaporeans with the cost of living today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The leadership transition from the third generation (3G) to 4G leaders also presents a unique opportunity for each Singaporean to question what we can do to make Singapore a better home for all of us.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The leadership team is no longer just the political leadership.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singapore needs a special breadth and depth of leadership if it is to succeed; leadership in every field of industry from trade and industry to sports, arts and culture.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If Singapore is to thrive as the immediate geopolitical situation shifts – and separately, the challenge of an ageing society, inequality and an extremely low TFR confronts our small country – boldness should be part of our national character, too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At its core, the transition from the 3G to 4G leaders must be accompanied by a transformation of our society which creates the conditions to engender a confident people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The impetus and authority behind a new boldness in Singaporeans should harken back to the title of the President’s Address: a call for a strong people-Government partnership to build our future Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A people who exercises independent judgement and who are empowered to support Singapore and to move forward together.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers’ Party will always bear in mind the national interest in our deliberations and endeavour in the interest of Singaporeans and Singapore. 3.26 pm

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: One of the first things our workforce of the future would have to be prepared for is the increasing differentiation in job roles and, as a consequence, also of the skillsets that these roles will demand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's early success with employment growth had been founded on the same principle that other industrialised economies adopted, with mass creation of jobs to support large-scale manufacturing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As the President's Address indicated, the future of work will be very different.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike many other economies, however, Singapore had managed to sustain the early approach by recognising quite early on that a much more sophisticated labour market model would be required as global economic competition intensified.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, instead of differentiating industries, therefore, economic planners had the foresight to push for the workforce to graduate into higher value-added activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As the population's incomes rose, the workforce as a whole embraced higher skilled jobs, including moving much more quickly into knowledge work than other economies which had started out in a similar way.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: What we face now in Singapore are, in some ways, the problems of having been too successful too quickly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: With a workforce in which the proportion of degree holders is increasing rapidly, we now have an increasing proportion of professionals, managers and executives (PMEs) and, as a result, of knowledge workers as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Knowledge workers are subject to the same laws of demand and supply that all other resources must adhere to, and an excess of knowledge workers of the same type in any one area that is unsupported by demand will see the labour market prospects of that group dwindle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As an advanced economy, Singapore faces the same insatiable thirst for top manpower in a broad array of fields as other advanced economies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But the limited size of our population is such that the availability of skills it can supply will always fall short of the breadth being demanded by companies competing at the cutting edge of global competition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: To deal with this, the core principles which had guided early planners to their success remain relevant today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And that is to prepare early for the inevitable, to make difficult decisions to match seemingly impossible and incompatible objectives and, most importantly, to do so with a clear understanding of how much is at stake.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And many have already begun to recognise that the solution lies in preparing and revisiting the skills adequacy of their workforce, so that it keeps up with the evolving demands of the global economic competition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In order to improve their preparedness, advanced economies regularly make projections about their skills needs, appropriately harnessing the technology that is available today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: A picture of where the skills deficits are can be obtained which, no matter how imperfect, gives the modern advanced workforce a good sense of what the skills landscape would look like in the near future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: For Singapore, especially where the twin challenges of manpower shortages and skills deficits are never far from our minds, mapping the landscape of available skills will provide policymakers with an informed start to addressing the skills challenges of tomorrow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I agree strongly with the characterisation Minister Heng Swee Keat offered last week of the situation we are in, where he pointed out, in his media interview, that the solution to the problem we face should also be contained in the very technology which is causing the destructive challenges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The imperative for the workforce is to keep as much ahead of the curve as possible against the competition, leaving them in no doubt that even if tomorrow's jobs appear to be created, the Singapore workforce of today is prepared to be the first off the mark to acquire the necessary skills to fill them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Despite the scale of the challenge, there is room for cautious optimism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As the information in the skills framework is augmented, understanding that individual workers have not just the challenges that confront them in skills acquisition, the opportunities that are open to all of us in the skills landscape should begin to crystallise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I would like to talk about a role that may not be as clear but, certainly, no less direct, and, that is, the one that is played by the Ministry of Defence(MINDEF) and the Singapore Armed Forces in leading the impressionable young minds in 21st century skills mastery and leadership.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Skills training, in many ways, is part of what an organisation like MINDEF invested with heavy responsibilities for shaping young lives must dedicate itself to in order to stay relevant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As a small country, painfully aware of our natural limitations, there should, therefore, be no self-imposed limits to asserting the priority of progressive thinking but a need to pursue continuing skills improvements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This must naturally, therefore, begin with a 21st century military that should go beyond the call of duty in the pursuit of individual skills proficiency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Equality of opportunity benefits everyone in the long term because it strengthens the social fabric and provides a sustainable basis for each and every generation to pursue prosperity and individual fulfillment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It is almost no doubt that the days of mass job creation are over.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We need to create a much more differentiated workforce, one that can confront, even if not completely overcome, challenges of inadequate skills coverage.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I agree with the President that we need to develop a vibrant economy by strengthening local companies, supporting startups and investing in technology.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I also agree that we need to go through trials and tribulations before we reach that stage.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I learnt business the hard way because it is so dynamic.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I can never get it right all the way and I still do not get it right all the time.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I left Singapore in 1997, I lived overseas trying to do business in north Asia, Hong Kong, China, Thailand and India.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I tried to sell warehouse space, but then that did not give me any winnings or contracts.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I realised that the Internet was buzzing and progressing really well.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I kept changing the software and refining it by listening to the customers, make more changes, but I never changed what my core solutions were.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After about nearly nine months without any business, I got my first contract, a very small contract.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But it taught me a lesson that nothing is perfect and, if you try to find the perfection, you can never get there.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Business succeeds in its imperfection: finding gaps, filling them and succeed in its imperfection.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But that also taught me that you cannot have one size fits all for all customers.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: You just look at our coffee shops and the coffee.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It has got kopi c kosong, kopi, kopi o siu tai, lots to choose from.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, business succeeds not because it is perfect but because it is imperfect or because it impacts.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our policies and programmes will never be perfect.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But it must impact and we have to get it right; we have to get the broad directions right.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It has to go through the trials and tribulations but it will never be good enough.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, we have to keep reviewing it, keep refining it.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of our policies and programmes are well-intentioned.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They have the right objectives but, at implementation, we need to improve a lot more.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I think it will help if we achieve the outcome that is desired but, somehow, the implementation needs to be improved.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The broad direction was that we expect the industry to change but that needs a good number of enterprises to undergo radical changes.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Radical changes include business model change, workforce skills upgrade, product redesign, internationalisation, so that the sector can become more productive and competitive.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: You need critical mass for the whole sector to transform and to change.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But in every sector, businesses are at their different phases of development.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I look at it in three different broad categories in these phases of development: innovation, consolidation and expansion.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Within that, they are of different sizes, shapes, forms and different phases and they are built upon different types of structures.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: ITM can also not be about disbursing grants or transformation through technology.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Not all businesses can be transformed through technology.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, in reality, many of the businesses will tell you? "Before I transform, before I invest in innovation, where is the business volume?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Where do I get the contracts?" So, yes, innovation is critical.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But, more importantly is commercialising or realising the gains of what they have innovated.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Companies will have to compete internationally but there will be some that can never be competing internationally or go beyond the shores of Singapore, they will fall by the wayside.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, maybe ITMs have to go beyond work skills development or company capability development into opening up more paths and business opportunities.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That calls for more effective trade missions and also a more successful way to hunt as a pack.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) Chairman for Trade and Industry, Mr Liang Eng Hwa mentioned we need to hunt as a pack.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But our success rate of hunting as a pack needs to be improved, too.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We also have to give local companies a chance to work on public sector projects and contracts.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And with real business volume and in a tight labour situation, we can rest assured that the companies will have to become productive, to innovate and to transform.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Businesses need to play its own part because the responsibility cannot be shouldered by the Government alone.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They have to make changes and take steps.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In that sense, we will see business closures and that is part and parcel of the process to help the sector become stronger.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And when there are business closures, there is consolidation.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some sectors may slow down in order to scale quickly and we should facilitate that.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Sometimes, when a sector shrinks, it may not be such a bad thing to happen so that they can come back stronger; and stronger companies can rise up.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Administratively, you cannot deny some of the daily issues businesses face.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The process that companies have to deal with when applying for support and grants, we need to streamline that a lot further.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The administrative fees across different departments that add to the business cost; maybe we should review that.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Let us help to review and, if possible, reduce them.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe what we can do is not to add to the burden of the businesses.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Small or big businesses, they do create jobs.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That is why Enterprise Singapore (ESG) plays a very critical role.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Now that it is a one-stop agency for businesses, I hope that the ease of access increases.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hopefully, the integration is successful and they do not behave like International Enterprise Singapore and SPRING again but, really, as one, one-stop shop.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Not all 23 sectors that have launched their ITMs should be managed in the same mode.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As I have mentioned, transformation is either innovation, consolidation or expansion.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And once it is clear whether a company or a sector requires either of the different stages, Government support would then be holistic.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If we leave it to the market, there will be inefficiencies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: ESG should take a more active role in this process to strengthen companies and help them internationalise or consolidate.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It should take a more proactive approach than to just leave it to the trade associations.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Trade associations are a helpful vehicle but trade associations have their limitations.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That said, I would also urge trade associations to step forward, especially those which have received help, but, sometimes what they can do is far from what we expect.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They will do their best but there are limitations and there are different interests.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: ESG should continue to work hand-in-hand with them, take a more proactive role.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Trade associations must continue to play their part but make an effort to galvanise the industry, the sector, make that a priority, beyond just asking for grants or subsidies.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am sure between MOM, MCI and MTI or other Ministries that offer grants or subsidies to businesses, there are many of them out there, you can streamline them.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That way, there is a better chance for businesses to gain a better understanding, awareness and access to these grants and schemes with ease, and the effect and the impact can be more widespread.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I also believe that the startup environment is important because startups, although they are young companies, inject new life into the economy.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In Singapore, the startup environment has certainly progressed – Launchpad, Block 71 and many, many other pockets of development in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We see many more Singaporeans launching their new businesses, especially in the tech area.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But the reality of setting up a business is that it is not easy and failures are more than successes.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Startups achieve both social and economic objectives so we have to continue to support them.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They can influence a culture; inject new hope and new life into the economy.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We can focus on growing startups but create the ecosystem and environment, not just giving out grants or subsidies; create opportunities for them.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Being optimistic about startups means giving them hope, giving them encouragement but not unrealistic to think that the startups in Singapore can become unicorns.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Most of them would not become unicorns with the size of Singapore's market.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It requires a culture that encourages people to try things and test things and fail.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And when it comes to launching a product, imperfect is perfect – we cannot wait until perfection.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Every entrepreneur walks this fine line between what is fixable and what is fatal.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The important thing is that they push their experimentation to the limit but we need to embrace failure for success.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Government and private sector must work together, come together to help to build this environment and a culture with a vibrant ecosystem, enhance the platforms for people to start and offer equal opportunities to startups, not just the first-time startups, but serial entrepreneurs as well – those who have failed first time, failed second time and trying it again.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Allow more of them to bid for public sector projects and give them a chance to have a go at it.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This, in turn, will encourage entrepreneurial dare, thinking and doing.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Singapore economy needs a new vision, a new direction.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I support the initiatives of Minister Chan Chun Sing in developing Singapore into a data hub, attracting a good mix of talent, focusing on strengthening the local sector to become globally competitive and relevant.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have to know where we are going and how to get there.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It has to be a new direction that can sustain us for the next decade and we need a sense of where we are every step of the way.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to better reflect how our economy and local businesses are doing, and whether growth and wealth that we have created have really benefited people’s lives, jobs and wages.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One thing is for sure: what brought us here can no longer take us further.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Let us move forward with a new vision, direction and strategy.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With that, I support the Motion. 3.48 pm

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In her speech, the President spoke about the need for Singaporeans to work closely with the new generation of 4G leaders to write our future chapters.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are on the cusp of a new era.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Jobs automation, re-skilling, cashless payments, smart technology and so forth are becoming a part of our lives, regardless of whether we are resistant to it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A renewal of leadership comes at an opportune moment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the meantime, citizens, too, must partner this new Government and renew ourselves, so that we can navigate the new complexities as one.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given our lack of a hinterland and mineral resources, it is inevitable that Singapore will have to use new technologies, platforms and connectivity channels to overcome these constraints and build demand for our products and services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Globally, this will come fast and furious, unlike what we have seen in past phases of global industrialisation and technological advances.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Smart technology and automation save us a lot of time and effort which we can then use to indulge in other pursuits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For the less mobile and elderly, such technologies enable them to lead more independent and fuller lives and this is good news for an ageing society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yet, because new technologies are emerging and evolving every day, there is only a short window of time to adapt.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Those who are unable to catch up, particularly the seniors and the poor and less educated, get left behind and further behind.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time as this is happening, many are concerned about the changing nature of work.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The amount of self-employment is increasing, along with the fragmentation of labour into microjobs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, is it contingent that work, such as self-employment or gig work and the disappearance of salaried employment likely to become the norm?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would think it would be a gradual move towards more people working independently and not the complete disappearance of salaried jobs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this ecosystem of rapidly changing technology and evolving nature of employment and with tighter global competition, the labour market of the future will be somewhat tight and will get tighter.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it is essential to ensure workers' well-being in search of jobs, whether salaried employment or self-employment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is even more important as the only real resource we have is our people, our talents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I firmly believe that, in the future, countries that can attract the most productive people in the digital economy will disrupt the value chain in every sector and appropriate immense wealth, while other countries will have only the scraps.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The mobility of talented people will lead many of these wealth creators to migrate to countries that offer the best conditions, including the lowest tax.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To achieve many of these things, Singaporeans will need good jobs; jobs that will give them good incomes to sustain their desired livelihood; jobs that are fulfilling and challenge them to grow.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Unfortunately, some of them, despite being capable and well-qualified, are impeded due to discrimination against circumstances that cannot be helped.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The President highlighted the need to continue to strive for a more caring and inclusive society and the need to tackle inequality vigorously, she said.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: She had mentioned the need to provide the right additional support to those needing it – in housing, education, skills training and employment – so that meritocracy works well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Only then can everyone do well through hard work, talent and skills, regardless of their backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But for many people and, for the future, the right question is not whether there will still be work.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The real question is whether there will be enough jobs paying decent wages.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Most individuals want to be useful to society and work, remunerated or not, is one way for them to feel so; employment is one way we construct the social fabric.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps, people will be prepared to accept lower pay in return for this social bond.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the short term, however, the destruction of jobs is costly for those who lose them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The acceleration of creative destruction raises three questions: how can workers, with jobs or not, be protected?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can we prepare ourselves for this new world through education and regulatory changes?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Burying our heads in the sand is not a strategy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This brings me to the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) and I have raised this quite a number of times, including in my maiden speech in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It does so by encouraging and supporting employers who are able and willing to adopt progressive workplace practices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It then works with employers to change their practices and blacklists those who are unwilling to comply.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Understandably, it is not possible to completely weed out workplace discrimination, just as it is impossible to completely stamp out discrimination in any community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To prove discrimination is challenging, there are laws in place that employers must comply with.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Equipping TAFEP with legal powers to prosecute errant employers is something Singaporeans have openly wished for.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Meanwhile, preferential treatment of foreigners is also another common grievance.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On the flip side, there are also claims that Singaporeans turn down jobs because they feel the pay is too low, thus leaving jobs to foreign nationals who are willing to work at lower wages.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, my questions are: has any research been done on how true these claims are?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If there is some truth in them, how can we resolve these?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are companies doing enough to integrate foreign employees so that they do not gravitate to their own nationalities?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And should we also investigate whether employers are offering reasonable salaries that match the required job scope?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In a gig economy where job security is on the decline, there is certainly going to be more frustration and panic among a generation that had become accustomed to having stable jobs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I have heard from employees who have given up on legal action against employers because it is too expensive and troublesome.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the US, for example, the equivalent Equal Employment Opportunity Commission is responsible for enforcing the federal laws that make it illegal to discriminate against a job applicant or an employee.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The commission pursues litigation against errant employers who are found to be guilty of discrimination offences.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Similarly, in Australia, the Fair Work Ombudsman does the same thing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It has the power to initiate litigation against a national system of employers for contravening the Fair Work Act.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In Singapore, we recognise the importance and effectiveness of a tripartite approach towards resolving workplace discrimination issues.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As such, TAFEP is deserving of more powers to strengthen its capabilities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope this can slowly be part of the medium to long-term plan to ensure the ecosystem of inclusivity which can be further enhanced and all our talents can be maximised fully, regardless of an individual's physical disability, gender or ethnicity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Indeed, Singaporeans want to live in a fair and just society, one based on meritocracy but, at the same time, strives to leave no one behind.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I strongly believe a stronger TAFEP is needed so that meritocracy works well and would go a long way to allay fears faced by Singaporeans and Singaporean jobseekers in a tight labour market environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Disruptions caused by automation are another concern of mine.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: According to the UK think-tank, the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), middle- and lower-income workers are likely to lose their jobs to machines.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our Government has rightly been encouraging employers to send their employees for training to acquire new skills to manage the new technologies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With large-scale retrenchment a possible problem from automation, I think it is important that authorities also consider new guidelines that make it necessary for companies to help their workers to remain employable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The IPPR also suggests that automation can result in higher profits at the expense of employees' salaries, and thus, new guidelines for additional protection of workers would be necessary with the use of emerging technologies by businesses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But how can companies help employees without it being an additional burden on the companies?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Future Ready Fund can be used specifically to prepare our workforce in areas where they can be retrained or reskilled to meet the changes in the job market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, an SME can tap on it to focus on educating staff on being future-ready by having a monthly digitalisation online course, for example, for a start, and then focus on the relevant job-related needs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Company management may be better suited to guide the type of challenges and opportunities needed and tailor a future-ready programme for their employees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Switzerland has earned the reputation of having the friendliest and most welcoming environment for companies and tech firms when it comes to cryptocurrency regulations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: BitCoin is considered legal tender in the country and it is a hotbed for blockchain-based companies and advisory services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think we have good potential to be a leader in fintech solutions in the Asia region.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am pleased to note that some startups are offering their own cryptocurrencies, using initial coin offering (ICO) as a fund-raising platform.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And recently, there was even a fintech firm launching an ICO advisory centre.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think the Switzerland model could serve as a useful reference and guide towards possible liberation of regulations in regard to embracing the cryptocurrency culture in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also about mobile banking, investments, online wealth management and so forth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I hope more Singaporean fintech startups will think beyond cryptocurrencies and venture into other areas of fintech.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our 4G leaders, I know, are well attuned to this need.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We can play a part by introducing more teeth to TAFEP.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: It is our national language and a regional language.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: It is rooted in our geography, in our history.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: It is not only important to our sense of who we are and where we are rooted in the world; it is also important to securing our future in the region and share in the growth of the region.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Could we help those students who do not currently learn Malay in school to attain some basic level of proficiency?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: I know our children have a lot to do already in school, including learning English, Chinese or Tamil to ever higher levels of proficiency.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Many Members have spoken in this House on the importance of such learning and they are right.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: I believe it would be to the good if all our children could learn it to some basic level of conversational fluency.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Such learning will be good for the cognitive and intellectual development of our children.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: We will reflect on what it means to be Singaporean and on the common values and beliefs that bind us together.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The President says that “our diverse cultures and traditions are now interwoven…we have succeeded in nurturing a distinct Singapore identity.” Sir, I am not as confident as all that but I believe that we will be taking a step firmly in that direction when we make the learning of our national language a bigger part of our national education.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The President said that the focus of the future work before us would include the following: to work with regional partners to strengthen ASEAN centrality and unity, maintain an open and inclusive regional order and strengthen our position internationally, including in our region; to encourage local businesses to stay relevant and venture into oversea markets, including our regional markets; strengthen the education of different age groups, promote proactive lifelong learning among our people and be adventurous to venture beyond our shores.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Learning the national language will help us achieve these goals.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In the 21st year of the reign of the Qing Emperor Guangxu, Li Zhongyu recorded that Malay was commonly spoken in Southeast Asian islands and the Chinese born and bred and living in Singapore had all learnt the Malay language.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In other words, modern language, approximately a hundred years ago, all Chinese living in Singapore could speak some Malay with some facility.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Former Member of Parliament Mr Lim Huan Boon was a pioneer in encouraging the learning of Malay among Chinese Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: He took part in and won the 1963 Legislative Assembly Elections in the Bukit Merah constituency and represented his constituency in the Malaysian Parliament as one of the Members representing Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Learning Malay can help promote cultural exchange among our different communities and it is the duty of every Singaporean to do so.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.40 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 4.08 pm until 4.40 pm.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond the dollars and cents, renewing our economy, strengthening our fiscal position, which is important to our survival, the heartware of this nation is equally important.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How we care for one another, how we make sure no one is left behind, how we speak up for a better Singapore and how we have a culture of giving are crucial in the next chapters of the Singapore story.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My late father taught me to always give and, in his eulogy, I said "Daddy gave more than he received and that ultimately was his strongest philosophy in life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A philosophy I hold dear to my heart and one I will impart to my daughter as well." It was with this philosophy that I entered politics and the quote I used in my candidate video was: "There is beauty in giving more than receiving".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This spirit of giving is very much alive in Singapore and I see it in my work as a civil society activist for the past 17 years and as a Member of Parliament for the past three years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I see it almost every week when I meet my Legislative Assistants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps the most common question I am asked now is how on earth do I speak up so much in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How do I find the time to research and draft so many speeches and questions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Melissa has a full-time job, is actively involved in humanitarian work and is also my Chief Legislative Assistant.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If there is just one word to describe her, it is that she is amazing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She and my six other Legislative Assistants – Charmaine, Karen, Su, Roy, Jing Ling and Rachel – embody the spirit of speaking up and this spirit of giving.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Despite having full-time commitments, they give their time and energy towards the Singapore cause.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They care deeply about our future and, most importantly, want to play a role in shaping it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This spirit of giving is also very much alive in Nee Soon East.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Tan Meng, my CCC Chairman and also my left-hand, left-leg, right-leg, right-hand man, exemplifies this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He leads a team of dedicated volunteers and has been a grassroots leader for 26 years now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He serves with his heart and handles every feedback and every case so passionately, so meticulously and with compassion.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And he does this every single day as a volunteer.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Twenty-six years ago, he was curious and wanted to see how he can help improve the community and so he joined the CCC.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Twenty-six years later, he looks as young as ever; perhaps the secret of looking young is to volunteer more!

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And I know he will volunteer more and continue to serve till his last breath.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Siti Durriah is equally committed and I first met her when I was visiting a refugee camp in Aceh.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I met this young lady who was so passionate about helping people that she used her precious time off from work and her salary to volunteer to help others.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A physiotherapist by training, she was in Aceh to conduct developmental assessments for refugee children and teach them English.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And there are others who are so devoted that they have chosen to make a career out of it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I recently met Dr Sudha Nair when I joined President Halimah to open Safe Spaces, a Child Protection Specialist Centre run by PAVE.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The stories they shared with us that day were heart-wrenching.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The children made cards for President Halimah and, in one card, the child wrote about how she watched her father strangle her mother.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It takes a very strong heart to be able to handle all these abuse cases every day but Sudha spoke with so much passion and so much determination.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I thought this Executive Director must be quite new to this as she was so fresh, not jaded at all and was bursting with positivity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But she has actually been a social worker for more than 30 years now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are fortunate to have someone like her, devoting her time towards ending family violence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are also fortunate to have Kalai who devotes his time to end animal cruelty.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He has worked at ACRES for the past seven years now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He was previously a volunteer with ACRES before I conned him, I mean convinced him, to join ACRES full-time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He took a pay cut to pursue his passion.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He took on a job where the office hours are 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A lot of animals are indebted to him, from otters to owls, from pythons to pigeons and, most recently, a dolphin.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The recent dolphin rescue near Bedok jetty was perhaps the best example of his level of commitment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He spent hours searching for that wild dolphin which needed our help.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: His hard work paid off and he managed to find and free the dolphin from the fish nets the dolphin was entangled in.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He gave that dolphin a second chance at life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So many more civil society activists I have met who work steadfastly to feed one mouth, educate one mind and comfort one soul.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The question is how do we have more Melissas, Tan Mengs, Sitis, Sudhas and Kalais?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How do we support their efforts more and strengthen this Spirit of Giving here in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This could encourage them to willingly volunteer more often during their school days and after graduation, thereby promoting a culture of active volunteerism."  There are good VIA programmes, like the one at Hougang Secondary.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Rather than introducing volunteer work through ad hoc projects, at Hougang Secondary, it is a way of school life, a life of volunteerism that is inculcated from the very beginning and they even get the parents involved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are lots of lessons to learn from them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But at the end of the day, I do hope that MOE can review our school-based volunteer programmes and see if there is still a need to make it compulsory and provide rewards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also hope that we can consider giving people more time to volunteer.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Time is perhaps the most valuable commodity in today's world and lack of time is the most common reason given for not volunteering.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: NVPC has found that volunteerism rates drop once people enter the workforce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As John Mackey nicely put it, "A healthy society rests on three pillars: business, government and civil society or non-profits.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Each has a distinct and important role to play and all three need to work together synergistically to create the most value for society".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given the insights that civil society can bring to the table with their ground experience, I hope they can be better represented on the Boards of our Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Prof Tommy Koh stated, "When we appoint people to boards, we can also appoint challengers who are subversive and who have alternative points of view.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That's the kind of cultural change we want to see.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do not believe that we hold the key to the best ideas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that we can build more regular channels for dialogue between the Government and civil society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Already, there have been many instances of fruitful dialogues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One example is the roundtable discussions that MEWR conducted to engage green groups to galvanise action and efforts for the Year of Climate Action.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Participants shared with me that they came out of the session with greater optimism and a better understanding of the Government's efforts to tackle climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another recent instance was IMDA's consultations with filmmakers on amendments to the Films Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: IMDA had extended the consultation period upon request and had taken on board the suggestions by filmmakers in the final wording of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Jasmine Ng, one of the filmmakers I worked with, commented in a Facebook post that she "really does appreciate that this engagement with IMDA and with you and the other MPs has been authentic".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I was particularly struck by her comment that, "we felt that we were heard and understood, even though we may variously disagree on some points".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, even where there is disagreement over the outcome, there is greater acceptance of the end result when civil society understands the reasons for the Government's actions and policies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It was a beautiful session to say the least.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Both sides gained a better understanding of each other's concerns, challenges and constraints.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Most of all, both sides realised that we are all on the same side, on the same boat.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, we can fire up and mobilise the spirit and energy of Singaporeans if we engage more, consider more alternative points of views, empower more, inspire more and ensure people have time to give back when they are mobilised.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Nelson Mandela said, "There can be no greater gift than that of giving one’s time and energy to help others without expecting anything in return".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I was going to end with that quote but then I realise that, actually, while we do not expect anything in return, sometimes we do stumble upon something valuable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And this was the case for Joseph and Jing Yu.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Jing Yu was volunteering at ACRES in 2012 when she met Joseph who was working at ACRES.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They both gave their heart and soul towards helping animals and they also gave their hearts to each other.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And, so, for all the singles out there, start volunteering and you might find your true love.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Better still, ACRES has quite a good track record, so volunteer with ACRES and you will find your true love while helping to strengthen this spirit of giving.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, thank you for the opportunity to participate in the debate.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are living in exciting times in a region full of challenges.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I am confident that Singapore will be able to handle these challenges, harness these opportunities and thrive.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Or as the President has put it, Singapore will remain exceptional.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In the same way, we became exceptional at dealing with our water challenges through perserverance and innovation, even creating new jobs and exporting solutions abroad.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As we forge ahead, we must hold on to the sound principles that have guided us in our journey thus far.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: One of these is meritocracy which, I believe, is important for us to revisit once in a while.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
