text: In fact, it would not be wrong to say this was one of the values upon which Independent Singapore was founded, powerful ideal which Mr Lee Kuan Yew and our Pioneer leaders believed in.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: At its core, meritocracy is a principle of allocation.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Allocation of resources, allocation of opportunities and allocation of rewards.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: A society founded on meritocracy makes these allocations based on capabilities and efforts, not on race, not on gender, not on your family connections.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Over time, this will increase inequality and polarise society into the "haves" and "have-nots" – distinct groups living different lives in different worlds.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Over time, the marginalised will lose trust in institutions and others in the community.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: At the root of it is this: it does get harder for them to succeed and, eventually, it becomes impossible.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Slowly and quietly, society will break up from within.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: When that happens, we will not be able to overcome together to face challenges that call for national unity.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Indeed, we have seen worrying consequences of rising social inequality overseas. "Drain the swamp" was a key slogan in the last US election.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As Americans found social mobility hindered, the American Dream – to be middle-income, to own a home and to raise a family – was no longer within grasp for some.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It consequently saw the US retreat from free trade in a bid to revive the American Dream, an economic nuclear option which does not address the domestic causes of the problem.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We must balance our economic and social policies.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We cannot drive our economic policies on fierce pursuit of economic gains; but neither can we design our social policies with bleeding hearts.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: There is even a term in psychology for this: "attribution bias".

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: However, if we are successful, we should realise how lucky we are and not forget the support society has given us: a good education, a safe and secure environment and the mental and emotional support.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In our meritocratic society, we must ensure that the spirit of giving back is most apparent in the successful.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I read in a Dads-for-Life article where Mr Gerard Ee related how his father, the late Dr Ee Peng Liang and Singapore's father of charity, "transmitted good values through word and action".

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Ee family lived in a lower income neighbourhood at Geylang Lorong 13, and Senior Ee organised annual toy-giveaways at his home for children in the neighbourhood.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Junior Ee and his brothers were in charge of packing the toys.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: And while this happened 50 years ago, Gerard still remembers how the children so looked forward to receiving the toys.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Gerard continues his father's spirit of giving back.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: He served as Chairman of the National Kidney Foundation (NKF) from 2005 to 2012, having responded to a call to help NKF get back on its feet.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This was even after he had retired from active volunteering to take a deserved break.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This spirit also lives on in Mr Mohamed Abdul Jaleel, who recently launched the S M Jaleel Foundation.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: And in the philanthropic families of the late Dr Lee Kong Chian and Syed Omar Aljunied.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We, too, are successful in our own ways.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Share our time, talents and treasures with those in need.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Be kind to our fellow Singaporeans in their daily lives.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The question is: will the new generation in Singapore, some of whom will become very wealthy in record time in new areas, such as tech, have the same spirit of giving as our Pioneers?

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: And will the children of our new well-heeled, who have access to the best education in the world, still give time to help uplift the rest of us?

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: What is clear, though, is that only when the successful give back will society accept, rather than envy, their success.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is, indeed, why our Public Service model succeeds.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our most capable are awarded with prestigious scholarships – no small sums from public coffers – to pursue their education at the best universities all over the world.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Because they dedicate their best to Public Service, everyone in society benefits.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are fortunate to have good people who decided on a Public Service career, rather than more lucrative fields, because the Public Service offers them greater meaning.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: And society has been the better for it because the best of our Civil Service know, as President Bush Senior put it, and I quote, "There is but one just use of power, and it is to serve people".

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It is, as Bernanke puts it, "The only way for even a putative meritocracy to hope to pass ethical muster, to be considered fair, is if those who are the luckiest in all of those respects also have the greatest responsibility to work hard, to contribute to the betterment of the world and to share their luck with others." Mr Deputy Speaker, let me now talk about common spaces and experiences as one feature of Singapore's brand of meritocracy.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: No other country or city shares common spaces like Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We live together in shared neighbourhoods, eat at the same hawker centres, exercise in the same parks and waterways, and bring our children to the same libraries to read.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We must preserve this to ensure that every Singaporean has a stake in and a shared ownership of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We do this so that there are places and spaces where our community can come together, regardless of race, language or religion, to enable daily interactions in as many ways as possible.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But these common spaces are even more meaningful because they guarantee common access to quality public facilities and infrastructure for all.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will ensure that the most needy among us, who have not done well yet in our meritocracy, are not deprived of access to good quality public facilities.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The successful and yet-to-be successful will live equally far or near to new nodes of economic activity in Jurong and Punggol, to hawker centres, eldercare facilities and schools.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Members may smirk at the mention of this motto.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But it is a serious matter to remind ourselves to be thankful that we do not have a bifurcation where the elites send their children to expensive, private schools and the rest to poorly resourced ones.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In fact, many of our best students in national examinations come from our heartland schools.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our education policies must enable every Singaporean to pursue their aspirations and realise their potential, regardless of their family background, including those with special needs.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Indeed, we are one of the few cities in the world where parents have no qualms putting their children through pre-schools and Primary and Secondary schools where they live.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: That is part of our brand of meritocracy.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Investing in quality education is our way of ensuring a fair and good start to our children's journey, whatever their background.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: While some have the means to go overseas for studies, every Singaporean has the chance to receive a quality education at home.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Everyone knows that their degrees and diplomas from our local institutions carry with them a world-class reputation.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In every city, there are areas where the rich and successful live, with schools where only the wealthy and connected can afford to send their children to.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: And then, there are the areas which visitors are advised to avoid, typically where the low-income or new immigrants gather.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Even when rich and poor neighbourhoods exist side by side, their inhabitants never cross paths.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I am not talking of developing nations but of rich and wealthy ones.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: That is a failure of meritocracy that we have avoided and must never allow to take shape in our future.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Government must, therefore, not allow meritocracy to reward narrowly, but instead broaden and make alternative routes available.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam once put it, "multiple peaks of excellence".

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: And if I may add, "many chances of success".

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Second, our policies must enable self-reliance by supporting and encouraging work.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We must provide all Singaporeans with the opportunity to work and do well for themselves and their families, regardless of where they are within our system of meritocracy at that point of time.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This empowers individuals and families and strengthens dignity and purpose.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will also ensure that our meritocracy does not become a static snapshot, but a dynamic one where everyone has the opportunity to reap success throughout his life journey.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This recognises that potential is not just realised in school and provides the opportunity for late bloomers to realise new dreams at different stages of their lives.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Ultimately, it is trust between citizens and institutions that will strengthen the Singapore brand of meritocracy.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: To kindle this virtuous cycle, the Government must deliver on our policies and continue to actively and openly engage, except in matters that are sensitive, involving issues of security or commerce.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Deputy Speaker, please allow me to put on record our highest appreciation to Dr Yaacob Ibrahim for his outstanding contributions as the Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs for 16 years.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have truly benefited from his leadership during his tenure.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Although our community has retained our religious beliefs and safeguarded the social values and graces of the Malays, it is meritocracy that gave us unique characteristics.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The main impact of meritocracy is that we have shifted from a feudal society that emphasises rank, titles and wealth that can be inherited, into a community that values someone in terms of educational achievement and career.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have become a community that builds hopes and dreams for the future because it opens the possibility of a better life.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: After 50 years of Independence, Singapore’s brand of meritocracy has resulted in achievements that our community can be proud of.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is the total figure comprising both the young and old.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: If we look at today’s cohort, only 1% of Malay children do not complete 10 years of schooling and 94% of them attained post-Secondary education.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: At the University level, we have seen more Malays achieving First Class Honours each year.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They are our community’s latest assets and will become the stepping stone towards ensuring our future remains bright.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In the job market, we see more Malays in administration, managerial, professional and technical (PMET) jobs.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is an increase from over 7% of the total population in 1980 to more than 32% in 2015.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The household income of Malays also increased six fold within 35 years, from 1980 to 2015.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Perhaps, there are those who always criticise these achievements because it is seen to be lagging behind other communities.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But I feel pride instead because our achievements today are proof that we can succeed by making an effort and not by submitting ourselves to fate or being dependent on assistance.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is even more so when we look at the potential of the current cohort.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are the products of the system of meritocracy that does not side with any particular race or social status.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Therefore, to those who succeed and gained everyone’s confidence, our achievements are genuine.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In fact, the expertise of the Malays are recognised everywhere we work, because our passports are viewed the same way, it is as red as all others and as valuable.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is because there are three external factors that challenge us and we must overcome.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Otherwise, these factors will impede our community’s progress in the future.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: To a certain extent, these elements have managed to erode our religious and cultural values as Malay/Muslims in this Archipelago as well as our Malay heritage that we should be proud of.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These elements can also divide our community and even members of our families.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Here, the role of the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (MUIS) in supporting the socio-religious life of local Muslims and interaction with Singapore’s multi-religious society, is an important one.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will strive to ensure that our local religious teachers are equally competent and as good as foreign religious preachers who may appear more glamorous.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The second challenge is the economic disruptions that have become more frequent.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The world is facing many uncertainties economically, socially and politically.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Challenges arise with the expansion of the economies of Asia and our region.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our current position as well as regional countries have changed and we are being challenged to the extent that they have morphed into our closest competitors.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: New technological disruptions will be more competitive and impactful, whether they come in the form of artificial intelligence (AI), robotics or the digital economy.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Jobs disappear quickly and yesterday’s skills are not needed tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: On this aspect, MENDAKI can play an important role by tweaking its programmes.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For students, MENDAKI will continue to ensure that they possess basic education and strengthen those with potential, as early as preschool.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Therefore, MENDAKI will also collaborate with Government agencies and other Malay/Muslim bodies to focus on factors that cause our children’s education to be interrupted, especially when their families’ lives are disrupted.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is because dysfunctional families would not just prevent our children from reaching their potential, but they will also be more likely to be involved in crime and drug abuse.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Since economic disruption can make a university degree to become invaluable or a particular skill to become unwanted in the blink of an eye, MENDAKI has also been busy thinking of ways for our community to live a culture of lifelong learning quickly and ready for change in terms of skills enhancement for the new economy, as well as grab opportunities that will come.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The third problem is the impact of extremism from foreign religious influences.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It is not limited to just terrorism, because extreme behaviour have started to have links to exclusive behaviour, which can cause the Muslim community to isolate itself from the wider society.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: To a certain extent, it has already impeded the pace of integration between communities.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In facing those challenges, MESRA can also play an important role to ensure that our community remains in the mainstream.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: MESRA can play a proactive role so that our community has many opportunities to interact with all races in our daily lives and not just in school or at work.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This was how Singapore developed an integrated and harmonious society that interacts well with each other despite having different religions and cultures.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: At the same time, all of us know that the rights and responsibilities of our fellow citizens are not different at all.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is what makes us a cohesive society.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Therefore, MESRA must extend its reach so that it does not just focus on the language and cultural segment of the community.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I would like MESRA to be further strengthened in order to achieve two major objectives.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The other MESRA advisors – Senior Parliamentary Secretary Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Amrin Amin and Ms Rahayu Mahzam – have already started several innovative pilot programmes that involve professionals in new fields like health, legal and education.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Second, we will strengthen the ranks of good calibre leadership in MESRA.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I am grateful that several professionals who are outstanding in their respective fields have answered our call to work together to help our community continue its progress.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will work together to involve more professionals in order to give better service and contributions to the community in MESRA’s activities.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is the best outcome of meritocracy in the Malay/Muslim community, whereby our outstanding professionals who have succeeded return to give back to the community.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These three institutions are highly valuable assets to the community and the cornerstone of the Malay/Muslim community in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Although M3 comprises different institutions – MUIS as a statutory body, MENDAKI as a self-help group and MESRA as a part of the People’s Association – our system of meritocracy enables us to strengthen M3 with the best officers.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Meritocracy also ensures that renewal can be done if some parts are less than outstanding.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In addition, professionals at M3 should be able to and know how to have synergy and solidarity when working with one another.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: M3 has to drive efforts with the same aim and direction towards achieving progress for the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I will ask them to lead various initiatives and mobilise other partners.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As the African proverb goes, we realise that if we wish to run fast, then run alone.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But if we wish to run far, let us run together.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Third, M3 will further strengthen their respective networks.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: There are many innovative programmes being done by the organisations within M3.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: However, one weakness that should be addressed is the issue of last-mile service delivery.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The following story illustrates this example very clearly.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Her family faced difficulties when her husband was detained for drug offences.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The rules state that she is not allowed to rent a home.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: She cannot purchase a new house because the CPF amount is in her husband’s account.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: When grassroots volunteers knew about her situation, we hastened to get help for her.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Clearly, there are many available programmes to help her.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The main one is getting the attention of the Social Service Office (SSO) and HDB.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Family Service Centre of the Singapore Buddhist Lodge Vision also provided counselling as she began to have depression.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They referred her to opportunities to undergo training and, with this support, she started work even though she never had a job before this.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As she was very determined to be self-reliant, there were times when she was willing to do several jobs.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Her life journey was full of challenges, but her family stayed together.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Her husband has been released and returned to their family.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Her husband now works as a driver and they have moved to a 3-room flat.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The most wonderful thing was that her three children are now studying in Polytechnics.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Because volunteers managed to get in touch with Mdm S early and society quickly supported her and accompanied her in her difficult journey, her family was able to rise up again.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: That is why it should be developed and strengthened.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: If we can overcome the attitude of "Not Invented Here", or not supporting others’ initiatives and guarding our own turf, or worry that our influence will be affected, our community can make more discernable progress.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We must make use of our community’s full potential.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are already admired by visitors to Singapore as a model minority community that succeeded because we have been strengthened by Singapore’s system of meritocracy.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It will be unfortunate if we only create a community that is prosperous only in terms of wealth.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Let us listen to the lyrics of a song by Malay rock legend Ramli Sarip titled “I Seek Eternal Peace” from his album, Sadaqa.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: His lyrics are: “I do not seek abundant wealth To live like a rich man I do not seek millions of dollars To live lavishly I do not seek friends To live a life of indulgence” Our prosperity should also make our community feel so grateful that they are moved to have the spirit of giving.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This spirit of giving, in turn, will encourage us to have the responsibility to develop the community on the basis of the gotong-royong spirit.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This was also my message to a group of tertiary students recently at Berita Harian, that is, when they eventually become successful, they should give back and engage the community.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: At the very least, they can inspire others to succeed as well.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is in line with what I said earlier, whereby, if meritocracy only manages to make us successful, it is an imperfect system because it does not inculcate the desire to give back to society.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In line with the coming month of Ramadan, let us renew our pledge to give blessings to all.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: With that, we can achieve an objective in life that is consistent with the message from Ramli’s song earlier, that is, “to have a life of eternal peace”.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Let us build an exceptional Singaporean Malay/Muslim community in the Southeast Asian Archipelago.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are at a key juncture in our nation’s journey.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In this journey, we will preserve our place in the world; Singapore must remain exceptional.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: And we must do so with the Singapore brand of meritocracy, one that is not merely a way to allocate resources but to do so also fairly and effectively.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: With the aim to ensure that Singapore remains a home for all, not just for the rich and successful.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: A Singapore where nobody is left behind and a Singapore which continues to provide opportunities for everyone to realise his dreams.   5.28 pm

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, during a recent business lunch, I was relating how some families in my constituency were relying on pay-as-you-use or PayU meter and could not even afford a refrigerator, a basic household item to many.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: One of the successful business leaders at the lunch suddenly cut me off by saying she could not believe there was a device like PayU meter in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: She quickly changed topic by saying how she and her daughters from a top girls' school would only stay in Marriot Hotel when they travelled overseas.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: She did not come across as a person who was particularly arrogant, ignorant or heartless.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: During the 45th Gallen Symposium in 2015, Deputy Prime Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam talked about our policy with regard to housing estates and ensuring a certain racial quota.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: He said the policy would not have come naturally: “The most intrusive social policy in Singapore has turned out to be the most important,” as it melded a nation where the people considered themselves Singaporeans first and foremost.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In my speech today, I would like to urge the Government to urgently tackle the issue of class-based divides with the same intent, purpose and rigour as we did in the past in ensuring racial and religious harmony, or the “CIMO” policy as it is known by ordinary Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: What do we mean by class-based divides and social divides?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The IPS report has broadly categorised the social divides in two aspects: one, comprising people staying in private or public housing; and another, arising from what most Singaporeans believe to be from "elite" and "non-elite" school backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: How do we encourage people staying in the private estates to make the effort to mix more with people staying in the public housing estates?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many speakers before me have made very good suggestions.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Through volunteering, sports and developing common interests, we can encourage mixing of social class.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For me, I just want to focus on one housing policy that may help to mitigate the social divide between people staying in public and private housing.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I understand that MND has a policy of reserving land just beside MRT stations for private housing.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The rationale is that the reserved land can be tendered out so that the prime land can be sold at a market rate that reflects the true value of the land beside MRT stations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If HDB were to build public housing just beside the MRT station, there is a limit to which HDB can price the HDB flats significantly higher than those further away, from a social standpoint.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As a result, those who succeed in obtaining such flats through balloting would be deemed as enjoying too much of a windfall.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, such a policy has had its unintended side effects.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The private housing built beside an MRT station often blocks the direct path between the public housing estate and the MRT station.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: So, the MRT station is here, the reserve land is in the middle and the public housing estate is on the right.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The pavement built in between the HDB estate and MRT station often blocks the direct path and the residents cannot walk directly to the MRT station but they have to make a big round.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In Potong Pasir, for example, URA has tweaked the policy to mandate the developer building the condominium beside Potong Pasir MRT station to maintain a public passageway for the residents in the Potong Pasir HDB precincts to have a direct path to the MRT station.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: So, I urge URA, HDB and LTA to consider rectifying the past errors based on the Potong Pasir model.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Next, I would like to turn our attention to bridging the gap between those from "elite" and "non-elite" school backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: About 30 years ago, Raffles Institution (RI) and Raffles Girls’ School (RGS) recruited students from a large base of Primary schools, "elite" or "non-elite" Primary schools through merit, basically through the PSLE results.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: From my understanding, 30 years ago, students from "non-elite" Primary schools, that is, from all the different schools made up more than half of the RI, RGS students.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: MOE probably has the figures and I hope the figures can be shared publicly.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: At least the immediate-past principal of RI had admitted that, I quote, “RI is now a 'middle-class' school that caters to the affluent segment of Singapore’s population.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Wealthier families have been able to give their children an edge through tuition and enrichment, leading to examinations, such as the PSLE, no longer being the level playing field that they were intended to be", and I agree.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Similarly, most RI alumni interviewed also agreed that RI had become less diverse in its student population.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The concern is that the "haves", with their connections and advantages, get more and more economic, social and cultural capital, while the "have-nots" struggle to even get a foot in the game even if they work hard from the start.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Today, a good number of us in this House came from humble family backgrounds, including myself.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thirty years from now, will we see a similar composition?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is a deep and complex issue with many causes and points of approach but I would like to suggest that we start with our education policies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Much has been said about investing in pre-schools and giving all children a good start in life, which is commendable.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The concern is that the rich, the well-connected parents have the means to “protect access” to the best schools – and perhaps even the best opportunities in life for their children, excluding those who are not so well-off.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, such a student may come from a disadvantaged background and perhaps could not afford the enrichment or tuition that caused him or her to miss the PSLE T-score of the top school cut-off point by one or two points.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Will such “nominated” students feel inferior in a top school?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Will such a student continue to experience unfair disadvantage as he or she cannot afford a personal laptop or co-pay the overseas field trip?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is where additional help in terms of financial and mentorship will be useful.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Perhaps, a Junior Raffles Institution Scholarship of $1,000 cash a year offered by RI can be modified to cater to this group of students.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Otherwise, it will remain only a handful of successful applicants each year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, financial assistance or scholarships may not suffice.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Author Shamus Khan, who wrote “Privilege: The Making of an Adolescent Elite at St Paul’s School”, makes an interesting point about how those from disadvantaged backgrounds given scholarships to the school are never quite on the same level as the entitled.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Academic performance notwithstanding, they are deferential and do not have the same air of success and confidence, traits which would serve them well in later business, politics and public life.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The top school may have to institute a mentorship scheme whereby the successful alumni who came from similar humble backgrounds can periodically provide guidance, encouragement and connection to this group of “nominated” students.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Next, I would like to turn our attention to the Special Assistance Plan (SAP).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: SAP was introduced by our founding Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew in 1979 to preserve the best Chinese-stream schools so as to develop effectively bilingual students inculcated with traditional Chinese values.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I am from the second batch of SAP students and I have benefited from the system tremendously.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: So has our current Minister for Education, Mr Ong Ye Kung.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Mr Ong had confided that he would not have attended Maris Stella High School if it was not a SAP school.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: SAP schools have existed for nearly 40 years and many people have asked to examine their relevance today.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With China becoming a major global player and the second largest economy in the world, it is even more pressing and necessary for SAP schools to churn out youths who are comfortable with the Chinese language, culture and values.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This has and will continue to help Singapore to deepen our relationship with China.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It will help facilitate trade, business and cultural exchanges with the mainland Chinese.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   I am from the second batch of SAP students.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I am able to speak in Parliament in both Chinese and English and credit must be given to the SAP system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Next year, 2019, SAP schools will be celebrating their 40th anniversary.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The Chinese like to celebrate the "5s” and "10s” to review the past and look into the future.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: SAP was introduced by founding Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew in 1979 to preserve the traditions of the Chinese schools and to cultivate effectively – bilingual and bi-cultural talents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With the success of its economic reform, China has become the second largest economy in the world.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With its One Belt One Road initiative, the Chinese influence in Asia and the world is becoming more and more significant.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Not only are more Singaporeans willing to learn Chinese, foreigners are also sending their children to Singapore to learn Chinese.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: So, learning Higher Chinese is no longer the monopoly of SAP schools.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many Secondary schools are now offering Higher Chinese and the take-up rate has been increasing over the years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: To learn a language is not just for examination or being able to speak and write.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The important thing is to know, understand and appreciate the culture.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Just now, in my English speech, I mentioned that educational background has become a faultline in our society; students from the elite schools and non-elite schools tend to stay within their own inner circles.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For example, to allow non-Chinese students studying ordinary Chinese to attend SAP schools.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Allowing non-Chinese students to study in SAP schools provides Chinese students with the opportunity to mix with non-Chinese students.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It has shown that graduates from SAP schools, whether they go to JCs, polytechnics, universities or National Service, can generally mix well with non-Chinese Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, we should not refrain from promoting Chinese culture in SAP schools just because there are non-Chinese students in the school, just like the Mission schools or Buddhist schools will not reduce their religious aspect simply because there are non-believers in the school.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Non-Chinese students going to SAP schools will have to accept exposure to the Chinese culture.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is not necessary to make a hasty decision.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, encouraging non-Chinese students to study at SAP schools is a sensitive topic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, we have to face the situation squarely as we tackle the issue of class divides along educational background.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Class was certainly not so much of an issue when the words of the Singapore pledge "regardless of race, language or religion" were coined.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We now want to build a democratic society, regardless of race, language, religion or class.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With this, I support the Motion. 5.45 pm

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There has been much discussion about fighting inequality and blurring emerging social divides.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Is the glass half empty or half full?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We have a functioning meritocracy with various pathways of success.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Rather than arguing about whether the glass is half empty or half full, can we get everyone to join in to fill up this half empty and half full glass called Singapore?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The answer, I believe, is what psychologists have termed as the "Ikea effect".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Simply put, the "Ikea effect" says that we cherish what we build.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Many of us have struggled with self-assembled furniture.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The instructions often look easy: insert a screw here and turn an Allen key there.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But the results are usually far from perfect and certainty not what we see in the showroom.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, despite the imperfections, we are intensely attached to our self-built furniture, far beyond their useful years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At home, I still own a few Ikea stools that I built during my university days.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They made it through eight house moves and I lugged them through half the world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This is the "Ikea effect": we cherish things that we build and labour leads to love.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, when we get Singaporeans to come together to build a better society, we value not just the shiny successes, but also the imperfections, the work in progress.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I often see this happening on the ground when we come together to do some meaningful social work.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: After a successful project, the better-off among us appreciate the challenges and inequalities that less fortunate Singaporeans face.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We also realise that our own success is not just a result of our hard work and talen,; but also of circumstances and the help of others along the way.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, the needy among us get lifted up, not just because of the material assistance that they received, but also because of the wisdom and life-skills, because they felt the warmth and solidarity of fellow Singaporeans and because they learnt that those with less also have something to give.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Most importantly, whether we are the better-off or the needy, we all appreciate society with its imperfections, because we all know that, on that day, we made society just a little bit better.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We can make volunteerism a defining aspect of what it means to be Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: SG Cares encourages individuals, companies, schools – to work together to build a more inclusive Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: SG Cares provides the technology, combines the needs of various communities and serves as the bridge to major companies and institutions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Some CDCs, such as Northwest CDC, also have good social work programmes and can mobilise people to do good.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With the data, technology and added volunteers from SG Cares, as well as project management and funding from the CDCs, the grassroots can be an effective last-mile coordinator of assistance to the needy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, in my constituency, Kebun Baru, thanks to the strong support from Mayor Teo Ho Pin of Northwest CDC, we are implementing two priority long-term programmes for social work: to build up the best community support for cancer patients and survivors, and to build a dementia-friendly community.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We are also exploring getting technical assistance from SG Cares.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And from 2020 onwards, we roll out this collaboration nation-wide.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, I also hope that SG Cares can mobilise our people to help pockets of Singaporeans that are usually unseen, such as children and youths at our various homes and the young offenders serving time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Over time, I hope that SG Care can make volunteerism a defining characteristic of being Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: SG Cares can transform the Singapore psyche and turn Singapore into a Democracy of Deeds.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, MOE encourages students to do VIA programmes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We can use this platform to incentivise youths to do more social mixing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Specifically, MOE can provide bonus VIA points to encourage collaborations between different schools.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the cluster level, the MOE school leaders can work hard to nurture collaboration between elite and non-elite schools, so that students from different educational backgrounds can forge friendship from a young age.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: MCCY and MOE can also create a parallel track for youth sports, so as to encourage social mixing outside the schools.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, we can grow ActiveSG's Sports Academy and Clubs to absorb more youths from different schools and give them CCA points under the LEAD framework.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, MOE can also invite Sports Academy and Clubs to send teams to join inter-school sports competitions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And, in general, ActiveSG also brings people together through regular sports competitions and activities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There is more we can do to encourage them to extend their camaraderie beyond the soccer field or badminton hall.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And when Singaporeans willingly come together to socialise, they will treasure the bonds they build.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: To the third set of ideas: supporting our needy to break out of the poverty cycle through some policy enhancements.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: First of all, we can do more to promote financial literacy and prudence of our needy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There are many VWOs who are willing to go to the schools, army camps, the community, or even the prisons to teach financial literacy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: These will benefit all Singaporeans, but especially the needy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Second, we can consider reviewing our Registration of Criminals Act, to temper justice with mercy, to rehabilitate and to re-integrate.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We all know that a prison conviction can have a tremendous impact on a person's ability to get hired.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: That, in turn, creates financial hardship for the family and contributes to poverty and inequality.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: These former inmates can volunteer for five years at VWOs that are IPCs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: A national panel can review their volunteer efforts and recommend to MHA on whether their criminal records deserve to be spent.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, we can provide a better rental housing environment for our needy while they battle to improve their lives.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, we can factor in household size as a major criterion to rental flat size.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For singles who are working hard and cooperating with the social workers, we can consider waiving the joint-single requirement if no suitable room-mates can be found.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There are many exciting possibilities if we can overlap our data and digital capabilities with Singapore's physical and financial connectivity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We have built our new National Trade Platform (NTP), which serves as our "national single window" for trade.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We are also connecting our NTP to Japan, to China through the Chongqing Connectivity Initiative (CCI), as well as to Hong Kong through the Global Trade Connectivity Network (GTCN).

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As a result, physical trade documentation is minimised.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Default and transaction risk in trade financing is reduced.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Through the Project Ubin trials, MAS is using distributed ledger technology to circumvent slow and expensive bank-to-bank transfers technology.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore companies are also coming together to build the Fast Track Trade Platform (FTTP).

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This SME trade platform is a block-chain powered digital e-commerce marketplace, with many added financing and insurance services built on it.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In turn, these three projects can open up new possibilities for Singapore, especially if we can integrate them into a national e-business platform.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can we allow our banks and financing companies to tap on these trade and transaction data, so that they can determine more efficient ways to provide finances and issuing credits to our companies?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can we connect up the supply chain of players of various industries to identify real-time opportunities?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, during low-demand periods, can three-party logistics (3PLs) and warehousing companies tie up with PSA or CAAS to offer discounted services, so that we can encourage more ships and freight planes to stop by Singapore?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can we integrate this platform to our digital security efforts, so that our emerging digital service providers can work with next-generation technology?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, is there scope for us to extend relevant and non-competing aspects of our national e-business platform to the rest of ASEAN because ASEAN can be a single economic ecosystem, with Singapore at the heart of it?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond this, digital technology can also help us drive our Government's productivity, which has an impact on business productivity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The National Trade Platform can be described as a "National Single Window" for trade for all companies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can we build other "national single windows" digital platforms for other industry clusters?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, developers, builders and architectures within the construction sector have to work with various agencies to get the permits and approvals.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can we get various agencies to redesign their approval processes, identify conflicting or overlapping requirements and create a common and current depository of regulations for all?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This means the entire sector can efficiently transact with the Government through that single national window for most key processes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And if we can come up with a "National Single Window" digital platform for the construction sector, another obvious choice is the lifestyle cluster, which frequently has to deal with various agencies on F&B, zoning and Police permits.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: To conclude, our debate on the President's Address gives us the opportunity to cast our eyes to a further horizon.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I share many of the priorities that the Government has highlighted.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, I believe there are exciting opportunities to use data and digital transformation to drive the economy and also believe that there are some policy adjustments that we can do more of to fight inequality and bridge social divides.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Most importantly, if we can infuse SG Cares into the Singapore soul, inspire our people to build a better Singapore, we will all be happy and happier for it because people value what they build and because labour builds love. 5.58 pm

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Building a well-connected world city, developing a vibrant economy, forging a cohesive, caring society and nurturing a Singaporean identity that we can be proud of.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Trust is a commodity that cannot be taken for granted and is not easily earned.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: These are powerful words and I hope very much that the 4G leadership will heed this very wise advice, Sir, as trust and connecting with the people are the foundation stone of the social compact between Singaporeans and their leaders.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, how should the 4G leadership connect, maintain and build on the trust that their predecessors have had for all these years?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: My sense is that this is already happening.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We have arguably the brightest and most able talent of their generation on the 4G leadership bench.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But in today’s digital world, where reputations are made almost instantaneously – and lost just as quickly – how our next generation leaders engage with Singaporeans will be particularly crucial.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Behavioural experts will tell you that how you are perceived is often the starting point of how your message is received and understood and this intuitive impression you make on your audience is very much a function of the multiple visual and social cues you send out.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Successful leaders know where their natural inclinations lie and use this knowledge to boost those inclinations, or compensate for them.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: As they transition to become the future leaders of Singapore, I hope very much that they will strive to remain fully aware of the aspirations and concerns of Singaporeans on the ground, beyond the traditional avenues of feedback.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They exemplify the trust and connection with the people that President Halimah spoke about.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I did not have the privilege of working closely with Mr Lim Hng Kiang and Mr Lim Swee Say, but I have seen how well they connect with the ground and how trusted they are.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Prior to working with him, I had the privilege of lining up behind him at a popular briyani stall at Newton Food Centre when he was Minister for the Environment and Water Resources, probably in the mid to late 2000s.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: What struck me then was his humility and graciousness.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: No one would have noticed that a Minister was in the queue.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: He was friendly, approachable and got his food without any fuss; all this, with his trademark smile.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob and I met formally when he was the Minister for Communications and Information.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Because of my appointment to the then-MDA Board and also several other MCI committees, I had the opportunity to work closely with Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: What strikes me most about Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob in my interactions with him over the 10 years is his awareness of those around him and how he makes it a point to make those around him feel comfortable and at ease.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In 2013, I hosted Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob to a dinner at a television market in Cannes, France.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: My events team in London had made reservations at a halal restaurant in Cannes, which was a challenge back then as there were only a handful of them.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It was a Middle Eastern restaurant which they said was a highly recommended seafront restaurant.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, we sat down to dinner at that restaurant, ordered our food and everything was going well.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In the middle of our main course, loud music came on and, to my horror, a belly dancer emerged.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: She went table to table to try to get diners to join her on the dance floor.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I broke out in cold sweat, hoping that she would not stop at our table to ask the Minister to dance.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob patted my hand and said in his usual calm manner, “Ganesh, don’t worry about it; just enjoy your food.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I’ve encountered this in my travels to the Middle East many times and they won’t disturb you if you are busy eating your food.” And true enough, the belly dancer skipped our table.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond the belly dancing episode, Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob was always connected, calm and gracious in work settings, so much so that it is quite hard to disagree with him.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And even on occasions when we have disagreed, Dr Yaacob would always make it a point to explain his side of things.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: He is, to me, an excellent example of a leader who is self-aware, connected and genuine.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And this, to me, is why he is trusted by all who have worked with him and the people he serves.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: (In Tamil):   Last week, President Halimah Yacob mentioned in her speech several points on how the 4G leaders should lead our country.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They must receive the support of the people.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They must have a good relationship and trust among the people, she said.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The 2G and 3G leaders have built a relationship as strong as a tower with the people.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This will not be easy for the 4G leaders.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They still have much more to learn from senior leaders in our Parliament.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Let us take Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim as an example.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: He had been a Minister for 16 years and a Member of Parliament for 22.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I was a Board member at the Media Development Authority for some time with him and had the opportunity to interact with him.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: He always had a smile on his face.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And from the Permanent Secretary in MCI to all who still work in the Ministry, everyone was simple and interacted courteously like him.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The 4G leaders would have much to learn from their experiences and lead the country well.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In today’s digital world, the messenger and the way the message is delivered are sometimes more important than the message itself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: President Halimah stressed the importance of leadership in an "uncertain and volatile world" and aptly advised that the 4th generation leadership must "fire up and mobilise" the spirit and energy of young Singaporeans and grow with the people we represent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Leadership renewal is well underway with the recent Cabinet reshuffle.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Each generation of leadership change premises a new social compact – one that is based on a set of core inclusive and shared values; one that also builds on our past and embraces our future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Confucius once said: "Study the past, if you would divine the future".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: An astute Singaporean political observer once shared with me this: he said that when Singapore was first founded from the embers of the British Empire and the brief interlude in Malaya, the founding fathers of the first-generation leadership saw the need to build the country and its institutions as quickly as possible, in the face of external threats and internal strife.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: The relationship between the polity and the political leaders could be summed up as "No Voice and No Choice".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: There was no luxury of space for discourse or time for discussion with the people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: People accepted this because existential threats were not rhetorical questions or strategic questions to be answered but they were actually day-to-day issues that needed to be tackled in the business of running Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: This new consultative leadership, could be summed up as "Got Voice but Little Choice".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: We hear you, and, indeed, we want to hear from you, but we will still have to make the hard decisions because we still know better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: After another 20 years, the 3G took over.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: The 3G team started taking over the responsibilities of running Singapore in 2001 even though the 2G leaders kept a watchful eye.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: The 3G team formally took over in 2004 with the appointment of the current Prime Minister.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: REACH stands for Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry @ Home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: I think some of us may have forgotten this little factoid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Active citizenry is necessary because the Government recognises that it does not have all the answers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Political and policy solutions used to be formulated for the people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: In the 3G age, solutions have to be formulated and implemented with the people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: The relationship has now evolved to "Got Voice and Got Choice".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Where and how should Singaporeans and their 4G leaders go from here?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Whether it is "No Voice and No Choice" or "Got Voice but Little Choice" or "Got Voice and Got Choice", one fundamental force remains over the last 50 to 60 years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: The trust between the PAP Government and the people has largely remained strong over the years, despite the many tests and tribulations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Trust not just nurtures and edifies, but, if not betrayed, trust perseveres and overcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Trust, is difficult to quantify or value precisely, but, in its absence, renders almost everything else worthless in a relationship.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Trust endows us with courage and cohesion, which are what we need going forward.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: I am not talking about individual courage but courage as a nation and as a people to forge a future together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: As Aristotle once said, "Courage is the first of human qualities, because it is the quality that guarantees others".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Courage as a group is based on trust.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Cohesion is a little bit more difficult to understand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Cohesion is not simply uniformity and does not occur just as a default option due to the lack of diversity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Of course, if a group shares the same genetic, cultural and geographical factors, then cohesion may be much easier to achieve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: But the hard truth is that the hand that nature dealt Singapore is not an easy one – Our multiracialism, multi-religion and multiculturalism may be a strength, just as much as it can be a challenge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: And we will always have to work through the cards we are dealt, one by one to get the best possible result.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: This is and will be the work of generations of leaders of Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Just as our Founding Father Mr Lee Kuan Yew had reminded us, "This is not a Malay nation, this is not a Chinese nation, this is not an Indian nation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Everybody will have his place: equal; language, culture, religion." The challenges are many for the new 4G leadership.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Some may think that existential and basic questions no longer dog us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: We no longer worry about the roof over our heads, about clean water or having enough food for our children and having a chance to get a decent education.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: But this does not mean we do not have challenges that threaten the very basic fabric of our society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: These challenges are more subtle but no less fundamental and visceral.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
