text: One major challenge is how do we maintain cohesion in Singapore?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Cohesion is formed from a sense of identity, shared values and singularity in purpose.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: The old challenges of race and religion to cohesion are still there.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: It will always be a work-in-progress in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: To me, there are three key challenges on building cohesion facing Singapore and the new leadership.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: The gap between the "haves" and "have-nots" is becoming more pronounced.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: How do we keep the country going together when different social classes may be living, literally and physically, further and further apart?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: On one side, there may be families who take holidays in European ski resorts without a second thought and, on the other hand, many other families can only afford to take a coach to Malacca for holiday, if at all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: These outcomes may be entirely due to a meritocratic system sorting out society and also due to market forces and may be even entirely justifiable from such perspectives, but, in the long run, what will be the effect on cohesion?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: And what do such outcomes reflect on the values we profess or, at least, claim to profess?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: It has been said that if one can capture the middle ground, then one is usually victorious in politics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: But as we have seen in many post-fact democratic societies, one sometimes wonders what is the middle ground?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: In most issues in the past, the spectrum of opinion of the polity could be described by a Gaussian distribution, or what we call a bell-shaped curve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: If the entire chunk of the bell-shaped curve supports you, you are home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: I am not sure if the bell-shaped curve is still so prevalent anymore in the multi-polar world with many different viewpoints and groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Anyone can publish a blog or be an influencer with a following of thousands.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: There are now thousands of moderately loud voices versus only several very loud voices in the past.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: It is getting harder and harder to discern what constitutes the middle ground and what does not.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Or whether the middle ground now is simply a collection of smaller interest groups, temporarily coalescing out of shared self-interest and undergoing dissolution soon after?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: There are now too many choices and voices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: How then do we lead and foster cohesion when the middle ground is either not so middle or grounded?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Consequently, it may become harder and politically riskier to prescribe what we think is frankly unacceptable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: This may not be apparent in peaceful times, but in times of crisis and uncertainty, hard choices will have to be made.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Remembering the words of Mr Lee Kuan Yew, "Whoever governs Singapore must have the iron in him." Indeed, even as a tiny red dot, we must stand up to our principles and beliefs, and we will not be pushed around.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: There is a place in your heart that just warms up when you visit the same coffee shop or hawker centre that your father brought you to as a kid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: You feel a sense of security and joy when you tuck into the same nasi lemak and kaya toast with soft-boiled eggs that had been made by the same folks for the past 20 years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Humans being humans, we anchor our lives to persons, places, moments and experiences that defy the imperatives of economics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: These anchors define what is truly "home" to us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: I will be honest: every time I see a favourite hawker retire or a coffee shop close, a little bit of a sense of "home" dies in me.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Even though I can understand why he is retiring, maybe because his children have all graduated from university.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Yes, change is inevitable; we either change or be changed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: How we then lead Singaporeans to face and embrace change so as to stay relevant in a world of ever-shortening business and technology cycles and diminishing distances between competitors and yet keep and grow the sense of home within all of us, is a major challenge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: But our life anchors often do not answer to questions of economics, even though our economics and physical well-being demand that we answer and respond to these same questions adroitly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: How do we foster trust and cohesion between Singaporeans from different social economic classes who may lead very different lives?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: How do we rally Singaporeans together when the middle ground may not be so middle or grounded?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: How do we maintain cohesion among Singaporeans by anchoring them to Singapore as home even when we need everyone to embrace change so as to remain relevant and economically viable?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: With trust and cohesion as our shield and sword, we should be more than alright.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The business community generally agrees with this stance and expects our country’s 4G leaders to continue consolidating the new era’s Government-business collaborative relationship which is based on mutual trust and mutual learning, and pushing for economic transformation with dynamism and resolve.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In the past Singapore had succeeded many times in finding breakthroughs in economic transformation.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Our first-generation founding leaders succeeded in creating Singapore’s economic miracle when Singapore struggled for survival in adverse circumstances.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Their far-sightedness and precision in positioning Singapore while relying on the people's trust and support amid an extremely unfavourable environment, paid off.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Ten years ago, that is, when the financial crisis erupted in 2008, the 3G leaders and the businesses confronted it together.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: They rolled out employment subsidy programmes and encouraged upgrading of skill to help workers keep their rice bowl, taking Singapore on a quick bound after it bottomed out amid the global economic recession.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Today, Singapore is once again in an unpredictable international environment.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses expect 4G leaders to be both talented and virtuous and be attentive to the lives of the people while understanding the vagaries of recent industrial developments.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: They are expected to demonstrate courage and determination as leaders while injecting new vitality into the economic transformation.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, the new era requires the creation of a new form of collaboration between the Government and businesses which will let enterprises have a greater rein in terms of initiatives in economic development.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In the early years of nation-building, due to the special political and economic situations then and the constraints of domestic education, the Government exercised full control on the direction of economic development.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Today, the international market is open, information flows freely and technology keeps renewing to no end.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: With the spread of digital technologies such as big data analysis, it is easier for enterprises to muster resources while the trends of industries are more diversified.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Next, it is necessary for the trade associations and enterprises to be more involved and in control.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Going forward, the responsibilities of the Government are to clarify the directions and allow companies full play on a level playing field and promote mutual trust with enterprises in the transformation.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: To this end, Governments and businesses must strengthen their mutual interactions and deepen mutual understanding.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: To grasp the development opportunities amid rapid changes, 4G leaders must listen to the voices of businesses, pay close attention to the developments of the industries and broaden their visions so that they can formulate pro-business policies more accurately.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I remember that, in the 1990s, Singapore eliminated the garment-processing industry while developing high value-added industries.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Later, the garment industry continued to develop in Hong Kong as its base, bringing about a fashion design hub and a related logistics supply chain that brought high returns.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: For example, Singapore’s import and export trade accounts for a very high proportion of our total economic output.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In the future, we can continue to explore how to leverage these existing advantages in new circumstances.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The Government can keep in touch with companies through platforms, such as trade associations and chambers, to adjust policies in line with the latest trends.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: If the Government wants people to live well, they must first let businesses do a good job.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: To this end, I urge businesses to actively establish a new Government-business relation.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: They should not just make good use of Government assistance programmes to develop their businesses, but also understand more about economic policies and provide constructive suggestions to Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Today, not only are the Government leaders passing on the baton; so too are the business leaders.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Besides, there are many young entrepreneurs who are making great achievements in emerging industries, such as in technology and Internet-related industries.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Also, I look forward to the leaders grasping the dynamics of industries accurately and offering them effective help.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Going forward, we are ready to build a better future for the country with the new leadership team. 6.31 pm

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While Singapore faces many challenges in the coming years, it is good to see a clear identification of the issues we need to address and the road map for dealing with these challenges.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And notwithstanding these challenges, I am also heartened that there is still an important part of Singapore's plans to secure a place for ourselves in the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore's success in the previous decade has been built upon being an open economy and staying relevant in an ever-changing world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Almost immediately after Independence, Singapore's economic plan was to engage with the world, to bring in investments, to be a platform for trading, and EDB and other institutions helped to build Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore's security was also built having strong defence relationships with countries both near and far.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These important relationships were developed because Singapore had an outward focus from the get-go.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the growing trends that is of concern to us is growing insularity in many parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In Singapore's early years of Independence post-World War II, the global architecture was being set up.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Bretton Woods institutions, including the World Bank and the IMF had been set up in the 1940s, a few decades before our Independence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And the trend was very much to support investment and growth in the developing world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At that time, the western powers had realised that it was necessary for the whole world to prosper in order to ensure that peace would continue.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In parallel with the Bretton Woods institutions, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) oversaw the liberalisation of world trade and this Agreement eventually developed into the World Trade Organization.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Together, these institutions have brought down trade barriers in many countries, including Singapore, which have benefited and grown.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These institutions were also complemented by regional organisations that are focused on bringing down internal barriers and facilitating trade.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The bigger alliances included ASEAN in our region, the North Atlantic Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) in America, and, the most comprehensive integration, which was the European Union (EU).

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The President's Address highlighted important events that seemed to suggest a global shift from this trend and I will elaborate on some of these.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is unprecedented in EU history and, although the EU looks like it will survive Brexit, it is clear that the concerns that triggered the British decision to leave were also resonating in other parts of Europe.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It has reiterated its intentions to become a world player.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the time of the President's Address, the Malaysian elections had not yet taken place.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am sure, if it had, she would have highlighted this as an important development as well, given that our relationship with Malaysia is one of our most important bilateral relationships.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My heartiest congratulations to Prime Minister Mahathir, who has prevailed against all odds and is set to be Prime Minister again.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is a small country with no control over what happens in other countries and changes in other countries take place at paces that they dictate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While other countries may change their minds on how far they wish to engage, I think Singapore still needs to find a way to stay relevant.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think even as countries change and governments' outlooks in the world change, what has helped Singapore and certainly with the generations of leaders so far is a way to stay relevant in this ever-changing world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is built largely on relationships that have been developed over the generations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In relation to Malaysia, I think Prime Minister Lee was one of the first to congratulate Prime Minister Mahathir on his appointment as Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it was important to reiterate that many of the projects that have been developed are in both countries' interests to pursue.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of Singapore's greatest assets has been the strong standing of our leaders and the many relationships that have been built up over the years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even as countries appear to lean away from multi-nationalism, I think it is the strong standing of our leaders and the reputation of Singapore, the diligence of the many people in our Foreign Service and our trade representatives who have helped us get a listening ear from the senior leaderships in other countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it is important for us to continue to build these relationships and for the next generation to also continue to nurture them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our position as ASEAN Chair in the coming two years is a golden opportunity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even as Singapore's 4G leadership comes to the fore, I certainly hope that the previous generation of leaders will stay around to nurture relationships and to help guide and lend a helping hand, where possible, because human relationships are very important.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This issue was brought to the fore by the Institute of Policy Studies’ (IPS') Study on Social Capital in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It was subsequently raised by several hon Members of this House during the Budget Debate earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There has also been much discussion in academia, the media and online platforms amongst all segments of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It does because it cuts to the heart of the foundational values of our social compact; values, such as meritocracy, equal opportunities and self-reliance.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It makes us sit up and question these values, their relevance in the context of modern-day Singapore and whether they have become the metaphorical “sacred cows” that are impossible to slaughter.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I disagree, however, with detractors who recklessly attribute the widening inequality as a consequence of our existing policies.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Public policies are made within the context of its time and it is not reasonable to suggest that our existing policies have not served us well.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Singapore, as a country, and Singaporeans as a citizenry, have come a long way since 1965 and our policies over the years, implemented by our Founding, second and third generation leaders, contributed significantly to our success.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But change must be for a purpose, especially if it is to a policy or system that has served us well.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I remember not too long ago, a Parliamentary colleague brought up the possibility of abolishing the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE).

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Good valid arguments were made for and against.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But I managed to speak to many parents of primary school children after, and their views were mixed.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Some felt changes should be made, but most were not in favour of abolishing the PSLE completely.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And yet, as the prevailing view that the PSLE is a high stakes exam that has serious ramifications on our young students’ future remain, the problems of stress on our young students and anxious parents will continue.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But not all possible solutions require the slaughter of a “sacred cow”.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Pilot projects that consider alternative models can be explored.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There must be a careful calibration of what requires “tweaks” and what should be “boldly” changed.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As Singapore grows and evolves, her context changes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: New issues, such as widening inequality, have arisen.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The more important question now is therefore, not an inquest into fault, but about what needs to be done moving forward.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Can the next generation leadership team exercise political leadership to “tweak” or “boldly” slaughter any “sacred cows” where necessary?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: One argument against “doing more” to deal with widening inequality lies in the fundamental principle of one of our foundational values – meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Inherent within the concept of meritocracy is the ideal that if an individual works hard enough, is determined enough and possesses the ability to succeed, he or she will.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This has worked well for Singapore for two to three generations where many Singaporean families have bettered themselves, through education, hard work, grit and determination.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The argument on the other end of the spectrum, however, is that meritocracy works well, if the gap between the "haves" and the "have nots" is closer.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This was, indeed, the case during the days of our parents and grandparents.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The gap in resources available to families with higher income and those with lower income is stark.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In Singapore, formal education begins at Primary 1.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Students of different backgrounds, where the perceived “difference” – and I say "difference" in inverted commas – in ability between students, such as the ability to read, write or count, could stem from the environment of their homes and the resources of their parents instead of their true inherent abilities.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And when these students are streamed and valued in our education system, sometimes quite early on in their formal education, they may then be denied the opportunity to succeed as they may, if the playing field was more level to begin with.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, we all appreciate that the issue of widening inequality in Singapore is decidedly more complex and requires much more attention than just the preschool arena.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is an acknowledgement that there are Singaporeans amongst us, especially the children, who are placed at a disadvantaged starting point, because of the widening inequality and the rigours of our system.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I await with anticipation the action plans that will bring this promise to fruition.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Because deep within our social compact is a belief, a belief that, as a community, regardless of race, language or religion, we will always improve our lives together.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The delta of improvement may differ, as a meritocracy mandates, but we move forward as one.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is the desire of every parent to see their children better themselves and lead fulfilling lives.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Similarly, every generation of young Singaporeans growing up have their own set of dreams and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Their goals may differ, but the result that is hoped for is always the same – to improve themselves and achieve what they set out to do.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In this House yesterday and today, we have seen wide agreement across the Members that inequality is one of the great challenges of our modern era not just in Singapore, but also across many nations, many societies around the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Much of the discussion in Singapore and around the world as well has been about redistribution, about redistributing resources, opportunities and so on.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But there is also a deeper theme, which is that of social cohesion, whether fellow citizens, whether fellow Singaporeans see one another as brothers and sisters with a common destiny.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because if you do not see your neighbour as your brother or sister, then the question of whether you are your brother’s keeper or sister's keeper does not even arise.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That is why our policies to maintain social cohesion, that sense of friendship and fellowship with each generation must continue, and must continue being deepened and reforged.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But, Mr Speaker, is it enough just to have redistribution and social cohesion?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But are they enough to sustain a fair and just society into the future, not just for one term of government or one generation, but for generations to come?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Quality growth, so our people can rise and live better with each generation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some countries around the world are facing that.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There has to be growth, good quality growth.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is the knowledge work by experts with deep learning and interdisciplinary skills.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I am told today that there are lawyers learning blockchain and studying how it will transform ledgers and transactions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Two very different disciplines; yet, coming together to create new domains of knowledge work.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Innovation works as ideas are generated and implemented.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Makers making the future, often in scenarios where buzzwords become the factories of tomorrow.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Advanced manufacturing, where robotics, 3D printing and additive manufacturing combine with the Internet of Things.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Factories which might have seemed like something out of science fiction a decade ago, but which are rapidly becoming reality.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Entrepreneurship work, the work that young Singaporeans go about when starting a business, building those skills, creating opportunities to rise together with co-workers and employees.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We also continue to learn from the experiences of other countries.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The role of government and businesses working together; how working together can be reinvestment to regenerate shared resources and grow the shared common space and common resources that all can benefit from.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If I may tell the story again in a slightly different way.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Earlier this decade, there was a Harvard study by Michael Porter.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They looked at many United States (US) businesses, and the Harvard study suggested that some US businesses could invest more, that they were not investing enough, according to the Harvard Group; not enough investment in workers' skills, not enough development of supply chain networks, not enough regeneration of infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even though investment would have helped all companies do better, it did not always make short-term business sense for individual companies.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And we must continue encouraging companies to invest in skills upgrading because this uplifts the worker and uplifts other companies in the sector as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It must continue to be part of a deepening culture and social compact between our employers and workers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Likewise, helping our fellow Singaporeans to go regional to find new opportunities is part of this, too.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Economists like Mariana Mazzucato have written about this.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She pointed out the example of the iPhone, how it is built, not just on private enterprise, but on many innovations originally funded by the US government.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, the Internet, once upon a time, started out as a project funded by the American defence establishment.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But today, it is part of the innovation commons that powers so much on innovation and entrepreneurship in the US.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Touchscreen technology was initially developed at the University of Delaware, with partial public funding.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Closer to home, Mr Speaker, if I may talk about food, because food is a great passion for all of us in this House and fellow Singaporeans at large.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Basically, it is a machine that involves many precision parts which would require a large capital outlay.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It may not be so easy for a small business to buy one.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Not every business can afford to buy one.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But when agencies establish a shared resource, many companies benefit, including the smaller small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And this helps level the playing field and create opportunity.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have seen programmes, such as those on the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), or on Consumerism for Indonesia.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We see programmes investing in our workers and mid-career professionals as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Many of us would have heard stories of veteran entrepreneurs sharing their knowledge, sharing their own social capital and networks to mentor younger peers and younger entrants in the SME sector.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, quality growth, Sir, is very much part of the mission of all our economic agencies and our businesses, creating opportunities for young Singaporeans of all backgrounds.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Opportunities to rise, whether you start in a multinational corporation (MNC) or whether you start an SME yourself.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: An SME that may start small but, someday, grow big, maybe even become a unicorn.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And being able to do that, whether you are born in a private property or in a rental flat.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Opportunities to grow through picking up skills and experiences, either from your peers or through partnerships between trade associations and agencies.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Opportunities to grow and learn, no matter what background you come from.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Opportunities to take flight, to learn management and leadership, to get overseas work exposure to develop your potential, regardless of whether your parents have pre-existing wealth or entrepreneurship networks.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have to keep those opportunities coming to fellow Singaporeans, so that our younger generation can continue to rise and grow.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And we must be brave and we must be bold.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so long as we pull together, strive together, brave and bold, I know we will survive.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):  : Mr Speaker, like other Members, I would like to record my thanks to President Halimah Yacob for her Address.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The things that the President mentioned should certainly be adopted as a guide and direction for national leaders, especially the 4G leaders, to propel the country towards further success; the kind of success that can be attained and enjoyed by every Singaporean, regardless of race, religion or background, especially those who are less fortunate and the needy.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: She also said we must have bold thinking and make bold changes that are exceptional, when facing a situation where changes can take place rapidly and sometimes in the blink of an eye.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: She called on the leaders, especially the 4G leaders, to sustain and strengthen everything that has been implemented and achieved by previous leaders but, at the same time, also produce new and fresh ideas while navigating a future that is different and distinct.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I wholeheartedly agree with and support President Halimah's call on the importance of having bold thinking and making bold changes, that is, doing something exceptional so that we can enhance Singapore's standing and relevance internationally and, at the same time, enhance the benefits to every Singaporean because our people are the heartbeat and backbone of the nation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These two matters are equally important and are closely linked to each other.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, I am of the view that the well-being of Singaporeans must be given priority because a society's well-being is the factor that determines the level of motivation and innovation of that society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A motivated and innovative society can produce a strong and progressive nation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, it is important that not only the leaders, but also Singaporeans collectively, must have bold thinking and undertake bold measures in our journey and efforts to achieve our shared aspirations, which are to build a democratic society, based on justice and equality and, therefore, achieve happiness, prosperity and progress for our nation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It would be good if every Member in this House, including myself, especially myself, to do some introspection or self-reflection before we continue our journey.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is so that we are all clearer and more aware, as custodians of the people's voice, about the necessary measures to be taken for the good of the nation and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In this introspection or self-reflection, I would focus on President Halimah's advice about the need to have bold thinking and undertake bold measures or doing something exceptional when the situation calls for it.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: And in the process of self-reflection, some of the questions that we can ask ourselves as lawmakers are: first, have we managed to think and act boldly at this time when making changes to national policies in order to fulfill the basic needs and for the well-being of the nation and Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Second, are there policies that need to be improved or changed, that is, policies that brought about undesirable implications that affect the well-being of Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If so, what are the steps that should be taken?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In short, regarding the issue of motorcycle COEs, I proposed measures that should be taken so that the low-income are not burdened and can carry on surviving and continue to be self-reliant.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, the Ministry's response is that they are also very concerned about the financial hardship faced by the low-income who are affected and burdened by the motorcycle COE prices and urged that these groups visit the Social Service Office (SSO) to get financial help.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Are we not, as a society, also asked not to adopt a crutch mentality or be dependent on financial assistance?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: On this issue, we can see how the Ministry is not quite bold in making changes to the COE policy for motorcycles and, in fact, has adopted an approach that is rather contradictory to the principles that we have promoted, which is to be self-reliant and not to have a crutch mentality, by urging that those whose income are affected by high motorcycle COE prices to seek help from SSO.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This issue has been touched on by many Members, current and past.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Government must take bold measures to manage the problems that have burdened single parents in our society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The question is whether the current public housing policies have brought benefits for single parents and their families.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is why changes must be made for these single parents, so that they can enjoy the benefits for themselves and their families.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We can think back to a debate where I was not allowed to voice out an issue in this Chamber that was deemed to be sensitive.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We need to be more open in order to achieve a democratic society based on justice and equality.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps we can learn from Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad and the Malaysian people who have demonstrated an exceptionally bold spirit for the good of their country.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Here, I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad on his appointment as the seventh Prime Minister of Malaysia recently.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These practices are necessary and very crucial in the process of making and changing national policies, so that we, Singaporeans, can achieve Happiness, Prosperity and Progress.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the President’s speech, she highlighted what our nation has done well so far, outlined the challenges that we face and clearly set out the priorities that this Government has to focus on doing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I agree fully with the priorities set out and would add that this Government and this House must continue to take bold steps in creating a new world of opportunities for Singaporeans and continue to invest in our people so that this and future generations of Singaporeans will continue to thrive together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, in terms of bold steps for a new world of opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In our 53 years of nationhood, Singapore has undergone several transformations that demanded bold vision in our leaders and courage in our Government and people to trot uncharted paths.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We took risks, forged ahead and developed successfully from Third World to First.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Here we are, once again, in the midst of yet another transformation, as we embrace a digital economy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to embrace the digital economy for Singapore’s long-term good.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many countries around the world have been profoundly impacted by the advent of the digital economy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The way we organise our society, the way business is conducted, and the way people transact and interact with one another are all changing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As technology disrupts the world, Singapore must find a niche for ourselves to stay relevant and continue to be of service to the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Past successes do not confer us any advantage, and we must not be unnecessarily burdened by legacy achievements.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must move fast, seize new opportunities and entrench the advantages gained before others do.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In doing so, the Government has a critical role to play in creating a conducive environment, building a supportive ecosystem, and nurturing strong public-private partnerships so that social good will guide the innovative private sector.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I commend the Government for forging ahead in our Smart Nation project.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There is interdependence between a smart nation and a digital economy; they reinforce each other.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, there are still areas that are not progressing as fast as it could and should.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One example is e-payment, which received several national mention and much attention.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Several commentators have noted how fast China has transformed its payment landscape to do away with cash, especially if one considers paper-form money was invented in China in the seventh century.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But of course, China and Singapore are in different circumstances.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For the Chinese, cashless payments may be more reliable and more secure.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: China also has a different regulatory and business environment that catalyses innovations much faster.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In Singapore, the use of cash is deeply entrenched.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Thirdly, while technology can fail, cash never fails.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, to substitute cash and change habits, we will need a cashless solution that is superior to cash in the user’s experience.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A personal encounter may be helpful in illustrating my point.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Once, I visited a hawker stall to purchase a cup of tau huay chui or soya drink.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I asked to pay via quick response (QR) code since I have PayLah installed on my phone.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But to her, it is simply inconvenient, consumes electricity and, whilst there is no direct financial cost to her, there is not much of an incentive for her to actively use it as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Moreover, cash is a great medium of exchange, which she is used to and has never failed her.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Adoption goes beyond having good technical solutions, though in this case, it would help if Aunty can verify the payment on her mobile phone rather than use a separate machine.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is also about outreach and promotion, perhaps even consolidation, to avoid confusing consumers with too many options.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, one wonders why e-payment is still not taking off.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Is it because our market is too small but players too aplenty, resulting in a highly fragmented market?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Or is it because the incentives are too little to lure consumers and merchants away from cash?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must also not be locked into legacy systems and legacy corporations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Otherwise, it will be extremely difficult for e-payment or any type of transformation to take off in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have to use the solution that offers the best user experience if we are to hope to lure consumers and merchants away from cash.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We will need to push hard, take bold steps and be ready for disruptions to existing players.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Next, we need to invest in our people to move ahead together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to do more to prepare our people for a digital economy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is useless to "chiong" towards digital economy if our people are not ready for it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must make sure that our people are able to benefit from this transformation and not be left behind.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Currently, we have a strong curriculum in mathematics and science from primary to pre-university level.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This must be preserved even while we adapt the pedagogy to suit the needs of different learners at each level.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must equip even those students who may not have the aptitude for these subjects with a reasonable foundation, to prepare them for future job opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And for those who can stretch a little more, supplement their science and mathematics learning with coding skills, as part of building the STEM foundation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many countries have introduced coding lessons to their curricula.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Examples include Israel, New Zealand, Australia, Denmark and some German states.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our workforce needs to have ready access to courses and training opportunities with constantly refreshed curriculum.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: SkillsFuture must continue to be an important upgrading asset for workers, along apprenticeship and practical work opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We also need to pay attention to helping women to achieve their fullest potential.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Digital fluency not only opens up new career opportunities for women in the digital age but also enables women to exploit smart solutions that help to create capacity and options.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With the right smart solutions, women and men can remotely manage situations and monitor their young and old at home while they are at work.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Smart solutions can allow women to work productively and respond efficiently even if they have to be away from their offices, thereby enabling flexible work.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Digital platforms can allow women to exchange useful information and create job opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: E-commerce platforms, for example, can help stay-at-home caregivers monetise their skills or overcome resource constraints in starting their businesses and, in the process, maintain financial independence, stay plugged in while continuing to care for their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Women can also make use of these platforms to raise funds, find mentors and network with other women entrepreneurs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to help our elderly to be digitally ready.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Whilst future generations of elderly will be better educated and tech-savvy, we must not neglect our current generation of seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need Smart Seniors for a Smart Nation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to harness technology to supplement our shortage of eldercare manpower and help more seniors live independently in the comfort of their own homes and community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to harness technology to help them stay connected to news and information, to support networks, to friends and families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To do all these, it is important to ensure that they are digitally ready.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Digital readiness is the very first step and a critical enabler for our elderly to fully exploit the benefits of technology.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Engendering a smart nation need not only be the responsibility of the Government or big enterprises.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Local communities can also contribute since we know local needs and gaps best.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should allow innovative ideas, which may be simple ideas with simple benefits, to flourish.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These help to create a conducive environment, familiarity and a positive attitude in the community towards digital solutions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In MacPherson, we have quite a few ideas that can help the elderly and families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But to do so costs money which we, as local grassroots, can ill-afford.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Current Government funding schemes do not cover digital project, at least not yet.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We also have aspirations to expand it to “game-fy” daily tasks to encourage active living and also enable predictive analyses of their overall well-being so that appropriate medical or social interventions can be introduced.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We had to raise funds and could only raise enough to do a watered-down version of what we had in mind.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We used the limited resources to build a minimum viable product.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Speaker, Sir, allow me to continue in Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, digital economy is the future trend.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The emergence of digital technology has brought about earth-shattering changes to modern lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Various mobile apps have greatly reduced the time spent on daily tasks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With the prevalence of smart phones, high-speed Internet, big data and artificial intelligence (AI), the digital economy has disrupted the old way of life and doing business.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many countries in the world are promoting the development of digital economy so as to bring convenience to their people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As an international financial centre and information hub, Singapore cannot neglect this trend.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In order to ensure that all our citizens can share in the benefits of digital economy, we have to make sure that all can board this express train and be connected to this mega trend.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In terms of technology and innovation, Singapore is ahead of many countries and holds first-mover advantage.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With the popularisation of smart phones, people can access the latest shopping and transport information and be connected to many resources and services through mobile apps.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With the touch of a finger, we can order food and buy things online and have them delivered to our doorstep.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With these apps, family members can monitor the health conditions of their elders and ensure their safety.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, technology, when properly harnessed, can bring about many benefits to the country’s economy and people’s lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In particular, we need to pay attention to our elders.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many of them are trying to catch up with the pace of digital economy, but many are hesitant towards learning these new technologies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government must do more to create a more pro-elderly learning environment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should use pro-elderly designs to encourage them to seize these opportunities and master digital skills, so that they will not be left behind in a rapidly changing society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Regions around us are quickly catching up in developing the digital economy, in terms of e-commerce and universal digitalisation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must continue to innovate to keep up with the times.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In English): This next transformation will not be an easy journey.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It has to be a national effort, not just the work of the Government.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It will require all Singaporeans to contribute actively with their ideas and efforts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Whether we are able to do so successfully and quickly is, therefore, a matter of public interest affecting our economy and businesses, the lives of Singaporeans, as well as our international reputation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I urge all Singaporeans to work together, to make sure that this national effort succeeds.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are all well aware that the world is undergoing unprecedented rapid technological changes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The fast pace of change is having a major impact on how we work and earn a living.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For Singapore to be competitive in this new arena, we need to be hungry.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Businesses will need to transform, our towkays will need to change their mindsets, and our workers will need to be eager to learn, to upskill and continually upgrade.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These critical strategies have been mentioned numerous times, but we are not acting on it fast enough.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We need to improve our workers’ productivity and employability skills.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Companies and workers must embark on this transformation journey now.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Labour Movement will push the transformation agenda by working even closer with the Government and businesses, and this is how the Labour Movement will be here to assist.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Labour Movement will fully support employers in the transformation of their businesses because it will ultimately benefit our workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Businesses will have to play a leadership role by leveraging technologies to transform their businesses.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our workers must support businesses by working smarter and becoming more productive.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Labour Movement will support workers who are willing to improve and upskill.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Currently, we have high employment and our workers have enjoyed real income growth over the years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: So, when businesses do well, our workers will benefit, have better wages and higher quality of living.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But in this short time that I have joined the Labour Movement, there are concerns on the ground.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And I would now like to touch on some of these concerns.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: There are worries about buying a home, their retirement savings, healthcare costs and having enough for their children’s education.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They sometimes feel that no matter how hard they work, these needs may not always be adequately addressed.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These concerns are all about the rising cost of living.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In a conversation I had with a very close relative, he pointed out to me that coffee prices have been increasing and are set to increase again.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: He said that while the price increase may only be 10 cents, the number of increases has been too often and these expenses have added up over time.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Union leaders on the ground often share similar concerns as well.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They are on the shop floor and daily expenses are always on the radar screen of our workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Many older Singaporeans are worried about rising healthcare costs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Government has introduced numerous policies like the 3M framework of MediSave, MediShield Life and MediFund to assist Singaporeans in their healthcare needs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Nevertheless, Singaporeans still have concerns and I can understand their anxieties.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For our workers, retirement adequacy is another anxiety.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They are worried that their Central Provident Fund (CPF) savings will not be enough for them to enjoy the quality of life they seek once they stop working.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: More crucially, if they lose their jobs unexpectedly before retirement, will they have enough savings?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Can they be assured that if they work hard, save and contribute to their CPF savings, their basic needs of housing, children’s education, healthcare and retirement will continue to be taken care of?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Singaporeans now have longer life expectancy and the issue of retirement adequacy will become more and more pressing.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is reasonable for Singaporeans who are working hard to have such concerns.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: How do we ensure we uphold the principles of meritocracy and equality that have brought Singapore to where we are today?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Labour Movement believes that the best way to improve the lives of our workers is gainful employment, in good jobs and good wages.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We need employers to maintain a nimble mindset and workers to help themselves by upgrading their work skills.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Both employees and employers must stay relevant in the evolving business environment.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is the best solution because wages can only increase with productivity gains.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Real wage increase is necessary to keep up with inflation to cope with the cost of living.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Weishen Industrial Services, a cleaning company, is an example.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The company embarked on the Inclusive Growth Programme and was able to exploit driverless ecobot technology.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The employers deployed this new technology and were able to redeploy their employees to higher value roles with corresponding higher pay.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But I know workers on the ground have experienced growth differently: some have done a little better, others have progressed a little slower.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is the reality when technology disrupts businesses.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: While we push to transform, I am particularly concerned with three groups of workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The PWM has done much to alleviate hardship of low-wage workers in the cleaning, security and landscape sectors.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, there are other sectors with low wage growth.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For them, I propose that we expand the use of the Inclusive Growth Programme and find pathways forward to support more workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I note that the Tripartite Workgroup for Freelancers and Self-employed is currently working in this area, and we are keenly watching their progress.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Another group of workers that I am concerned about is our mature workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Recently, I chatted with two uncles, both of whom are 75 years old, at the curbside in Changi Airport Terminal 2.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They were sprightly and fit, and while they chatted with me, they told me that they appreciated that they could still contribute, work and earn a living.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: So, on one hand, I was happy to see them healthy and active but, on the other, I wonder if provisions for their retirement are adequate when they are no longer fit to work or when they finally choose to retire.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, being part of the Baby Boomer generation, they also wondered if they could be better protected with more assured terms of employment.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They cited that we can legislate retirement and re-employment ages but, on the ground, we cannot legislate mindsets.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The real question here, therefore, is whether employers are willing to employ senior workers instead of having the fixed mindset that these workers are a burden, more expensive and untrainable.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Union leaders and I are worried for this group of workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For many of them, the job is essential.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Just like us, they have expenses, mortgages and dependants relying on them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Tapping on WorkPro, the Labour Movement continues to work with companies to implement age-management policies and practices and redesign their workplaces.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In addition, through the Special Employment Credit, the Government subsidises employers the net cost of employing mature workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We should empower the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) to look into this area of concern and do more.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The third group I would like to talk about are the middle-aged/middle-income workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They may be currently employed, but their earnings are just sufficient to meet their needs and their income growth is not high.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is because some of their skillsets are diminishing in demand, or they lack the opportunities to progress.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: There are currently several Government schemes outlined for this group of middle-income workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, similar to mature workers, the entrenched mindset against hiring middle-aged workers is worrying.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Labour Movement will need more support from the Government and business leaders to redesign jobs, encourage our workers to upskill, stay relevant so that they can progress in their careers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will continue to look into career-matching programmes, programmes to change employers' and workers’ mindsets; and for the displaced middle-aged workers, work towards giving them a second chance at employment.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As Minister Josephine Teo and I chatted, she told me that employers want “plug and play” workers, but the reality is that workers need to “plug, train and then play”.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Beyond addressing the current concerns, we also want to help all working people seize opportunities that the future will bring.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Hence, I would like to touch on the ITMs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The best way forward for the Labour Movement is to operationalise the ITMs and continue to work with the tripartite partners to translate these ITMs into tangible outcomes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We need to make ITMs real for all our working people, whether it is a professional, manager or executive (PME) in the financial sector or the worker on the shop floor, by distilling the ITMs into actionable, purposeful training programmes for them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For example, in the aviation sector where I had interaction when I was in the Ministry of Transport, SIA Engineering, together with union representatives, are empowering 3,000 workers with the skills to handle technology in maintenance operations, including real-time data to facilitate more productive work.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: With this outcome, workers can look forward to better jobs and future wage increases.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We need to stay relevant by making lifelong learning a habit.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The concept of lifelong learning is not new.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Chinese saying of “活到老, 学到老” is a teaching dating back thousands of years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: By embracing lifelong learning and making it a habit, we will be better prepared for future challenges.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: There will always be challenges along the way and even hardship.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But if we work smart and stay ahead of the curve, we will find solutions, progress and forge a better living for ourselves.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: (In Mandarin):  : Globalisation, the use of technology and digitalisation, all these changes impact not only our businesses but our workers as well.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The next phase will be the implementation and operationalisation of these ITMs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our economy, businesses and jobs are undergoing transformation.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) is helping our workers to do so by simplifying the complex and making the tough easy for them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: There are macro-level policies to achieve long-term goals, strategies to deal with future challenges and a list of future opportunities.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The information is too complex and high level for many workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We must simplify and personalise it for them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: What our workers want to know are: will I be affected?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: After we help our workers understand how the changes will impact them, the next step is to help them adapt accordingly.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Workers want to change but they do not know what to do next: what skills do I lack?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: With so many training courses, which one is suitable for me?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I need to work and look after my family at the same time, how do I find the time and energy to go for training courses?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: No matter how things change, our ultimate goal and outcome must be better jobs and lives for our workers, and a brighter future for our people.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: (In English): My Speaker, we need to take better care of our low-wage workers, our middle-aged/middle-income workers, as well as our mature workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But needless to say, solutions are only possible if employers, workers and Government work together.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is critical that our businesses take the lead and do the right thing, that when our workers do their best, remember to share the gains with their workers and give them what is fairly theirs when their businesses thrive.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Help will always be available to those who need it, whether for employment, housing or education.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Those who have done better should reach out to the less fortunate.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In our Singapore, no one, no one should be left behind.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We hear you; we are with you; and together, we can make it real for Singapore, and for all our working people.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Last two weeks, our Labour Movement celebrated Labour Day 2018 with the annual May Day Rally and May Day Awards, paying tribute to those who have worked hard to make Singapore a successful nation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is poignant that 58 years ago, in his inaugural May Day Rally speech in 1960, the same year that Labour Day was gazetted as a public holiday, the then Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew announced that the Government was committed to the welfare of the workers in forging ahead on industrial expansion and nation-building.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am heartened that the Government of today is committed to doing the same for Singapore and our working people.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the 1960s, Singapore was a young nation facing mounting internal and external challenges on various fronts while trying to find our footing to be economically viable and provide for our people.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The immediate economic tasks facing the Government then were to restructure the economy and to alleviate the unemployment problem.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The industrialisation programme was put in place to create employment opportunities and to provide a new diversified economic base to replace our entrepot trade.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: NTUC also undertook efforts to modernise the Labour Movement and build strong tripartite ties to arrive at win-win outcomes for employers and workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The hard work of our Pioneer leaders and Pioneer Generation has paid off and has brought Singapore to where we are today.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As the generations who have come after and have had the good fortune of sitting under the peaceful shade of our Pioneer Generation’s tree of labour and enjoying the fruits born of their grit and determination, we must be prepared to do the same for the next generations of Singaporeans to come.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Today, we are facing the headwinds of a rapidly changing economy and changing global order.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While we are no longer a nation in our infancy, our Government of today must possess the same pioneering spirit of those who have come before to enable Singapore to advance to the next plane of growth, break through new ground and conquer new frontiers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As a nation, Singaporeans must also draw on the pioneering spirit in their blood to chart new courses and embark on new opportunities in this Brave New World.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Of pressing concern to me is the need to raise the urgency to future-proof our business and our workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As stakeholders, the Government, employers and workers need to talk about how job roles will be transforming and raise awareness of the job roles and skills which are likely to be at risk of displacement due to technological advancements and global competition.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These potentially at-risk jobs will not be gone tomorrow just because of these conversations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As stakeholders, we need to use this time, while our workers are still employed, to upskill and prepare our workforce for the higher value jobs of the future so that when their current jobs are eliminated, they can still remain employed and employable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We can use this time to discuss and influence the adoption of progressive employment practices in times of change.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While no one can definitively predict the future, we can and should do what we can today to prepare ourselves for what is foreseeable on the horizon.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
