text: In order to raise awareness and urge people to take action, our leaders must have the moral courage to talk about such issues and be open to sharing information and co-creating solutions with partners to ensure speed to market.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I believe that there is value in providing such frameworks of understanding for our people and to strengthen Singapore's brand as a trusted economy and I continue to call on this Government to look into these suggestions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While inertia has oftentimes been attributed to the mindset of employers and employees in preparing for change, in the design of our policies and interventions, we must be cognisant of underlying concerns and address them in a targeted manner to move the needle in transformation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There is no one-size-fit-all solution and nuanced collective action has to be designed thoughtfully for the intended audience.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Future Jobs, Skills and Training capability at NTUC has developed a framework for collaborative action to change mindsets towards future-skilling.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Stakeholders can work together at each stage of the framework to leverage their respective strengths for greater reach and effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These include efforts to address information asymmetry, raise awareness, inspire action, provide holistic support, create positive feedback loops and encourage the flourishing of change-agent mentality.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Participants at the Forum also participated in a dialogue with our NTUC Secretary-General on topics concerning future jobs, skills and training.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Besides ensuring that our people have the means to fill their bellies, we must not forget about our people's desire to fill their hearts and pursue their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is the additional challenge in nation-building that our Government faces today.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While our Pioneer Generation leaders were focused on ensuring Singapore's survival, today, it is also about the flourishing and continued sustainable growth of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Concerted efforts need to be taken to integrate diversity, encourage inclusiveness, mitigate the effects of social stratification and improve social mobility and "liveability" for our people.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):  : The 23 ITMs have already mapped out the future economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We must work hard and build a better future together.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am most concerned with whether businesses and workers can cope with the challenges of the future economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, when dealing with complicated working environment, there is no one-size-fits-all solution.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We have to customise our solutions to meet the different needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I urge our 4G leaders to not only meet the material needs of Singaporeans, but also their hopes and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Government must make our society more inclusive and increase social mobility.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I hope people from all walks of life can do their part, move with the times and build a better future together.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In English): To conclude, against a rapidly changing landscape, evolving needs and limited resources, we must ask ourselves what guides and orientates us in a spinning world – what is Singapore's True North?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What core values do we hold steadfast to in this new era?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What makes Singapore our home in a highly-globalised and migratory world?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What ignites the fire in our people's bellies to take Singapore to greater heights?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In spite of all the uncertainties, I am optimistic about Singapore's future and I believe we can stand strong together against adversity and find the answers to these questions together.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Through the sharing of the Government's agenda in the President’s Address, I am heartened that this Government is committed to refining our vision for the future and in leading us to build Our Singapore, Our Future as one united people.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In his Ministry's Addendum to the President's Address, Minister for Transport Mr Khaw Boon Wan pointed out that good connectivity bolsters Singapore's vibrant economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Regardless of whether the Government may think that the worst of our rail unreliability and frequent train disruptions may be over, we must not forget the lessons learnt from the poor maintenance management, the poor planning of our rail system and infrastructure, or the impact of train delays on our economy and commuters.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even as the Government plans and brings about the expansion of our rail network, I hope the same lessons will provide a firm reminder to get the planning, equipment, infrastructure and even the ethos right from the beginning.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps the Government can share more details on the new MRT lines that will assure the public that the designs for the new lines, trains and stations will be forward-thinking and will cater for the projected increase in our population and commuter traffic load in the next 50 years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Minister Khaw Boon Wan also stated in the Addendum to the President's Address that we will develop a workforce of capable engineers and technicians.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope that with the Rail Academy as well as good human resource (HR) practices, we will not merely develop a strong team of capable and experienced engineers and technicians in the years to come, but we should also aim to develop good managers in different aspects of rail operations and management, including senior management.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The President mentioned the building of the Kuala Lumpur-Singapore High Speed Rail (HSR) and the Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) in her speech.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope that we can start the building and operation of the HSR and RTS with the right focus on sound design, engineering and operating system as well as a good maintenance regime supported by a professional and well-trained staff working with the right corporate culture and avoid the design and maintenance issues we have seen with our MRT system and trains.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The drive towards a Car-Lite city and Active Mobility for the First-and-Last-Mile Connectivity for public transport has led to the Government's focus on the use of shared bicycles and personal mobility devices (PMDs).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The popular use of shared bicycles brought with it more problems as we have heard in the House in the past year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Government truly thinks that a Car-Lite city as well as First-and-Last-Mile Connectivity are important for the future of our transportation system and will, in the President's words, "play an important part in a metropolis that embraces the future", I feel that this is a critical moment for us to get it right as far as the safe and proper operation of transport modes for First-and-Last-Mile Connectivity is concerned.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Government wants to promote PMDs and bicycles for First-and-Last-Mile Connectivity, it needs to really focus on building a good riding culture, something that is really lacking at the moment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we have to go about setting right this riding culture now and, if not, we may miss the boat again.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is why I am raising this issue here today.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Think of the accidents or near-misses involving PMD users and pedestrians, think of people walking along footpaths or walkways being startled by inconsiderate cyclists or PMD users, think of cyclists not stopping at red lights or cycling against the traffic, think of PMDs using roads illegally.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In recent months, we have seen much publicity of the Land Transport Authority (LTA) taking various enforcement actions against errant use of PMDs, and e-scooters being impounded for illegal use on roads or illegal bicycles being impounded.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While enforcement is important, it alone may have limited effect in creating a good riding culture.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Only people who are caught are punished and sent for safe-riding courses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Or in breach of our laws and get away with it as our law enforcement officers cannot be everywhere?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Or those who ride inconsiderately, frightening or inconveniencing others, for example riding close to pedestrians or not giving way to those in need like the elderly or those with mobility issues?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Similarly, the Government's plans to register all PMD users will not automatically create a good riding culture among users.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Like current enforcement efforts, it may, to some extent, deter reckless and illegal riding at best.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Deterring reckless or illegal riding alone can be our only end-goals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Inconsistent enforcement against errant cyclists remains an issue.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We still see, for example, cyclists cycling against the flow of traffic or beating red lights, but there is relatively little enforcement compared to PMDs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the proliferation of shared bicycles and by allowing shared use of footpaths and walkways, we need to sort out our poor cycling culture, too.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to evaluate how effective our public education efforts in promoting legal, safe and considerate use of PMDs or bicycles are to the majority of our people.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Public education is important and must go hand in hand with consistent enforcement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the moment, education only reaches directly to limited groups of people, for example, students, offenders, foreign workers or people who voluntarily sign up for such classes or read up on such literature online.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ultimately, how is the Government going to ensure that the ethos of safe riding and good riding etiquette can be understood by all, regardless of riders or pedestrians?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Riders and pedestrians seem to have the mindset that they each have the right of way in footpaths and walkways and even on public connectors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To change this mindset, there is more for us to do to educate the public beyond what is being done.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Government plan to expand its public education programme to reach out to the masses beyond its current efforts?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will end this part of my speech with a suggestion to the Government to improve the situation for safe and considerate use of PMDs, in particular.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think this is still an unsafe speed and I would invite the Minister to take a walk with me along a busy park connector and experience whether it is safe for PMDs to travel at 25 km per hour in a park connector, especially during peak periods.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, many PMD users exceed 15 km per hour even on footpaths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The President said that we will invest in infrastructure to keep Singapore as one of the best-connected cities in Asia, citing our Changi Airport expansion as an example.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Changi Airport expansion is exciting and promises much about staying ahead as an international and regional air hub.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, the President also said that we want to live in a world-class city and an endearing home that is clean, green and efficient, fun and connected.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Minister for the Environment and Water Resources Mr Masagos said in the Ministry's Addendum to the President's Address that since Independence, we have pursued our vision of a liveable and sustainable Singapore, balancing environmental protection and economic growth.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our homes, our living spaces and our green spaces are never far from our offices, industrial premises, ports and airport.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, within a few kilometres from Changi Airport, you will start hitting private residential estates, condos and HDB estates in Changi, Tampines, Simei, Pasir Ris.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The popular Changi Beach is literally just at the doorstep of one of the airport's runways.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Recently, I raised some concerns in Parliament about noise and air pollution arising from expansion of Changi Airport and the possible impact of Singaporeans near the airport and on the eastern and north-eastern parts of Singapore, pointing to the aircraft as well as vehicular traffic emissions associated with the airport.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I mentioned that the toxic emissions associated with airports included various pollutants, including carbon emissions, which were the subject of the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), a scheme implemented under the Aviation (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill in March this year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: CORSIA is the carbon offset scheme; it does not mean zero carbon emissions from the aircraft plying Changi.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With a bigger airport and more flights, there will be more emissions and, hence, more pollution from the various toxic emissions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also asked for the present levels of various pollutants as well as the projected levels when Terminal 5 opens.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Environmental pollution is a key consideration when building airports or airport extensions or runways in many developed countries.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A metropolis that embraces the future must be one where developments and progress must go hand in hand with good management of our environment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In closing, let me end with some brief words on the third category of transport – maritime.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I declare my interest as a shipping lawyer and a member of the maritime community.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I spoke of my concerns for the shipping industry in my speech during the Budget Debate this year and I would like to reiterate my call for the Government to focus on helping our local shipping SMEs, as opposed to Government-Linked Companies (GLCs) or the foreign-owned businesses operating in and from Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In her Address, Mdm President spoke about the need to develop a vibrant economy with more opportunities for our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore is right in the middle of her next big economic transition.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Much effort has gone into developing the ITMs, which form an important part of the Government’s strategy to address each industry’s changing needs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But what do these ITMs mean for our workers?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many workers tell me they want to be part of the transformation but are asking how they would be impacted.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Thus, the key imperative now is for the Government to work with its tripartite partners to articulate the roadmaps in a manner that is compelling to our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As Minister Ng Chee Meng put it earlier, "we need to make the 23 ITMs real for all our workers".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is no surprise that many are concerned with the security of their job, as the future is filled with inevitable disruptions to the status quo.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For instance, drivers face disruption from autonomous vehicles, and workers in a manufacturing plant face disruption from ever increasing automation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My interaction with workers reveals three common fears.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Process automation and mechanisation have made many manual jobs redundant, and many worry that their jobs would be the next to go.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, some fear losing their jobs in the near future as digitisation and new technologies continue to disrupt traditional industries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, even as our workers grapple with the uncertainty of their own future, they fear that their children would not be able to get a good job in the new economy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These are key questions that we need to answer as we move to operationalise the ITMs, cluster by cluster, sector by sector, company by company, worker by worker.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to distil each ITM and articulate what it means to the individual worker.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need every worker to understand where the future lies for him or her.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the same time, we need to excite the next generation of workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But it is not all doom and gloom on the ground.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In my visits, I have seen many success stories of workers who have not been afraid of new technologies and automation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Rather, they work with the new machines enthusiastically and take charge of transforming their own jobs before they are made redundant.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mui Sin started as a Machine Operator in 1980 with electrical equipment provider Yokogawa.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: She performs repetitive tasks along with many others in a production line back then in the 1980s.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Throughout her career, Mui Sin continued to upskill herself, going for training, first to become a Store Assistant, and attending information technology (IT) courses supported by her supervisors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, Mui Sin is a Production Planner, managing several vital computer systems to ensure manufacturing schedules in Singapore and Batam are in order.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Her work impacts hundreds of production operators, vendors and customers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Yap Kok Keong is another good example of how one can continue to keep pace with technological advancements through continuous learning.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Kok Keong joined Panasonic Appliances Refrigeration Devices Singapore in 1987 as a technician.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Throughout his career, Kok Keong attended many training courses to upgrade himself both in technical skills as well as management know-how.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, Kok Keong is a Factory Manager and supervises 120 workers on the production floor.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But he told me his learning cannot stop.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Just last month, Kok Keong attended a SkillsFuture course on Computer-Aided Design and Additive Manufacturing to better prepare himself for the Industrial 4.0 transformation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, both Mui Sin and Kok Keong are earning better wages because they have taken on higher value jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But what we can learn from both of them is their attitude towards lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is not easy to go for training while having to worry about your work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, I must also commend their companies for providing the necessary support to help their employees upskill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This spirit is crucial as Singapore transitions towards the future economy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, let me touch on the need to get our workers ready for tomorrow’s jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, we have many programmes and initiatives to match today’s unemployed to today’s jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More needs to be done to prepare our current and future workforce to take on tomorrow’s jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, workers, companies and the Government must Re-imagine the future of work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is especially important as automation, AI and robotics become more mainstream and threaten to displace the jobs of today.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How would jobs look like in the next 10 to 20 years, with AI possibly at the centre of most of our industries?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We will have to re-imagine the future in order to disrupt ourselves before we get disrupted.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, we need to Re-design our jobs, our work processes and our business models to be future-ready.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The ITMs provide a strategic plan for the industry but they do not tell the individual company and the individual worker what they need to do specifically.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This may be why not many workers are excited by the ITM right now.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some tell me the ITMs are too “cheem”, too stratospheric.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But not Mr Fang Chin Poh who works for SBS Transit.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chin Poh started his career as a bus conductor 37 years ago.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When the bus company adopted the one-man operation bus service in the 1980s, his job disappeared but he went for training and he became a bus captain.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, Chin Poh is a Chief Bus Captain.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As the General Secretary for the National Transport Workers’ Union, Chin Poh was involved in the development of the Land Transport ITM.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He tells me that when autonomous buses do ply our streets one day, he wants to become a fleet commander, overseeing the buses remotely from a central command.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chin Poh can articulate so because we have started to re-imagine the future of work in the public transport industry and to re-design today’s jobs for tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But Chin Poh and many others would need to reskill to take on new and future jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Reskilling and upskilling our existing workforce are, therefore, extremely critical.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Technology can help play a part in making learning easy and convenient.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Now, we can learn while on the go.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When I take the public transport, I notice many commuters looking at their mobile phones throughout their journey.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the U-Leap app, you can now access useful training contents on your mobile phones.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Optimising current infrastructure can also make learning convenient for our citizens.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can we open the computer labs in our neighbourhood schools for night classes on digital skills?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the same time as we do that, can we also open the schools' sports facilities for use by the community?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This way, we can keep fit and healthy in both mind and body, without having to invest in new infrastructures.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In time, AI will be at the core of many of our industries and we need to prepare our young for such a future.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But our young cannot be contented to grow up to just be consumers of these AI products.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must discover and nurture those with the potential to invent and create these products for the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is, therefore, crucial for schools to expose our children to statistics, coding, IT courses and IT programmes at a very early age, and to do so in a manner that is fun to learn.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Since our Independence, Singapore has always managed to overcome the economic challenges thrown our way time and again.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Much can be attributed to our strong tripartite partnership among the Government, the Labour Movement and employers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Twenty-nine months ago, in this Chamber, I devoted my entire maiden speech to the need for us to continue to invest in tripartism, the magic ingredient for Singapore's enduring competitive economic advantage.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am, therefore, glad that Mdm President, too, highlighted the importance of tripartism in her maiden Address last week.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am confident that as long as we continue to work together as we have always done, we can turn fear into strength.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As long as we work together and stay united, we can ensure that Singapore will continue to remain a land of opportunities for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I agree with Minister Chan Chun Sing who said yesterday that our challenges do not define us; our responses do.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, the future is in our own hands.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We have a Government that upholds the rule of law, a well-educated and skilled workforce that upholds meritocracy, a cohesive society cemented by multiracial, multilingual and multi-religious beliefs and values.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In the last 50 over years, we have developed as a nation comparable to any First World Nation, but we should not rest on our laurels.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Unions in other countries tell us that, in their circumstances, it is not so easy to replicate or emulate Singapore's successful formula.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In 1996, Mr Lee Kuan Yew, our Founding Father had said, and I quote, "Singapore has enjoyed harmonious industrial relations for almost three decades because of the successful tripartite cooperation among employers, unions and the Government.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This has been a major achievement in our industrial relations – a complete turnaround from the bitter, confrontational practices of trade unions in the 1950s and 1960s." We have to ensure that the younger generation and workforce understand the importance of tripartism, as well as bipartism relations at the company level, too.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I am very concerned over the fact that many of our working population do not understand or perhaps appreciate the history behind our successful economic development and growth.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Over the last five years, I have been teaching tripartism and industrial relations to aspiring younger working cohorts doing their degree programme in HR.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I am, indeed, surprised and amazed that through the years, I have only come across a handful of working cohorts who understood the working mechanism under tripartism and even the National Wages Council (NWC) recommendations.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We are not talking about ordinary workers with minimal education, but graduates and those doing postgraduate studies.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If we place much importance on industrial peace and justice, it is about time that the whole of the Government, employers and working people understand and cherish this national treasure.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There have been several calls to have this as a main core curriculum in school but, beyond this, we need to do more at every level to ensure that this is entrenched into every generation of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: HR professionals are the key to ensuring the sustainability of bipartite relationships at workplaces.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Government officials and employer representatives are the keys to the sustainability of tripartism.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Strong tripartism and bipartism should also help Singaporeans move towards social equality.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: SkillsFuture initiatives and lifelong learning can only be sustained if employers partake in the responsibility of training their workers, employees embrace change as a constant, are willing to learn, unlearn and relearn without having to chase after academic qualifications alone.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Government also should provide a conducive environment for all forms of learning to take place, be it online learning, bite-sized training, on-the-job training or structured training.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There must be regular engagement at bipartite levels and with workers to know what are the jobs at risk and what are the jobs of the future.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We are seeing incoherent speed of transformation happening in each of the industries.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How does it translate to workers on the ground, and if it translates into meaningful outcomes of better skill, better jobs and better career with better wages?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) has some of the indicators.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: But to be holistic, we should not only track but form tripartite task forces in each of the sectors to drill down and improve the outcome in each of these aspects with clear deliverables.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Though we pride ourselves to be an envy of the world, but we are not quite there yet when it comes to women in the workforce.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In this Chamber, many of my fellow Members of Parliament have spoken on the challenges that women are faced with during the first half of the Parliament for this term.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to further reiterate what I had mentioned during the last Budget speech on working women issues.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I am, indeed, heartened by the Minister for Manpower Josephine Teo for initiating several initiatives.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Josephine Teo has been a strong advocate on flexible work arrangements (FWAs).

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I applaud the success so far even though the adoption of Tripartite Standards on FWAs has been gradual.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I urge MOM to closely monitor the labour participation of women in the respective industries.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The assumption is that there are more women in the service sector than any other sectors.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: But we need to post-mortem those issues and strategise tripartite initiatives at the sectoral level to further improve the overall labour participation rate across Singapore.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, in recent years, the Ministry of Health (MOH) has done pretty well in attracting non-practising nurses and stay-at-home women back to nursing.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I must thank Minister Josephine Teo and her Ministry for organising the Adapt and Grow appreciation lunch last Saturday.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It was attended by employers, career coaches as well as clients or recipients of jobs and their families, each to share their journey.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Several recipients of jobs shared their emotional stories of being unemployed and the joy of being gainfully employed.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is, indeed, heartwarming to hear some of these stories.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, these are inspirational anecdotal stories that we need to compile and share with more workers or potential workers, so that they do not lose sight of resilience and the hope for a bright light at the end of the tunnel when one loses a job.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I was glad to see several women who came forward to share their stories, one of whom was inclined to work because of employers' support for FWAs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: A colleague of mine cynically commented that Singapore is very advanced in many ways and with laws on bicycle parking and provision of parking spaces but is yet to have a provision for dedicated enclosures for lactating mothers at the workplace or in shared office buildings.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It can start with new buildings, but we have yet to see any progress in this area.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: To be truly inclusive at all levels of the employment and economic fronts, we need both tripartism and bipartism that thrive at all levels.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need the political will to move things for the long-term and greater good of all working people, including women.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I am confident this will happen expeditiously in the good hands of our woman Minister for Manpower Mrs Josephine Teo.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to take this opportunity to thank Mr Lim Swee Say, the former Minister for Manpower, for truly walking the talk of tripartism, bringing about incredible positive change for the working people and for jobseekers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Through implementing various measures and innovative initiatives, this had resulted in a win-win outcome for many working people and employers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Lim Swee Say, I would like to thank you for that.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I quote, "In Government, I have never forgotten that it is in the interest of the workers and their unions that we must strive for growth and development.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In other words, growth is meaningless unless it is shared by workers, shared not only in wage increases but indirectly in better homes, better schools, better hospitals, better playing fields and, generally, a healthier environment for families to bring up their children." In short, it is about ensuring workers have good jobs with fair and progressive wages for us to aspire towards greater social equality.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The labour landscape has changed tremendously ever since our late Minister Mentor first helped the group of workers from the postal services in 1952.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are now different types of employment, from the traditional employer-employee relationships to the self-employed freelancers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Nevertheless, every worker aspires to the same – Better Jobs, Better Pay and Better Lives.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is only possible if economic gains from our growth are shared fairly with the workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What would then be a good indicator that gains are being shared with low-wage workers as well?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe a good indicator would be a narrowing gap in real income inequality.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a unionist, I see this as one of the key defining challenges for our 4G leaders as they confront the question posed by our President, “What is next for Singapore?” Without a doubt, rising inequality is “a clear and present danger” to any government of the day.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Let us heed our President's rallying call to “tackle inequality vigorously.” For a start, in helping better the life of low-wage workers to be "betterer", we must start by doing things differently.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Doing different things differently then must stem from every stakeholder thinking differently when they are looking at trying to address income inequality.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Moving ahead, our 4G leaders must continually think differently to be able to catch and ride on the next "S" curve of better income growth for low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But to think differently, we must first question our assumptions behind the current policies on low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are the assumptions still valid, given current circumstances?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Only then, can we have the mindset change required to come up with better policies that can make a difference to the lives of low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Only then can our 4G leaders make bold changes and not, as what our President said, “be content to tweak things at the margins.” Mr Speaker, what can the Government do?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The question is, "What’s next?" While the term of this tripartite committee has ended, we now have many sectoral ITM committees.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is important, otherwise we place our vulnerable workers at risk of having the progress made to better their lives amount to nothing in the face of inflation and technological disruptions.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For a start, each ITM committee could start by contextualising the various ITMs to see how they can help the vulnerable workers to have the means to make a future living.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Each ITM must talk of skills that will also be attainable by the spectrum ends of society, such as the aged or those with low educational qualifications.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we ensure that they also receive the necessary skills required under the ITMs?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can they attain the necessary help for them to have a job more befitting of their skills and qualifications?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we help those at risk of being displaced adapt to the changing job market while still working at their present job?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I understand that, right now, we may not have all the answers to these difficult and inconvenient questions but, if each ITM committee spends time to focus on the vulnerable workers, then we are taking the right step into the future where no Singaporean will be left behind.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Likewise, questioning assumptions must also involve the employers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Conventional wisdom dictates that you try to bid for contracts by cutting costs or keeping labour costs to a minimum so that you can win the contract or increase profit margins.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, is that really wisdom in this time and age?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In 2015, Forbes released an article discussing how some companies, such as Gap, Starbucks and Walmart, are pushing their revenue to the next level.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was not aggressive marketing, nor was it ingenious product innovation.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was something much simpler, and one that many of our companies can adopt as well.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was simply living up to a sense of social responsibility to be fair and treat workers, especially the rank-and-file workers, better.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These progressive companies went beyond the idea that only a token pay rise is needed to increase the morale of their workers within their companies.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Instead, they started to treat their employees better, like giving better pay packages, generous worker benefits and creating a more positive work environment.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When workers are happy at work, they become walking ambassadors for these companies, often going beyond the call of service to do a good job.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are smiling at work, and customers begin to believe in not just the companies, but also the workers as well.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the companies I cited have shown, we need to create a new work culture among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have always taken pride in showing that Singaporeans are some of the most productive and highly skilled workers in the world.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yet, reports on aspects, such as happiness and work-life balance, always seem to shed a different light.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To me, this is a sign that there is, indeed, a need for change.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When companies do not pay workers enough, everyone pretends they are working.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are not willing to ensure that jobs are carried out as they should be.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Service providers are then forced to cut corners.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It creates a vicious cycle that has one simple flaw – their mentality that labour, especially rank-and-file workers, is a cost that needs to be driven down.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, labour needs to be more than that.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It needs to be one where work is given the remuneration it is due, when the low-wage workers among us are not merely numbers in a contract but treated as human beings with dignity and with dreams for themselves.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Workers must have the right mindset to be ready for the future.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must be ever-ready and have the ability to adapt our skills to the changing needs of the workplace.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When I talk about skills upgrading for the future, some people have asked me, “What does it really mean?” Is it more certificates and attending courses?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a worker, when you upgrade yourself, it means that you can do more and do it better.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: New skills should help you take on new tasks and responsibilities you may not have been able to do before.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Productivity increases mean that you can now do more as one employee either by leveraging technology or simply doing things better.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is the future I see throughout our whole workforce, and especially so for the low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I want to see a world where they are now able to do more for themselves and be recognised for it.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Too many times have I heard an unfortunate comment that suggests that these people are to be blamed for their circumstances.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I tell them that they merely have not seen them fight to break out of it.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we worry about how Singaporeans will cope with this new future, it can be very easy to overlook people who are already struggling to cope with the current realities that they face.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is my dream that Singapore’s future is one that will benefit each Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Not just the privileged, not just the educated, but also the hands that have worked hard in manual labour to continue to build the Singapore that we know and love today.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):  : To help low-wage workers, we need to challenge our own assumptions when creating policies that are meant to help these workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such questioning is necessary in order to generate a different type of thinking so that we can create better policies or have better planning in order to help low-wage workers have a better life.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This has been proven to improve worker productivity and enabled workers to get better pay.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Perhaps, this is the best way for us to achieve greater social equality.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.05 pm.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.44 pm until 4.05 pm.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In Singapore today, women and men are a little more equal than in some other countries and more than we used to be.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our Global Gender Gap Report showed that we need some nudging along in two areas.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In particular, firstly, political empowerment; and secondly, representation at professional and managerial levels.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If gender equality is the goal, then I say, gender mainstreaming is the strategy for us.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Closing up the gender gap is really a journey that is happening and must continue to happen with the development and transformation of Singapore itself.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is also linked to our continued growth.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Gender mainstreaming is the push for meaningful inclusiveness of women in all areas – in every area, every sector, every arena.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It must not be an "add-on" just to please, or a "by the way" kind of thing.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How gender perspectives can be identified remains at the core.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Now, it is not uncommon for us to hear women, women groups and even men sometimes pushing for gender equality.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: When the focus is primarily technical or technological, people – both men and women – will not be adequately considered and it is challenging to include a gender perspective.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Even if we reach a 50:50 mark for gender representation between men and women, are we women – and men – going to be happier, more comfortable, well-adjusted in our jobs and our lives, and feel the fulfillment that we so desire?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Will our work be done when we reach this ratio?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Indeed, success to women, and men, have different definitions and connotations.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, let us be realistic and practical when handling the topic of gender equality.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, are enough women pushing the envelope and coming forth?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Where are the women at times when we call for them?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And sometimes, it can be challenging to get the numbers, especially in some areas, some disciplines, and you will have to agree with me on that.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Perhaps we need a new innovative way to engage and bring women forward.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Perhaps mainstreaming techniques need a review with fresh eyes.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Men or women, they must be of the right mindset to contribute and be a part of it all – part of nation-building and a part of Singapore.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is also because each person, each woman, has her own issues, considerations, priorities, work-life balance, family commitments, expectations, concerns about publicity, public scrutiny and other interests.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: As the fairer sex, let us also ask ourselves "are we hungry enough?" Or are we just pushing for the sake of pushing?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In pushing for gender equality, clarity, practicality and awareness of all the factors and confounding issues must be seriously considered for a balanced approach, with appropriateness.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Consider Scenario 1: an elderly lady, aged 78, had a fall at home.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The family called the emergency ambulance services, she was sent to the nearest acute care hospital and she sustained fractures in her hip region.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: She experienced a lot of pain and, therefore, movement was not possible, neither was ambulation.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: She was hospitalised and an orthopaedic surgeon became her primary doctor.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In the ward, she was referred to the physiotherapist for rehabilitation and exercises.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: She was also referred to the pain specialist for pain control, as oral medications were not sufficient and an endocrinologist was called in to help with her diabetes mellitus management, as her sugars were always high.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The medical officer also asked the dietitian to review her and talk to her family about her food intake and regulation to help with her sugar control.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: At admission, a blood test was done and it showed that she had renal impairment, so a renal physician was also called in to help.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: A nurse in the ward, while giving instructions, noted that her responses was slow and she kept forgetting.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, she highlighted this to the medical officer who then felt a psychiatric consult was necessary.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The psychiatrist came to see her and then he said that a geriatrician consultation will be appropriate because she had signs of dementia.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And after many, many consultations and a week in hospital, she was still there and yet there was still no outcome as to when she would be going home.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Her family was concerned about the medical costs and the bills and they were told to approach the Business Office to discuss this.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Now, let us move on to Scenario 2: a 78-year-old lady sustained a fall at home and landed on her back.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Her neighbours heard her and they called the neighbourhood family physician who came and visited her at home and discovered the tenderness in her hip.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They kept her daughter informed and updated her as she could not leave work.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Now, what will it take for us to move from a model of care in Scenario 1 to that of Scenario 2?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Scenario 1 is a hospital-based, hospital-centric, multidisciplinary model.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is also traditionally a very physician-centric model.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Scenario 2 is a more community-based model which is patient-centric, in alignment with the notion that the patient should always be at the heart of all that we do and in our care delivery.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Are we ready to challenge the status quo and ensure healthcare affordability for our population in the longer term?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Which model will be able to meet our needs and the expectations of our population?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Importantly, we have to review which model is economically sustainable in the medium to long term, especially with our rapidly ageing population.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Now, Sir, in our community-based care model, it must be evidence-based.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It must have platforms for efficient knowledge sharing, maintaining confidentiality, of course, and our National Electronic Health Record (NEHR) is a good basic start to this.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It must also have a means of educating and influencing mindsets of our population so that we can change their behaviour about healthcare choices.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Only with these can we have the connectivity and decentralisation of a community-based model of care, as in Scenario 2.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It will require care teams with credibility and the required training; reputable and strong institutional backing and support, such as from our academic medical centres, which are already in existence; a strong sense of ties inter-professionally; and efficient implementation, responsiveness and, of course, always, always a degree of flexibility.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Scenario 2 must be made up of interdependent individuals and groups united by a shared goal, with practical vertical as well as horizontal integration.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is a critical consideration for all of us, both healthcare providers and healthcare consumers, in Singapore.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is a decision we must make and accept together.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):  : Singapore's Malay/Muslim community continues to move forward, is more progressive now, with many more professionals, more students at the university and postgraduate levels.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There are more success stories and excellent achievements amongst our youths, entrepreneurs as well as our workers.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: All these take place within our unique society, in a multiracial and multi-religious Singapore, where the different races interact and integrate and which also requires us to have open minds and be big-hearted.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: These values are inculcated in our children from young when they are taught about meritocracy.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They want to stand shoulder to shoulder with the other races and communities and compete on the same issues.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Moving forward, there are several distinct challenges that I would like to share.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This happens not only in relation to the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS), but also in other aspects of Islam.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This also happens in other religions and has been a global trend.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Some think that this happens due to changing times, immigration and the spread of beliefs and ideologies.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Radicalism and extremism are thorns in our society’s side.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This wave is upon us and we must open our minds to keep pace with the times.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Students, our new and Pioneer workers, teachers, religious teachers and Malay/Muslim organisations must ride the Smart Nation wave as well as its accompanying initiatives.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Do not allow ourselves to be left behind.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Third, increase involvement in the areas of research, experimentation, mathematics and all the sciences.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: While there are those who have embarked in these fields, but the numbers are still very low.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Improvement in these areas can further strengthen our Malay/Muslim community’s strategic position in the nation.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Fourth, a deeper understanding on legal matters, legal rights and the law.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Many have made the wrong move or took the wrong path due to ignorance of this area.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Hence, moving forward, we must enhance education efforts and community dialogue sessions on these topics.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is essential for them to safeguard their rights and concerns.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Let us all make a commitment, open our minds and aim to continue learning, with full of determination.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are two important macro-economic changes that will impact Singapore’s workforce significantly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They can impact our job and wage growth and, ultimately, our social compact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Macro tech-inspired economic changes, such as automation and AI, will accelerate workplace changes and create new types of at-risk workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The rise of AI and automation has left some to speculate that many jobs could be lost.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The demise of human jobs has, to date, been largely over-exaggerated.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Technology generally creates more jobs than it destroys.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In Singapore, for example, automation has taken away jobs, such as the bus conductor.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But it has created a generation of route-masters and technicians over time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But some jobs might, indeed, be made redundant.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, many telemarketing jobs and call centre jobs are already replaced or complemented by AI.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Less than a week ago, Google demonstrated the Google Duplex technology powering the Google Assistant making a hair salon booking with a human hairstylist.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I watched the demonstration and was rather tickled by the sounds "umm," "uhh" and tonal inflections that created a convincing, realistic cadence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But I started to worry when the Google Assistant could decide on alternative booking slots when the preferred one is unavailable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our admin executives and even concierge services must take notice.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What it does mean is that some jobs will be redefined and others lost.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, while it is relatively easy to identify at-risk jobs, it can be difficult to retrain and move workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I met Mdm Tan in her mid-50s who has been working in the printing industry for the past 20-plus years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: She does some order processing and basic typesetting.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is rather typical of work in a traditional SME printer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: She knew that she was in a sunset industry as consumers move to digital images and her work has been automated quickly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, when I encouraged her to make plans early, she declined to change industries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: She lacks direction on which job to change to without significant loss of income.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Her children have yet to start working and she needs the income.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many Members of this House would have encountered similar examples.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The consequence of us not making such a change earlier would be eventual retrenchment and extended unemployment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The rapid disruptions have also caused anxieties for our workers, even including the younger ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many knew that changes are coming but what to move into is usually a much tougher question to answer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And the training to undertake that leads to a successful job switch is even tougher to make.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The demands of the new economy requires a new job market that is more fluid and responsive to the needs of both employers and workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I suggest three key features to this new job market.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: One, this new market needs companies to evolve new jobs quickly, with workers ready to train.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If they do not evolve fast enough, our workers’ wages would be stagnant and they might eventually lose their jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, our ITMs must be pervasive and help our companies to transform.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is a point also brought up by Minister Ng Chee Meng and Mr Melvin Yong.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, asset pooling, such as sharing of technology, can help our SMEs overcome their lack of resources and inertia.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Working with NTUC to introduce customised training is another.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Two, we need a better matching of jobs and workers facilitated by AI-enabled platforms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The latter sounds ironical but is the shot in the arm for the job market.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It has embedded capabilities to learn and get better at matching jobs to workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, it will need refinements to improve participation by the smaller employers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Reaching a critical mass is essential for AI to be effective.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many micro SMEs or smaller SMEs have yet to post their jobs on the platform.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many workers, especially the older ones, have also not used it because of language barriers that we need to address quickly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many more workers need help to look beyond their current industry and navigate to new possibilities which they find it very difficult to use.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our ageing population requires new job types to sustain the economic vibrancy and competency of our Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many older workers prefer jobs that are less physically demanding.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, many jobs still require shift-work or extensive amount of time at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Technology disruptions and economic restructuring have the potential to affect the jobs of our older workers disproportionately.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even our policy changes can affect them adversely.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, I have a Chinese-educated resident who found it very difficult to pass the Private Hire Car Driver's Vocational Licence (PDVL) for private hire vehicles even though he has been very adept at his craft for the last two years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to find new job types within the community that can best meet the income and lifestyle needs of our older workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In 2011, the North East Community Development Council started the Community Employment Programme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These are not full jobs and are not meant to be so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The scheme shows that there are good possibilities in both the private and public sectors for similar and better-paying micro-jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, our older workers can help to engage residents and run the administrative functions in a Senior Activity Centre.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need such job-creation capabilities to continue to keep our residents in the workforce beyond 67 years old, especially when one in four Singaporeans will be more than 65 come 2030.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, let me share some thoughts about the next macro-economic change and its impact for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is the rise of the Southeast Asian market.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The investment and job opportunities for Singapore and Singaporeans are tremendous.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because investment structures in this region are not fully developed, there are opportunities to develop solutions for such inefficiencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, such market inefficiencies have given rise to a generation of fast-growing Southeast Asian companies that can compete globally, such as Go-Jek.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, if you try Go-Jek, it is already more than a ride-hailing company.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They have Go-Clean for cleaning, they have Go-Med for healthcare, they even have Go-Massage if you need a massage.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need our people to better understand the region in order to thrive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: More importantly, the larger market allows our companies to expand and create more and better jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have a 60-year-old resident who was retrenched from his Oil and Gas job nine months ago.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When I visited him recently, I thought that he might be despondent from not finding another job easily.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Fortunately, he had leveraged on his network in Thailand which was established in an overseas posting quite a few years ago and had found another job in Thailand rather quickly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can similarly build such resilience in our system by looking at the Southeast Asian market as an extension of the Singapore domestic market.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This then requires our companies and younger Singaporeans to better understand the region.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our schools, Public Service and trade associations have already started exchanges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must continue to deepen engagements at all levels.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With Singapore as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Chair, this is an important opportunity for our different entities to lay the foundation for deeper ties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Rather than just attachments to companies in Singapore, America or the United Kingdom (UK), our students can be given opportunities to study or work alongside their Southeast Asian counterparts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The MNCs which operate in this region can be useful partners under the Global Innovation Alliance to scale up such opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We should also seek to establish business councils with Southeast Asian countries where there is currently none.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This provides companies with bilateral and multilateral opportunities to deepen understanding of the investment climate and structures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Having the fastest-growing region at our doorsteps is an unparalleled chance at economic expansion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must be mindful that it also brings along regional companies eager to partake in the growth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We will have competition and opportunities in equal measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While economic restructuring and technological disruptions have affected jobs and caused uncertainty, we are restructuring from a position of strength in a high-growth region.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of the fastest growth countries in the world are Southeast Asian.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, we need a new, a different job market to help our Singaporeans to navigate the vagaries of the changing market.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We will need longer-term investment in Southeast Asia to ensure longer-term economic growth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have the correct foundation in Singapore, but we must all participate in this change so that all Singaporeans can grow together as one.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, like many Members of the House, I would like to talk about the issue of inequality.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And fourth, while accepting that there is inevitable income disparity in every society, do different groups interact well with one another?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, to put it simply, the gap, the core, the churn and the mix.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, let us look at the gap between the top and bottom income segments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One indicator is the ratio of incomes at the 90th percentile to the 10th percentile.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I use household income per household member here for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Compared to countries, such as the US, South Korea, the UK and Finland, our ratio is quite high.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we must take into account the fact that we are a city state.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we compare ourselves with other major cities around the world, I think we will not be out of kilter.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have been moderating income disparity through polices, especially with a progressive tax system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are, in turn, redistributed to lower-income Singaporeans through schemes, such as the Workfare Income Supplement, the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Vouchers, higher subsidies for lower- and middle-income households in education, healthcare, housing and so on.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Middle-income families receive $2 for every tax dollar.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This rate of redistribution is higher than the $1.30-$1.40 that middle-income households received for every tax dollar in the UK, US and Finland.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What is equally important is that high-income earners also give back to society through philanthropy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Throughout our history, we had been blessed with successful businessmen and philanthropists – people like Lim Nee Soon, Tan Kah Kee, Syed Mohamed Alsagoff, Govindasamy Pillai.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This giving spirit is still very much alive today and we must continue to encourage it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With the muscle of progressive taxation and redistribution, and the spirit of giving back, we can moderate the impact of an income gap.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What is more important is the distribution of income between the top and bottom extremes and whether we have a strong middle-income core.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The most well-known indicator of income distribution is the Gini coefficient.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The closer it is to zero, the more equal the society.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Conversely, the closer it is to one, the more income is concentrated at the top and the more unequal the society.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We did not compute Gini coefficient until 1980.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we know that in the 1960s, inequality was very high.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, many Singaporeans were poor, did not have proper roofs over their heads, never attended school.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Yet, there were many wealthy traders and estate owners.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, one study estimated that in the 1960s, the Gini coefficient probably was around 0.5.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it was very high – shot through the charts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But to drive growth and create jobs, we opened up our economy, industralised, attracted foreign investments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Singaporeans saw their income and standard of living rise.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: During that period, as Members can see on the chart, the Gini coefficient trended downwards, right into the late 1980s.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In 1997, Singapore was hard hit by the Asian Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In 2001, the burst of the US dot.com bubble affected us, too.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the aftermath of both events, we observed the Gini coefficient spiking very steeply, as Members can see on the chart.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
