text: Fortunately, the global economy picked up over the last 10 years, and we have seen inequality moderate over the same period.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There have been studies to show that gross domestic product growth actually exacerbates inequality.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, as Members can see from the chart, our experience is that the fall in Gini coefficient coincided with periods of growth.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And the reason is because ours is a model of inclusive growth that benefited the masses, where there is tripartite cooperation between workers, employers and the Government and when there is a belief that we share the fruits of success, as we all eat from the same rice bowl.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, as a result, you will find that when there was growth, we actually moderated our Gini coefficient.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are, however, higher than other European countries and Japan because of their comprehensive welfare systems, a topic that I will come back to later.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To measure the strength of our core, we use median household income.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In Japan, the US, UK, Denmark, Finland and many countries, the real median household income either stagnated or experienced close to zero growth between 2006 and 2016 – all the blue bars on the chart – very low growth or no growth.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And this is a result of income growth across the board, including for the lower-income segments in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The strongest evidence of a healthy middle-income group in Singapore is our changing lifestyles over time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Birthdays and festive celebrations in restaurants, living in bigger HDB flats and executive condominiums, family vacations overseas.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are not enjoyed by an exclusive few but by the broad masses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is also not a natural occurrence, but a result of our model of inclusive growth.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The challenge ahead is that many middle-income families hope to do better and for their children to be better off than them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But given the high base we are at, the climb is getting harder.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will still improve but it will most likely be in steps and not in leaps.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We should also not define a better life purely in economic and material terms but also other aspects of a holistic quality of life, from a more pleasant and greener environment to a more cohesive and caring society and with greater pride in being Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The third dimension of inequality is churn or social mobility.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Ministry of Finance has studied the incomes of young Singaporeans in their 30s compared to their parents.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is an important part of the Singapore character and one of our biggest national achievements, that Singaporeans are able to transform the lives of their families over one generation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A major contributing factor is our belief in meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But public policies play a big part as well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We ensured universal access to good general education which uplifted the population.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We do what we can to remove barriers erected by financial difficulties.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Additional support is provided for children from lower-income families.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because of that, many students who would have dropped out of school, were able to continue to be engaged in their studies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This explains why in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), our 15-year-old students from disadvantaged backgrounds performed much better than their peers of similar backgrounds in developed countries, not just in literacy and numeracy but also in other critical soft skills, such as collaborative problem-solving.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Compared to other countries, Singapore has one of the smallest proportions of low performers in PISA.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, if Members look at the chart, all the way to the right, is Singapore, the lowest bar, that is, the percentage of low performers in PISA.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, there are no more bars to our right.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In other words, we have one of the smallest education underclass in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And if we wish to equalise the education outcomes further, we can, and there are two ways.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We can, first, reduce academic rigour across the board so that everyone performs more or less the same.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Or we can strive even harder to help those at the bottom level up, as we have done all these years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: By nature, we are hardworking people, and that is a virtue.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will continue to work hard, we will do what is right for students, support as many of them as possible to do what they like and love and be the best they can be.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We also provide broad access to tertiary education.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our home ownership policies played a major part in social mobility, too.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: HDB provides significant housing grants to help Singaporeans buy their homes, with the lower-income getting more help than the higher-income.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, in my constituency, we have many new Build-To-Order (BTO) flats.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When I do my home visits, I meet many families who have moved out from their rental flats into a flat that they now own with great pride and often with the help of additional housing subsidies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the success of our policies has led to a new set of issues.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Families which did well are able to pass down the privileges to their children, through better coaching, enrichment classes and exposure to the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For families which cannot move up despite the stronger and better support that is available now, we find their circumstances more dire and challenging than poor families of the past.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Singaporeans have always been relatively blind – to race, income and family backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I used to play football at Bukit Merah Secondary School.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I was just talking to Mr Azmoon on this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He also used to climb over the fence and play football, at whichever school I do not know.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I played in Bukit Merah Secondary School legally, until my knees got busted, because without fail, every weekend, on Saturday, someone would book the field, open up the gate, and whoever wanted to play would just play and I would always go there, and people living around, other groups, would just join in.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And then we did chut-ho-bay, o-bay-som; we divided ourselves into two teams, and we just played.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Nobody was bothered who was from where and what background.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And this was really the relaxed Singapore way of life.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This culture is organic, but it is also carefully nurtured and reinforced.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At least three public policies play a part in doing so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Every precinct or community is planned with a range of housing types, so that every estate has a good mix of Singaporeans from different backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We meet one another along neighbourhood coffee shops, hawker centres and community centres.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our playgrounds are getting better and better and more interesting, and we see kids from all backgrounds, with parents and grandparents in tow, playing together.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The People's Association and other community organisations hold many activities to encourage communal interactions and forge bonds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a universal rite of passage for every Singaporean male.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: NS is not just a security apparatus, but also an important national institution which fosters social mixing at different stages of our lives.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The great majority of primary schools in Singapore have students from all socio-economic levels.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And children, being children, they will play and learn together.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The study by the Institute of Policy Studies on a nascent class divide has often been cited.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng mentioned that, too, yesterday.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, some schools, due to their history, culture or programme offerings have a large proportion of students from the higher-income groups.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That has raised concerns and a few principals have pointed that out in their public comments and speeches over the years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our policies will need to work against this trend to actively bring Singaporeans of all backgrounds together.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, let me summarise, after I have gone through gap, core, churn, mix.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In many developed countries, inequality had been characterised by stagnation of wages and economic opportunities for the masses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In Singapore, our median income is still rising.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Lower- and middle-income families continue to experience real income growth and social mobility.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Singaporeans have been enjoying a rising standard of living and are motivated to do well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is both a result of our culture, of who we are, as well as our public policies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But transforming from Third World to First has created new problems and new forms of inequalities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, a rising middle class which aspires to do even better, but material progress is getting increasingly difficult, given our high base.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, some low-income families find it difficult to uplift themselves and stratification risks becoming entrenched.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And third, some amongst the higher-income segment are becoming socially distant from the rest.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Some think that universal welfare can be a solution to all these problems.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It means making assistance broadly and easily accessible to not just the lower-income but also the middle-income.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Proponents argued that with universal welfare, there will be no stigma associated with social assistance, and the dignity of the lower-income will be preserved.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But make no mistake; no handout is actually free.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To support universal welfare, taxes need to go up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we want universal welfare, taxes on ordinary folks, including the middle-income, will have to be much higher.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the greater concern is the impact on motivation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I noticed that yesterday, Mr Pritam Singh alluded to it, and it is a concern that should not be dismissed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, a few weeks ago, in a public dialogue, I called for views and suggestions on how we can better tackle inequality and I thank everyone who contributed and wrote to me.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One young man left a comment on my Facebook page.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: His name is Chee Kian and he is now a teacher.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: His father was a taxi driver, his mother a cleaner.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He said, "I benefited from the meritocratic system in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I worked hard through the education system to achieve what I am today.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, I notice that it is getting harder for poorer students to break through the system like the past as privileged kids garner (many) advantages since young...and stay ahead.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: (We need to) bridge the gap between the rich and the underprivileged through education so that more Singaporeans are able to succeed through working hard." This is a young man who clearly empathises with the challenges of the low-income.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But his solution was for the system to enable people to help themselves, not welfare.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We make help available to them, but we also preserve their motivation, so that they continue to strive, instead of being passive recipients of welfare.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members of this House have worked with low-income families week in, week out and understand their plight.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Others outside of this House might have read about them and their plight.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But let us not forget the ethnographies of those, like Chee Kian, who have worked hard and bounced back, thanks to the social trampoline we have.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Government must continue to extend assistance to the disadvantaged, and it will.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But making handouts easy and unconditional is not dignity; self-reliance is.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What can we do in the next phase, especially for education, and how should we do it?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The phrase "bold changes" in the President's Address received a lot of attention.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While we should be bold, we should not be reckless, for this will undo what had worked and undermine the fundamentals of our system and all that have helped serve our students well over the years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We must be bold, and we must be wise.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To do this, we must put our ears close to the ground, listen to the voices of all segments of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we listen close enough, we will also realise that the "voice of the people" does not deliver a singular message, rather it offers a diversity of views, conflicting and complex, even as they remain compelling.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Take, for example, the call for streaming to be abolished.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The argument is that it will remove the label and the stigma of the Normal streams.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we also need to put ourselves in the students' shoes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We cannot assume that the students all want to be in the Express stream.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Some prefer the pace of learning in the Normal streams.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Many students will tell you – and I am sure they used to tell Minister Ng Chee Meng when he visited them – they prefer to be a big fish in a smaller pond, rather than a small fish in a bigger pond.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Many students in the Normal (Technical) course also like the more applied and hands-on curriculum which they feel plays to their strengths.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we cannot ignore how these students feel.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Remember, stigma is not an education policy, but the result of our own attitudes and biases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is also the call for PSLE to be abolished, one of the hot favourites.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, that way, we take away the stress and the unfairness, because those from better family backgrounds can afford additional help and prepare their children better for their examinations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if you speak to enough parents, you will also realise that many support the PSLE system because the PSLE experience teaches their children to work hard and to demonstrate what they have learnt throughout primary school years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Many parents are also not overly stressed by it because they do not see PSLE as an exercise to chase for high marks, but rather as an objective and transparent way to decide which secondary schools their children will go to.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For many families and students from humble backgrounds, PSLE is their way to do well and go to a school of their choice.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The alternative, which is, to go by residential location, is even more unfair.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With this change, we will not differentiate students so finely for Secondary 1 posting.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If the scores are no longer so fine, how do we then allocate secondary school places?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am confident that this will reduce the stress on students and help them enjoy learning more.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is a big step change and it is coming in three years' time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have also heard many considered views and arguments on how we can improve the education system – better help the disadvantaged – and we have acted on them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will see results in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One strong view over the years which resulted in a consensus is that one of the best ways to help children from lower-income families is through quality preschool education.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At MOE Kindergartens, children do not mug, study and get trained academically.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Through these activities, they develop confidence, social skills, as well as a foundation in literacy and numeracy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We heard the voices of people, such as Ms Denise Phua, who has always championed a programme-based rather than class-based approach to cater to different learning needs and interests of students.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we are ensuring more porosity between such classes and streams.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We introduced the Polytechnic Foundation Programme where good performing students in Normal (Academic) streams can articulate directly to polytechnics, and they did very well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think more can be done in this area.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We received so much feedback about stress in the system and too much rote learning.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, over the years, our curriculum and pedagogies have continuously evolved and changed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Long gone are the days where children were expected to do well just by memorisation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, primary school students face their first examinations only at the end of Primary 2.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We embedded 21st Century Competencies, which are critical soft skills, into the curriculum.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The way higher education is being delivered in the Institute of Education (ITE), polytechnics and universities has also been drastically transformed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is nothing like what parents remember them to be.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have also put in place more help for the young from vulnerable families.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Ministry of Social and Family Development has roped in social workers, counsellors, nurses, paediatricians and educators to provide holistic support to these children.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In lower primary, we will continue our efforts, including through the Learning Support Programme.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Through the Programme, which is conducted in small groups of eight to 10, we dedicate resources to help weaker students.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is why even though our student to teacher ratio is at the levels of other developed countries, MOE has refrained from implementing a general reduction in form class sizes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Smaller form classes across the board can be beneficial to students, but it will deprive weaker students of the more dedicated support that we are able to provide today.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, embedded in our class size practices is also our social compact.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Students need a supervised and secure environment to complete their homework, study for tests, and seek counsel and guidance.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Admission policies greatly affect diversity in our schools.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The major education and assistance programmes are funded and run by the Government in an ethnically-neutral way.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Self-Help Groups come in, complement the effort by reaching out to vulnerable members of their communities and offer additional help.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, is that of Mdm Sharinna Tan, a single parent to four children.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They used to live in a 1-room rental flat in Bukit Merah.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Various organisations – Government agencies, The Straits Times (ST) Pocket Money Fund, public hospitals – stepped in to assist her.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Chinese Development Assistance Council (CDAC) reached out to her, and her children benefited from one-to-one tuition under the Supervised Homework Group Programme.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, Mdm Tan is working as a sales coordinator, earning about $2,000 a month.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: She is the proud owner of a 2-room HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Her eldest son just graduated from Ngee Ann Polytechnic and he won an award for the most outstanding academic performance in his course.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The other three children are studying also in Ngee Ann Polytechnic, another one in ITE and the last in secondary school.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The second story is that of Mr Hairul Hakkim Khuthibutheen.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When he was 14, his father passed away.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The mother had to return to the workforce to support the family.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: She worked as a factory operator and a service staff in a fast-food restaurant.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Hairul received help from various schemes, including from the Council for the Development of the Singapore Malay/Muslim Community (MENDAKI), the Singapore Indian Development Association (SINDA) and bursaries from the Muslim Trust Fund.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He graduated as the top student from NUS Law Faculty in 2016.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, he is a Justice Law Clerk at the Supreme Court, very nearby.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are two of many Singaporeans whom our system has helped.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If meritocracy is confined to academic excellence, success is defined narrowly as being a university graduate holding a professional or managerial position, then pathways will be limited, possibilities reduced and opportunities curtailed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is a pertinent question in Chinese: 为什么要千军万马过一个独木桥？Why ask an entire army to cross the river using one plank, a single plank?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Why can we not have many pathways to success?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Children, together with their parents, make those choices at a fairly young age, based on their talent and interests, with little or no stigma associated with any of the choices.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, we can celebrate our children choosing to be a coder, cybersecurity expert, chef, event organiser, creative designer, hospitality professional, nurse, early childhood educator, filmmaker or craftsman.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And they have to undergo the requisite training, not necessarily in a university.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is not the case 10 years ago.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But a lot more needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will have to develop even more pathways and opportunities within our education and training system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Employers' hiring and HR practices have to wake up to this new mindset.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Societal mindset will take even longer to evolve and change.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will continue to improve our policies, and we will not stop at these measures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: My invitation for ideas and suggestions remains open.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: From the multitude of voices, we will discern that singularity of action, a choice that is right for Singapore, and one which we must explain well, persuade people and be able to defend publicly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, bold moves need not always be major changes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They can be a change in the way of thinking, a spark to add to the Singapore flame.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This has to be supported by an entrepreneurial attitude towards tackling problems, such as inequality.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will actively look out for fresh ideas and try out new solutions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we come across an interesting and promising approach, we will be prepared to consider it, develop it further, run a pilot programme and see how it works.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I do not mean that it will ever be finished.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It will always be a work in progress.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, we may be in a better situation than many other developed countries.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It was so for the first men and women who sat in this House when our country was mired in turbulence, violence and uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, we live in an era of peace and prosperity, an era where much wealth has been created, but much inequality still exists.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To tackle this challenge, we must once again pledge ourselves, as one people, no matter the circumstances of our birth, no matter the luck of our draw, no matter the successes and failures that attend our lives, to create a more equal society.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We must do so by appealing to the sense of unity of Singaporeans, never by pitting one group against another and pandering to the diverse, divisive forces in society.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Indeed, when debating the President's Address and, particularly this time around, with the 4G leaders drafting it, it is very important to look further forward.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: It is heartening to hear what kind of society, in terms of equality – which is a very important subject – the 4G leadership intends to forge for our future Singapore.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Corrado Gini developed this in the early 1900s, that if the number is high, it is bad; if the number is low, it is good.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I remember that in many of the pre-Cabinet discussions that we were involved, we looked very specifically at household income by deciles.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: We are not blindsided by just one big average number.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: It is good to know that such attention was still paid to it.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: This upward mobility in terms of churn, it is very important because it gives hope to society.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The other aspect which he talked about, which is "mix", it defines the day-to-day experiences in Singapore under the 4G leadership.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: How is it like as a Singaporean living in those years, mixing with people of different social economic groups and so forth?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat always says when he was former Minister for Education, every problem in the world boils down to education; it is always education's fault.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But what the Member asked, therefore, shows that it is really not just about education.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, NTUC, MOM, employers coming together is such an important institution that we have.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That goes back again to Minister Ng Chee Meng's speech and how that economic model can benefit us.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While we do all that, continue all our social programmes – NS, housing, education, making sure that Singaporeans continue to mingle, continue to feel as one – and I can continue to play football in Bukit Merah Secondary, notwithstanding my knees.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other apps which came and left include Easy Taxi and Karhoo.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most recently, Go-Jek and Jugnoo arrived on our shores.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Disruptive technologies will come and go, and we can expect this trend to continue.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By now, we are familiar with how ride-sharing apps have radically transformed the taxi industry.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These new technologies change the way we commute as more turn to such apps to book rides.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This also means more job opportunities for freelance drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When ride-sharing apps first came onto the scene, they were pitting themselves against the taxi operators.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Alliances started to form through products like JustGrab and UberFLASH.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Eventually, we saw two large alliance Uber and Comfort versus Grab and the others.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Uber employees were asked to pack up on the day of the announcement and to go home and wait for further notice.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Commuters were worried about Grab monopolising the industry.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Freelance drivers were not sure how their livelihoods would be affected.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many had signed on to these ride-hailing apps to make a living.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some even changed jobs, bought a car or leased it long term to enter this market.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They were perhaps lured by the promise of flexibility and good income.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps, disruptive technology brings along with it disruptive management.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, it is only right to ask: is this typical of how management of such disruptive technology firms will operate in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I guess, like most things in life, it depends.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are many other apps-based platforms operating here, ranging from food/retail delivery to talent matching services, benefiting many freelancers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recently spoke with the President of the Sharing Economy Association Singapore and he assured me that his members desire to be responsible corporate entities to freelancers and consumers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But how will we know if freelancers embarking on the gig economy or availing themselves to such platforms will not be left to deal with another Uber disappearing act?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I propose four areas to strengthen the support for freelancers and those who are considering this career option.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I work in the NTUC and I look after the welfare and needs of taxi drivers, private hire drivers and freelancers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One, do more to educate our jobseekers and school leavers on what to look out for if they choose to embark on freelancing as a career option.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just last month, we met with 100 Education and Career Guidance Counsellors from MOE.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The aim is to update them on the developments within the freelance communities.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This enables them to better advise students who might be considering freelance work.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similar efforts are in place with career counsellors for adult jobseekers on what sustainable freelancing is like, the risks involved and the possibilities.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many freelancer communities and platform operators have also volunteered to share their experiences and industry tips at these engagement talks.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One way is to embrace the recommendations made by the Tripartite Workgroup on Self-Employed Persons.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is an encouraging move and parallels existing efforts by taxi operators to help cabbies with their MediSave.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Insurers have been approached by the Tripartite Workgroup to design such a product and I hope it will be available soon.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Coincidentally, in today's Straits Times Life section, there is also an extensive write-up about the lives of freelancers in the audio, stage lighting and rigging work and the need for protection when they are faced with an injury and long-term illnesses.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Mdm President’s speech, she also reminded us that we must continue to strive to become a more caring and inclusive society, especially for our workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Freelancers, Mr Deputy Speaker, are an important part of our workforce, and a good place to start is to provide a safety net for them.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thirdly, accord recognition to the dispute resolution framework set up by the supervising Government agency.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Info-communications Media Development Authority, MOE and LTA have already put in place such a system for media freelancers, sports coaches, instructors as well as taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such dispute resolution systems allow freelancers to work through payment disputes with the production houses, schools and the taxi operators.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More Government agencies should set up such a framework so that freelancers under the purview of their respective sectors can be better supported.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fourth, caveat emptor or buyers beware is a great reminder to buyers to be careful when a deal looks too good to be true.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is true that we want to remain a nation of opportunities, where we can invite new ideas from the world to come to Singapore and take root.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our workers, including freelancers, are also prepared to adapt to evolving market conditions and embrace technology.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Businesses, likewise, need to demonstrate a willingness to be in sync with our workers’ commitment.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are we still an economy that welcomes new ideas, allows testbed for innovations and involves our local workforce in these exciting ventures?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Despite this Uber episode, we want to tell those with the best ideas and technologies to come to our shores.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: In the part of her speech about forging a cohesive, caring and inclusive society, she said, and I quote, “Singaporeans want to live in a fair and just society, one based on meritocracy, but at the same time strives to leave no one behind.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, we are each prepared to do our best, but also to walk alongside fellow citizens who need help to keep up.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: In Singapore, people must always be able to get ahead through effort and excellence.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: We must open up more progression pathways and celebrate a broader range of successes." She went on to say, "We must tackle inequality vigorously.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to provide the right additional support to those needing it – in housing, education, skills training and employment – so that meritocracy works well.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Only then can everyone do well through hard work, talent and skills, regardless of their backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to pay special attention to the growing population of the elderly.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: We will continue to help older workers stay employed, earn fair wages and save more, so that they can age with dignity and purpose." Sir, this resonated deeply with me.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: For many years now, I have been speaking up for the fair treatment and strengthening of employment and employability opportunities for older workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: I am very happy that the President’s speech emphasised this.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: And, given that the speech bears the imprint of our 4G leadership, I believe that older Singaporean workers can now have the confidence, comfort and expectation that this commitment will continue to be kept.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government and the tripartite partners have worked closely over the years to enable workers to prolong their working years.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The most obvious measure has been the extension of the Retirement Age, followed by the introduction of the Re-employment Age and the further raising of the Re-employment Age ceiling.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Beyond that, there have been a range of measures aimed at strengthening the competitiveness and attractiveness of employing older workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Companies and entire industries are facing disruption caused by rapidly advancing technologies and changing business models.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: I think we hear a lot of examples in the speeches of Members today.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: In manufacturing, additive manufacturing technologies will have a big impact on the traditional assembly line.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Autonomous vehicle technology will mean that people can be conveyed in vehicles from point to point without the need for drivers.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Robotics and machine learning will mean that that arena previously open only to humans, for example, arenas like advisory services, can now be remodeled.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The spread of e-commerce and online shopping is certainly reshaping the retail scene and will have a deep and wide impact on the relevance of large physical store networks and distribution, and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: While it is easy to recite these disruptive changes, it is much harder to figure out what to do with them and how to deal with the impact.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: And for this very reason, we must do our best to gauge their impact on the use of labour and to plan ahead.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: In industries and occupations with a higher proportion of older workers, such planning, in my view, is even more critical.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to develop specific, viable development as well as transition plans for these.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: We cannot just depend on individual initiative and general provisions and exhortations to deal with this challenge.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: I, therefore, suggest three ways to help focus Government and tripartite efforts in this quest.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The first one is: where do we focus on?

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: I looked up the data from MOM's Labour Force in Singapore Report 2017, and I came to the following understanding.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: First, the proportion of workers aged 50 and above in our resident workforce had increased from 25.7% in 2007 to 34.4% in 2017.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: So, the ageing trend is clear, it is persistent.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Two, out of a resident workforce of 2.175 million, around 750,000 are workers at or above the age of 50.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: So, as I have mentioned just now, as of 2017, it came to 34%.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: So, that is one in three in the resident workforce above the age of 50.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The three occupational categories in the resident workforce which have the largest number of workers aged 50 and above are: first, the category of cleaners, labourers and related workers, that is, 120,000 resident workers above the age of 50; service and sales workers, 110,000; plant and machine operators and assemblers, 99,000 workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: So, that is looking at it from occupational types.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Whichever way of looking at it, either the three occupation groups or the four industry types, they will add up to about half of the older workers in our resident workforce.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: How do we then use these data to help our older workers who are particularly numerous in these industries and occupations?

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: I think a good starting point would be to assess which of these industries and occupation types are already facing the impact of changing technology and business models.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Earlier, I mentioned the advent of autonomous vehicles, e-retailing, manufacturing 4.0 and so on.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The question is, do we see a correspondence between these new technologies and business platforms and the occupations of the industries that I have just listed as having more older workers?

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: It is very clear that the industries that these workers are in are, like all the others, not exempt from experiencing disruption.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: They are also experiencing the disruption, and the pace can only pick up with time.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: We must, therefore, initiate action to plan for the older workers in them, so that while there is still time, those who can be trained, updated and upgraded are given at least an equal opportunity to do so, compared to younger workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: For those who face displacement because the technology might be wiping out particular occupation groups in the foreseeable future, or for those who see better longer-term prospects in other occupations or industries – such occupations will become larger as a result of an ageing population, for example – then they should be prioritised for help to convert.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Otherwise, if we do not do these plans, we do not target and we do not help and explain and nudge and make it happen, then the risk to both older workers and the system will snowball.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: And when the current technology or the business model that they are in is discontinued, you can see that there will be very quick and concentrated dislodging of workers from these occupational types or industry, and that may then overwhelm the help mechanisms at that very point.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: So, it is a question of digesting it away while we can in a very constructive way.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Companies will also find that they cannot employ enough workers with relevant skills if they do not upgrade those that they have currently, regardless of their ages.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: But please do not neglect the older segment.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: It is easier, safer and smarter to plan and act earlier and progressively to digest away the problem while there is still time.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Done correctly, the older workers could, in fact, enhance their relevance and value and strengthen their working terms and prospects.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: By tackling the challenge as early as possible, we minimise the number of older workers who will be displaced through irrelevance.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: In this way, we enable older workers to continue earning incomes.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: This will not only help them meet ongoing living expenses but also strengthen their retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: As we like to say in the Labour Movement, "A job is the best welfare".

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Now that we have a better idea where to focus, the next question is: what needs to be done?

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: In essence, I think we should do three Es.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: As we do so, we strike an increasingly better and more sustainable balance between older workers who have a real chance and choice to remain in work longer while simultaneously ensuring that their work creates real value for their employers.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Government agencies in charge of coordinating and spurring the progress of these plans must have accountability towards this outcome.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The tripartite partners must support the agencies to track progress and flag obstacles in the journey.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The desired outcome will not happen by chance.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Only constant vigilance, mutual accountability and a relentless attention to detail can get us there.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, step up Work Redesign for Ageless Workplaces.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Unless we believe that the vast majority of companies are already very "ageless", which we cannot be, not so in their thinking and the way they operate based on our experience on the ground, then, obviously, what must be done is that we must find ways to ramp up the outreach and the take-up, so that the impact can reach and help many more older workers in time.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: After we are clear about where to focus and what to do, I would add a final ingredient, which is, how do we nudge both management and older workers towards the desired mindsets and behaviour?

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a story that goes like this: there were five birds sitting on a branch.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: There was a hunter nearby and he took aim and fired a shot at them. "Boom".

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: All five birds heard the gunshot and knew that they should fly away for their own safety.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The question is: how many birds were left on the branch?

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: This is because knowing is different from deciding, and deciding is different from doing.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Knowing and deciding will not save us or give us the edge over the competition.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: It is in the prompt doing of the necessary that survival and success are to be found.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: By naming the good and taming the rest, we can then say truthfully and with confidence and a good conscience that "based on justice and equality", we will maximise our chances "to achieve happiness, prosperity and progress for our nation".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We are living through an era of rapid technological progress which is likely to make automation much more pervasive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Technologies are now being applied to areas which we usually regard as being carried out only by people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Just last week, Google showcased an AI system which is able to make appointments over the phone.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Those of us who watched the video saw how the AI interacted with a person without a script.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Here in Singapore, some of us would have seen the automated tray-clearing robots being trialed in our coffee shops and hawker centres, or the self-driving vehicles that are making their way around parts of one-north.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As automation technologies continue to develop, they will continue to be able to perform more tasks which require more complex skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, whether one is a blue-collar worker or a white-collar worker, these changes can make us feel vulnerable to being replaced by technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: There is a sense that these changes are beyond our full understanding and control, leading to fear and anxiety regarding an uncertain future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is understandable and it is expected to be so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This might lead some to resist the technologies, feeling that society should push back against automation to protect jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Some may wonder why the Government is actively supporting the process of economic transformation, instead of protecting existing jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Some worries go beyond workers, with businesses fretting about business model disruption, students worrying about whether their knowledge and skills will remain relevant, and older people wondering how they will cope in a society that requires more and more familiarity with technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I can empathise with such fears and anxieties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I have also seen this in patients facing an uncertain prognosis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In these situations, I find that seeing the situation in the right context is often helpful to reducing anxieties and, more importantly, to galvanise positive actions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our companies and our workers, too, must see the challenges in the right context and understand that while technological disruptions can create uncertainty for businesses and workers who fear being left behind, they also present new and exciting opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As consumers, many of the technology evolutions are driven by consumer needs and demands.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As consumers, many of these changes do improve our lives with better and faster products and services, as well as more convenient ways of doing things.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, e-commerce can disrupt the value chain and maybe threaten some jobs if you are in the retail business but, certainly, e-commerce also provides access to a much wider range of products and services available from the comfort and convenience of our homes, and people do enjoy shopping online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As workers, automating away tedious and strenuous jobs will make our work lives more productive, engaging and perhaps safer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Digitalising work processes will also allow us to be more effective and productive at our jobs while allowing work arrangements to be more flexible, such as working from homes, leaving us with more time to pursue other goals or maybe spend more time with our families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With automation, we will also be less constrained by our physical limitations even with an ageing workforce, as work-related experience will count more than just mere physical strength.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As business owners, many understand that disruption from technology and automation is a global challenge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With an interconnected world that we live in, we are not in a position to prevent or slow down technological change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Companies understand that if they do not disrupt themselves, someone else will do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Instead of wondering how we can protect ourselves from change, we should instead push to be at the forefront of change, even as we have to consciously work towards mitigating the negative impact on vulnerable groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I would say our prognosis is fairly good.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, our people are well-educated and highly skilled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our position at the heart of Asia puts us in a region of fast-growing demand where these skills can be put to good use to meet the needs of Asian consumers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have a strong scientific base that is built up over years of investment in science and technology, giving us a strong research base, strong research institutes and globally-leading Institutes of Higher Learning which can support industries in their transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Last but not least, we have a vibrant startup ecosystem driving innovation in the economy and serving as a means to capture economic value from upstream investments in research and development.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Yet, with all these prerequisites, success in economic and industry transformation is not a given.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As Member Melvin Yong has said earlier regarding his thoughts on ITMs, we have much work to do together and there are hurdles to a successful transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Executing the ITMs and economic transformation will not be a once-off process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Hence, business models will have to adapt repeatedly to meet these needs, and our workers will need to continually upgrade their skills to remain relevant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But the speed and pervasiveness in which the technological change and disruption are taking place are unprecedented.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Tackling changes posed by the technological revolution, therefore, requires a fundamental DNA evolution on our part.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: A fundamental mindset change is needed, regardless of whether you are a business owner or a worker.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With new medical discoveries and new treatment modalities coming on stream every few months, learning new skills and knowledge and adopting new technology are something that healthcare workers have embraced as part of their work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Each time a new infusion pump is introduced in the wards, a new surgical instrument is adopted within the operating theatres, the entire team, from the doctors, nurses, operating theatre technicians, supporting staff and so on, undergo training, recertification and refresher courses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The hospital management actively plans for this and also ensures that the personnel are kept updated on the latest knowledge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, lifelong learning is very much a part of the DNA of our healthcare workers and the hospital management.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We need to inculcate this mindset of lifelong learning across all our industry sectors so that change is not something that we need to fear but something we embrace as our mission to remain competitive and deliver better products and services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We need to put in place a well-oiled system to facilitate the need for such lifelong learning across all sectors of our economy involving all stakeholders: institutions, agencies, TACs and our unions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The mindset change, however, must start with the employers because they have a very important role to play in this as they lead the change to adopt innovative business models and technologies that keep their companies competitive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Employers are also critical in developing their employees and helping them to ride the fast-moving waves of technology advances, because only after the employer has decided to transform and communicated this to his workers can the workers respond by picking up the relevant skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And armed with these new skills, the workers can better support the company and take up the better jobs available and, in turn, making the company more competitive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Employees must also maintain a positive mindset towards new technologies, not thinking of them as complicated and beyond their abilities to cope.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For this to happen, the transformation must also be “user-friendly”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The fear of technology can be overcome by ensuring that the “user-interface” is an intuitive and friendly one.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, my five-year-old niece does not need to be taught how to use an iPad.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Within a matter of a few hours, she can trigger the games app, figure out how the interface works, and can start playing the game.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have all seen this in many of our kids when they are given a device like an iPad.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Many of us also would not need to read the instruction manual of a new smartphone that you have just taken from the phone store.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Within a matter of a couple of days of tinkering around, you kind of get used to how the interface works and you can probably use 80% of the functions of the phone without so much as reading the user manual.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Similarly, some SMEs in the manufacturing sector are able to do so and ensure that the user interface of automation is as simple as the interface of an iPad.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I have visited some in the manufacturing sector and they have made the control of industrial robots via the use of iPads certainly very intuitive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The operator in this situation is, in fact, interfacing with the iPad and would not have to bother about the technology behind the robot itself unless, of course, they are the technicians charged with servicing the robot.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In the words of a mature worker, as far as they are concerned, the robot is there but they are actually interfacing directly with the iPad and it is something that any smartphone user will find that, with minimal training, you can get used to it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We need to change our mindsets and not see technology as something complicated and beyond our abilities to cope.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: An example of a company that demonstrates this is PSA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: During the visit, I met Mr Aw Eng San, a 53-year-old crane operator who has been with PSA since 1994, but who, despite his years, displays a positive mindset towards change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The training was well-designed and it eased the process of change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: After just three weeks of classroom training, as well as subsequent on-the-job training, he has since settled into his new role in the automated yard operations control centre, managing exceptional situations for a fleet of automated cranes using a joystick and hi-definition cameras, rather than being isolated in a crane cabin which can be hot on certain days and for which he has to climb up a ladder to get access.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The new job now allows him to work indoors and interact with his colleagues in an office environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: By keeping a positive mindset towards change, Mr Aw has learnt a new skill and stayed relevant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As a result, he has contributed to an improvement in PSA's overall performance, and his pay package has also increased through higher performance incentives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: He is now even encouraging his friends from the other terminals to join him on this journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: From a typical blue-collar job, his job is now technically an “office job” that is less physically demanding, much safer and, certainly, much more fulfilling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With the expansion to Tuas Mega Port, I am sure many more exciting jobs will become available.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It is not only the “big companies” that are capable of transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This SME, Swee Heng, invested in a new 60,000 square foot factory that is semi-automated and houses state-of-the-art equipment, such as two tunnel ovens that make baking much more efficient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As a result, manpower can be redeployed to perform more intricate tasks, such as cake decorating.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Swee Heng has also digitalised much of its manual processes and upskilled their older workers to become more tech-savvy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Beyond mindset change, how can we better leverage our strengths to effect a successful transformation?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Well, one of our key assets is a well-educated population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We need to better engage and co-create policies with our people to harness the power of an increasingly educated and better-informed population towards the creation of better outcomes for everyone.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I remember when I was a student, patients in those days tended to be very highly compliant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But they are much more dependent on their doctors to play a paternalistic role in looking after their health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Those days, we were often frustrated that patients were not able to comply with the treatment instructions in the regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: They either did not finish their antibiotics when they were supposed to, or they were not using the asthmatic inhalers as we instructed them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, often times, diseases were not very well controlled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: They do not somehow feel like they want to be empowered.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: They are better informed, and they do not necessarily take their doctor's orders so easily at face value.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Sometimes, they come with a stack of papers printed from the Internet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: You get a test right on the spot.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And they will only comply with the doctor’s advice after the doctor has spent some time explaining his decisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But once we are able to get the patients to understand the issues and empower them with the knowledge, more patients today are taking charge of their own health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It is thus a much more satisfying partnership for our doctors to work with their patients towards achieving better health outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Government needs to be flexible and be prepared to make changes where necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have to better communicate to our people the challenges and limitations that we face so that we can make the necessary tradeoffs and partner our people so that we can remain as a competitive “Team Singapore”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The second strength we have is also our uniquely Singaporean secret sauce – our strong partnerships and tripartism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Sister Thanaletchimi shared that our Government works hand in hand with TACs which represent businesses, and unions which represent workers, crystallising the essence of our tripartism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is something that sets us apart from many other countries which face the same challenges we do in economic transformation, but without that secret sauce that we have.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But the ITMs are only of value if they can be executed and executed well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The tripartite partnerships involved in each ITM are, therefore, crucial to bring together this integrated perspective.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Just as important, we also need to continually reinforce our society’s capabilities to support its more vulnerable members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These are concrete ways in which we can ensure that Singaporeans are not left behind in the midst of economic progress and keep inequality at bay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As Mr Thomas Chua mentioned yesterday, we need to continue to empower the TACs to do more with the employers to help businesses better understand the transformation journey they can undertake in their own sectors and support them in taking the first steps.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We need to find more ways in which the unions can participate in the training and reskilling of our workforce, to catalyse the mindset change I spoke about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: More importantly, we need to ensure that the fruits of economic transformation translate to real tangible benefits for our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, beyond the usual measurements of productivity gains and value-add per worker, we need to have better ways and better parameters to measure how our workers actually benefit from the transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: A good example of such tripartite effort is seen in the Air Transport ITM, which was developed in close collaboration with the Air Transport Industrial Tripartite Committee (ITC).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Meeting every quarter, the ITC aims to shape and drive manpower and productivity initiatives for the sector through tripartite collaboration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Notably, the ITC has a Workforce Transformation Workgroup through which it regularly updates members, such as NTUC and the union, on the progress of industry transformation and workforce issues in the sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The inputs obtained through the ITC’s channels on Government initiatives and ground sentiments have proven valuable in helping our agencies further refine their schemes and programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In my concurrent appointment as Senior Minister of State for the Ministry of Trade and Industry and Deputy Secretary-General of the NTUC, I hope to be able to further bridge the gap between Government agencies and the Labour Movement, particularly in the implementation of our ITMs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Throughout all these, the Government must remain nimble and be prepared to change our approach when needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Even within the ITMs, where necessary, we have taken a tailored approach in the formulation and implementation of our ITMs, as each industry segment has a different makeup and faces different challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is a reflection of what Mr Teo Ser Luck pointed out yesterday that, even within each industry, different approaches will need to be taken for different groups of enterprises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will continue to review and adapt our ITMs to meet the needs of each industry, even as these needs change over time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To illustrate, for enterprises in more innovation-intensive industries, for example, in the manufacturing sectors, the capabilities the enterprise needs to develop can be highly enterprise-specific.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: They can subsequently be supported through schemes like the Capability Development Grant (CDG) to take up these technologies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And in the OTR, we also work with them to see how best they can level up the skills of their workers to manage technologies that they are bringing in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: On the other hand, for sectors like logistics and air and sea transport, the technologies required are much more similar across different enterprises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In such cases, we adopt a more broad-based approach which allows many firms to benefit very early on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These are also open to all firms in the industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: All things considered, Singapore has all the ingredients for success.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Globally, everyone is facing the same set of challenges as a result of the rapidly changing environment, but Singapore is well-placed with distinct advantages to embrace innovation-driven economic growth for our enterprises and people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Government is prepared to support our enterprises and people in their transformation journeys.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Everyone has a role to play as we move into the innovation-driven economy of the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And everyone can participate in it, whether as a worker submitting an innovative idea to improve work processes, as a student through school projects, or a first-time entrepreneur coming out to start your own business, or even a retiree who has a good idea.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The key is being open in our thinking and being prepared to make the necessary changes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industy (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With that, Sir, I stand in support of the Motion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will deal with three aspects of President Halimah's Address in my speech: social inequality, cost of living and the task of the 4G Government leaders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: President Halimah, as highlighted by a good number of Members before me, signaled that our Government will tackle inequality vigorously.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is important, however, to understand the Government's objectives in addressing the issue of inequality.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Both within and outside Singapore, political leaders have often incorporated the phrase "income inequality" in their speeches, but do not necessarily have the same understanding of its impact on society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We just heard a masterful speech on the same topic by Minister Ong Ye Kung a few minutes ago.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some political leaders have sounded apocalyptic warnings about the effect of income inequality on society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some have referred to income inequality as providing people the motivation to do better and improve their lives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some other opportunistic politicians blame immigration and free trade as contributing factors to income inequality.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Doubtless, such accusations can exacerbate divisions within a society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I found the chapter on inequality written by Prof Steven Pinker of Harvard University in his recent book "Enlightenment Now" instructive on this point and wish to share his insights with hon Members of this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Prof Pinker asserted that income inequality, usually measured by the Gini coefficient, is not a fundamental component of well-being.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is not a basic right, such as the right to health, education, security and so on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said, and I quote: "Income inequality is not itself a dimension of human well-being and it should not be confused with unfairness or with poverty nor is decrease in inequality always good.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
