text: Most effective levellers of economic disparities are epidemics, massive wars and state collapse".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We should not conflate inequality per se with unfairness.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Against this backdrop, it can be readily appreciated that our country's Gini coefficient figures, which solely measure income inequality, do not provide a full picture on the Government's effort to deal with social mobility, poverty, access to Government services among our low-income families and social mix.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I believe the hon Member Mr Cedric Foo made the same point earlier.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this context, the Government's stated intent in the President's Address to open up more progression pathways, celebrate a broader range of success, giving every child a good start in life irrespective of his family circumstances and help children at-risk, deserves this House' full support.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is not to say the Government should not be mindful of income inequality.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to deal with the impact of GST on lower-income families.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung just spoke about this when he touched on the topic of redistribution to lower-income families in Singapore in his speech just now.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As low-income families do not pay much income tax, most of the tax they pay would, therefore, be GST.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I respectfully suggest that in determining the impact of GST on low-income families and measuring the sufficiency of the transfer benefits to help them with their cost of living issues, we should not just use how much GST a low-income family pays as a yardstick.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The assumption that low-income families use quite a bit of their disposable income in directly paying GST ought to be tested.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is more likely that a member from a low-income family would buy food from businesses at the wet markets or from a hawker centre, which are not GST-registered, as opposed to a supermarket or restaurant in a shopping centre.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Ultimately, to ensure that the transfers are sufficient to offset the impact of GST on cost of living, the Government must be mindful of the inflationary pressures on the lower-income families, especially if their wages do not keep pace.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One defining action to ensure social mobility is the provision of access to good quality education.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This has and will continue to be a great leveller for our society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So long as the individual puts in the effort, he or she can achieve good results and enjoy the opportunities it brings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, the beneficiaries of our system must actively contribute back to society that helped them achieve success.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is the Singapore brand of meritocracy that Minister Masagos referred to in his speech yesterday.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to share a good example of a product of the Singapore brand of meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Ms Chong Hui Xian is an active community leader in Bukit Batok over the past seven years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She is an auditor with one of the top four accounting firms.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Her father, now retired, was a kitchen hand at a hotel.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She could not get into an Express or Normal (Academic) stream.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She went to Normal (Technical) stream at Yusof Ishak Secondary School.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: From there, she went to ITE West for a year and then to ITE East for two years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She did sufficiently well to get into an accounting course in Ngee Ann Polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: By that time, she had gained sufficient confidence to compete, in her words, with "the single O-level pointers".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, she decided that she must do something for our community.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She and her friends set up an ITE chapter in Ngee Ann Polytechnic to help ITE students better cope with their studies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She continues to help youths by sharing her story and motivating them to be the best they can be.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Her focus, borrowing Minister Masagos' words, is on "building a good society, not a richer society".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Government, in the Committee of Supply (COS) debates, urged caution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister Desmond Lee stated that "use of legislative levers is insufficient on its own".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My point, respectfully, is that there is no legislative lever in the first place.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But so long as the powers are well regulated, used judiciously, I do not see a significant downside.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is the likelihood of him entering the criminal justice system, compared to a person who completed school?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For the Benthamites amongst us, is it not more likely that, in the end, the state will be compelled to spend more money on him to deal with the consequences of him not being in school?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One connected issue to the Government's agenda in forging a cohesive, caring and inclusive society is the housing policy concerning the physical location of rental flats.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This relates to the fourth dimension of income inequality that Minister Ong Ye Kung spoke about in his speech dealing with social mix.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As Members know, a good number of standalone rental blocks have been built in the recent past.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Yesterday, we heard the hon Member Ang Wei Neng forcefully endorsing the Government's ethnic mix policy in HDB housing estates.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hon Member Henry Kwek made a clarion call to promote social mixing among classes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan suggested renting older housing units to those needing interim housing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do have a concern with the building of standalone rental flats.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Usually, they are built at the fringes of mature housing estates.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We miss a chance of getting family members from these rental flats to mix with members in regular units.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With better interaction, we promote awareness, empathy for low-income families and, hopefully, this will spontaneously generate more help for them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We can also motivate the low-income families to better their lives through their own efforts, mirroring the efforts of their friends in regular units.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to the issue of money because it is so easy to forget that whilst we want the Government to do more to increase social mobility and help with cost of living, our fiscal position, as the Minister for Finance reminds us, is getting tighter and tighter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We cannot afford these figures to go up all the time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We must focus on individual responsibility to slow down the increase in social spending and talent development to grow our economy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the latter point, I do not have time to do justice to this big topic in my speech today, but I wish to share an example which shows that Singapore offers a great platform for innovation and economic opportunities for all, irrespective of their personal backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I met Mr Fock Mun Hong, aged 48, two weeks ago at his late father's funeral wake in Bukit Batok.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He shared with me that his late father, who had no formal education, was his biggest mentor.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His father was the sole breadwinner in a family with two children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He recounted that his father used a discarded cardboard, some aluminium foil and a vegetable steamer to create a personal sauna for just less than $50!

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A graduate of NTU, his Singapore company just discovered enzymes that can dissolve styrofoam.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Ordinarily, it takes thousands of years to degrade styrofoam.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With this discovery, he plans to take part in Temasek Foundation's Liveability Challenge to address urban waste.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hopefully, he will be able to commercialise his idea and that will, undoubtedly, be good not just for Singapore but our world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Returning to the issue of addressing the increased costs of social expenditure, there is scope to use data analytics to ensure better targeting and reduce moral hazard.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do appreciate the complexity but I exhort the Government to consider utilising data analytics to get a better picture of who should be helped.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They sought financial help over and above the CPF LIFE annuity payment they were getting.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Unfortunately, they were not getting sufficient support from their children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When I suggested that they participate in the Lease Buyback Scheme, they demurred, stating that they want to pass on the full value of their flat to their children upon their demise.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, what lessons can we draw from this?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This does not accord with our nation's values.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to my final topic, our 4G Government leaders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am heartened to note from the President's Address the humility of our 4G Government leaders in recognising that they need to demonstrate leadership and resolve, listen to the views and feelings of our people and earn the right to lead.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This, I believe, will go some way in building the relationship of trust with the people that hon Member Ganesh Rajaram referred to in his cogent speech yesterday in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Ganesh Rajaram also referred to the challenge of communication in today's digital world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As far as communication is concerned, I dare say that the task of the 4G Government leaders is likely to be more difficult than it was for our Government leaders in previous generations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We all know about the advent of deliberate online falsehoods in social media.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We also know about the heightened potential for non-Singaporean players with ulterior motives to influence the Singapore political scene through media platforms.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is now the long tail of expectations and demands which makes it more difficult for us to reach consensus on policies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is where we need to forge a climate of constructive politics, always putting Singapore and our people first and to avoid short-term populist measures that will weaken Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And I am glad to note that Mr Pritam Singh, on behalf of the Workers' Party, fully endorsed this principle in his speech and I take the opportunity to congratulate him on his election as Secretary-General of the Workers' Party.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But constructive politics is not just the domain of Members of Parliament and political leaders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We need to ensure that the environment of trust and respect that exists between our people and political leaders will continue whilst political leaders remain fully accountable to our people for their actions at all times.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They, their parents, their spouses may feel it is just too much of a sacrifice for them individually and for their families.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will be dangerous as, in the end, we will not be able to build a strong foundation for the future, which was referred to by Minister Chan Chun Sing in his speech yesterday.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, together, in and outside this House, we need to work together to make sure that our politics remains constructive.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish them well in forging the bonds of trust with our people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also wish them every success in their endeavour to ensure that Singapore remains, in the words of our President, "an exceptional nation".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: You either improve or you decline, relative to every other country.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And sitting in a comfort zone in the corner for too long will prove costly.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Most Singaporeans, including myself, would accept and would not argue with this logic.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Our country's innovation journey has often been framed as a national fight for survival.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As the Government unveils new polices over this week and recognises Singapore's undeniable successes, there are points that ought to be addressed as we go forward.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: First, while Singapore can attract talent and build an ecosystem of entrepreneurs, investors, corporations and research institutes, some might say that we, nonetheless, lag behind in the culture of risk-taking.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Chan Chun Sing said yesterday that international exposure is key for tertiary students.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I would agree, but I hope that this quest for learning, learning from others' stories of successes and failures can start at an even earlier stage, pre-tertiary, and then continue with a devoted commitment to lifelong learning.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Before founding Alibaba and becoming a multi-billionaire, Mr Jack Ma failed his college entrance exams twice.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He failed to then get into Harvard which he applied for 10 times.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He proceeded to be rejected from dozens of jobs and I would sheepishly admit, as an academic and educator, that we are often accustomed to not looking beyond the grades that one is awarded.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But how wrong I would have been had Mr Ma gone for his education within our system, if I had this simplistic bias.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Simplistic to think that grades alone would determine someone's professional identity.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As a nation, we should strive to ensure that our education systems and our educators allow our entrepreneurs-in-waiting to thrive and, importantly, to never feel ashamed by any failures they experienced.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And, as Minister Ong Ye Kung very articulately expressed, the various dimensions or the four dimensions of inequality and how we could actually try to overcome any barriers that we would face.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: That is the first point, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: These afflictions, Mr Deputy Speaker, do not affect only vulnerable adult persons.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans should be encouraged to talk about their mental health.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They should be given the resources, skills and language that they need in order to take action to overcome mental health issues.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Labour Movement, which we heard from through several speakers earlier, should be mindful that as we ask the workforce to ensure that professional standards and targets never slip, the people are nonetheless given the time to take better care of themselves, take some time off and take care of their mental and physical well-being.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If I may just use a metaphor that Minister Ng Chee Meng used earlier, it is not just to plug, train and play.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I would say it would be to plug, train, play, recharge, maintain and then play.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: She said, movingly, that the Government should provide more support to young families and make Singapore a great place to have children, help families cope with the cost of living and enable persons with disabilities to lead a full and active life.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The next generation of Singaporeans, if my students are anything to go by, Mr Deputy Speaker, want to be included and involved at every stage.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Would you like for her to go first?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We are structuring our economy in a world of rapid change – shorter technology cycles, automation, digitisation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These trends are causing disruptions but also creating opportunities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the same time, we are also facing greater competition due to globalisation, as other economies around the world also restructure and adapt to the changes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Having just joined the Government from industry, I see businesses all over the world coping to adapt to the changing global landscape, as trade flows, automation and other factors, such as Brexit, come into play.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Companies are transforming to provide differentiated products and services, and also to be more productive as they come under cost pressures.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: While Singapore has done well economically to attract businesses here and created an environment where our local companies can also thrive in this international hub, our next phase of development has to go beyond just creating a vibrant and attractive business environment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As we help companies transform, we cannot just look at automation or process transformation without helping our workers to stay relevant and agile to cope with the changes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We must ensure that as companies change, the quality of jobs get better.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Change should not just be about lowering costs, which would run counter to our productivity and quality goals.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Singapore needs to provide the best business environment and secure the best talent.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If our companies do well to transform and grow, our workers will be able to take up quality jobs and earn better salaries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, this is easier said than done because it also means getting our policies right and helping every worker develop an agile mindset.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: While Ernst and Young has a wide range of capabilities to serve its clients, it is best known for its audit services, and a large part of its workforce provides audit services to clients.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Most of such work is statutory, as companies need to comply with audit regulations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, its clients are also under cost pressures to reduce compliance costs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As more and more financial systems today are run by software, analytics have in recent years been introduced to make audits more efficient and effective.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, even more recently, many audit firms have been exploring the use of AI that can crawl through data a lot more quickly and perform basic audit functions which auditors spend many hours doing traditionally.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The accounting profession, one of the oldest professions around, finds itself evolving.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Even highly-trained professionals are not spared from disruption, and they, too, need to evolve and develop deeper domain skills, be proficient in data analytics and adapt to higher order skillsets in order to be relevant to boards and other clients.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, no matter which sector or occupation we are in, we cannot afford to insulate ourselves from change.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will have to adapt to change and disruption and position ourselves to benefit from the opportunities that it brings.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The changes that we see around us are not just transforming the content of jobs, but also the employment norms and working arrangements.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In many developed countries, companies are turning to contingent workers and retaining only a small core of permanent staff, so that their workforce can ramp up or ramp down quickly with business cycles.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In these countries, the notion of traditional permanent employment is fracturing, that long-term employer-employee relationships are becoming less common, and workers face more uncertainty as a result.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is because we have taken care to keep our labour market policies tight and flexible, so that permanent employment remains available to those whose seek it.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Even so, in Singapore, we are seeing gradual shifts away from the idea of lifetime employment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workers are more likely than before to work for multiple employers in their lifetime, and experience more frequent and fluid career transitions.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: While some workers do so voluntarily in search of better opportunities, others are forced to do so due to displacement from technological advancements, economic restructuring or business cycles.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I have met many residents going through such changes, so I know that this is not a simple challenge.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is easy to be overwhelmed by the pace of change.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That is why, even as we take personal responsibility in charting our careers and adapting to change, the Government also has a role to play in helping workers manage uncertainty, and to build confidence – confidence to adapt to the changing environment, and confidence that Government schemes and policies will support them through uncertain times.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To do so, we must make our economy vibrant, keep our labour market responsive and ensure that our support systems are inclusive.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: By driving the adoption of prefabrication and automating the production process, these hubs significantly improve the productivity of the construction industry.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is important as the ITMs cannot just be plans on paper that are disconnected from the needs of companies on the ground.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have to make the ITMs relevant for both companies and individuals, as Member Zainal Sapari had spoken earlier.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Companies can then better understand industry developments and plan ahead for future opportunities, while workers know what skills to pick up.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I also agree with Member Heng Chee How that this would be especially useful for older workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Apart from making the ITMs relevant, we should also speed up the pace of adoption of ITMs so that industry transformation will not lag global industry developments.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We want all our companies to transform and grow amid the restructuring economy, and to remain agile to opportunities, including opportunities overseas.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is something that I have seen in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Many companies are based in Singapore because of our highly skilled and adaptable workforce.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We must maintain that as a competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As the economy transforms, we must keep our workforce relevant, responsive and flexible.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Take, for example, Mr Shawn Koh, who works as a senior engineer in SembCorp Marine.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Shawn does engineering design in the Engineering and Instrumentation Department.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: He was previously working more on oil-related offshore projects, but when SembCorp Marine saw an opportunity to further penetrate the Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) markets, Shawn was selected to go through the PCP for Marine Engineers which was offered by Workforce Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This gave him the technical skills to now take on gas-related projects as well.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These new skills are taken into consideration when it comes to his promotion and career progression.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The PCPs exemplify how companies can tap on Government support to prepare the workforce for new opportunities while also allowing workers like Shawn to stay relevant and pick up new skills.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is especially important for our mid-career and mature workers, some of whom face greater difficulty finding jobs after being displaced, as shared by some Members in this House earlier.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: A&G schemes like the PCP and the Career Support Programme help to address mismatches in skills and wage expectations, thus boosting labour market mobility and agility.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The A&G programmes have been ramped up over the past few years, and I believe that such interventions are crucial in this phase of transformation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And even as we have been doing much on this front, we can continue to do better to help workers adapt to the changing environment to transit into new and good careers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the same time, for our workforce to be agile, we must continue to be open to foreign manpower that complement our local workforce.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Our foreign workforce policy is guided by three objectives.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: First, to calibrate foreign manpower growth to spur restructuring and productivity-led growth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Second, to enhance the quality of the foreign workforce, so that we can do more with less.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Third, to provide flexibilities for emerging business needs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: While most foreign specialists with skills-in-demand should be able to meet our prevailing work pass criteria, MOM is working with the economic agencies to provide selective flexibility for those who may be unable to qualify for work passes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In addition, we can tap on these foreign specialists to develop our local capabilities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Capability Transfer Programme announced earlier this year helps to facilitate the transfer of capabilities from foreign specialists to local workers, so that our workforce can be equipped with leading-edge competencies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In this fast-changing environment, the fruits of growth are sometimes unevenly distributed.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I share similar concerns with many Singaporeans over income inequality, in particular for our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Over the past five years, the real income of full-time employed Singaporeans grew faster at the 20th percentile than the median.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, we must continue our efforts to uplift our low-wage workers to bridge any divide and help them support their families better.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In order to improve wages in a sustainable manner, we must work to improve the productivity of our workers and companies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: More importantly, it provides them opportunities to upskill and become more employable.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Lower-wage workers in these sectors have a clear progression pathway, which sets out how they can enjoy wage increases as they upgrade their skills, take on new responsibilities, and improve their productivity.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For example, Mdm Farah Aqil started off as a cleaner with NAFA Systems Service Pte Ltd about 10 years ago.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At that time, she earned about $750 a month.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Over the years, she accepted the need to upskill herself, operate new machinery, and take on supervisory responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As her skills were upgraded and productivity improved, she moved up the PWM wage and job ladder.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I am glad that Minister Ng Chee Meng earlier shared the same view.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, I hope that the unions and employers will continue to make a tangible difference for our workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: (In Malay):  : Changes and disruption are nothing new in this rapidly changing world.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Over the years, the changes that we faced, whether in terms of education, career or businesses, have become the norm.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, in these last few years, the scale is bigger and faster, involving the entire sector and affecting every citizen.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Looking at the business world, we have already seen how the trend of budget airlines has become more prevalent and affected the bottom line of the major airlines.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But one positive benefit from that wind of change, among many others, is that it allowed more people to enjoy air transport, apart from opening more career opportunities for pilots, cabin crew as well as engineers and technicians.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It has also added vibrancy to the tourism sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Perhaps many of us still remember the introduction of the one-man-operation (OMO) buses in the 1980s, which are buses that have only one operator each, that is, the bus driver, and do not need any bus conductor to collect fares.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: When this system was introduced, there was a lot of outreach efforts being done to help the public adapt to this new operation, which was more productive and manpower-lean.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In other careers, professionals like doctors, engineers and architects need to constantly upgrade themselves with the most current knowledge in their respective fields to remain relevant.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Rank-and-file workers like technicians and delivery workers also need to supplement themselves with technological skills.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: A degree alone is not enough now without having expertise, experience and knowledge that require constant upgrading.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In fact, there are more opportunities to progress for those without a university degree, based on their abilities and experience.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Our way is to ensure that every member of society receives quality education.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For those left behind, we need to give them hope and guidance to further improve themselves.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The importance of knowledge and education cannot be dismissed, whether an individual aspires to be an entrepreneur or a worker.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Education is the basic foundation for our future.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I am grateful to be handed this responsibility.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I am certain that self-help bodies like MENDAKI can help at the various levels of education and upgrading requirements, especially for the disadvantaged, so that we can close the gap between the successful ones and the less successful.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Without workers who are educated and equipped with skills, entrepreneurs and businesses would not be able to function well and sharpen their competitive edge.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will also explore the best ways to help entrepreneurs enhance their potential.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These inclusive and collective efforts require everyone to work together, and I hope that such an approach will further motivate the needy to improve themselves.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Most importantly, we must help open up opportunities and give hope to everyone.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: (In English): The 4G leadership must evolve and strengthen our social compact with Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It must be our moral responsibility to build a Singaporean Core in our workforce.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It must also be our moral responsibility to create better quality jobs that our workers can access and earn better incomes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It poses challenges, but also opportunities, and the only way for us to tap on these opportunities is to position ourselves to adapt to the changing environment and to move forward together, inclusively.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I am excited to be part of this new team and will try to contribute the best I can.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There is no better privilege than to serve the nation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I will continue to do my utmost for our country and serve the needs and aspirations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Miss Cheng, would your speech be longer than eight minutes?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: If it is, I would like to move the extension.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, Mdm President’s inaugural Address laid out several important concepts and our 4G leaders’ philosophy on good governance and leadership.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She has also said, “Singaporeans want to live in a fair and just society, one based on meritocracy, but at the same time strives to leave no one behind.” This is the crux of the topic I want to raise today.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Education has been a key driver of social mobility.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our successful transition to a knowledge-based economy within one generation has been a direct result of our education policies.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But more importantly, education has levelled the playing field for families with varying resources, allowing children of all backgrounds the potential to rise to the best of their abilities.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Looking at the horizon, we can do better to ensure education continues to be an enabler of social mobility.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The setting up of MOE Kindergartens is a big step in the right direction.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Access to quality preschool education will ensure children from disadvantaged families would not be deprived of foundational learning prior to formal primary school education.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, most help is needed for disadvantaged children from the lowest income group.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There are obviously families out there that, for reasons of their own, do not see the importance of their children going to preschool.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: How can a child focus on learning and keep on par with the others if they do not attend school regularly?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: When these disadvantaged children start compulsory education at Primary 1 and realise that they lag behind the rest of their classmates, it discourages them and generates a sense of low self-esteem and other disruptive notions.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Parents must recognise the importance of foundational learning and make every reasonable effort to give their children a complete preschool education.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is commonly regarded that Singapore’s education system is world-class.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, I see a dark cloud looming over the horizon – elitism amongst the school children and apathy towards others.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Even though there are existing opportunities, such as the Outward Bound School (OBS) for students of different backgrounds and schools to mix, we must do more to reduce these artificial "class" barriers that have been built.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For a start, schools in the same cluster can conduct their co-curricular activities (CCAs) and related trainings together, to encourage social mixing.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Such partnerships among schools should be made formal, and students will have the opportunities to build more established friendships based upon passion and common interests with their peers in other schools.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In my own youth, my secondary school, which was highly regarded in my neighbourhood, shared a common field, facilities and CCAs groups, like the Marching Band, with a neighbouring school of lesser fame.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We made friends and played games like basketball and volleyball together.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, while our education system continues to mould our younger generation in their formative years to have grit, determination and the drive to achieve, we must not neglect the softer side of education, specifically, empathy.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is a hugely important issue that I cannot emphasise enough of.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In today’s high-tech, fast-changing world, we tend to favour communicating via devices over engaging personally in person.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This results in a certain apathy towards others as we lose that human touch.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Empathy is an essential skill that can help to strengthen relationships, understand the perspectives of others and make our society more gracious.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We need to start bringing back this specific skill to our young, via our education system.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The current syllabus focuses on the classroom and the imparting of theoretical knowledge.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: While that is important, we must give students practical opportunities to impart empathy, getting them to walk the talk.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Schools can adopt a kindergarten, old folks' home, voluntary welfare organisation or pet shelters in their neighborhoods.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The students will be responsible to help run the facility, the programmes, engage the residents or helpers so that they can learn the responsibility of caring and attending to the needs of others.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am heartened to know that a group of 10 university students who clock their Community Involvement Programme (CIP) in their secondary school in an old folks' home continue to take the 6.00 am train every Saturday to the same home in which they were volunteering then.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I believe we can seed the caring heart of the next generation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Last weekend, at our Tampines East ITE Edusave Award Ceremony, I shared the story of one of my colleagues in my company.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Chris started working for my company at age 16.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She started as an hourly paid admin assistant.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She is not the only one taking the path less travelled.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We must continue to ensure our young have different pathways to success and the necessary environment to achieve their aspirations.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: A D7 grade in English should not be a death sentence for someone who is passionate about Accountancy or Chinese Studies.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: No one must be left behind due to our stringent education system.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am glad that there are so many examples of people today who have not travelled the typical journey and have made it.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But each time the story is framed around the immense challenges they had to overcome.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I wonder if more of such successes could be had, if we had a more inclusive education system, especially targeting those of the lower-income group who have the least family support and most difficult challenges.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, Singapore has built a world-class education system from scratch and, because of that, we have been able to navigate the uncertain seas and come out better than before.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Education will continue to be one of the most important factors to affect Singapore’s future, giving our young the right skills, tools and knowledge to chart their futures.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is imperative that we continue to educate and mould our future generation to be ready for the world, and for their future.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Not just with technical knowledge and skills, but also with an empathetic heart and soul.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   The President said in her speech that Singapore has entered the next phase of development.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the past, we can learn from other countries and catch up with them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that, when faced with these challenges, the Government and the people must work together to find solutions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The mindset of the whole country must change as well.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Government, large enterprises and individuals should take our SMEs into consideration when making purchases.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the area of education, many countries are still exploring how to teach according to the students’ aptitude, while upholding education standards and fairness.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Singapore, we have tried many different methods.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Our education system has been evolving constantly from our generation, our children’s generation to our grandchildren’s generation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Parents should not just focus on academic performances.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They should also encourage their children to participate in co-curricular activities (CCAs) which interest them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps that particular CCA may well be the key to their future success.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope parents and the schools can work together to find a more suitable education method for each child.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When are the designs going to be upgraded?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The population in Yishun is increasing and there are more and more young families.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can we rebuild the older gymnasium and the swimming pool into a sports complex with swimming facilities for children to have fun in?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Tampines has Our Tampines Hub; Bedok has the Bedok Integrated Complex; Woodlands has Kampong Admiralty.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the relevant authorities can heed Minister Ng Chee Meng’s call yesterday, "We hear you, we are with you, together we will make it real." We look forward to the day when we "make it real".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As Members of Parliament, we often need to deal with cleaning or neighbourhood dispute issues.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: More often than not, these issues cannot be solved by the relevant authorities alone.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It takes the parties involved to make compromises and shoulder part of the responsibilities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In this area, we need to work harder.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are no standard answers for the above questions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Members of Parliament, public servants or the Government must continue to listen to the views of Singaporeans and work out workable solutions together.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, I rise to put my vote of thanks to the President for delivering a speech that not only inspires but points us to the direction that we must collectively work towards in the coming years.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Our next generation of Ministers are all lined up and ready to run the next lap.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And we are fortunate to have a system where there is an orderly handover of the torch, so that the flame continues to burn.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As I look back the past weeks, the milestone events from the Select Committee hearings to the appointment of new office-bearers would doubtless show our resolve to continue with the way we have been running our country, in the best interest of our people – that is the Singapore way, whatever the naysayers may be hooting.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Unlike them, we are proud to be Singaporeans.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Unlike them, we do not set sail in the same boat with the likes of Sinbad the Sailor.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We do not believe in “whatever will be will be”.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We believe in charting the right course after taking all the relevant readings on the compass.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Regardless of which school your children go to, as long as they are happy, they learn, they make good friends, they are in good schools.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: All schools have the same core syllabus and the teachers and principals are rotated around.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Not every school can be like Raffles Institution (RI) or Raffles Girls’ School (RGS).

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have been very bold in the past few years in tweaking our education system to put less stress on our students and introduce experiential learning.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many of the new ideas introduced are commendable.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Students do not just go to school to gain knowledge.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They are also exposed to community service, there is a lot more outdoor learning, and even at the ITEs, polytechnics and universities, they are put on internships.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These would greatly help to build up a talent pool of thinking and adaptable people as they stream into the job market.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: All these efforts in producing a new generation of young people.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think our country may not have seen the full impact of this new learning because many of the students are still studying, and the numbers that have gotten into the job market is still small.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But I have seen many who come to help me in my Meet-the-People sessions and I must say they are impressive.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As we take steps to move away from the very staid and rigid old system of education, we as parents must also give encouragement to our children and assure them that the school that they are in is a good school.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I want to ask that we as a community would have to move forward with confidence.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, we do not have to go around “chope-ing” seats, rushing into trains, or pretending not to notice that you are taking up the seats meant for the elderly and pregnant women in the train.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need to learn to be more gracious.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Yes, graciousness is something that we all can adopt.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have a children playground in a private estate in Nee Soon South and it is very popular among children, especially in the evenings.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The man living in the unit upstairs was not happy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The man who smokes said, "I have all the right to smoke in my own home".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The man living upstairs said, "I have all the right to have clean air and to protect my health and my family members' health." So, if everyone argues like the two examples above, where do we go from here?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can we be more considerate and show compassion for others?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are we too quick to point fingers at others?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Have we ever paused to think if we are doing enough for our community, our environment and our nation?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can we make the bold change in behaviour, attitudes and so on for the next lap so that we can together have a stake in building up the gracious Singapore?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Help the less privileged and those with special needs so that they too can participate.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, when introducing new policies please ask how this will help to bring down the barriers and let people mix together, irrespective of economic class, race or religion.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We must review what we have done and look at where we must improve, for example, our SMEs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are we not able to do more for SMEs?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need to stay relevant to the world.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Leadership is never so challenged as it is in today’s world.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The need for us to adjust to meet the changed social environment has been a long time coming.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We will build on the foundations laid down by our pioneers who have set the ground.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need to continue to work hard which is our virtue, perhaps harder than our founding generation as the world is changing at very fast pace.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In doing so, we must exercise good judgement and not discard what is working just for the sake of being bold.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We must get some basics right such as getting our society to be more gracious and more considerate.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To accept that we live in a closely-knit community, this initiative and effort must begin with us.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We see very conflicting demands from different people, each with different ideas and each claiming they have their rights to this and that.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If we do not start to address this "your right and my right" issue, the narrative will separate people.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We must act now if we do not want to be known as "a one divided country with divided hearts". 1.46 pm

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To heed the President's call for us to forge a cohesive, caring and inclusive society, particularly for our seniors, I would like to take this opportunity to raise three ideas about how we can smoothen some of the bumps and ripples in our healthcare landscape and to remove some of the friction where it is not needed, so as to promote more equal access to medical services.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As my following comments do concern some adjustments of a fiscal nature, I would like to declare my interest currently as a medical practitioner in a public healthcare institution.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Ministry of Health (MOH) has certainly done very much in this regard, by introducing and expanding many schemes such as the Chronic Disease Management Programme (CDMP) and, more recently, the Flexi-MediSave Programme.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They have also allowed greater use of MediSave for medical scans, and so on.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These measures are effective but can be complex and, at times, may be too restrictive.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The concern, of course, and it is something we all appreciate, is that too loose a policy on MediSave withdrawals could lead to an earlier depletion of our accounts, leaving nothing for us to rely on in later years when medical needs and expenses could be greater.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I am not sure that this worry is always necessarily well founded.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If you look at the statistics over the past few years, the mean MediSave account balances among Singaporeans have been increasing steadily, and a significant number do pass on with remaining balances of fairly appreciable amount in their accounts.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But it could make a meaningful difference to the elderly with multiple or less common conditions requiring more specialised and expensive medications, or who require more medical investigations to better manage their conditions.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Presently, for a patient who has exceeded his MediSave claims limits and who finds it challenging to pay the remainder in cash, he or she has a few options.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One, he can appeal to the Ministry to withdraw more from his MediSave.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Two, he can apply to the Medication Assistance Fund and other welfare schemes.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Or three, he or she could just simply choose to forego treatment or to forgo some of the treatment in excess of what he is willing to pay for in cash.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Allowing for greater MediSave withdrawal in these cases can help a patient avoid trying the welfare route, which ultimately adds to public expenditures, and also encourage compliance with treatment.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If the patient follows on with treatment, then the future consequences of his condition, if left improperly managed or sub-optimally managed, would be less and the eventual costs to both the patient and society would ultimately be lower.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am of the opinion that further loosening of the MediSave purse strings would not lead to over-servicing or over-consumption.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our treatment management schemes have been strengthened over the past few years.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, agencies such as the Agency for Care Effectiveness (ACE) are now putting in place guidelines about what constitutes effective treatment and what is not.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The introduction of the PG package, for instance, a few years ago, with very generous benefits, has also not led to worrying levels of over-consumption or over-servicing within the public healthcare system thus far.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, I think it is just and right that the Government has been absorbing the GST charged to subsidised medical services in public healthcare institutions for many years now, at considerable cost to the Ministry.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We are also trying, of course, to shift our model of care beyond the hospital and back to the community by strengthening our primary healthcare networks.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While the majority of hospital care is now provided for by public hospitals, the majority of Singaporeans still choose to visit their family doctors or general practitioners (GPs), rather than polyclinics, for their primary care needs.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would be a major deviation from our GST framework, which favours a flat system with later reliefs or Government transfers.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Philosophically, I realise this is a slippery slope, but in practical terms it would be very much in keeping with the intent of current policy that already absorbs GST from subsidised healthcare services.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I wish to emphasise that this suggestion refers only to primary care services and not for hospital or other types of medical care.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also appreciate that, at present, most solo practices, for instance, are not GST-registered.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But with the emergence of more group practices and with the increasing cost of healthcare, the number of healthcare providers that need to pay GST may increase in the future.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What constitutes a provider of primary healthcare services can be defined and licensed, and this is also an issue that can perhaps be addressed when we debate the Healthcare Services Act later this year.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I appreciate that there will be issues with the implementation of such a scheme, but I certainly believe that it merits consideration.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Although a hallmark of MediShield Life is that no one is excluded, including those with pre-existing conditions, like virtually all medical insurance systems, there remain some gaps.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For instance, I would like to draw your attention to two areas.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have been strongly encouraging parenthood and it would serve as greater assurance to would-be parents that the mother’s medical care can be covered in the uncommon instances of complications related to the pregnancy.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have come a long way; we have passed 50 years successfully as an Independent nation, and we are now moving on to 200 years after the founding of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We now have a new generation of Singaporeans and Singaporean leaders that will steer us towards SG100.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is my hope that our healthcare system remains future-ready, and also friction-free where it counts.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I was moved when the President reminded us that we are an exceptional country.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes, some of us take our existence, rights and privileges for granted because we compare ourselves with other developed nations of the world.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But as we all know, we do not have what they have – no hinterland, no natural resources, not even enough natural sources of water.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Due to these insufficiencies, despite our stability, prosperity and progress, anxiety and insecurities about our future surface from time to time.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On quite a number of occasions, people I met asked me whether Singapore would be able to continue to survive and if a bright future would remain for our children.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One person I met recently asked if Singapore would continue to do well in 20 years’ time.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think citizens all over the world ask themselves similar questions about their nations’ economic and political future, but not questions about their countries’ existence and survival.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I do not think any of our ASEAN neighbours have any doubt that their countries will still be around for their future generations, regardless of political turmoil or economic crises.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My answer to the question about our existence is another question.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are many answers to this question, including our roles as a global transportation, commerce and financial hub.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It all boils down to our usefulness and relevance to the world.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, as long as we have value, our survival is guaranteed; and when we add value, we thrive.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Every generation has to find its own raison d’etre.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because we are so small and there are so few of us, literally, we have to work exceptionally well as a team.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In all the best teams, leaders and team members are constantly communicating and updating one another to facilitate the necessary adjustments and corrections.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must keep channels of feedback open and continuously address the issues affecting our people.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: People have to be able to trust our leadership and Government which must remain honest, have integrity and be free from corruption.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Very importantly, the Government must ensure a fair and equitable system for all, which will assure Singaporeans and motivate everyone to put in his best effort.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They will be able to see that there are multiple paths to success and unlimited opportunities.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As long as they work hard, they can be assured of upward social mobility.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps the Government can look into providing such guidance and assistance services permanently to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How do we resolve the inherent conflict between meritocracy, which rewards ability, skill and talent, and the resultant income inequality?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A compassionate community which is inclusive of people from different strata will help to ensure our country’s stability and success.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When one of ours trip and fall, we should stop to help him get up again so that we can continue the race together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important that our system has values, such as mutual support and cohesiveness.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the face of challenges posed by a disruptive innovative economy, we need to ensure that Singaporeans can manage such rapid advancements confidently and leverage upon them for our benefits and life improvement.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We shall not be limited by our physical and ability constraints.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The disadvantaged can also benefit from technological innovation and get elevated socially.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Increasingly, in an integrated globalised economy, opportunities are no longer limited by borders.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The cost of living remains one of the key concerns among those I meet.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have Pioneer Generation offices (PGOs) that did the good job to support those in the PGs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A similar approach could be considered to ensure that such households are assured of attention and assistance by the Government.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government also needs to keep in tune with the younger generations and ensure that the polices are up to date that could be tailored to meet their aspirations as they are vital to our nation building.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to continue to strive for real income increase and guard against the rise in cost of living as the impact on the middle- and low-income groups may not be easily eliminated by redistribution through grants and subsidies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The lower income groups are not only affected financially but emotionally and psychologically as well, as they perceive escalating prices pushing items beyond their reach.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have to put in more effort to monitor the challenges faced by our lower-income and middle-income groups closely and policies are updated to ensure that their aspirations are within reach.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our existing public housing policies have been successful and should be preserved.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I urge prudence in changing the ratio as it serves Singaporeans well in racial and community harmony while meeting the aspirations and dreams of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: HDB should or could challenge its present parameters and further expand the provision of flat types and facilities to meet the higher expectations of Singaporeans while retaining affordability and reach.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, a new type of flats could perhaps be privately designed with condominium standard or the like but are built and managed by HDB and Town Councils without fences to encourage integration with the other HDB flats around.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It warrants a rethink of the potential impact on the efforts to build a cohesive and inclusive society and preventing widening social impact of income inequity.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These three characteristics have their pros and cons.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They have generated the spirit of perseverance and the drive for progress of our people.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, they also created some problems at the same time.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If they are not dealt with appropriately, they can also generate utilitarianism and make people profit-driven and indifferent towards each other.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will hinder our efforts to build an inclusive and united society.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I feel we need to redefine what success is.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I agree that the Government should broaden the definition of success.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Success should not be just about academic achievement and material comfort.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We continue learning as long as we live.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should emphasise skills training, create opportunities for each Singaporean to fulfil his potential and achieve success, thereby building a prosperous society enjoyed by all.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Where there is a will, there is way.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should turn the three "K"s to three "B"s – “bo kiasi"（不怕死）, "bo kiasu" (不怕输), "bo kia jingzheng" (不怕竞争).

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In other words, not afraid of dying, not afraid of losing and not afraid of competition.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: You may remember that during the five-kilometre run in the 2016 Olympics, an American and a New Zealand runner tripped but they helped each other to get up.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During the 2017 UK Marathon, a runner, Swansea Harrier Matthew Rees, stopped to help another runner, David Wyeth, to complete the last segment of the run.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is how we should build an inclusive, caring and prosperous society.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, we are descendants of people who had created a miracle island and I am confident that we will be able to overcome these challenges and build a stronger Singapore for our future generations. 2.09 pm

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Two approaches to achieve this are: first, tackling inequality by providing the right support to those who need it, such as in skills training and employment; and second, rolling out policies for the growing elderly population, such as helping older workers stay employed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I speak in support of this with special focus on older workers and, especially, baby boomers, and women at the workplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: One barometer of an inclusive society is having an inclusive workplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This means helping different groups of Singaporeans who are able and willing to work, to stay employed and find fulfilment, even as circumstances change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: An inclusive workplace is not an automatic nor easy outcome.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But there are concrete ways the Government and our partners can work towards in order to create and sustain it, such as being inclusive in helping mature workers and being inclusive in creating flexible work arrangements, which is especially helpful for women.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We need to help our mature workers, including the baby boomers who are now entering the retirement phase of their lives, by keeping them active and connected to society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: While some seniors will want to retire to spend time with their grandchildren and hobbies, some will find purpose in continuing their current roles, and others may wish to take smaller, bite-size roles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Some mature workers are also in transition between careers and welcome opportunities in the care sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will need to cater to their different wants to keep them integrated in society while playing a meaningful role.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The World Economic Forum points out that by 2020, the global population of those over 60 years of age will reach one billion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: By 2050, it is expected to reach two billion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This trend, combined with a general decline in birth rates, is leading to a situation where the world’s old will outnumber the young.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is not just a statistical quirk, but a demographic result of great significance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Oxford Economics and Haver Analytics posit that there will be sharp deceleration and, indeed, negative labour supply growth, and Singapore could be among the worst hit in terms of its impact on economic growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: However, in Singapore, as Minister Chan Chun Sing said on Monday, we should not let challenges define us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Instead, we should see ageing as an opportunity to do things differently, or as Mr Ravi Menon, Managing Director of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, puts it, “Demographics is not destiny”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The good news is that our healthy life expectancy is also increasing, with people staying healthier for longer, and there is also an opportunity to better leverage the abilities of those over 60, by adjusting workplace policies and redefining what “retirement” means.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Seizing opportunities arising from productive longevity is, therefore, crucial to Singapore’s success as a nation and it is a key priority.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Extending working life and promoting senior entrepreneurship are increasingly perceived as economic drivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Fostering both can enable older people to leverage their institutional knowledge, wisdom and insights to continue contributing positively to the community and economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For existing healthcare workers who wish to continue in their current roles, we facilitate their re-employment through strategies such as job re-design, training and re-employment facilitation workshops.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In the case of nurses, who form the bulk of the healthcare workforce and where we most need manpower, we have also seen an increase in the number of nurses working past the retirement age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This flexibility supports older nurses so that they can continue to contribute at a pace that they are comfortable with.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our public healthcare institutions have also implemented workplace initiatives such as elder-friendly features like placing a magnifying glass on medication carts, and larger fonts for signages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We are also automating some labour-intensive care activities such as lifting and transferring of patients using mobile hoists and bed transporters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This will reduce the strain on older workers and allow them to continue in their roles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For those who wish to take on part-time or smaller, bite-sized roles, we have also been working with our partners to increase the number of micro-jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For example, several of our public hospitals have created Basic Care Assistant (BCA) positions, where locals with no prior healthcare experience are trained to provide care in areas such as feeding and patient transfer in the wards on a part-time basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For mature workers looking to switch careers, we provide multiple pathways and training to facilitate picking up of new skills to join us in our care transformation journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
