text: This PCP will complement the current PCP-RN diploma programme at Nanyang Polytechnic and provide an additional pathway for mid-career conversion into nursing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We are also working with WSG and e2i on programmes to facilitate employment and transition of mature workers, especially professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) who may be displaced due to restructuring in other industries, into suitable roles in the healthcare sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Older workers as a segment of the workforce do not represent a monolithic group.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: They are of differing ages, educational backgrounds and circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: While some work simply because they want to remain gainfully employed, others, like Minister Ng Chee Meng said yesterday, need to work as they have expenses, mortgages and dependents relying on them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Hence, I support Minister Ng's idea of forming a new Tripartite Committee to take a closer and perhaps more granular look at ways to support mature workers to continue working if they choose to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Singaporeans in different life segments and at different life stages have varying needs in their careers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Those starting a family or looking after their elderly parents or grandchildren may be looking to balance their work with family commitments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Many women ask for this support in flexible work arrangements (FWAs) and actually the men too.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Adopting FWAs will help us better cater to the needs of our healthcare workforce at different life stages, and retain them in the workforce, especially our women and older workers, for a win-win.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For instance, we have piloted FWAs for nurses, who are the largest staff group in the public healthcare sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have engaged nurses, and we know that this is important for many of them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Today, more than 100 wards across the public healthcare institutions have adopted FWAs for nurses, in the form of more flexible shift work hours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This helps them to avoid the binary option of either being employed or unemployed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To further scale up FWA adoption for nurses, the public healthcare institutions will progressively move to electronic rostering, or e-rostering, starting from the second half of 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This shift will help to support nurse managers in managing more complex shift rostering of staff and empower them to support FWAs in a bigger way.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Globally, gender pay gap persists, including in Singapore, although we rank relatively well even among the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries, ahead of countries like Australia and the UK.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: A reason often attributed to this pay gap is men's greater share of senior jobs as more women drop out of the workforce due to family care-giving duties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: An article in The Economist noted that men’s and women's salaries start diverging from the child-bearing years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This "motherhood penalty" is often followed by a "good daughter penalty" when elderly parents require care and daughters often prove more conscientious than sons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: So, here, I am tempted to note that the men just do not get it!

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Quoting figures from the UK's Office of National Statistics, the median pay gap is only 2% among full-time workers in their 30s yet jumps to 14% in their 40s and 16% in their 50s.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As our population ages, a so called "caring economy" is emerging.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The need to provide care to the elderly can have a significant impact on the workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Working caregivers must often take time off or leave the workforce altogether.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As The Economist article highlights, the "caring economy" disproportionately affects women because they make up the majority of caregivers, which also negatively impacts gender parity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: FWAs, such as flexi work hours, work from home arrangements, or part-time work would better allow caregivers to remain in the workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Besides providing funding support and the Tripartite Standard on FWAs, moving forward, we could, adopting a tripartite approach and help companies who may not have the know-how to implement FWAs to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Over the years, we have been increasing support for caregivers, such as expanding day care and home care capacity, providing caregiver training grant and training, respite care and elder sitter service for dementia patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Nonetheless, as our population ages and caregiving needs increase, we must look at more ways to better support caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources and Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Policymakers can continue to roll out initiatives to foster and support such an environment but creating a truly inclusive workplace would require individuals and companies – shareholder, management and staff – changing within themselves in terms of mindsets and prejudices and changing their corporate culture.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: One of the key priorities the President set in her maiden Address was for Singaporeans to live in a fair and just society based on meritocracy, and at the same time, to strive to leave no one behind.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This aspiration of building an inclusive society is a familiar reframe in this Chamber.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: At each change of leadership or milestone in our political calendar, it is prudent for this Government to take stock of the well-being of Singaporeans from all strata of society to ensure no one gets left behind.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But beyond such periodic refrain, I certainly welcome the challenge put forth by the President for this Government to go for both changes this time and not to contend with marginal tweaks in the next phase of our nationhood.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: While we can choose to live in awe and respect of what our pioneer generation had achieved, we certainly should not be tempted to dwell in the shadows of the past just to avoid rocking the boat.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We also should not be tempted to just apply a patchwork of measures to fix any system that is out of sync with the changing times, in the hope that some of the problems will go away.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Although this Government has acknowledged its concern over the lack of diversity in our schools and housing estates, it is somewhat not as alarmed by the finding as explained by Minister Grace Fu early this year.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Nevertheless, we can certainly agree that if this class divide is left unchecked, our aspiration of building a nation undivided by race, language or religion would be tinted by the ugly reality of class-based society.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The lack of our diversity in our school is one issue we need to address to tackle the problem of social inequality.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This is important because this Government views education as a key pillar of social mobility and I do support that wholeheartedly.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Long before the release of the IPS study on this issue, the principle of Raffles Institution in 2015, proclaimed that the school has become a middle-class school, catering largely to affluent families and was no longer truly representative of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: He said, and I quote, "A long period of conditioning means that we often fail to see elitism even when it is staring at us in the face." Although what he said then was not something new, such frank admission by an insider from one of the oldest schools in Singapore is certainly noteworthy.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But what struck me most in that speech was the challenge he put forth.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: He went on to say, "What really matters more now is what we do with this reality and knowledge." So, how can we address this inequality and the lack of diversity in our schools to prevent a class divide from taking root in our society?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It also wishes to actively promote interaction amongst students of all backgrounds through applied learning, co-curricular activities (CCAs) and Outward Bound School camps.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: They will send their children to expensive tuition and enrichment classes and there is no shortage of firm believers in such classes to deliver the high T-score and distinction for their children.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This will perpetuate the message that if you have the money, your child will stand a better chance of getting good grades.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The lack of diversity in our schools will only grow.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As for the proposed initiative to promote interaction amongst students of all backgrounds, I must say those interactions are rather fleeting in nature and are confined to small groups of students each time.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Such interactions, I am afraid, are rather piecemeal in nature and they will not even put a dent on the class divide issue.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Does MOE know how many students in GEP have undergone test preparation even though MOE has stated in its website that parents should not enrol their children for such activities?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: MOE says such GEP preparation activities could inflate pupils' scores and not reflect their actual potential.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Such acknowledgment by MOE offers simple proof or ample proof that parents can give their children a headstart if they can afford it.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What will the profile of GEP and Special Assistance Plan (SAP) students tell us about race and income then?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Does MOE know whether students from elite schools are spending more time on tuition and enrichment then their counterparts from the neighbourhood schools?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Does MOE know whether the tuition culture here had a hand in helping our students achieve the impressive test results in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2015 chart that was presented in this Chamber yesterday?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am sure MOE would agree and knowing this number is important.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Any measure formulated to address social inequality or lack of diversity in our schools must take into consideration the entire education ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Without this information, any formulated measure would be, as in the words of the President, "tweaking things at the margin".

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Does the Minister not agree that it makes a world of difference when smaller neighbourhood schools are resourced with the same amount of funding as the popular schools?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Is the Minister willing to do something bold in the area of equitable funding for all schools?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This move will ensure a good mix and spread of students from all spectrum of primary schools going into the popular secondary schools.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This will definitely introduce diversity into the so-called elite schools.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This will also prevent elitism from entrenching itself in any of the popular schools.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For parents who want their children to attend a popular secondary school, every primary school is now a good school to start the journey.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some may question that this is not meritocratic.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: They have certainly earned their place with direct admission into a school of their choice by finishing top in their respective primary schools.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The proposal is still based on meritocracy but at the local level.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: If you have the resources, the money, the proper nutrition, the proper training, the proper technique, you will stand a better chance of coming top in whatever you do.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Can we honestly say every student is starting from the same base because every school is a good school, so may the best student win?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What we want them to learn and experience in school now will determine what the future holds for the next generation.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We can either teach them about the importance of equality and diversity or let them live it and experience it first-hand in the fair and just society that leaves no behind as set out by the President.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The late Encik Yusof Ishak in his first President's Address to a newly elected Parliament in 1968 outlined three objectives to achieve for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The first two objectives were to build an effective defence capability and to achieve greater economic growth.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: These two objectives were to be brought up time and again, in one form or another, by subsequent Presidents, and for good reasons.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We live in a world that is constantly changing and evolving.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: These objectives will need to move with the times.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The third point highlighted by Encik Yusof was about the need to enhance our national consciousness of the problems that will beseech a young nation in time to come.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Specifically, he said Singaporeans must learn to place national interest above personal or sectional interests.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Now that we are conscious of the issue of social inequality in society that is gravitating to a class divide, what more can we do with this reality and knowledge?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: And I welcome his commitment that this Government will continue to improve its policy and not to stop at the proposed measures.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 2.55 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 2.35 pm until 2.55 pm.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The President’s speech marks the formal opening of the Parliament session.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The speech itself describes the Government’s agenda for the rest of the term.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Addenda to the speech then lay out the specific programmes of each Ministry.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is a tradition we inherited from the UK, where the Queen delivers a speech drafted by the elected Government – although it is called the Queen's Speech – and the speech highlights the Government’s legislative programme.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The global order, which is based on openness, globalisation and free trade, has come under great pressure.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Relations between the big powers – especially the United States (US) and China, and also the US and Russia – are under stress.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is not clear whether the institutions and international rules that have underpinned world peace and security for the last few decades will change.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if they change, there will be significant long-term implications for Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are opening a new chapter after SG50.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It will be a new phase of our social and economic development.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have the responsibility, and the privilege, of reimagining and rebuilding Singapore over the next 50 years and more.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are also going through a significant generational change.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I gave my inputs and I endorsed what they produced, because as a Prime Minister, I am still ultimately responsible for the Government's agenda.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But my main role is to be supportive, to help the 4G Ministers present and implement the agenda, and to see through as much of it as possible while I am a Prime Minister.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Today, I will speak about five aspects of the President's Speech.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: First, coping with the external changes; next, growing our economy; third, ensuring social mobility; fourth, maintaining social cohesion; and finally, ensuring good politics and leadership.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Globalisation, which has delivered growth and stability for many countries, including Singapore, has come under pressure.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Countries, particularly in the West, are questioning the benefits of openness and free trade, and of the free movement of people.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The US has been, thus far, the champion and sponsor of the post-war international system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They were generous to others, sharing technology and know-how.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They spent blood and treasure to maintain global peace.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They believed that all these was in their own "enlightened self-interest".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But now, many Americans no longer believe this, including the Trump Administration.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They feel that other countries are benefiting more from the global system, and benefiting at the expense of the US.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They want to make sure that the US will always benefit directly – item by item, country by country, and not just generally, from upholding a system which is good for everybody and therefore indirectly good for the US.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, the US has made trade a top issue, especially trade with China.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In other words, it is not just the two participants who are affected or the amount of, whether it is steel or aluminium or soya beans or cars which is not exported and which cannot be traded, but the whole multilateral system, the system of rules which ensures that countries big and small, have played on a level-playing field have their place in the sun and can contribute to and benefit from this international network of cooperation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And it is a system which we have depended upon in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Therefore, the trade tensions threaten global prosperity, especially for smaller countries like Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The trade disputes can also affect the overall relations between the powers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The US and China are jockeying for position and advantage.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The US is still stronger, especially militarily, but China is growing in power, influence and confidence.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if there is mutual distrust and rivalry between the two, it is but a small step from a trade disagreement to a wider and more serious quarrel.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The US and China are far from going to war with each other, but it is not clear which way their relations will tilt.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If they tilt towards more conflict, it will be bad not only for the two powers, but for the rest of the world as well.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But if relations tilt to the other extreme, and the two powers agree to divide up the world between them, and set rules that only benefit them, that would be just as detrimental, especially for small countries which will have no say.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As a small and open country, Singapore will always be vulnerable to what happens around us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As Mr Lee Kuan Yew used to say, "When elephants fight, the grass suffers, but when they make love, the grass suffers also".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Therefore, we must be aware of what is happening around us, and prepare ourselves for changes and surprises.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Close to home, Malaysia saw a historic change last week, in its General Election.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As Malaysia's closest neighbour, we need to pay close attention to our relationship with them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The two countries have deep historical, economic and people-to-people ties.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have enjoyed good relations with Malaysia under the former Prime Minister Najib Razak and cooperated on major projects that benefit both sides.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have also worked with Dr Mahathir and several of his team before.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We completed joint projects with Malaysia when Dr Mahathir was last the Prime Minister, including building the Second Link at Tuas.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And I also know Mr Anwar Ibrahim well because he was my counterpart when I was Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Indonesia is having elections too – local elections this year and national elections the next.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have good working relations with President Jokowi, as I did with President Yudhoyono before.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I hope we can maintain friendly and productive ties with Indonesia too.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Regardless of political cycles or election outcomes, we will work hard on relations with our two neighbours.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Their success makes for a more peaceful and prosperous region, and that is good for us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the President's speech, she spoke about how Singapore must remain a nation of opportunities.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This, to me, is the heart of our nation-building journey.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our forefathers came to this land, because they sought better lives for themselves and their families.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When Independence was thrust upon us and the odds were stacked against us, our pioneer generation dug in and slogged to build a nation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Their children and grandchildren took up the torch after them, and improved Singapore year by year.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This sense of opportunity, of possibility and hope is the spark that has inspired generations of Singaporeans to dream big, and to work hard to realise those dreams.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must always sustain this confidence that we can build a better life for ourselves and future generations of Singaporeans, that we can make tomorrow better than today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Nationally, this means growing our economy, creating new possibilities and expanding our horizons.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Individually, it means improving the life of every Singaporean, in a fair, open and a cohesive society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: One of the top priorities of the Government is therefore to keep the economy growing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are in a strong position today, because our economy has grown steadily for the past 50 years and more.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have enjoyed high growth for much of this half century – even from time to time exceeding 10% per annum.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Today, our per capita income is higher than Japan's.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They worry that their children will not have better lives than they themselves do today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But let me put the numbers in perspective.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: First, 2% to 4% is in fact quite good for a mature economy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: South Korea and Taiwan are growing around this rate too.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Second, 2%-4% is just an estimate, based on our current stage of economic development.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is not the limit to our efforts or to our ambitions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Individual companies and individual industries can certainly do better, especially if they come up with a more innovative product or if they expand into new markets, till virgin ground.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are pushing ahead with our economic upgrade.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The only question is whether we can seize them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In Indonesia, in Jakarta, the tech scene is vibrant, buzzing with energy and talent.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They are companies which have become worth more than $1 billion; and Indonesia has four of them – Gojek, Traveloka, Bukalapak and Tokopedia.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Vietnam, Thailand and Malaysia have lively tech sectors too.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, if we can build up our own tech sector while connecting with theirs, we will prosper together.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are making good progress also, developing frontier technologies in artificial intelligence (AI), fintech and in advanced manufacturing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have attracted leading AI researchers and companies to Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Nanyang Technological University (NTU) has built a reputation as a leading centre in AI.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Alibaba Group recently opened a research institute on AI together with NTU, which is its first outside research institute outside China.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When I visited Beijing recently, I went to see Didi Chuxing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is the equivalent of Grab or Uber.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And the Didi Chief Technology Officer (CTO), Bob Zhang, told me the graduates were doing very well.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In fintech, MAS has developed Singapore to become a fintech hub, just within the last two to three years – the right rules and the right encouragement, the right openness, the right light touch and the flower blossoms.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: More than 400 fintech firms are now based here and so are over 30 innovation labs and research centres set up by multinational corporations (MNCs).

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In advanced manufacturing, the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) is collaborating with multi-nationals, with local companies and universities to develop new technologies in aerospace and precision engineering.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, there are many possibilities for us to grow our economy and to reinvent and redevelop Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Individual Singaporeans must see progress in their lives, must feel that the future is bright and must know that each one of us has our stake in it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This means sharing growth widely and equitably to improve the lives of all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It also means fully maximising the talents and efforts of our people, and getting the most capable and reliable people into the most consequential jobs where they can make the most difference and the greatest contribution.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In other words, making sure there is social mobility so that our meritocracy continues to work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How do we know if our meritocracy is working?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And finally, a capable person must face minimal social impediments, minimal social impediments to be accepted, to contribute and to be in a position to lead in society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And in the long term, this last part – keeping the social impediments down – is the most difficult to sustain.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We want Singapore society to maintain an informal and egalitarian tone, where people interact freely and comfortably as equals, and there are no rigid class distinctions or barriers that keep good people down.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is important but it is beyond the Government’s ability to bring about alone.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Society itself has to be open and permeable.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Each one of us must carry those attitudes, values, and norms, that willingness to welcome talent and welcome ability to keep the system the way it is.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Any society which has been stable for a long time tends to stratify and it becomes less socially mobile.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For example, the UK and India have long entrenched hierarchies and very fixed notions of class and or, in India, caste, which they have found very difficult to overcome.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Singapore is still a young country of 50 years and notions of class and hierarchy have not yet calcified.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our social cues, our markers, our norms – they are still evolving, and we do not want them to evolve in a wrong direction and contribute to class divisions and rigidities.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Social cues are important because they can become ways to pigeonhole or to exclude others, knowingly or unknowingly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In Britain, your accent and the way you speak, can define your status in society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Do you have a posh private school accent?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Do you speak like a professional who has been to Oxbridge?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Do you speak as a working-class person, with a local accent, regional accent?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Then, you know you come from a certain part of London, and you are a certain class of person, not very high up the totem pole.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: George Bernard Shaw wrote, “An Englishman’s way of speaking absolutely classifies him".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It pigeonholes him into his social class, you listen to him, you know, do you respect him, do you look down on him, do you give him orders or do you say "Yes, Sir?" And he went on to say "absolutely classifies him.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The moment he talks, he makes some other Englishman despise him”.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And it is true, if you do not have an upper-class accent, you are marked down straightaway.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that is why Singapore schools put emphasis on teaching students to speak good English.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In other words, if you cannot speak proper English, well, you are down there.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If you can speak proper English, the doors open for you.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And I think this would close the doors on many from less privileged families.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that is why the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI) continues to have campaigns to teach people to speak proper English.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There are other social markers that can signal and entrench class differences.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Members may recall the recent fuss over an unauthorised secondary school Social Studies guidebook.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It contained a table that had sweeping generalisations about people in Singapore from high and low socioeconomic status (SES).

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For instance, those from supposedly low SES speak Singlish, play soccer or basketball and eat at hawker centres, while those from high SES speak formal English, play golf or tennis, and only eat at fine restaurants.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Luckily, it was not a guidebook approved by MOE.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Lifestyle choices can indeed become separators in society, distinguishing marks.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What you eat, how you dress, where you go for holidays, what games you play, what clubs you belong to.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In every society, people have ways to show who is in and who is out.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You take one look at a person, or you listen to him just for a moment and you can already place him.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But the general tone in Singapore is one of restraint.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If you wear a chunky gold watch and dress flashily, instead of being impressed, people may think you are a loan shark!

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must discourage people from flaunting their social advantages.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We should frown upon those who go for ostentatious displays of wealth and status, or worse, look down on others less well-off or privileged.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We should emphasise our commonalities, not accentuate our differences.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And so, you see, if you look around the Chamber, everybody informally dressed, discussing serious matters of state.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They occupy the key leadership positions in society – in government, in academia, in business, in professions, in politics.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Members of the elite share similar backgrounds, interests, and social spaces.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They may be alumni of the same schools, they may have done business with one another, or they may have worked in the same professions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They know one another and have interacted with one another in different roles over long periods through their lives.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They are useful for people to know one another, to get things done informally, to share an implicit understanding of the interests of their society, and to feel a collective sense of responsibility for the society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They must not close up, they must not form glass ceilings.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It must not be difficult or impossible for others with talent or ability, but lacking the right backgrounds and connections, to be welcomed into the elite group, to rise to the top, to take their rightful place and make their full contribution.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If this happened, not only would social mobility be frustrated, but soon, the elite group would start to only look after its own interests and fail in their duty to lead and care for the rest of society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Raffles Institution (RI) is one of our most popular schools.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I did not go to RI, but I can tell you it is a good school.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The new RI principal has been putting in effort, speaking to parents of potential students in primary schools across Singapore, to encourage them to apply to RI.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To his surprise, some of the parents told him they did not want to send their child there.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Not because they thought their child could not keep up with the academic demands, but because they feared he would not be able to fit in with other more well-off students.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And all the students get along confidently and comfortably.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, no parent needs to worry that he cannot afford to send his child to RI or that his child will feel out of place.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But if such a perception exists and discourages promising students from applying to the school, it is not good for RI, it is not good for Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: RI knows what it has to do in order to uphold its egalitarian tradition.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Government policies and programmes must, and do, support social mobility and meritocracy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We make sure that the fundamentals are done well – quality education, home ownership and affordable healthcare, which improve the life of every Singaporean.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We give everyone a good education, and now we are investing heavily in preschool, to give all Singaporean kids and in fact, almost babies as well, a good start in life.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have a strong social safety net, with targeted assistance schemes, so that those with difficulties are not left behind and forgotten.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And we intervene with extra help – whether in education, housing, healthcare or jobs training – for those who need it, to enable them to take full advantage of the opportunities.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Above all, our education system must stay open.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have set aside places in primary schools for children without affiliation to these schools, and we will do more if necessary.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are expanding opportunities for students from different schools to interact, through sports, community activities and the Outward Bound School.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Last year, I visited Outward Bound School for their 50th anniversary celebrations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I had attended the course 50 years ago.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I chatted with Nicholas Conceicao, who is the Executive Director of OBS.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And I told him that when I went to OBS 50 years ago as a 15-year-old, they only took in two students per secondary school.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, in a group of 130-odd, there were people from 50 to 60 different schools, different language streams and very different social backgrounds.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And we all had to get together because they had us mixed up properly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We went through the course together, we became good friends, and came away understanding the diversity of our society better, and how we could all work together.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because for 17 days, at that impressionable age, it is an intense experience.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You are put through physical stress, you are emotionally put to your limits, you have to work with others, there is very little that you can do alone.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if you do not make friends, you are miserable.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And you have to make friends across boundaries.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, I recounted this and Nicholas told me that today, well, because of the larger numbers, they cannot take in students from 60 or 70 schools at a time, but they take in students from two to three schools at a time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And nowadays, the students all speak English, but still, he finds clear differences in the cultures and interests of the students from the different schools and even in the way they use language.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, it is all speaking English, but different interests, different vocabulary, really different world perspectives, almost.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: At OBS, the students still learn to work in teams.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, when they pitch a tent or build a raft, or safely belay someone on an obstacle course, they must work closely with teammates; you cannot do it alone.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And so, the students learn to bridge their differences and to trust one another.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When that opens, even more students will benefit from this experience.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are doing many things to improve social mobility, but I have to be honest with you – there are no easy solutions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Many ideas have been proposed and tried out.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Political philosophers, statesmen, all powerful human minds have been brought to bear to try to deal with this conundrum of how to keep the society spry, open, stable and there have been no magic bullets.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And the most successful models perhaps are the Scandinavian countries, but even they have seen widening social inequality in recent times.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have to understand that this is what they call a wicked problem.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is a problem with no easy solution, which we will discuss rightly, repeatedly in this House through the years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our strategy in Singapore has been more successful than most.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And now that our society is more settled, we must work harder to keep the pathways open and to level people up.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We will learn from our own experience and the experience of others.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Spot what looks promising, but please also recognise what will not work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Some people have suggested, I read in the newspapers, a Universal Basic Income, which is a neat idea; so far, unproven anywhere in the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Finns tried it and aborted the experiment early.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is in fact very hard to do.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if anyone can come up with a better alternative, certainly, we will consider it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the end, the Government must focus on practical, effective policies.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As a society, we must uphold clear social norms that minimise social barriers and encourage mobility, so as to keep our meritocratic system working well for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Meritocracy is about individuals having opportunities and being successful.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But we must also be successful together, as one people, one society and one nation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that is what social cohesion is about.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must feel a sense of social responsibility and concern for our fellow citizens, without which our society cannot hold together.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What holds us together is not our pink NRICs, but the shared experiences that we build together over time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We grow up together in national schools, and we are comfortable around each other, regardless of our family backgrounds.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We go through National Service, building brotherhood and camaraderie when we march and fight together.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We eat at hawker centres, regardless whether we are rich and poor.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We learn the habits and preferences of different races and religions and we help neighbours out when they are in need.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And unlike in some other countries, there is no social stigma to living in public housing or taking the bus or the train.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We celebrate our successes together, such as SG50 recently, and every National Day.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And when crises hit, we go through them side by side.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Or even 20 years ago, before the 9/11 and before SARS.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But nation-building will always be a work in progress, because the forces that pull Singaporeans in different directions never go away.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Race, language and religion are enduring fault lines.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: From the start, we knew that they could divide and destroy us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Take, for example, the influence of China and India on our own ethnic groups on Chinese Singaporeans and Indian Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: These are two vast nations, even civilisations that are growing in strength and confidence.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It will be a very long time before we become immune to their ethnic, cultural or economic pulls.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Furthermore, the relationship is complicated, because on the one hand, we want to maintain our separate identity as a multiracial, sovereign country but, on the other hand, we want to say we speak Mandarin, we have overseas Indians, we have ethnic links, we have cultural ties, we have an inside track.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, between the two, there is a tension and we have to keep that balance and maintain our position, and our cohesion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Over time, a Singaporean Malay identity has emerged clearly but still, it overlaps with the Malays in Malaysia, both in terms of race as well as religion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And the call for a global "ummah" – a community of the Muslims around the world – has powerful appeal.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Beyond race, language and religion, we must work at building bridges between different groups in society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Traditionally, when we talk about social cohesion, we think of race, language and religion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But if you look at it in other dimensions, there are other gradients, other possible fault lines, other ways where we have to strengthen our social cohesion and become closer together.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: One of them is between unions and management.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Another one is between old citizens and new.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Labour Movement is one institution vital to our social cohesion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because of the tripartite partnership, labour management relations are a source of strength for us, unlike in many other countries where unions and managements are bitterly opposed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Whereas in Singapore, labour harmony is secured with the help of a strong National Trades Union Congress (NTUC), as we sing at every May Day Rally, slightly out of tune.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And now, Mr Ng Chee Meng in NTUC will carry on this work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Another bridge we need to build is to our new citizens.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: First generation immigrants into any country will always take time to settle down, to understand the nuances of the culture and character, and to progressively integrate into the society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that is what happens in the past with previous waves of first-generation Singaporeans over the last 200 years and that is a necessary process which has to happen, as we continue to have an inflow of people to join us and become Singapore Citizens.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The new arrivals have chosen to make Singapore their home and they will contribute to our country, our society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have to make every effort to mix and to interact with everyone else.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For our part, we should welcome them, we should support them in their journey to become Singaporeans, as others have helped our forefathers and helped ourselves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Therefore, there is much work to do to maintain our social cohesion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To continue to grow Singapore – reinventing our economy, creating new possibilities for the future.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To ensure that Singapore is always a land of opportunity, a meritocratic, fair and just society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To hold Singaporeans together in one cohesive society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Can the next generation of leaders build on our shared experiences of 50 years and maintain the sense of collective mission?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Can they work to improve the lives of all Singaporeans and not the interests of narrow groups, so that they pass on an even stronger and more united Singapore?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They are overseeing their own portfolios and projects, they are explaining their ideas to Singaporeans, they are implementing policies and making them work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Many of them joined in the last three GEs, from 2006 onward, so about over the last 12 years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have also promoted promising backbenchers to become office holders, including in the recent reshuffle.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is a strong team of able men and women, with a balanced combination of skills and strengths.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They are gaining experience, they are willing to serve and, most importantly, their hearts are in the right place.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We need new leaders for each generation, from each generation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because each generation has its own challenges to tackle and tough choices to make.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The international order may well also be different.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Some hard truths will always remain for Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But even old problems may need new solutions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must be pragmatic and not ideological in our approach.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Keep an open mind, and make decisions with both the head and the heart.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Last week, at the Opening of Parliament, I had a chance to chat with Mr Low Thia Khiang.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Somebody snapped a picture of us and the Workers’ Party (WP) posted a smiling photo of two of us on their Facebook page.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I think Mr Low would not mind me sharing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I asked him – the WP is having a leadership transition too.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What will change, now that the WP has a new leader?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Don’t you agree?” I agreed with Mr Low.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As an opposition party, the WP plays a role in our political system, whoever is their party leader.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In other words, the ruling party, the People’s Action Party (PAP), does not have a monopoly of power and does not have the right to rule Singapore indefinitely.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So long as the PAP Government performs, it keeps the voters’ support, it stays in power and the opposition cannot gain ground.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But if the PAP Government becomes incompetent or corrupt, then, of course, the opposition will grow.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, our system gives the PAP Government, given any government, every incentive to perform, and to keep the opposition performing its role, where it is, namely, in the opposition.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We treat every election as a serious contest.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Political parties do not have a fixed lifespan – a time to live and a time to die, as Ecclesiastes puts it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How long a political party continues in government – or in opposition for that matter, because parties come and go in the opposition too – depends on whether it can renew itself, continue to serve the people, continue to bring progress to the nation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If the PAP can keep on successfully doing that, we can stay in government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But if we ever fail, we deserve to lose.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, my message to all PAP Members of Parliament is "work hard, serve the people, hold the ground, and win the elections".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This does not mean the Government will shy away from difficult problems.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if Ministers are not prepared to govern, then give it up.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because that is your duty; that is what you are here for.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And governing means that from time to time you have to do difficult things when they become necessary.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Leadership means you have to explain, persuade, and convince people that you know what you are doing, and that you are doing it for a good reason, and it is a right thing to do.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is the way to maintain people's trust, and trust is crucial.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The previous government had introduced the new tax three years ago, and it had caused great unhappiness in Malaysia.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was not the economic merits or demerits of the GST.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But politically, Malaysians linked the GST with other complaints they had with the previous government, and they rejected the explanations and the persuasions, and they say, "No.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Out with it." Does that mean no government should ever raise taxes?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Then, the government must convince the population that it is raising taxes for a good reason, for the right reason.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And whether the voters accept that will depend not just on the arguments, but also crucially on whether they trust the government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because with arguments, for every right argument, we can produce five doubtful ones which look quite plausible.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And during elections, there is no shortage of producers of such arguments and people can get confused.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if they do, you vote for them, and you will take all things which need to be done as one bundle.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I think this is the right lesson to learn.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It would not dare to do painful but necessary things.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And politics becomes the art of pandering – a bidding war between the parties – who can give more, who can offer more?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You say you reduce the tax; I say I abolish the tax.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And then, you say, "I will give you a hongbao" on top of that.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And how to pay – well, we can think about that after the elections.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have been working together, learning to complement one another's strengths and weaknesses, making decisions as a team and taking collective responsibility for these decisions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To me, this working together is as important, if not more important, than the question of who should be the next Prime Minister.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because for the next Prime Minister, I know there is more than one qualified candidate.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are fortunate that this is so, because it provides strength and depth to the team.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Now, it is about the team coming to a consensus on the best option.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But to work together as a team, that is not a choice because there is no other option.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Whoever becomes the next Prime Minister, the team has to work closely together for him to succeed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If they cannot or do not do so, then the next Prime Minister will fail, whoever he is.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Even in the best of times, and certainly in times of severe crises, Mr Lee Kuan Yew did not run the country by himself.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Neither did Mr Goh Chok Tong, nor myself.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: One year, Mr Lee received the Freedom of the City of London, in 1982.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was a grand occasion – he dressed up; he made a speech.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He said: "I feel like a conductor at a concert bowing to applause, but unable to turn around and invite the accomplished musicians in his orchestra to rise and receive the ovation for the music they have played.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For running a government is not unlike running an orchestra, and no Prime Minister ever achieves much without an able team of players." I think I can speak for Mr Goh Chok Tong when I say that we both feel the same way.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: All three of us were not sole leaders, but primus inter pares – that means, first among equals.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But the emphasis is we are equals, but we are just the first among equals; first among equals with our colleagues.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We take their views, we take them seriously, we benefit from their advice and their abilities and their skills.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have fierce arguments as to what to do but we are on a team together, with strong enough bonds that we can deal with issues together and there is leadership, but it is unforced.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The team accepts, respects and knows that it has an important role to play.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They are not there just to carry out orders.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We were all fortunate – Singapore was fortunate – that the Prime Ministers had such stalwart colleagues.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Lee had a core team of very strong Ministers supporting him – Goh Keng Swee, S Rajaratnam, Lim Kim San, Hon Sui Sen, and Othman Wok.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Emeritus Senior Minister (ESM) Goh had a talented team too – Ong Teng Cheong, Tony Tan, Wong Kan Seng, S Jayakumar, S Dhanabalan, Abdullah Tarmugi, and George Yeo, just to name a few.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If anything, ESM Goh's team was even more comprehensive than Mr Lee's.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And when I took over as Prime Minister, I inherited ESM Goh's strong team and Mr Goh himself stayed on, and we added talent to the team.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Now, he has stepped down, I rely on my own core team, which now also includes several of the 4G Ministers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, the next Prime Minister must have, and will have, his own stalwart colleagues too – his generation, and I hope, also younger ones.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I know everyone is anxious to know who the next Prime Minister will be.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Well, the leader must command the respect and loyalty of his whole team.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He must enjoy the support and confidence of the broad mass of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And these things take time; they cannot be forced.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I do not believe we are ready to settle on a choice yet, nor is it helpful to treat this either as a horse race, or a campaign to lobby support for one or the other candidate.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Let us give them the time and space to do their own work, to work together in their new roles and to get better known by the public.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For these 14 years as Prime Minister, I have been working with the 4G team, guiding them, assessing them, preparing them to take over the reins.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When Mr Heng Swee Keat rounded up the Budget debate this year, I was happy to hear him describe the Budget as one that not only meets the needs of today's generation, but also accounts for the needs of future generations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It showed that the 4G Ministers understood that their deepest responsibility is to be a steward of Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Government is certainly not the owner of Singapore, but neither it is just the manager of Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is responsible for taking good care of the country, for holding it in trust, building it up and handing it on in due time to future generations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Government must keep faith with past generations who gifted this country to us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It has to be responsible to the present generation who continue to build on what we have inherited.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have built something truly special here in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Countries near and far look to Singapore as a model of governance and development.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: People want to live here, do business here.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Even the US and the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) are planning to hold their meeting here!

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In many other countries, political leaders plan only up to the next election or the next crisis.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But in Singapore, we are able to think beyond the immediate, beyond ourselves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We care about our community, our country and our future.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our religious leaders visit temples, churches and mosques together.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They give their blessings on one another's milestone celebrations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our neighbours and friends invite us over for makan during Chinese New Year, Deepavali or Hari Raya.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They come back eager to apply what they have seen and learnt around the world back home.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our grandparents and parents bring us up and nurture us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They are living examples of how by working hard, we can build better lives for ourselves and our children.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, we are all living the Singapore Story, keeping it alive.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must sustain and pass on this shared vision of prospering together, progressing together.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That way, we will make this little red dot shine bright in the world as well as in our hearts for many, many years to come.   4.00 pm

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Who are his parents?" Is it bad to come from the Civil Service or the SAF?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Is it good to have people from a wide range?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I do not know how many people are running.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And the stronger this team is, the harder I make Mr Low's job.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I think I will have a tough job today.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: First and foremost, this is the speech after the Prime Minister; secondly, with all the Ministers in front of me, even much tougher now.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):   Hon Speaker and my fellow hon Parliamentary colleagues.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In our search for success to achieve prosperity and stability, let us not forget those who may struggle in this race of life.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I am quite concerned with our highly competitive life – whereby "success" is measured solely from one’s economic status or the position that one achieves in one’s career – to the extent that sometimes, we forget how to be a society with a heart.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The global situation remains volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous, or what is known as a VUCA world, so it is important that we continue to learn and re-learn, so that we can be resilient.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Disruptions and economic changes, whether globally or locally, are clearly becoming more frequent, and this requires adaptability.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I am confident that those who are able to adapt can survive, ending in success and progress.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The need to adapt is not limited to any particular community, and no one is exempted.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, every member of society needs to adapt and change with the circumstances.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We are presented with many success stories about the community.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: There are more Malays in leadership positions, as well as holding key appointments in various organisations and companies – in both the public and private sectors.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, as I mentioned earlier, we need to measure success holistically, by looking at how far the whole society has progressed together, with no one forgotten or left behind.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Since the Malay community is a small community, this means that the "gotong royong" spirit of helping one another can be easily implemented and expanded.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I would like to call on those who are successful in life to step forward and give back to society.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us all help not only those in need, but also the whole society.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Helping someone does not necessarily mean giving financial help solely.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, help can be rendered in many forms, for instance, spending some time to help out or contribute ideas to organisations that need it.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: There are many Malay bodies that are constantly looking out for capable members of the community to serve in their board of administrators and work together in community service projects that are co-organised.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The expertise of someone with a successful career can be used to benefit society through sharing sessions and exchanging of intellectual ideas.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: For example, our youths can benefit from people with rich experience who become mentors to those who need it.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, in order to answer the President’s call that we become an exceptional nation and society, we must be bold enough to challenge ourselves in terms of the current way of running things.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is impossible for us to become an exceptional society if we do not change our ways.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Change must come first if we wish to achieve progress and success.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Although our community has progressed and achieved success in many areas, we are still hampered by social issues.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Obviously, this is a problem that we are not proud of.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I admit that many efforts have been launched and implemented.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, the outcomes are less than satisfactory to me.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us unite as a society with a heart and be able to work together so that our community can progress and prosper, in line with the nation’s objectives.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English) Mr Speaker, please allow me to continue my speech in English.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In the President’s Address, President Halimah reminded us of the need to continue progressing and to build an exceptional nation.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In the Address, her Excellency encouraged us to consider taking bold steps to challenge the status quo, if it can lead us to reach the pinnacle of "extraordinary".

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Encouraging the 4G leaders to explore and to do what is necessary to make Singapore an exceptional place, I am heartened.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Not only should we achieve economically, but also achieving as a gracious society, and society with a heart.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, the volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous (VUCA) world that we live in now means that challenges abound for all of us.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Each challenge means differently to each of us.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Some of us may thrive, while some may falter.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
