text: My fear is that in our zealousness to face and overcome these challenges head on, we may forget the ones who are struggling and falling behind and eventually forget how to be a society with a heart.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: But, surely, those who are better off will feel a certain amount of anxiety as well.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: When that happens, does it mean they will tighten their purse strings and keep their wealth for a rainy day instead of helping others who are in dire need of help?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that we, as a society, will do our part in helping others overcome the challenges associated with a VUCA world, be it through volunteer work, donations or some other ways.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Only when we keep a look out for each other and ensure we advance towards the future together, can we then claim to be a society with a heart.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: There are many facets in building a society with a heart.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from encouraging Singaporeans to be kinder, more empathetic and generous, the Government too has a responsibility to ensure all segments of Singaporeans are well taken care of and division does not happen.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We owe our thriving city to our parents, grandparents and the generations before them who helped mould Singapore into the country it is now.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, enough time has passed that some of us may have forgotten their contributions and take them for granted, leading to inter-generational conflict.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While these scenarios are likely and can possibly cause conflict between generations, I believe our Government, and especially the 4G leaders, shall have the wisdom to ensure the needs of all Singaporeans are satisfactorily met and not at the expense of others.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: But we must remind ourselves that again, success can be truly measured by how we advance and progress together as a whole, and this sometimes entails making small sacrifices to ensure those in need are not neglected.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, I am certain that if we band together and lend support to one another, we can emerge stronger through the adversities and challenges.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us work together and achieve the exceptional nation we want to become.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Singapore has always been a place of promise and possibilities, attracting many ashore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And today, we continue to create new opportunities for Singaporeans from all walks of life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: President Halimah’s Address has set out our vision towards developing a vibrant economy that invests in the skills and talents of our people.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We aspire to be a caring and inclusive nation at the workplace too.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We envisage a Singapore where young graduates, older workers and women have ample opportunities to discover their potential and have a fulfilling work life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Last Sunday was Mother’s Day and my family celebrated it with a simple meal with my 67-year-old mother.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: She has always been our pillar of strength, and despite her age, she insists on working because it keeps her going.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: She had worked throughout her life, dancing a delicate balance between family commitments and her job when we were younger and later caring for my ageing grandmother.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Like her and like many mothers, we want the best for our family, and at the same time, we strive to give our all at home and at work.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Thankfully, Singaporean women today are better positioned to juggle between the worlds of home and work as we are starting from a higher vantage point than before.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Over the years, Singaporean women have made strides in education and at work.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Close to 40% of those who graduated from science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) courses in our homegrown universities comprise of women.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: More than a third of our STEM polytechnic graduates are also female.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In terms of women in full-time employment, we are now ranked sixth when compared with the OECD nations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With meritocracy and better education, our women are inching up the gender pay gap.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This places us in the company of the top 10 OECD countries, and ahead of countries like Australia, Germany, the UK and the US.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Median incomes of women in occupations like accountants, securities and finance brokers were higher than men.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: However, we still have some way to go.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I agree with Miss Cheryl Chan, Ms Thanaletchimi and Ms Tin Pei Ling that there is more to be done to encourage women to remain in the workforce.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: While our full-time employment rate for women is ranked highly compared to the other OECD countries, our part-time employment rate is not.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We want to close this gap as much as possible because employers as well as female employees stand to gain from Flexible Work Arrangements (FWAs).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Companies that offer FWAs do better in attracting and retaining the best talents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In addition, a survey in 2016 found that majority of such companies reported higher employee staff morale and improved productivity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Women who have the options of FWAs do not need to choose between full-time work and zero-time work, and they are able to stay in touch with the marketplace with their skills and with their experience.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Instead of having our women opt out of work, we want to empower our women with choices to opt in, and stay in the workforce.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With the right support, women can have the chance to fulfil both our family and also our career aspirations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: However, we also know that it is not easy for all companies to offer FWAs due to specific work conditions or rigid working hours.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Several Members of Parliament including Miss Cheryl Chan, Dr Intan and Ms Thanaletchimi spoke passionately in the House on this topic with ideas to legislate FWAs or other family-support leave entitlements.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: These suggestions are not new, and we know that laws alone do not change social behaviours and mindsets.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Our approach is a practical one, combining legislation and promotional efforts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In addition, advances in technology and communication can also help to facilitate FWAs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: MOM is strongly committed to growing the number of companies with FWAs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The grant also provides additional support for job-sharing arrangements, in recognition that it is harder for employers to provide this type of FWA.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: These employers have publicly pledged to offer FWAs and each of them will appoint a senior management member to champion FWAs in their organisation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: They are committed to exploring alternative arrangements with their employees should there be difficulties in forming FWAs in their company.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: At MOM, we want to encourage employers who have not pledged their support to do so.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With effect from 5 May 2018, companies can now sign up onto the Tripartite Standards through the Jobs Bank.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Previously, they can only do so through the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) website.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With one more additional platform, it is really now a lot easier for our companies to adopt the Standards.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Thirdly, MOM will continue to promote FWAs as part and parcel of the modern work life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In today’s age of technology and Internet of Things (IoT), managers, supervisors and co-workers can no longer equate face-to-face time and physical presence at work with an employee’s capability.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, Mr Speaker, Sir, we really need a mindset change that respects, a mindset change that provides and a mindset change that supports choices and supports flexibility at work.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This cultural shift will also mean that someone who puts up a request for part-time work or puts up a request for flexible work will not be deemed as a lesser employee.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Together with our tripartite partners, we will press on to deepen and also widen our efforts to support Singaporean women at work by making FWAs more pervasive and also across the board.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Women will have more power to make choices for ourselves and our families, and also the freedom to belong to the workplace as long as we wish to.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I want to thank Mr Ng Chee Meng and Mr Heng Chee How for their heartfelt and insightful thoughts on how we can help older Singaporeans stay employable and also adaptable and continue to be valuable contributors to our workplace and to our society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This resonates with what the fourth-generation leaders envision for an inclusive and caring Singapore workforce.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Throughout the years, we have made progress in supporting our older workers’ choice to work.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The vast majority of those who accepted re-employment in the same job did not experience any cut in basic wages.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Sixty seven-years-old Ms Margaret Tan is one of our older workers who has been with Mandarin Oriental Hotel for the past 14 years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As a Senior Guest Service Manager, she leads a team of over 80 staff.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: She is a keen learner; she earned two specialist diplomas in the last two years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: When she was 65 years old, she embarked on a specialist diploma and within two years, she earned two specialist diplomas.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The first one is in Leadership and People, the other one in Service Excellence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As Mr Heng Chee How pointed out, it takes two hands to clap.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We need willing and far-sighted employers, as well as able and also active older employees to join hands and make our workplace age inclusive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Like Mandarin Oriental Hotel, employers that embrace progressive workplace practices which prioritise a person’s abilities over his or her age, they really stand to gain from the deep experience, they stand to gain from the reliability and they stand to gain from the loyalty that our mature workers will bring with them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Older Singaporeans who are ready to adapt and keep on learning, like Ms Margaret Tan, make it attractive for employers to see their potential and view them as valuable assets.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I agree with Mr Ng Chee Meng, Mr Heng Chee How and also Dr Chia Shi-Lu that ageism has absolutely no place in our society or even workplace.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: MOM will focus on resources to support companies to unlock the potential of our older workers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Thirdly, we will push for more age-inclusive behaviour and move towards eradicating ageism.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In President Halimah’s words, and I quote, this “small, multi-cultural city state…must survive and thrive on the wits and will of its people.”  I believe our young Singaporeans have the potential to keep this red dot going strong.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We have invested in their education, knowledge and skills, and will continue to give them the edge to hold their own when they start their careers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: According to the 2016 Graduate Employment Survey, a good majority of new graduates in full-time permanent employment are also employed in jobs related to their fields of study and that is 81% from autonomous universities and 72% for polytechnic graduates.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In addition, the gross median salary of Post-Secondary Education Institution (PSEI) graduates surveyed approximately six months after their final exams is also on an upward trend.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We will continue to strengthen our efforts to help our new graduates maximise their potential to achieve positive employment outcome.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In a fast-paced and changing world, they need to be well-armed with information and also knowledge to navigate upcoming trends and future-proof themselves for what is ahead.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The rise of the gig economy and also disruptions to traditional occupations throw up a diversity of work options that graduates did not use to have.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With these in mind, we have deepened our work on these fronts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We have extended the annual snapshot of employment outcomes for fresh graduates on what is known as the Graduate Employment Survey, to cover all private education institutions with full-time employment programmes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This allows our graduates to make better informed decisions on their choice to work or to further their studies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: MOM keeps a pulse on the career trends and aspirations of students from our universities, polytechnics and ITE.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We work closely with MOE to guide the students in their career and education choices.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: A structured education and career guidance (ECG) curriculum and access to ECG-trained counsellors, teachers and lecturers help our students discover their strengths and their career interests.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: More details will be shared at a later date.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Please allow me to respond to some of Mr Png Eng Huat's points that he raised earlier.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I want to assure him that all schools are subject to the same level of funding for capital expenditure, such as infrastructure, IT and operating costs such as manpower and repairs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: All schools can also receive additional funding for special programmes such as electives, overseas trips for experiential learning.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: However, there is differential funding for building of facilities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We approve the building of non-standard facilities on a case-by-case basis, provided there is significant education value to our students.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And these schools will have to raise funds to fully pay for these facilities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore has been and must continue to be a nation full of opportunities for Singaporeans from all walks of life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: MOM’s ambition is for all Singaporeans who are able and willing to work, regardless of gender, age or background, to be able to continue doing so.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Helping all our workers, whether men or women, young or old, achieve their work and life aspirations requires change from everyone involved.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: First of all, our workers must adopt a mindset change to embrace new technologies, be open to change and upskill themselves to remain competitive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: If workers are willing to stay relevant by upskilling and reskilling themselves, their productivity and efficiency will be able to keep up with times.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I believe, by doing so, workplace ageism and sexism will be eradicated slowly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Thirdly, the whole society must also change their prejudice and support the culture of inclusivity, and embrace diversity in our workforce.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For our young people, we need to support them to leverage their strengths, and choose career and education pathways that will give them the greatest competitive advantage.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We believe that as long as Singaporeans leverage on their strengths and pursue excellence in fields that they are passionate in, they will find success.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I have just joined MOM and I look forward to working with the employers, employees and the community to develop a more inclusive workforce.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I also hope that Singaporeans from all walks of life can explore together how we can promote a more progressive, enlightened and inclusive workplace culture.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, amid an uncertain external environment, we can hold fast to our foundation of meritocracy and also inclusion, as well as joint aspirations for success.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Together, we can forge opportunities for all in the workforce, including women, the young as well as the old.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With a receptive mindset, our workers can embrace learning and new trends, and adapt to stay relevant throughout changing times.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Employers who invest in progressive work practices with foresight and with courage will attract the best talents and they are able to move their organisations forward.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, really, we need all of society, everyone, to support a culture of inclusion at the workplace with kindness, with understanding and with openness.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We may be small but when we come together, we are bigger than the sums of all our dreams and all our hopes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, we can afford to be bold, because with inclusiveness, we become stronger.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We have started on the road to progress.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, let us not set limits on ourselves, but together, let us blaze the future for a Singapore Unlimited.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In her speech on how the Government can build a strong partnership with people to co-create the Singapore of the future, President Halimah Yacob emphasised the need of the fourth-generation leaders to work with Singaporeans to build a vibrant Singapore that is full of opportunities, and to create a cohesive and inclusive society that caters to the needs of different societal segments.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is with this in mind that I would like to focus my speech on catering to the divergent and differentiated learning needs of a particular segment of children and how the Government could enhance education options for these children, specifically those who are of primary-school going age.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to declare my interest as Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of a private education organisation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore has a well-regarded education system that is both recognised and admired worldwide.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Bodies, such as OECD consistently rate our education system as one of the best in the world and, as we were reminded by the Education Minister in his speech, our students have achieved remarkable Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) results.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The primary school system that we have built is well-suited to cater to mainstream learners who are able to function and learn in what is predominantly an examination-based academic environment.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In such a system, students who were able to perform well in summative-assessments, such as tests and examinations would do well, thus culminating in what most parents will agree is the mother-of-all-summative-assessments, the PSLE.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I do not intend to comment on the PSLE in this speech.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that this has been commented on before and will indeed continue to be debated for some time in this Chamber at the future.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, I have to commend MOE for trying to lessen the examination-based academic aspect of the PSLE by providing for schemes like the Direct School Admission (DSA) to allow students to enrol in secondary schools using other criteria apart from their PSLE score.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The replacement of the T-score with wider achievement levels in 2021 is also a positive step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My point is that while the majority of neurotypical students in mainstream MOE primary schools tend to function well in this system, there are also those neurodivergent students with differentiated learning needs who would perhaps perform better in an environment and system that is different from the typical mainstream MOE primary schools.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am not referring to students with clear special learning needs that are already enrolled in Special Education (SPED) schools, such as those operated by Association for Persons with Special Needs (APSN), the Movement for the Intellectually Disabled of Singapore (MINDS), the Asian Women’s Welfare Association (AWWA) and other volunteer welfare organisations (VWOs) and non-governmental organisation (NGOs).

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: SPED school students often have moderate to serious physical and/or intellectual challenges that will make it difficult for them to make it in the mainstream education system, and it is good that MOE and the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) have worked with these organisations to provide options and opportunities for these students to form the foundation for independent and meaningful lives and careers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Pathlight has since grown from strength to strength, thanks in no small part to the vision and tireless work of a lady that I have tremendous respect for – my hon Parliamentary colleague, Ms Denise Phua.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And I am confident that Ms Phua and her team will continue to "light the path" for many children and young adults on the autism spectrum in the future.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The neurodivergent children I am hoping that MOE can provide enhanced educational options for are those primary school students who have neuroatypical conditions that are not so severe or challenging that would require them to enrol in SPEDs or Pathlight but are presently finding it challenging to cope with these conditions in mainstream primary schools.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, these students are not just able to merely grasp the mainstream primary school academic curriculum, many of them are even able to excel in it.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: MOE has, in recent years, worked very closely with educational and developmental psychologists to offer early detection and interventions for children with special learning needs and has also offered support programmes in mainstream schools for students with dyslexia, mild autism, and ADHD.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I sincerely hope that MOE will continue to do good work in this area, but I feel that these programmes are still insufficient to cater to increasingly complex learning needs of our children.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, unless the Allied Educators-to-students ratio is lowered, it is also very hard for these Allied Educators to cater to the needs of working with such a large group of students in mainstream schools.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would be in line with the Pathlight model, but perhaps on a smaller scale and with more autonomy given to the schools.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that there would be VWOs and NGOs like AWWA or the Dyslexia Association of Singapore who would have the expertise and know-how to set up these autonomous specialised schools.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other organisations who might be inclined to provide such services could be religious organisations or established private education providers, and interested parties could even be partnered with philanthropic organisations or charities, or even corporate entities who are willing to co-fund this initiative.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps, a cluster of smaller, autonomous specialised schools could even be housed in a single building to create a unique learning community for neurodivergent children.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These schools would be set up with the same national education perimeters and guidelines as the mainstream schools, with the same flag-raising ceremonies, the singing of the national anthem, the reciting of the pledge and the incorporation of the National Education (NE) modules into the curriculum.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I noted that my Parliamentary colleague Miss Cheryl Chan had earlier suggested for students with special needs to be given a "through-train" pathway to secondary school.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think that this is a suggestion worth exploring, but if MOE still feels that the PSLE is relevant to neurodivergent students, then students from these proposed autonomous specialised schools could still be required to take this examination.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The key difference is that these schools would have the freedom and autonomy to prepare their students for the PSLE in the way that they deem would be best to cater to these students’ diverse learning needs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am sure that there are potential concerns that fees of these autonomous schools, if they are privately funded for example, would price themselves out of the reach of students who need them the most.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It could also be mandatory for these schools to include a certain percentage of these students at subsidised fees.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This, Mr Deputy Speaker, in effect, helps to ensure a more equal distribution of resources from the community as those who have the means to afford such education would be, in effect helping those who do not.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And such guidelines would also ensure that these autonomous specialised schools could actually have a more diverse and varied student demographic than some primary schools from certain residential regions in Singapore today.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, one can set up such schools and ensure that they remain accessible.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Now, this I believe is an idea worth piloting.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These schools and their programmes have allowed students to explore many more tracks and pathways that cater to their learning needs, capabilities and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In recent times, MOE has also made an impact in the pre-primary early childhood education sector by setting up MOE kindergartens and mega pre-schools to ensure a base-line quality for early childhood education, while still allowing private early childhood education options to exist.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This has ensured variety and choice for parents who might want different types of education for their young children based on their preferences and whatever their children's needs might be.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having transformed the post-primary sector and with increasing involvement in the pre-primary sector, it now makes sense for the Government to go one more step further and look at diverse options and pathways in the primary school system.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that diversity actually creates a stronger and more resilient system overall, which will in turn enhance the entire education ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, I feel that the word “bold” has been somewhat overused in this Chamber in the past few days.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What I am hoping for is for the Government to continue the good work that it has already done in our education landscape.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What I am hoping for is an escalation of this progressive evolution, with a focus on facilitating the creation of more primary education pathways for neurodivergent children.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We are no longer in the Third Industrial Revolution where computers were mere tools to aid us in automation and productivity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In what many believe is the Fourth Industrial Revolution, artificial Intelligence (AI) systems can now self-learn and self-improve to the extent that one day, many more job groups including those in the middle levels such as radiographers and bookkeepers, jobs like that can disappear.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Jobs such as drone operators, app developers and sustainability engineers are jobs that did not exist 10 years ago.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Previously, handmade dumplings or 手工水饺 are now made in factories without human beings, or what the Chinese call 无人工厂 in China; and even beggars in China have already gone cashless, with many having their own QR codes or other online access for givers to transfer monies directly.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Closer to home, a friend of mine who incorporated a business and was looking for a new corporate logo.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Instead of using the traditional means to seek out a local designer, he approached an online global design service provider.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For about S$400, an automated online system organised a global competition of logo designers who submitted a total of 50 designs, out of which five were shortlisted and then after further briefing and discussion with the designers, one was selected by my friend.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is the sort of boundary-less global marketplace, global labour market that is impacting Singaporeans; a world that presents either threats or opportunities, depending on how future-ready Singapore is.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In a world such as this, whilst all of us will learn to be consumers of technology, many more need to be developers as well in order to stay relevant.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A dual economy of a different kind is emerging – people and businesses who thrive in this new world versus those who will barely survive; one that can cause inequality and tensions in a small nation-state like ours.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Against this backdrop, it is no wonder that President Halimah had called upon the 4G leaders to go for bold changes and not be contented to tweak things at the margins.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The boldest move in Singapore in education in recent years has been the inclusion of adult learners into the mission of MOE; a very bold move, a significant one that must be applauded.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Indeed, as German psychologist Eric Fromm puts it, why should society feel responsible only for the education of children, and not for the education of all adults of every age?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For the typical workforce, it is still early days to know if the SkillsFuture movement will fully realise its mission to transform Singaporeans to take charge of their own learning; be less obsessed with chasing the paper and to be more obsessed with mastering the skills and staying ahead of the game in their vocations, a mantra often repeated by Minister Ong Ye Kung.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Think about turning competent special schools into lifelong learning institutions or Continuing Education and Training (CET) providers to train their alumni or others with similar learning profiles.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It was only as recent as two months ago in this House that I had called for boldness in tackling the excessive obsession and time spent preparing for high-stakes exam in particular, the PSLE.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I will say a few words about it since it is a hot topic.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But Sir, it is unfair to ask Singaporeans to give up something when they are not given the knowledge or the hope for a better alternative.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: After all, doing well in high-stakes exams has long been seen in Singaporeans as the passport to top schools and hopefully, top jobs later; never mind the disproportionate amount of time, money and stress to prepare for it.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Lifelong learning is a mindset and habit often formed during one’s younger school days and a difficult one to cultivate when one is older.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Our schools will need the time and resources to do the upstream work that is critical in developing a curiosity and a love for learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And without this habit, it is futile in adulthood, to try to develop every Singaporean to his fullest potential – the mission of SkillsFuture.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Learning from other systems, more than once in this House, I had shared about other schools' models like the Yun-Ku School that was recently launched by Alibaba founder Mr Jack Ma, a former teacher himself.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have shared about his 10-year school system and also shared about other school systems in other parts of the world and inclusive models that have done none the worse elsewhere in the world.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Locally, I had the chance to witness a home-schooling system that had scaled up to a school.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I saw how a repository of learning resources are accessible to both students and staff; how each child is taught to be self-driven in this school to set his own learning goals; how each teacher is truly a facilitator; how their academic rigour in this school led to standards that met both local and overseas tertiary admission criteria; and although in this school, I saw that technology could have been applied more widely, yet it displayed many attractive features of what good education comprises.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am confident that we can learn from the strengths of our local systems and that of others to present a better alternative to the current model where the high-stakes PSLE has become the holy grail.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is up to the Minister and his advisers to decide if piloting a better alternative is a bold or a reckless move.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Questions to ask of our current school system.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is merit to learning from the experts from the OECD and the like; and to know where we stand versus other countries.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But the PISA is but a test of the skills and knowledge of 15-year-olds who have a whole life ahead of them, at least another 60 years according to life span statistics.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Four, what is the new curriculum, beyond coding and computational thinking skills, does our lifelong education system need to deliver in this rapidly changing world?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Five, what are the features of our current system that we must retain at all cost?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Six, what are the features that are causing pains but have become sacred cows that we have learnt to revere and even defend?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Seven, how do we maximise the potential of every Singaporean, regardless of their learning ability and profile, and ensure an inclusive education system for all?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The rest of us Singaporeans who care for our country, who are concerned for our future should ponder over them too.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Education is a crucial tool to help finish the unfinished business of addressing inequality.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Education equips Singaporeans to maximise their potential to work, to earn more and to enjoy a better quality of life; to be socially mobile and to provide the opportunity to learn and play together with fellow Singaporeans who are different from us.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It can empower us to become not only successful for ourselves, but also use the fruits of education to bless others beyond ourselves.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Education is thus too important to leave it to only the educators.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It affects all of our lives, and we should jointly envision, co-shape and support a lifelong education system that is uniquely Singapore and second to none.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government therefore can and should make changes to the system for the better and the longer good and ensure the education ladder in our country leans against the right wall.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As for the rest of Singapore, Sir, we too must take our place and support, build and climb that ladder that will lead us to the right wall.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Only then can the dream of fulfilling the potential of every Singaporean become a reality, and not a slogan. 5.00 pm

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I share the aspirations and concerns the President had expressed in her speech and I would like to take this opportunity to speak on some of them, namely the three "M"s: minimising the negative impact of inequality; mustering the courage to implement bold changes; and mastering technological advances.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am heartened that our Government is committed to minimising the negative impact of inequality.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore is a capitalist economy and a meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this environment, those who are talented, able and hardworking will be rewarded.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But in nature, talents and abilities are not equally distributed.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, what about those who are not as talented or skilled?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hard work alone will only take you so far.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should also not forget that health or personal conditions and circumstances may limit some people's performance at work.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Whilst we should continue to encourage reward systems based on output and performance as this is accepted to be fair and justifiable, let us not overlook the problems of the imperfect market.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Distorted remunerations of varying magnitudes exist, either paying too much or too little for contributions and work done.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This way, even the poor in our community can afford a reasonable standard of living.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We also face stratification and slowing social mobility.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our population is now more stratified across age groups and income and wealth.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Historically, Singapore has been fairly successful in promoting social mobility.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The story of our very own President is a good example and we all personally know similar cases like hers, where within one or two generations, families' circumstances are improved substantially.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But as our society advances, social mobility slows and the gaps between different income groups gradually widen as accumulated advantages and wealth gets passed on from one generation to the next.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a community, we should start a candid discussion about the strategies to overcome this problem before it becomes too entrenched and difficult to resolve.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We may need to modify our policies or social institutions.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should never accept the lack of social mobility as inevitable.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Education plays an important role in enabling social mobility.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Though MOE is committed to make every school a good school, each would still have different access to resources and therefore, indirectly limit the academic and non-academic options available to their students.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How do we discover a talented tennis player from a school that does not have a tennis court or offer the sport as a CCA?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are we able to nurture that child who could potentially be a chess grandmaster if he or she is in a school that does not have a Chess Club?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are those who can afford to send their children for private lessons outside of the school.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But for those who cannot, how do we level the playing field in both academic and non-academic areas?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Aside from education, policies and Government schemes will have different impacts on every individual and family as each face a unique set of challenges.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In other words, there would always be groups that fall through the cracks, and we need to look out for them.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Exercising compassion in the implementation of our policies is helpful in reducing the impact of income inequality in our society.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Though the issue of income inequality is not unique to Singapore, there is no one-size-fits-all solution that we can copy from others.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government needs to continue to pay close attention to the ground, as the price to pay as a result is not restricted to economic consequences but more importantly, could create a tear in our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another notable point the President made was about mustering the courage to implement bold changes and not limiting ourselves to taking incremental steps.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are not advocating recklessness but calculated moves into unchartered territories.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we do not take calculated risks, we risk becoming irrelevant anyway, with dire consequences.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is most important is that we must be prepared for trade-offs and failures and have the courage and tenacity to pick ourselves up and try again.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some changes would be unpopular, and our leaders must be able to carry them.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, firstly, they have to win the hearts and minds of the people so that Singaporeans would be willing to take a leap of faith together with them.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Geopolitics have changed much and so have technologies.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Have we made the necessary changes fast enough?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to constantly review the relevance of what we teach and how we assess our young.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps we need to revamp our "O" and "A" levels and the subjects taught.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When we implement changes, especially bold ones, we must ensure that both top-down and bottom-up approaches work hand in hand.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is because while focusing on visions in top-down policies, there may be gaps in the schemes, while bottom-up initiatives may miss the big picture even as gaps are filled.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope our relevant departments will bear this in mind for our Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs).

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To get rid of the old ways of doing things, we have to reduce unnecessary processes to free up time and space for thinking, creativity and problem-solving.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Increased efficiency and higher productivity are mutually reinforcing.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have witnessed how technology has disrupted how some commercial activities are organised and executed.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A good example would be how quickly e-commerce has changed the dynamics of traditional retail.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Similarly, it is timely to rethink how our administrative services can be organised in bold new ways, instead of just trying to incrementally improve how the existing Ministries operate.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will help us to be ahead of the curve to implement change rather than to deal with change.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My final point is about technological advances, which are radically changing the way we live, work and interact with one another.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must master these technologies and harness their power to seize the economic opportunities they present.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some residents have expressed their concerns over our drive to become a Smart Nation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are worried about new complexities and being left behind.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They feel that our Government may be pushing this initiative too quickly.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I empathise with them but I really do not think we can afford to slow down.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must help them to adapt and catch up through schemes, such as SkillsFuture, but we must get on the tech train.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have an ageing population, but our seniors are better educated than their predecessors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe that where there is a will, there is a way.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must understand that we do not really have a choice as we would rather be ahead of the race and not just be in the race along the technology runway.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is currently creating a lot of buzz and a lot of worries too.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Whilst we nurture our own talents and build our capabilities, we also need to be a player in the global transfer of expertise and technical know-how to boost local competencies which in turn strengthen the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We want to continue to draw investments which create good jobs for Singaporeans, including high tech companies, such as those in the field of AI, cloud computing and robotics.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, we are also experiencing an environment of increasing trade protectionism among nations.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can Singapore deal with this current reality and find a path to thrive?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The complexion of global trade, economy and foreign relations is changing at a pace that seems much faster than before.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our next generation of leaders will have to be clear in their strategies and nimble in their actions to be able to execute policies that bring Singaporeans together and move Singapore ahead.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I support the President's call to our new generation to unite and work together to keep Singapore an exceptional country.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In her Address, the President calls for Singaporeans to walk alongside the fourth generation (4G) leaders in partnership to achieve an exceptional Singapore.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The concept of partnership means that there is more than one person in this journey.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Partners bring to the table their contributions, their strengths, their capital, they have different roles and responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They have a single commitment but they also bear risks together.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: That is a concept of a partnership and that is what we need to bear in mind when we build our country.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The premise of partnership is trust and, in this debate, in my speech, I would want to focus on the issue of trust.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The debate is important because the President's speech is not only for the Second Session of the 13th Parliament.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is a call to Singaporeans to take Singapore forward beyond the 13th Parliament and way into the future.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This debate is important because it takes place at a significant juncture in the political history of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The issue of trust is critical to all of us.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We are blessed to be in a country where the Ruling Party and the leading Opposition party transit leadership in a managed process.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And that is not to be taken for granted.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But however well-managed, there will be concerns, uncertainties and fears on the ground.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Leadership transitions can reasonably be expected to be a time of vulnerability.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Such vulnerability is easily exploited and can be exacerbated by circumstances, such as we are in now: shifts in alliances between countries, changes in the domestic landscape, disruption in the global economy, security threats.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, understandably, citizens, like myself, are concerned as to where and how the 4G leaders will lead us, how the leading Opposition party will play its role as a check and balance vis-à-vis the Government.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: As Singaporeans, we have a stake in Singapore’s future.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Visions, plans and policies are important but, just as important, if not more, is whether and how the leaders actualise them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Checks and balances vis-à-vis the Government are important, but just as important if not more important is whether the checks and balances are executed in a constructive and pro-Singapore manner.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, whether you are the Ruling Party or the Opposition party, we, the citizens will watch how responsible you are to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I believe this applies to all leaders, even those who have been leaders for a long time.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, I am encouraged by the acknowledgement of the 4G leaders that they must earn the trust of the people and forge their own bonds afresh with the people and earn the right to lead.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They, having thus spoken, the citizens will wait and see.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We weigh the actions of the leaders against their words.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The words that precede their action, the words that accompany the action and the words subsequent to the action.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We watch their other actions, hear their other words.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The totality will be the basis upon which we make our assessment.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I will do the same for Opposition politicians and the Public Service.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I want to know if you mean what you say and you say what you mean.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The 4G leaders and the new leaders of the Workers' Party are not strangers to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But compared to their predecessors, they have had a relatively short time up to now to prove themselves.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: They have clearly proven themselves within their parties.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is now time to prove themselves to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And this is not going to be easy.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: You have heard different, discordant noises on the ground.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But all must be taken seriously because all emanate from hearts either of anguish or of passion for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, the issue of earning trust is fundamental.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And I believe that is why the 4G leaders say they got to earn that trust.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Because if I trust my leaders, no matter how vehemently we disagree, I will cast my lot with them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I will pay the price, together with my fellow Singaporeans and leaders, to pave the way for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But if I do not trust my leaders, they have lost me in the journey.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Building trust, however, is not a one-way effort.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It requires one party to reach out and another to engage.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It will be a long and difficult process.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Especially if impressions have been formed, assessments have already been made, rightly or wrongly.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, we will need a lot of empathy and open-mindedness from both parties.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We should not fear to speak and debate openly and frankly.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We should speak and debate with cold logic, but with a flaming passion for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is healthy but it must be done responsibly.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Let us be open with each other and only then will our enemies have one tool less against us.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In tackling our challenges and building our future, the element of trust is important.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: There will be differing views, strong views, strong voices, loud voices.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: From this tumult, our leaders must discern what is in the long-term interests of Singapore, while looking after the immediate and medium-term interests of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, you have said to us that you will demonstrate leadership and resolve.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: You will stand firm on principles and ideals while seeking practical solutions.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: You will listen to the people, you will not fear to mobilise public opinion in the long-term interests of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And, indeed, as a citizen, I expect no less of Singapore’s leaders and the Public Service.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: To do that which is right by Singapore, boldly but humbly.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Never fearing those who speak the loudest, or those wield the most power, making difficult decisions in the long-term interests of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: How will you know that I believe in you?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: How will you know that when you make that decision, that difficult decision, which I disagree with, that you will have me on your bandwagon?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is for you to reach out to me and it is for me to open my mind to what you have to say to me.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Besides courage and principle, I and many I know will throw in our lot with leaders who uphold universal values of compassion, integrity and loyalty.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: As a citizen, I will trust leaders who defend our Constitution and the sovereignty of Singapore, putting at all times the interests of Singapore above all.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I trust leaders who exercise righteousness, dispense justice and equity, uphold the rule of law.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I trust leaders who protect the people, who remember the poor and vulnerable, who grow the country economically, socially for all.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Who lead us and who are above corruption.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In my sharing of my aspirations of leaders, I have steered clear of what policies and schemes we should have.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: These have already been greatly discussed and I leave them to better minds than mine.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But for me, the element of trust, if you cannot build that, you have lost us.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The President also speaks about trust between the people.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This is the second premise of the partnership: between people and people.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If we do have trust, we cannot be united.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If we cannot be united as one people, we do not require another enemy.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We have done well compared to many countries.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In the midst of our progress, we continue to carry with us differences in background, abilities, ideologies, culture, race and religion.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: These are part of our identity as individuals, a part of our heritage.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We are, indeed, different from each other, but we must not be afraid that we are different.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We recognise that our differences have enriched the Singaporean fabric.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Our differences have made us more accepting, broadened our perspectives, made us better, made us stronger.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: As such, the same differences that have strengthened and enriched Singapore can potentially tear us apart.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Consciously, we must use our differences to strengthen our society.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: When I have ability, I uphold and I lift the person without the ability, the person with the disability.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: When I have resources, I share my resources to level the playing ground.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If I am weak, I look to someone who is strong to support me.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If I am strong, I share my strength with my brother.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not allow anyone to attempt to fracture our society.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not coalesce according to socio-economic status, race, culture or religion.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And we must never, never, never allow distrust to engender along these differences.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: There is so much that we have to do together as a people.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is not just the work of certain agencies or certain companies but it is the work of every person, so much that we need to do, no time to fight.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We must put aside prejudices, we must put aside snide remarks and insinuations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So much to do, can we construct and not destruct?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: After all, we have a precious common history and we do, we must, we will have a precious and common destiny.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We have gone through thick and thin together.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The Japanese war, riots, acts and attempted acts of terror, financial crises, SARS.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We fought together, cried together, worked together, grew together.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Will we throw that away at insinuations from people who may not even have any stake in our country?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Would we throw that away just by listening to others and being persuaded without much thinking.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We are proud to be Singaporean and we should be.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We are proud of our sons and daughters, regardless of their achievements.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We empower our workers, employers, persons with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We grieve with fellow Singaporeans when their sons suffer mishaps during and in the service of the nation.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: No trust in the Government, no trust in each other.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We will listen to the views of others about Singapore, we will discern.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We will improve, but we will not bow to criticisms by persons who have no stake in our country.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The crux of President Halimah’s speech is about how we move forward together to build our future Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And as I thought about the future of Singapore, I asked myself: what does Singapore mean for each of us?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Although not representative, I did take a quick poll amongst several young people asking them to write in their own words what Singapore means for them.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Initially, there was some reluctance to pen their thoughts but they did it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While each expressed it differently, interestingly, there were common themes and phrases used to describe how they felt: "home", "safe and secure", "provided me education and opportunity", "stability", "place I want to return to".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I also asked them what is the future that they wished for.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many hoped that Singapore can adapt to the fast-changing world and continue to stay secure, progress and grow, to have opportunities and allow aspirations to be fulfilled.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There was also a call for an inclusive, united and compassionate society with more human touch.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, as I studied how they felt, I realised that the answers reflected our shared experiences and identity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Shared experiences of growing up in a society based on, as what President Halimah in her speech called, and I quote, "our foundational values of multiracialism, meritocracy, incorruptibility, self-reliance, inclusiveness and openness to the world".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, as I thought about the Singapore identity and what is it that makes Singapore stand out, I struggled, I really struggled, to describe it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I see it, I see it every day, I can feel it but it is hard to describe.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I believe that it is a combination of many factors.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is the skills and capability and conviction of our people, based on shared experiences that are unique to Singapore, based on our values whether it is our multiracial experience, our educational system, our heritage and our networks of relationships at the personal, business and community level.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But what is most important is the harnessing of the power of our people and our shared values and experiences and our networks and relationships that has made Singapore what it is today.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But what is behind, what is it that has made it possible?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is built over the years from our track record of making things happen, our reliability, trustworthiness and, to some extent, although I did hear in this House, some of us did ask for our kiasuism to be taken away.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think it is also part of our kiasuism and also as being a country that tries to make it easy for things to happen, for example, for businesses,making it easy for businesses to set up.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is all of these, it is of this coming together that defines the Singapore and the Singaporeans we are.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But as we look to our future, President Halimah also stressed that we cannot "assume that Singapore will always continue to be successful".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are shifts and developments that we must understand and deal with and these will need new and bold approaches.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The pace and scale of change that we are witnessing across industries are driven by the momentum in Asia, with the economic shift, the technological shift or what many have termed the Fourth Industrial Revolution and, for Singapore, our demographic shift with an ageing population.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, the question is, are we prepared for this new economy?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How do we stay relevant and be able to compete with other cities and countries as they develop and get better?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In my speech at the First Session of this Parliament, I had spoken about jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I had said that to enable Singaporeans, no matter where their starting point, to continue to improve their lives, Singapore must be able to give Singaporeans fulfilling jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: At that time, I spoke about my belief that having meaningful work gives confidence to our people not only to make a living but also to feel included and, hence, a sense of belonging and commitment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the changes we have witnessed in the last two years and the momentum of change we continue to experience, I now realise that while jobs are important, it is more than jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is about partnership and participation and working together that will make the difference for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is not just about the skills we develop, or the jobs we attain or the place that we learn.
