speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is about partnerships to bring it all together and the interaction amongst people of like and different backgrounds that matter.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They provide platforms for engagement and they promote innovation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Criteria used included doing business, financial competitiveness and innovation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Block 71 is another example of how the Government can foster an ecosystem for innovation and, in this case, it is about bringing together a startup ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This platform is now transplanted halfway across the world to San Francisco with the setting up of Block 71 San Francisco as well as closer in the region in Indonesia with Block 71 Jakarta.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This takes the Singapore brand abroad and, more importantly, is enabling a network of Singaporeans, partners and startups to drive innovation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This participation is about the exchange of ideas, innovation and expertise.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am not sure if many of you remember but only about eight years ago, Singapore was seen as dull and where you could not find any startups.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: By having a platform for people to come together, it would be very powerful in supporting skills development beyond formal learning and skills training.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It may not be just formal learning or certification of skills, but also learning that comes from interaction and sharing of ideas.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The whole idea transcends from business to even a social and community level.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The key thread is participation – participation in a supportive environment of individuals, regardless of backgrounds and experiences, the diversity and different perspectives will benefit all.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, as we start writing our next chapter, building on the power of our people, our shared experiences and networks, as Prime Minister Lee had said, I quote, "we have every reason to be confident and optimistic about our future".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The world is changing, getting disrupted, becoming more complex and, hence, unpredictable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Amidst this change, do our policies speak well enough to everyone?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly – and this is actually a real person I met – a 25-year-old who is working in a full-time job but driving a private hire car at night, holding down two jobs so as to afford further part-time studies leading to a professional certification.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And fourthly, a 35-year-old woman who has just obtained a degree from part-time study at great cost, time and money who finds that her employability in the salary she can command is not what she expected.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can say that there are already Government programmes in place to address the needs of these groups like Wage Credit, PCP, WIS and TAFEP which is true.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can also say that these problems are not unique to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can say that these people cannot always expect the Government to fix all their problems and there is truth in that as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But if disruptive change is going to make such situations more and more common, is there more we can do for these Singaporeans, as a society?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One private university graduate made an impassioned post on Facebook last month saying, and I quote, "I graduated in the top 15% of my cohort.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It should have wiped out the disaster that was my "A" levels.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have sent out thousands, hundreds of resumes, every month, every week, every day.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I applied for job after job after job, hoping that someone would notice.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Until then, I crunched numbers and copy clauses from story after story and picked up whatever freelance jobs and short-term contract jobs I could find.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In eight years, I received nothing." What else can we say to Singaporeans like these?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, Singapore and Singaporeans have achieved much in the past and there is much to be grateful for.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The glass is half-full, as I have argued before in this House.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But some of us would see it as half empty.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As was famously said in a scene in the movie Star Wars Episode 6, much depends on our point of view.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sometimes, both good and bad effects can come from the system-design source.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Going forward, as a country, we face a choice.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do we stick with the same policy and institutional ecosystem and merely apply a plaster or a bandage to control the bad effects?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Or do we take the riskier approach of reforming the underlying policy, institution or practice, risking that the new approach, in seeking to reduce the downsides of the old policy, may wholly or partly lose the benefits of the old policy?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One way to decide this lies in seeing if the deeper trends going on in Singapore and the world will make the downsides worse than the benefits over time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If not, let us do incremental tweaks and plasters now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I was glad to hear references in the President's speech to an appetite for bold reform, which, of course, does not mean reckless reform.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And in the spirit, I suggest reforms to two broad baskets of policies where longer-term trends argue for reform.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of these ideas have been suggested by my colleagues and I on other occasions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such changes would not reduce the absolute size of the reserves per se but would slow down the rate of reserve growth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This question is not only a technical economic question but a deep, philosophic question about inter-generational equity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And on this question I would put it to this House that there are reasonable views on both sides of the issue.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After all, there was a time in the past when suggestions like spending some of the NIR or adding Temasek Holdings to the NIR framework might perhaps have been labelled as irresponsible.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nominated Member of Parliament Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin made an interesting speech which asked about our reserves, how much is enough.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would build on that and ask: no doubt we need emergency reserves, we absolutely need that, but what rate of reserve growth is enough?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are risks from reducing the rate of reserves growth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We gain additional security from a larger and larger emergency fund going forward.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But there are also risks from allowing costs and economic pressures to rise in the future, inhibiting growth in other qualities we need to optimise among Singaporeans, like risk-taking, long-termism, entrepreneurism, TFR.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Confidence that the future could be better than the past, confidence that the deck is not stacked against me, confidence that I need not run faster and faster just to stay in the same place.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Spending more on the current generations and reducing the cost burden may affect TFR.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As our reserves grow and the need to promote confidence among Singaporeans grows, the case for reform to this basket of policies strengthens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fact of HDB flat lease decay is rightly a part of this basket of issues.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a large and complex issue which the Workers’ Party intends to study in the months ahead, with a view to make constructive suggestions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, can we not review our education system, which was originally designed, we are told, such that tuition is unnecessary?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we not review the balance between content mastery and time for non-cognitive skills development or even time for leisure, hobbies and family pursuits which aid healthy character formation?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: No doubt, content mastery has been pared down over the years, but do exams test the pared-down content taught in the standard curriculum or do exams test for content that goes beyond, thus acting as a sharper stratification instrument, whether intended or otherwise?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One letter published in The Straits Times Forum said, "The textbooks recommended by the Ministry and used in schools offer basic information.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, when it comes to examinations, the questions asked are often way above the level of the information in the textbooks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the main reason students seek tuition".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, is there room to re-balance further between developing cognitive skills on the one hand, which are important, and non-cognitive skills and leisure time on the other?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Amidst the relentless advance of AI and robotics, as simple tasks become automated and a higher and higher premium falls on skillsets like creativity and leadership, the case for education reform in this respect grows.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we not review our class size, to take advantage of falling enrolments while leaving the teacher population stable, as I argued in an earlier Motion?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Smaller Learning Support Programme (LSP) classes for weaker pupils could stigmatise those pupils.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, smaller general class sizes could reduce the number of pupils falling behind that necessitates those smaller LSP classes to begin with.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is evidence that smaller class sizes can yield significant education, non-cognitive skill and social mobility benefits.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our general class sizes are well above the OECD average.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And can we regularly measure and debate social mobility, as my Party Chairman Ms Sylvia Lim has eloquently argued for?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our system has many devices that favour stability.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To be sure, stability is a good thing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But with such a framework, are we not sacrificing diversity?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does our institutional ecosystem do enough to promote diversity of ideas in the public square?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we not scale back the extent, if, indeed, there is any, of the "influence, resources and enforcement powers" of the Government being brought to bear on the way news is reported by mainstream media (MSM) outlets, such that MSM editors and journalists report the news as they see fit, within broad regulatory parameters pertaining to sensitive issues like race and religion, as I suspect most journalists would want to do?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An Ombudsman may uncover policy gaps or institutional shortcomings that are not related purely to corruption or finances as dealt with by CPIB and AGO.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Traditionally, many national leaders have emerged from Government scholarship holders, some of whom go on to populate the top rungs of the Civil Service, GLCs and the Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This tends to reduce the pool of talent available to the private sector and civil society and it is important for both of these sectors to be strong in the future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, this pattern can produce political and GLC decision-makers who lack private or not-for-profit sector experience.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans were very surprised when the new incoming CEO of SMRT was another former General.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Did our Pioneer Generation Cabinet have such a high proportion of ex-civil servants?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If necessary, we can ramp up the scholar cohort size to ensure sufficient scholars remain to meet Public Service needs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition to these points, the other huge part of the equation is how to generate economic growth, to grow the size of the pie.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Technology is changing and our people’s needs are evolving, creating demand for new infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Expectations are always rising and, despite all that we have achieved, there is always more to do.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We need to rethink how we build, what we build and how we pay for it.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To meet the challenges ahead, I wish to make three suggestions on ways to improve the infrastructure needs of our country.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My first suggestion is to improve the data infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Data is the backbone of our Smart Nation initiative.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, consumers will remember how the fire in Singtel’s Bukit Panjang Exchange building in 2013 affected consumers from multiple operators in the northern and western parts of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While some people joke that denying people WiFi is a violation of their human rights, it is no laughing matter as such disruptions have serious consequences for both individuals and businesses.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Former Minister Assoc Prof Yaacob Ibrahim identified redundancy as one of the four core components of a resilient network, the others being diversity, resistance and recovery.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The traditional argument against building another totally separate network is the prohibitive cost.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While the costs of not having back-up are constantly rising, the costs of building such a network are coming down as technology advances.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Connectivity providers in the UK are exploring creative solutions to traditional network laying.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Sewers, spare electricity cable ducts, highways, overhead lines and rail networks are being explored for the right of way to lay cables.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This creative approach to new networks is also being seen at a government level.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, in the UK, the wastewater pipe network of Thames Water is being used to deploy fibre optic cables, instantly creating new, cost-effective and diverse connections in key business areas.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The argument for an alternative fibre network is strong and getting stronger.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By leveraging existing infrastructure to reduce implementation costs and optimise asset use, the costs may not remain prohibitive.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I believe there is also room for private operators to play a bigger role, so that the Government would not have to shoulder the entire cost of implementation.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But what is needed are clear rules to allow for the usage of existing infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I urge the relevant Ministries to take a deeper look at the issue.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We should also look at infrastructure from a sustainability perspective and, hence, we return to a topic that I have addressed before – electric vehicles (EVs).

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What seemed like toys for rich geeks just a few years ago are now seen as the future of mobility.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My second suggestion is to provide more charging points for EVs.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many countries are already laying plans to phase out combustion engines altogether.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Indian government has indicated its intention to only allow EVs to be sold in India by 2030.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: China has raised the bar yet again for automakers when it announced late last month its proposal to implement aggressive new quotas for the production of new Energy Vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The world is moving towards the adoption of EV and such a move would be in line with our commitment to COP21.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore is well-placed to take the lead in the adoption of EVs, but despite its small size that is perfect for EVs, adoption has been slow because of the lack of reliable access to charging.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is a chicken-and-egg problem, if there are no charging points, car owners will not adopt EVs.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One way is to open up more of these charging points to the public eventually but, without the HDB and Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) carpark access, a pervasive network of public EV charging points will not be possible.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Government needs to support and encourage more public-private cooperation in this space.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My third suggestion is related to one of the common complaints that we hear from residents that there is frequent congestion on roads due to what they perceive to be uncoordinated roadworks by different utilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To them, we seem to be constantly digging up and patching up the same stretches of roads over and over again.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While there are, of course, legitimate reasons for this, can the coordination between utilities be optimised through the implementation of more common services, tunnels, such as the one that we have in the Marina Bay area?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Or would it be possible to leverage other tunnels, such as the deep tunnel sewerage system or the underground transmission cable tunnel?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Such a scheme can reduce traffic congestion, reduce risk of damage to utilities and allow for easier access for maintenance and repairs.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is important to have a regulatory framework to allow these private or public tunnels to be accessed and utilised by all.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the same time, it ensures that utilities owners are properly compensated.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is in the larger national interest of reducing congestion and improving productivity.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The first is to have a balance between public intervention and market solutions.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are moving into a much more challenging world and the Government needs to establish the right ground rules.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There must be the appropriate balance between Government intervention where it is needed and allowing the private sector to find the best solutions.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On more micro initiatives, where the right solution might not be clear and where the private sector can find the best solution, the Government should exercise greater caution before getting involved.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: An example is the many subsidies that we are offering to SMEs to adopt technologies.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In contrast, while many of the infrastructure developments that I have just discussed, there are strong economic arguments for Government intervention as the private sector may not be willing to undertake the level of investment needed.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As reliability and security are paramount for such projects, given the scale and national importance, the Government has to provide direction and ensure that the Ministries coordinate across all levels in a whole-of-Government approach.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The second suggestion is to develop a regulatory framework for public and private cooperation.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Where private stakeholders are involved, a framework must be created to ensure proper compensation to the stakeholders that finance and build each piece of infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While it is tempting to regulate by saying no to everything, this will not lead to the desired outcome.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There must be some spread of risk-taking because, if you take no risk, you will reap no reward and our nation will be the poorer for it.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The final suggestion will be on alternative ways to finance infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Only the Government has the financial clout to finance major infrastructural investments that we need.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Infrastructure costs are long term in nature while financing is short term.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This transfers the risk from taxpayers to private companies.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can go even further than just borrowing to finance investment as has been announced in the 2018 Budget.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is similar to the use of REIT to allow more people to benefit from real estate ownership.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are currently, lots of appetite both domestically and internationally, to finance long-term, stable assets.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Such a move will help to develop a deep, liquid and transparent infrastructure market for SGX.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The social compact during our early post-Independence years was simple, quite simple as it encompasses much of our ambition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: I recall it simply says the Government will create a better life for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our first generation Government forged this social compact with Singaporeans like my parents, when we were a nation struggling for survival and aspiring for a better living.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The Government promised a home with modern amenities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We all moved from our kampong houses to HDB flats; rental flats initially.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: But with economic progress, we moved to purchased homes, which appreciated in value over time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We wanted stable jobs in a dynamic economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: So, when the Government urged us to pick up manufacturing skills in vocational schools, we did.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In the 1970s and 1980s, those were our only choices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: At the same time, we were given access to quality education and many of us attained education and skills levels that our parents never thought possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We wanted to be able to defend ourselves after the British forces withdrew, so, when the Government introduced National Service, we served.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Against the odds, our early generation transformed a small country into a thriving economy, established a strong defence force in a volatile geopolitical environment and built national unity from a multiracial, multi-religious society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: During this debate, many Members of the House have spoken on social inequality and cautioned against the ill effects of social stratification.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Like them, I have come across cases of low-income families facing multiple challenges, raising concerns about the future of their children and wondering how is it that we still have such families, given 50 years of remarkable economic progress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It begs the question: have we failed in fulfilling our social compact with Singaporeans?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It is true that as our country develops economically, most Singaporeans saw improvements in their lives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We accepted the social compact forged at that time where meritocracy was the principal consideration and our priorities were to promote personal responsibility and optimise our scarce resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Despite these efforts, some continue to say that Government intervention has been inadequate and even argue that certain Government policies have led to this inequality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Reflecting on this, I am convinced that the recent tide of concern regarding rising inequality is not so much an indication of an unfulfilled social compact.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Are we looking for greater emphasis on compassion versus meritocracy?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The larger question then is: is the social compact of the past still relevant today?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Will young	Singaporeans share the same aspirations and outlook as their predecessors?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It is important for us to understand their concerns and aspirations, given that this generation will inherit and actively shape Singapore's future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our Government will need to partner them to write the next chapter of the Singapore Story and co-create the right social compact for their time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: To do so, we must note our next generation – the Singapore millennials.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: According to the survey, young	Singaporeans embrace lifelong learning and rated acquiring new skills and knowledge highly as part of their top life goals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: They are also more socially conscious, future-focused and have greater international exposure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Being a parent of two millennials, I must say that I am intimately acquainted with the challenges of trying to understand our children and youths of today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: However, this pan picture of our millennials as depicted by the National Youth Survey is a useful reference point for us to keep in mind and as we continue to explore the key design considerations of what Singapore's future will look like.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It highlighted five strategies to reach out to our millennials today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It spoke of, one, creating an experience for them; two, making things frictionless; three, allowing customisation; four, building loyalty; and, five, demonstrating value.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: While these strategies were originally conceived to inform retailers' efforts to win over the youth market, the insights are applicable to our context.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The repeated questions were, I asked myself, how do these prescribed strategies upend our traditional business models of governance and public policymaking and, further, what further areas of governance, or what specific areas of governance can we infuse these strategies into?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: First, the strategy to reach to out the	millennial is to create an experience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: But today, our	millennials are developing their own definition of success.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Encapsulated by the so-called "YOLO" or you only live once attitude, our youths want to be excited where to live, work and play.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: To this end, our youths can look forward to raising families in homes that will boast the physical and digital connectivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Just imagine, by leveraging artificial intelligence, smart homes could render current day household chores an afterthought.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: At work, our millenials will also come to grips with the challenges of participating in the extremely competitive global labour marketplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: More would job hop with high attrition rates in some professions because just earning money is not enough.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Young people want to know that they have made a difference.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: They look for newer experiences and want to learn new things as they know the possession of single and static skillsets is not sufficient to thrive amidst the competition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: To balance work, our young people want a Singapore that is fun and vibrant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: From hunting down the latest "insta-worthy" hang-outs to taking part in various arts or sporting events, the extent to which we can make Singapore the most liveable city is clearly only limited by our own imagination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The second strategy to connecting to millenials is making it frictionless.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In the context of governance, perhaps, in re-imagining Public Service delivery.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Today, our youths have increasingly grown accustomed to living in a frictionless society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Thanks to advances in telecommunications and the Internet, private sector companies have been able to leverage innovations and technologies to make our daily lives more convenient and hassle-free.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In transportation, for example, private hire mobile applications, such as Grab, that provide door-to-door services with seamless payment solutions have become commonplace and effectively disrupted how our people consume transportation services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Reminders like "do not board a stranger's car" do not resonate with young people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Similarly, e-commerce has changed the retail experience, making it possible to now make purchases of all sorts from the comforts of home at just the click of a button.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This is the reality that confronts the Singapore Public Service: that these forms of corporate innovations increase our citizens' expectations of service delivery, which, inevitably, extends to the provision of public services as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This issues a clarion call to the Government to raise our standards of Public Service delivery to satisfy the expectations of our people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This is our opportunity to re-imagine many areas of governance, such as housing, health, social services, education and transportation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In this aspect, we can be encouraged by the progress that has been made by our Smart Nation initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We have already made inroads in some of these areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The parking.sg app is targeted at making the tearing of carpark coupons a thing of the past.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: I am sure that some still do tear the carpark coupons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: These ideas represent but the tip of the iceberg on how Singapore will bet big on technological solutions to transform the way we deliver healthcare, employment and financial services to the population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This Government will have to convince fellow Singaporeans we are ready to get on with the times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: To be daring and bold in exploring all ideas that will help ensure that our services are accessible on the go, available on demand, absent of cumbersome processes, supported by the use of safe and secure databases and equipped with feedback mechanisms for constant improvement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Through this, we hope to deliver the service standards that our citizens desire and deserve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Many of us in this Chamber can recall the days when kopi came mostly in recycled condensed milk tins and a kopi si siew kai counts as a special order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Today, walk into any modern cafe, often run by young entrepreneurs and you can select from a menu that ranges from nitro-cold brews to hand-brewed drip coffee with hints of cherry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The coffee beans will also be sourced from across the globe, catering to every palette and preference.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: No previous generation has ever had such high expectations for variety and customisation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Nevertheless, our young Singaporeans are proving themselves as more mature than older Singaporeans sometimes give them credit for.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Many young residents have shared with me that their perception of Singapore's value is not determined only by our plentiful economic opportunities but also by the extent that Singapore is home to people and places they love.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: They understand that Singapore, as an advanced economy, is unlikely to experience double-digit economic growth, but can still sustain a good standard of living if we remain dynamic in our outlook.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: What the millenials	seek, in the next bound of our development is greater involvement in shaping policies and the living environment that sets the conditions for our country's dynamism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: They want the opportunity to customise aspects of their nation, just as they had grown accustomed to in many other facets of their lives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: I believe our younger Singaporeans seek to revisit a social compact where the Government had a monopoly on master planning the public good and create a greater role for citizen participation in city design and policy formulation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This playground had features conceptualised, designed and built by residents living in housing estates in Sembawang.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The outcome is a facility that is fun for young residents with design elements that reflect the precinct's heritage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Now, I am told, there is also FOMO: Fear Of Missing Out, a prevalent mindset of apprehension that you will miss out on something great.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: So, to the young Singaporeans, there is huge potential for co-creation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Do not miss out on this opportunity to create the future with the Government and forge a new social compact where every citizen has the opportunity to shape policies and public goods which they hold dear.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This way, Singaporeans can take ownership of our country through the process of co-creation and everyone can be proud to call Singapore home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The fourth strategy to reach out to the millenials is building loyalty.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In this context, the implication for the Government is making Singapore where the heart is.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Indeed, what gives our young Singaporeans a stake in Singapore will evolve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For a generation that is better educated, more-travelled, articulate and confident than their predecessors, the world is their oyster.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Home ownership and stable employment might not be enough to keep our young Singaporeans anchored in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: On the other hand, the ever-growing demands of a small city state on its populace have not gone away.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We will still need every Singaporean son to defend us from external threats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As we remain a diverse society, mutual respect for Singaporeans of all races and religions to uphold racial and religious harmony remains non-negotiable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Life and living as a Singaporean come with responsibilities of citizenship.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For our young Singaporeans whose skills are valued by major cities across the globe, what makes Singapore their home of choice?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: What drives our love and yearning for home despite its imperfections and our household responsibilities?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: I do not profess to know the answer for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For my family, the trials and tribulations we have been through and the unbreakable trust we have in one another has held us together over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: By extension, forging a sense of common destiny and winning the confidence of its citizens are imperatives of every Government and an essential ingredient for effective partnership between communities and their leaders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The 4G leadership of Singapore is no exception.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As we tackle inequality head on, we must be cognisant of what social mobility means for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It is a popular index of a country's income inequality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: But it actually does not tell us much about income distribution and very little, in fact anything, about social mobility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The Gini coefficient is a relative measure and, therefore, has many limitations for tracking key issues, such as income or social class differences, and, particularly, how people are progressing in socio-economic terms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Yet, we know these societies are vastly different when you look at the social and economic conditions of people's lives across these countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: A better handle on measuring social mobility is needed to discuss meaningfully the causes of inequality and policies to tackle it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As Prof David Chan from SMU has highlighted, tackling social inequalities involves understanding people's aspirations and achievements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Today, young Singaporeans have come of age in relative affluence but we will soon have to confront the cost of sustaining an ageing society and closing the inequality gap.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: They, too, should have the opportunity to articulate their desired social compact.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Beyond influencing policy, I urge young Singaporeans to be the change you wish to see in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: If you feel strongly for causes to improve the lives of the less fortunate amongst us, step up and take action.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We see many more elderly in the community living alone and at risk of social isolation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: They need the support and our youth can respond.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: I am heartened that, increasingly, many young Singaporeans are answering this call.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: They asked me for support for a location that they can conduct this distribution process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As a nation, let us take pride not only in an economy where people's physical needs and wants are met, but in a strong Singapore society which we can all call home because of our individual and collective efforts to foster inclusion with fellow Singaporeans from different backgrounds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Speaker, today is the first day of the month of Ramadan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Please allow me to wish a Blessed Ramadan to all Muslims in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: I wish them well as they perform their fast throughout the month of Ramadan and may they receive His blessings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Therefore, I have a special message for our younger generation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As you work hard and progress, do know that the definition of success that we know today can, and will, change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: You need to create and open your own pathways towards a brighter future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Do not be bound to the old school of thought that over-emphasises academic results or sets too much limits on your career choice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Feel excited about where you live, where you work and where you play.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: And be bold enough to challenge the status quo together with the Government and seize opportunities to sharpen your skills and let your natural abilities shine.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: But stay confident and strong about your identity and your culture – in fact, use it as the cornerstone in all your efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The path to success will not be easy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The road will be tough – it requires both sacrifice and hard work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Because, now, you own this journey from start to end.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Do not let your station in life today define who you want to be and where you want to be tomorrow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As a successful young people, you also have a role in spurring progress and developing the Malay/Muslim community in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As we celebrate your success in various fields – be it academic, sports, arts or the professions – there will still be those who are lagging and left behind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: But we are certain that their situation is only temporary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Therefore, they can move towards the next station in life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: So, let us reach out and help them to ride the wave towards success, whatever the field may be.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: With the combination of your youthful enthusiasm and your “YOLO” spirit, you can create creative solutions to mobilise your generation and help our community progress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As your generation likes to say – hash-tag go-je-don’t-scared.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This is a new hash-tag, I am told – #gojedonscared.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It means, just go, do it, do not be afraid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Singaporean millennials would have to address many new challenges, including disruptions brought about by their peers across the globe.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: To do so, they need to have instincts, mental dexterity and skills that their global competitors possess.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Sometimes, we all take for granted what we have.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The next chapter of the Singapore Story must continue to capture the imagination of the storytellers, Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our earlier generations have undertaken a similar journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Now, we must go through our own journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Each of us has a part to play.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: To the parents, of all the obstacles we clamour to remove in our children's development, our preconceived notions of success is a good start.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Success need not be about achieving or achievements of goals but the fulfillment of self, including the joy of being able to be useful to others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Indeed, we should suspend judgement and be willing to listen to what they have to say.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Let us, as good stewards of Singapore, empower the next generation to succeed and take Singapore to greater heights.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: To the millennials, the path to success will not be easy, however we define it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The road will be tough and requires sacrifices and hard work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Yet, the journey is meaningful because you will own it from start to end.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Let your station today not define who you want to be tomorrow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We must continue to meet the future's challenges with a "YOLO" mentality and channel any "FOMO" tendencies towards a collective greater social good.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We must, therefore, band together, rally behind a common aspiration to build our Singapore of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There is no fear of missing out on tea break.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 4.10 pm until 4.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Over the past 53 years, Singapore has done well as a nation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We are one of the more successful countries in the world with a high Gross Domestic Product (GDP) per capita.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We are known to be non-corrupt, transparent and efficient.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Whenever I travel overseas, many foreigners that I speak to, compliment Singapore and they hold us in high regard.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Singaporeans are known to be hardworking, dedicated and trustworthy.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is a good reputation to have and something that all Singaporeans should be proud of.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But yet, sometimes, when I speak to Singaporeans, I do not sense the same level of pride of being a Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some of them are concerned about the future of our nation, being small and without resources.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some worry that the growth opportunities which my generation had may not be available to the future generations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some are critical of the Government even though they know that Singapore is well-run.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The frequent criticism is that the Government is well-intended but unwilling to listen to other views or is too defensive.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: My experience with the 4G leaders that I work with is that they are genuine and sincere about wanting to serve the people.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They want to do their best to improve the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, governing is a complicated process and no government, no matter how well-intended, is perfect.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As the 4G leadership team leads Singapore to the future, I hope that they can improve on the way that we engage our citizens.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I hope they will be more consultative in the policies and approach.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I hope they can be a more receptive and kinder Government when dealing with people of differing views.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: At the same time, I hope that Singaporeans, too, will rally behind and support a sincere and honest Government because no matter how good our policies, a divided nation will always fail.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As citizens, we can all be part of a solution by working together for a common purpose of making Singapore a better home for all of us.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: With better explanations, Singaporeans will be able to discern what are good policies; beneficial for our people and for the nation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But we need to work hard to explain our policies to earn the respect of those who may not agree with or understand the policies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Our leaders must also learn to trust that Singaporeans are mature and know what is good for them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I feel that there are several challenges facing Singapore for the future.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: One of the challenges is to ensure that the economy continues growing and Singaporeans continue to have access to good jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The reality is that our competition is the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Painful as it may sound, getting a good job is not an entitlement for any of us.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Each of us must find a way to provide better value to our potential employer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And when I read of the high unemployment rates in some of the more developed countries, I am glad that Singapore is still able to manage its unemployment figures.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But we should never assume that full employment is our entitlement and will stay with us in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Singaporeans hope for a better life for the future.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: An increase in cost of living will reduce their disposable income and affect their aspirations for a better life.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Government must keep a close tab on the increases in living expenses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Whether it is for water, transport fares, medical costs or food costs, we must be mindful that whatever the reason for these increases, when taken together, they will adversely affect the livelihood of our citizens, especially those of the lower income.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In my constituency, I have many residents who either live in private homes or bigger HDB flats which were purchased when they were younger, working and economically better off.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, today, many are retired with no income and some are unable to find similar paying jobs due to their age.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And their frustration is that they always get left behind whenever benefits are announced in the annual Budget.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is essentially a non-event for them because the SG Bonus, GST vouchers or S&CC or utilities rebates are usually not for them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They feel that the Government has little appreciation for residents living in better homes despite their past years of contribution to nation building when they were working.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am not suggesting simply giving handouts for them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is about better appreciating those who had contributed to Singapore during their working years, those who had paid income taxes, but served the nation in different capacities.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, I urge the Government to adopt policies which signal to our citizens that they are appreciated for their contributions to nation building.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This will give them a sense that they are Singaporeans, too, whenever the Budget is announced, instead of it being a non-event.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It does not make sense why the CHAS system penalises someone for working harder and earning more.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are many other policies which can be improved upon.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But it does not mean that the policies are wrong.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, with minor adjustments, we can make the policies better and create a more positive impact on our citizens.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: My appeal to the Government leaders is to be always open to suggestions for improvements; for our civil servants to adopt a framework of asking, "How can I do this better?" Mr Speaker, I am confident that our current leaders have the ability to plan for the future of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, I wish to sound a word of caution that Singapore should not be seen as a company where everything is simply transactional.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We are a nation and a home that all Singaporeans can be proud of.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, I urge the Government to develop policies which will strengthen our nation's core values; to inculcate in our citizens the importance of values like meritocracy, self-reliance, incorruptibility, diligence, honesty, humility and loyalty to the nation as we all continue writing the Singapore story.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singaporeans must be mindful that we are living in a highly competitive world and we must continue to develop the drive to be innovative and competitive, without losing our ability to stay grounded in reality.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must stay united as one people so that we can progress together for a better future.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, transforming our built environment for the future economy; second, transforming our built environment for quality living; and, third, transforming our built environment for retail and recreation.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First: transforming our built environment for future economy.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are three ways we can transform our built environment to support the industry transformation.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, review of land use planning policies and regulations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: More planning reforms, such as plot ratio increase or change of use, should be implemented to attract industry champions to spearhead industry transformations and developments.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: With the proposed industry transformation, it is, therefore, an opportune time for the authorities to review their respective policies and regulations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The provision of some breathing space from excessive regulation may help to foster a more vibrant and innovative business community which will inevitably contribute to the economic well-being of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Second, provide more flexibility in our building, environment and manpower regulations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: For instance, the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) should continue to encourage buildability and maintainability of buildings.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: But it should allow more flexibility for the industry stakeholders, such as developers, consultants, contractors and suppliers, to develop solutions for productivity and quality improvements.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Where possible, the industry clusters should also be located at places well-supported by our transport and logistics infrastructure, such as MRT stations, seaports and airports.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Next, transforming our built environment for quality living.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are three ways we can transform our built environment to improve the quality of life of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, encouraging families to stay near each other.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, encouraging families to stay near each other.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is particularly so in HDB towns where young and old families stay together.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our housing policies must continue to encourage families to stay near one another.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Although various developments are in place to support ageing, there is an urgent need to make every home to be elder-safe, every community to be elder-safe and make Singapore to be an elder-safe country for both Singaporeans and tourists.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need to take stock of the existing town amenities and shops and take bold steps to change the amenities and tenant mix of shops to better serve our seniors.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: For instance, some town centres have many similar types of shops, such as hair salons or renovation shops in one location and, thus, do not serve the needs of the residents, especially seniors.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As such, seniors in these towns have to travel to other places to buy elderly products and services.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must identify the range of elderly products and services and provide these amenities in the community so as to improve the quality of life of our seniors.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These elderly-friendly amenities will also encourage seniors to develop self-reliant capabilities, thus, improving their quality of life.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These standard solutions will encourage more families to make their homes elder-safe thus, encouraging family members and friends to visit each other.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Popular amenities for seniors include fitness gym, multi-purpose court, walking track and community garden.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Town Council can also provide better connectivity within the town by building more footpaths, cycling paths and covered linkways.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will encourage more residents to walk and cycle, thus, enhancing their health and well-being.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: At present, many buildings and places do not have barrier-free access.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our public transport system is also not fully integrated to provide seamless travel for all seniors and wheelchair-bound commuters.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need a whole-of-Government approach at the Ministerial level to enhance the barrier-free connectivity of our built environment as many Government agencies are facing many barriers presently.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Swimming is a low impact and wholesome exercise suitable for all age groups, especially the seniors.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: With an ageing population, many seniors are experiencing knee and joint problems and, thus, have reduced or stopped physical exercises.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Furthermore, many seniors are not keen to take up swimming due to the hot and wet weather conditions in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Sheltered swimming pools will provide a more conducive environment for seniors to enjoy swimming and water sports in our public pools.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: It will also increase the usage of our public pools at all times during the opening hours, including adverse weather conditions and days.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Transforming our built environment for retail and recreation.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need to take bold measures to revamp the retail industry in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I wish to propose three ideas to support the retail industry transformation in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In this regard, I would urge the Government to review the development plans for Tampines, Jurong East and Woodlands regional centres to transform them into mega shopping hubs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These underground shopping malls can be located at residential areas and parks so that people can walk, shop, eat and relax in the parks.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, we can build an underground shopping mall connecting Ang Mo Kio to Bishan Park and Thomson area.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These underground shopping malls can also become evacuation or bomb shelters in times of emergency.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Last year, Bukit Panjang transformed its Bangkit neighbourhood centre into an art street selling a wide range of products and services.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The transformation has attracted many more shoppers to the neighbourhood centre and provided much vibrancy to the town.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Residents can now enjoy shopping in a barrier-free and weather-proof shopping environment.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need to align the built environment transformation to support the industry transformation so as to provide better jobs for Singaporeans, a better living environment for Singaporeans and a better quality of life for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: But Sir, we cannot rely on foreign talent alone to transform our built environment, we need to nurture Singaporeans to be world-class built environment professionals.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need to train more Singaporeans to be world-class project managers, facilities managers, architects, engineers and quantity surveyors to build and maintain our world-class city.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, the method in which we plan for such a transformation has to be purposeful.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: A vision of a built environment which is bold and creative while remaining grounded in reality will be of great value to current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Together, we can make Singapore a world-class city.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We must grow so that Singaporeans can have good jobs and opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We must grow so that we have the resources to build our home, to take care of one another and to protect ourselves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We must grow for our children, to give them a better future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But growth is much more than just GDP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Earlier this week, Minister Chan Chun Sing painted the vision of Singapore Unlimited.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We can grow in productivity, so that our companies and workers do things smarter, faster and better than others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We can grow in skills, so that if you want to get difficult things done reliably and creatively, you will get it done through Singaporean workers and Singaporean companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We can grow in innovation, so that if companies want to create products and services to serve the fastest growing area in the world, which is Asia, they will come to Singapore to turn their ideas into reality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, we must be pro-business in our rules and regulations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, we must be pro-Singapore: believe that our local companies and workers can compete with the very best.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And, third, we must be pro-talent so that our people can have the best opportunities in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our focus is to set good rules and regulations, to protect our consumers and to foster a pro-business, pro-worker environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Because poorly designed or outdated rules can have unintended consequences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Where possible, we want to allow market forces to work efficiently, so that enterprises can compete fairly and achieve the best outcomes for society and consumers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And we know we have to regularly review our rules because technology and business models change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When rules are set smartly, fairly and in a pro-business manner, our people and our companies benefit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This nimbleness sets us apart from other countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Companies want to set up shop in Singapore because they know that here, they can operate in a trusted and reliable environment which is dynamic and connected with the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They can pioneer a new business idea in Singapore, prove that it works and then export it around the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, we will proactively seek feedback from businesses to make it a part of our DNA and our instincts to be pro-enterprise; to continuously improve our rules and licensing framework, speed up processes and facilitate new business ideas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One example is how AVA and SCDF worked with the Singapore Manufacturing Federation to enhance regulations for cold stores.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Previously, fire prevention compartment walls in cold stores posed hygiene concerns as they could attract pests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Based on industry feedback, the agencies worked with SMF to allow an alternative insulation material which will retard the spread of fire without posing hygiene risks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is a win-win outcome, which helped companies save several thousands of dollars per year for each cold store.
