text: But without additional revenues, how are we to meet the growing healthcare needs, as well as the many other proposals that various people, including the Workers' Party, have been asking for?

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And both Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Leon Perera have reiterated the call to change the rules on the use of reserves so that we can draw more from the reserves.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And this was done not too long ago.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: What does it say about us and our mindsets and attitude, if the minute we need the money, the first thing we do is to relax the rules?

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Surely, that will be ill-disciplined, imprudent and unwise.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This goes back to the issue of responsible governance.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Look at the challenges that other First World democracies face – their politics have become more fractured, chaotic and unpredictable.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One common thread across many of these countries is that they are in fiscal difficulties.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because the politicians pander to the electorate; they spend more than they collect in taxes and run up unfunded obligations and debt.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ultimately, the ones who suffer are the citizens, especially the most vulnerable.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We level with our people, so, everyone knows what to expect and what hard choices we need to take.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We work to serve the interests of all Singaporeans, not just for one or two electoral cycles, but over the long term.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is what we have been doing and will continue to do.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Earlier, I likened the city to a living organism, where we either adapt or perish.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In some ways, our next phase of development is like pushing a boulder uphill.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It requires constant effort to keep going up.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The moment we relax and let go, the boulder starts moving downhill, slowly at first and then at uncontrollable speeds and then it will be too late.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The higher up the hill, the greater the tendency for the boulder to roll down.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And, indeed, we are now at a higher point on the hill.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we need all hands on deck to keep pushing the boulder together and to reach even higher peaks of excellence.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That does not mean that you have to agree with every Government policy; if you have a different idea or proposal, we stand ready to listen and to review our policies.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But please do not disagree just for the sake of doing so.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I recall a speech that Mr Rajaratnam once made where he said, "It’s easy to win attention by disagreeing with the Government.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If the Government says ‘white’ and you advocate ‘black’, you will be hailed at the next cocktail reception as an original and bold thinker." But in the end, what is important is that we all come together with the genuine interest to solve the real and vital problems affecting our nation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The academic I mentioned earlier on the CPF matter, Prof Walter Theseira, when he clarified his remarks on the CPF issue, also wrote on his Facebook page: “It’s easy to make fun of policymakers and it’s also easy to critique policy.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Finding workable solutions that promote the public interest is a lot harder but, more than ever, we need to work together to help improve policy in Singapore.”  I fully agree with him.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This endeavour of building our future Singapore cannot be done by the Government alone; it must be a collective effort involving all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for National Development and Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We want to build a city that reflects the aspirations, the values and the spirit of our people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister was speaking of a debate we had when the NIRC formula was amended to include Temasek.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In that debate, if I remember correctly, the reasons given for the change were higher expenditure on healthcare, higher expenditure on ageing and infrastructure development.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And just to get a sense of the Government's plans in future, given the accumulated surpluses at hand, largely, I would believe as a result of Temasek's inclusion, do we have some understanding of what new projects or even endowments will be created by the Government for the years to come?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They were specific to certain contributions from MAS which we have explained.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is indisputable because the population is ageing; and it will rise very sharply.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, on healthcare alone, the increase is significant and we have to cater for this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the revenue side, if you look at our revenues, there is a part of them that is linked to income and taxation, largely to the economy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we know that the economy is not going to grow in the same way that it used to in the past.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Growth is moderating and so revenues from these different taxation models will moderate too.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is already the single largest item in our revenue source today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It will just provide a steady constant stream of revenue as a percentage of GDP.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We do not expect that to go up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, there is a risk that it may even come down.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because if you look at the trends in the asset markets today, interest rates are at historically low levels.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If you look at equity valuations, they are highly elevated.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, there is a risk that long-term asset returns may be lower in the future.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, if you look at this overall picture, spending beyond the term of Government going up, inexorably and clearly going to happen, revenue uncertain and, if anything, there are more downside risks than before, then I think you would appreciate that our fiscal position is, in fact, not that strong and we need to take steps to further strengthen it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Just two points of clarification for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Or is it something that is set in stone and cannot be changed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The second point for the Minister: would the Minister acknowledge that there are other costs on the other side of the equation?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The more future Governments are to raise things like GST, the more that raises economic pressure and, potentially, anxieties experienced by Singaporeans and the more that can affect other things which are important for the country and also important for economic growth, like TFR which, I think, has been said is an existential issue for Singapore, like entrepreneurship, risk-taking, long-termism, innovation and things like that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If we give more room to those things, might there also not be the possibility that these things could raise economic growth and, therefore, raise revenue further down the line?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But my point on the NIRC rules is this: that this was debated at length only not too long ago.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We went through this discussion in this House, debated thoroughly the points and we settled on a framework.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A framework that we think best meets the needs of both current and future generations and balances that fairly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we decided to enshrine these rules in the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Let us not be so quick to rush the minute we need money and say, "Can we tweak the rules again?" So, that is on the first point.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the second point, would cost of Government impose a drag on the economy?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, what I would very much like to hear from Members of this House is: if you think this is a concern, please let us have proposals, not to spend more, which we keep hearing, but to spend less for a change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: At that time, I was a volunteer and an activist with Mr Sam Tan at his Radin Mas branch.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There was some tea involved, not all of which was drunk.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The next thing I knew, I was invited to deliver a speech at the PAP party convention in November 2009.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I made a speech about a couple that I had met who ran a bicycle shop and from whom I had bought a bicycle.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The speech was about the way they had run their business, they had pivoted to a new business model; and the opportunities that they saw, I suppose, today, I would have used terms like "disruption", "SkillsFuture", "resiliency".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But really, my agenda was to talk about cycling and to put across the idea that cycling had an important role to play for commuters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I had been cycling as a commuter for some time and I found great difficulty as a result of one rule.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And that rule was that I was unable to take my folding bicycle on the MRT, except at some very peculiar hours, very early in the morning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And this one rule got in the way of my ideal commuting solution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: So, I used that platform to talk about how we should allow folding bicycles on the MRT at all times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Some of them were related to transport, the Bus Service Enhancement Programme, free rides on the MRT in the morning as a way of dealing with congestion, and several more about cycling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Nine years later, I find myself posted to the Ministry of Transport (MOT).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Never let it be said, Mr Deputy Speaker, that the Members of this House do not have a sense of humour!

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There have been new industry models that have affected our public transport framework.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have the Bus Contracting Model where the Government owns all the assets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This model allows us to be far more responsive to changes in ridership, to the needs of commuters, to drive better competition, better efficacy and better efficiency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have seen that trial of free MRT rides in the early morning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: All trains have space for a wheelchair and handrails in the central carriage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Over the last couple of years, we have seen the technology around digital motors and battery technology improve to the point where a significant number of power-assisted bicycles have appeared on our roads and e-scooters have appeared on our pavements as a result of which we had to have the Active Mobility Act, dealing partly, amongst other things, with which device goes where and which pedestrian commuter or mobility solution has the right of way.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have seen the appearance of bicycle-sharing service operators, dockless bicycle-sharing service operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This has significantly improved the last-mile connectivity, but it has also disrupted plans that we have had for docked bicycle-sharing services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It has created a whole set of disamenities and complaints and concerns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The number of HDB cycling towns has now increased to nine, with the paths and associated bicycle parking spaces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And some years ago, finally, I was able to take my folding bicycle on public transport at all times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: None of these happened because of any one speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Many Members of this House have spoken on these matters, many volunteers, many activists, have made representations and there continues to be an on-going serious, significant channel for public feedback.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In that same one year, 1,000 media enquiries and 200 media releases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: A constant process of engaging with academics who are interested in this space.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And the academics are a combination of engineers, public policy academics, but also economists and urban planning specialists.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We engage with industry, people who operate our services, the people who run research and development programmes, the trade associations and the unions on policy, regulatory and operational matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have engaged with local communities, grassroots organisations, grassroots' leaders, advisors, interest groups and activist groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: My colleagues and I in Punggol may have contributed significantly to some of those 850,000 enquiries over the last year, my apologies to my new colleagues in MOT and LTA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Over the same period of time, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Faishal Ibrahim has started and led the Active Mobility Advisory Panel, now in its second term reviewing the effectiveness of the interventions that they have introduced.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They engage in a process of consultation that requires in-depth interviews with a wide range of commuters, pedestrians and active mobility users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: A public survey that went out to over 5,000 people, focus group discussions with hundreds of people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Similarly, we have had the Family-Friendly Transport Advisory Panel co-chaired by the Chairman of the PTC, Mr Richard Magnus, as well as our colleague Mr Sitoh Yih Pin.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And similar consultative exercises for our Land Transport Master Plans 2008 and 2013.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Online surveys, focus group discussions, an international advisory panel, grassroots organisations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Singaporeans have been whole-heartedly engaging in this process, enthusiastically, and, sometimes, not so pleasantly, but, in general, with a view to improving our system and processes and making this work better for them and for our country.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is no surprise because our land transport system is a significant part of our lived daily experience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is an important part of our daily experience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But the Government's role in this is not just about operating and effectively managing a feedback channel.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have to act in a certain series of dimensions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have to firstly safeguard the public interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In this, we have to look at basic infrastructure, the core components, roads, tracks, stations, depots, railways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And difficult, if not impossible, for a purely commercial interest to take the right kind of perspective, the long-term horizon and balance out the public interest with the opportunity for profit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We also, in the same space, have to think about regulations and safety standards, service quality; we have to ensure that the equipment is maintained and lives up to performance, using levers, such as licences and contracts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But we do not want to remove profit completely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We want to ensure, through our second thrust of work, that we level the playing field to allow private enterprises to step in, to allow businesses to develop new models of work, new commercial operators to come in, to minimise the regulatory barriers and to use as light a touch as possible to have the benefits of commercially-driven innovation and fair practices and a competitive environment for business, to bring to bear those benefits that are available for our land transport system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: So, in this area then, what are the changing circumstances, the changing environment and the new opportunities that we will need to respond to for our land transport system?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have seen the growth of on-demand bus services and bicycle-sharing services and are likely to develop new products, new solutions, to meet those needs and those aspirations that commuters have.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Simultaneously, we have had a sense of increasingly diverse needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have an ageing population, an increasing number of commuters with mobility challenges and we will need to look at increasing accessibility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We are proud of the number of our services, stations, trains and buses which are wheelchair-accessible or barrier-free.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But just like that one regulation had impeded and hindered my commuting journey, when it comes to issues of accessibility, when mobility is a challenge, it does not take much to get in the way between the intent or the idea and the ability for someone with a mobility challenge to effectively use public transport independently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: A small step misaligned, a small design flaw and it gets in the way of a functional outcome that is necessary for that person or that family.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And families need to be considered, specifically, for the future of our public transport system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We need to be increasingly family-centric if we are going to take our car-lite approach seriously, then families with small children especially, need to be able to navigate our public transport system effectively, comfortably and see it as a viable alternative to owning a car.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These areas will need to have a greater degree of access to them to bring in those flows of workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We need to make viable, full transport, this vision to have employment close to home for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But not every Singaporean who works in those new areas will live in those areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will need flow to those areas and we will also need flow between those areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These changes to the patterns of flow of people will affect how we design our connectivity nodes and the main pipes for our land transport system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Some of our new behaviours, the rise of online shopping, this idea that you will have goods delivered to your door instead of going down to the shops, this has disrupted traditional freight movement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is extremely convenient, it means we have access to goods from around the world but, again, it causes potential disamenities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: You need space for the delivery trucks to come in, drop-off points for people to leave those trucks while they take those goods in, lockers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And we will need to think about how we calibrate that balance between the convenience for the consumer, the demand for that convenience and the congestion that it generates, even as we maintain the opportunity for new business models to be developed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: People are developing new types of jobs – flexi jobs, flexi place, telecommuting – and these shifting patterns of behaviour will also affect how our land transport system is used.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And, as always, as we have done, repeatedly, we want to do so in consultation, in collaboration with Singaporeans from all walks of life: families, workers, parents, grandparents, industry, academics, activists, grassroots.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We want to bring everybody into this process because this matters to our land transport system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It makes it relevant and responsive to the needs and aspirations of the public.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But also because, the public, we, have a large role to play in making an effective and pleasant land transport system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Whether it is the choice of the route, the choice of our transport modality, the choice of how and at which time of day we travel.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Or the choice around our behaviours: how we choose to board the bus or the MRT, how we choose to stand or sit, how we look out for each other on the roads.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have a plan and we know what we have to do.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We know where we have to get to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But how we get there, how quickly and at what cost, what are the priorities?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These are the things that we need to hear and we want to hear your views about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Please come and let us know, add to those 850,000 emails and phone enquiries that we have.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Frankly, if you have a view not just on this journey that I have described but also the destination, if you think that that shape of a strategy, that shape of a big plan about where we want to get to, if you have views on that, let us know.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Let us have that discussion and let us have that contest of ideas, so that we can generate the best possible public Land Transport Masterplan for Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: With our efforts, we think we know what Singapore needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But if you are in a position to know better, please, come to us with your proposals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: What is the direction, where is the destination?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Whatever we have seen in the last few years, whether it is about the point-to-point industry, private hire cars, bike-sharing and, now, e-scooter sharing, who knows what is going to happen in the next five years?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Whatever comes along, we need to find a way, we need to design our public transport system in such a way that whatever comes along will be easily integrated and be part of the solution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In some places, people talk of Mobility-as-a-Service (MAAS).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: What do they mean when they talk about Mobility as a Service?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The implication is that you will have multi-modal transport.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Perhaps a shared bicycle to the MRT station.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The MRT takes you to a destination at which point you have a point-to-point car waiting for you that will take you eventually to your place of work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: That journey should be seen ideally as one journey, as opposed to three separate journeys.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Perhaps you can arrange and make a decision about how long it will take you, how much it will cost you on one app, or one platform, or one decision point.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: That end-to-end transportation solution is referred to as Mobility-as-a-Service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There are calls that we should do this as a Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There are people who feel that this idea should be driven by the state.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But, ultimately, if we do so, we would remove commercial opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will remove the opportunities for businesses to come in with their ideas and their ability to drive innovation and innovative practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And frankly speaking, if you look at what we have today, we have a mixture of state-provided solutions, platforms, services and assets as well as industry-provided, business-provided services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: That seamless feel, that integration from end-to-end of your solution and your service, it does not have to all be provided by one entity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If you look at, for example, what people do on their phones: someone sold that to you, you have got your telecommunications subscriptions, the service that you are accessing, if it is a journal or a website, you may have a subscription.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But at the end of the day, you use your phone seamlessly and your experience is relatively blind to the various commercial providers you engage with.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Similarly, if you use cable: who owns the cable, who owns the telco, the subscription that you have paid for and perhaps your pay per use, pay on demand that you have subscribed to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But, ultimately, we want to allow that space to be present for businesses to thrive in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: When we think of that aspiration in the light of the changing mobility challenges, the changing demographics in age especially, this is going to have an impact on resource and resource allocation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: How do we do this in a way that is fair and feels just to Singaporeans?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will need to have a conversation on this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We may have to prioritise transport connectivity to these areas so that economic activity is made available close to Singaporeans' homes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: That seems reasonable but that will have an impact on our overall planning on our priorities, where we will allocate transport connectivity and resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Again, we will need to have that conversation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And as we do so, it will have benefits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It will have benefits through our system in terms of the loading capacity and the congestion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It will have benefits to our health in terms of our ability to get a bit more exercise in our day whether it is walking or cycling and it will have benefits to our environment in terms of the emissions as well as our carbon footprint and energy consumption.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our land transport system connects people with their jobs; goods with markets; connects ideas together with opportunities; and brings friends and families closer together in communities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is essential to the experience of living in this wonderful tropical island that Singapore is, the city-state that we call Home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Transport (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And this, our public land transport system, is one of the key defining characteristics of our home.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: First, I would like to thank the President for the Address.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I have heard many in the House speak about inequality and the urgent need to address the growing gap between the wealthy and the less privileged.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The book is "Pedagogy of Hope" written by Paulo Freire, who is a Brazilian pedagogue-educator.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In the book, Freire recounts a talk that he did for workers about freedom, authority, punishment, reward and dialogical education, based on his own research and field studies on the ground in Brazil.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: During the talk, Freire argued for a dialogical loving relationship between parents and children in place of violent punishments, especially amongst the underclass.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: After his talk, a man, aged about 40, looking worn-out, asked to speak.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: After he had praised Freire for his nice work, which presented complicated ideas in simple terms, he posed a question to Paulo Freire.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I quote the question: “Dr Paulo, Sir, do you know where people live?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Have you ever been in any of our houses, Sir?” And then, this man began to describe their houses: the lack of facilities and extremely minimal space within which the families must cramp into.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: He spoke about how lacking they were in basic necessities.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Freire had visited these houses but never lived in them.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Then, the man asked another question, “Doctor, I've never been over to your house, but I’d like to describe it for you, Sir.” The man then started describing Friere's house, complete with its amenities: running water, rooms for his children and his personal needs and so on.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: These are the same amenities that the man himself did not get to enjoy, but which Friere had become accustomed to.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Then, the man said, “Now, Doctor, look at the difference.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: You come home tired, Sir, and I know that.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: You may even have a headache from the work you do.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Thinking, writing, reading, giving these kind of talks that you’ve given now.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But Sir, it’s one thing to come home, even tired, and find the kids all bathed, dressed up, clean, well fed, not hungry.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, it's another thing to come home and find your kids dirty, hungry, crying, and making noise.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And people have to get up at four in the morning the next day to start all over again -- hurting, sad, hopeless.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: If people hit their kids and even ‘go beyond bounds’, as you say, it’s not because people don’t love their kids.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: No, it’s because life is so hard they don’t have much choices.” It was a sobering sharing for Freire, but he felt very misunderstood.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, he complained to his wife but in response, his wife said, “Could it have been you, Paulo, who didn’t understand them?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They understood you, but they needed to have you understand them.” There are two issues here.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To acknowledge it means you are admitting that you are where you are at in life not solely because of your merit, but because your privilege has -- knowingly or otherwise -- helped to get you to this position.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Meritocracy must be not an end to itself.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, I believe that it is merely one of the means to a greater end.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is to ensure that Singaporeans and anyone living and working in Singapore are given respect and dignity as an individual being.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: By that, I mean respect for his or her emotional, spiritual, physical, social and political well-being.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And to achieve this, mere economic policy would not be sufficient.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We need a cultural shift to think about things humanistically.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I think that all of us sitting here in this House would admit that we are the privileged today, even if some of us may have come from a less-than-privileged background.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, we may even use ourselves as an example of how meritocracy can work.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We might say, “If I have made it, then others also can or will.” Yet, a statement like that does not acknowledge that each of us faces different challenges, which may affect the options we have and alter the paths we can take in life.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I have talked about vulnerable listening in the last speech I made during the Budget debate and, here, I would like to add one more quality to that, to look at the way we behave culturally.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Paulo Freire, through this experience, developed an approach on how to work with the underclass, the people who are oppressed.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: He said that one needs to listen with compassion and, importantly, one needs to be humble when listening.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As we listen, we need to know that we hold positions of privilege.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We need to acknowledge that knowing the facts or being intelligent does not mean we can solve all problems and offer good solutions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To take a recent example: in trying to save Ellison Building from being demolished and then rebuilt again, various civil society and heritage experts came in to offer solutions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: URA and LTA agreed that they would need to listen deeply, to be more attentive to the needs of all parties and acknowledge that they may not know the best solutions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Being a good leader is not about showing how visionary you are, but about letting people be part of that visioning process.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Lao Zi, in 道德经, or The Way, has these wise words for leaders: 不自见，故明；不自是，故彰。To paraphrase, one should not be prejudicial or you will lose your objectivity.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: With humility, one can then attain and allow for greater possibilities and discoveries.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We should not just think that our rights as citizens are merely about voting in the leaders.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As critical citizens, we must be able to express our views about issues of concern.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We should be able to engage in discourse with reason, passion, humility and empathy.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Discourse amongst people, between different sectors or between people and leadership should not be about winning arguments or about flushing out the other views.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is not about shaming, name-calling or bullying.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, discourse is about understanding and learning to live with the others.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We have acknowledged in this House many a time that the world we live in is getting increasingly more diverse.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We must look towards a heterotopia, a space for all that embraces these differences we have.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Maybe we will be less efficient in managing all these differences.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But I strongly believe that efficacy is more important than efficiency.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot just simply invoke this often-used mantra "agree to disagree", so as to expedite decisions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We need to find the time and a way for us to listen to and understand each other long enough so that we are able to agree to disagree, meaningfully.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And then, our disagreements will still resurface, but when they happen in future, these differences will not be contentious.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Because we have listened with compassion, because we have not assumed that our privilege gives us the ability to offer all the right answers every single time, because we know that, through this long engagement, we would build trust.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In this way, we can address disagreements with empathy and generosity.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Two months ago, Prof Tommy Koh invited me to speak on a panel at Tembusu College, discussing Singapore’s hopes for the next Prime Minister.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The College had also selected a student leader to speak on behalf of his cohort.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And to prepare, this student leader spent a whole month running focus groups and surveying his peers.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: That night, he read out an open letter addressed to the future prime minister that summarised the themes emerging from his research.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Prof Koh, who chaired the discussion, and the rest of us panelists recognised it as the best speech of the night.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: You might have already seen that speech online that went viral and, if you have not, here is the printed version.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many have already weighed in on this letter online and some praise it for being inspiring but others have slammed it for being naive.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And whatever your inclination, it is worth a read because it reflects the perspective of a new generation of voters that will be making themselves heard, regardless, at the ballot boxes in the next few years.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I was nominated into Parliament to give insight into youths’ concerns.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I will thus orient what is probably my last major speech around the three big questions in the students’ letter for they resonate with the themes brought up by Mdm President last week.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Their second and third questions for their future prime minister are: “How will you unite Singapore?” and “What is Singapore to you?”.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This ties in with Mdm President’s call for leadership to deal with social inequality and cast a more inclusive future vision that can “fire up…the spirit of young Singaporeans”.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I will explore the questions and make suggestions that I hope are respectful enough of Mdm President’s call for bold changes versus marginal tweaking.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: First, “How much do you trust us?” In their letter, the students shared their uncertainty about whether their voice in the public square would be welcomed if they did not share pro-establishment views.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They wrote: “Do you see us as equal partners, leaders you want to empower, or as citizens you need to govern?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What kind of role do you trust us to play?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We are prompted in school to think critically and voice our opinions, but we see some naysayers being treated negatively.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We are encouraged to push boundaries…yet, those of us who write articles online are reminded to respect existing boundaries.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And we are taught it is important to learn our history, but are certain narratives preferred over others?” The youths believe that having dissenting views does not mean they are any less passionate for Singapore’s good or less loyal to Singapore’s interests.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They speak out because they care and they want to see their leaders model curiosity and compassion in their engagement with divergent views.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And lest we brush aside these dissenting young people as just part of a “vocal minority” that can be ignored, I find their youthful opinion matches the sentiments I hear from a number of 20- to 40-something professionals from the quieter middle ground.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This is partly because many people in this segment are unlikely to answer such polls in the first place.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They do not like registering their dissent openly, be it on survey or social media or any form of record.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The reasons why these people keep their dissent to themselves vary.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some honestly assume that their opinion is unimportant or unqualified; some like getting along and fear that their honesty will invite an open rebuke or a cold shoulder from the establishment; and others say it is just self-preservation based on their past experiences.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Whatever it is, their quiet dissent is real and such withholding of views may give the leadership the wrong impression that all is quiet on the western front.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is a well-known phenomenon that one unintended effect of being in a powerful leadership position is that people surrounding you may start to presume, wrongly or rightly, that their job is to tell you what you want to hear, rather than what you need to hear.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: One of the most poignant reflections I read about this problem was from former US Secretary of State General Colin Powell.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: To ensure he always had a clear picture of the ground, Powell said that he made his staffers stick to four simple rules: “Tell me what you know.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And always distinguish which is which." But even so, those four good rules still could not prevent the issue of withheld dissent which caused him, and his country, to make an astronomical mistake.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: He recounted, “There is nothing worse than a leader believing he has accurate information when folks who know he doesn’t, don’t tell him that he doesn’t.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I found myself in trouble on more than one occasion because people kept silent when they should have spoken up.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: My infamous speech at the United Nations in 2003 about Iraqi Weapons of Mass Destruction programmes was not based on facts, though I thought it was…A number of senior analysts had big “don’t knows” that they never passed on.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some of these same analysts later wrote books claiming they were shocked that I had relied on such deeply flawed evidence…So, why did no one stand up and speak out during the intense hours that we worked on the speech?…It takes courage to do that, especially if you are standing up to a view strongly held by a superior or to the generally prevailing view, or if you really don’t want to acknowledge ignorance when your boss is demanding answers.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The leader can’t be let off without blame in these situations…He has to relentlessly cross-examine the analysts until he is satisfied he’s got what they know and…what they don’t know.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, the leader must realise that it takes courage for someone to stand up and say to him, “That’s wrong.” “You’re wrong.” Or: “We really don’t know that.” The leader should never shoot the messenger.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I believe such polls may cause an unintended widening of the communication gap between leaders and the ground.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I do not think it is a case of "nobody" cared.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And now, these observers were not saying let us go soft on dissenters who are clearly professional agitators.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But they were asking: how far do we really have to go to bring down people with political opinions that may be different from our own?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What do we gain and what do we lose when we win the argument but display clear contempt of the other person?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Must it always be a zero-sum game in dealing with dissenters or can we work towards a win-win?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And these are not simply questions they are pinning onto political leadership alone but questions they are reflecting for themselves.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because many of them are leaders, too – from non-profits, corporations, public service.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They do work that does require them to work with dissenting stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, they are always looking for inspiration and role-modelling.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: One of Mdm President’s most memorable observations in her speech was about how the new leadership “will need to listen to the views and feelings of the people, and by their words and deeds, show that they have heard…And this is how they will earn the right to lead…In each generation, the people and leaders must work with one another…and forge their own bonds afresh”.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The student’s letter shows us how a new generation of voters would like to work with the new generation of leaders who desire the right to lead them.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They say, “We want you to trust that we do not disagree for dissent’s sake and that we can find unity even in the face of our differences with you…Disagreement is not weakness and your appointment is a chance for a new way for our differences to be received.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We truly believe that it is only in facing our differences together openly, honestly and fearlessly that our discourse can be strengthened, outcomes can be sharpened and our relationship can be deepened.” I train people in how to build trust through conversations and we have a simple rule of thumb.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In every argument, we really only have two end-games to play: you can either prioritise being right, or you can prioritise retaining the relationship and the results that come through that relationship.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This applies as much to arguing with your family as much as it does to arguing with stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When you prioritise retaining relationship over being right, what you gain is new ground to work together towards doing what is right anyway, towards the results you care for.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We can avoid unnecessarily adversarial relationships with our dissenters if we choose to be slow to speak and quick to listen for the truths our naysayers are offering.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If we want our system to be resilient, we need to boldly open up our echo chambers and learn to ask both friends and detractors, “Tell me what you know.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And help me distinguish which is which.” And if we have power, let us be aware of its silencing effects on people so that we can learn to lay it down purposefully to help others feel they have permission and safety to share their truths.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: As the founding Minister S Rajaratnam once said, “Don’t tell me things you think I want to hear; tell me things I should hear even if they make me feel uncomfortable.” I will now move on to my second point on income inequality.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In their letter, the youths echoed: "We are very worried that social inequality is becoming an issue that is dividing Singaporeans faster than we can mitigate it." As we zero in on meeting the needs of children from lower income homes, I hope we do not neglect their parents' needs.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We must not operate from a subconscious mindset of "save the children because the adults are a gone case".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because a child's well-being is tied to their parent's well-being.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Children's needs are tied to parents' needs, children's problems are tied to parents' problems.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Everyone is linked up, for better or for worse, for richer or poorer.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If we want to help the child, we help the parent too.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The same dignities we accord to middle- or upper-income families should be accorded to the lower income.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If we do not think it is culturally dignified or politically viable to tell two single, unrelated upper income individuals or a middle-income family of five to share one HDB room together, then let it be just as inappropriate to tell lower income people that they have to do so, and still achieve great outcomes.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Inequality has to be approached on a whole-of-Government examination of policy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because it is never just about income but power disparity as well.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, when policy declares, you and the child that you gave birth to cannot be officially defined as a family nucleus even if logically that is what you are, you are frozen out of the system and quite powerless to access certain good choices.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: You depend on access through more powerful individuals like a Member of Parliament or social worker to advocate for you on a "case-by-case basis".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: How much better would it be to go for a policy change that can let power thaw, flow and refreeze into a new, hopefully more empowering place, one where the previously disempowered can now help themselves and independently access the options they need to move ahead in life.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There, but for the grace of God, go we.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Who is to say one day we, too, may not come into a similar station in life?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Income is a vital and necessary indicator of well-being but it is not all-sufficient nor is it conclusive.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There are, currently, a few alternative indicators out there in the world: Bhutan's Gross National Happiness, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development's Better Life Index.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And if we think these indicators or others like Gini coefficient are flawed or not applicable to our Singapore context, then why not create one of our own?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A uniquely Singapore system of meaningful measures for well-being would help the people and the Government better communicate where we are and where we want to go.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We can raise our collective level of well-being if we knew which metrics mattered most.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What we do not measure will always be treated as something lesser.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We can criticise Bhutan's Gross National Happiness index, but we cannot dismiss the effect it had in kickstarting the world's thinking for years about what it means for economies to work on the things that matter most to people.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Canada's Well-being Index chooses to measure things like community vitality, culture and time use.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But we can base our well-being index: on what we believe reflects our unique values: unity between different races and religions, democratic participation, justice, equality, happiness and, of course, economic prosperity and progress.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The third and final question the youths had "What is Singapore to you?" is a provocative question to pose not just to leadership but to ourselves as an electorate.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The votes we cast, or do not cast.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The positions we support, or do not support.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The donations we give, or do not give.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The risks we take, or do not take.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The people that we serve, or do not serve.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is as bold, and as kind, as inclusive, as original, and as vital as we make her to be.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Our country is us, the sum total of all our choices.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Where it was their time to tear down, perhaps now is our time to build up.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Where it was their time to keep silent, perhaps now is our time to speak.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There is a time for everything and a season for every one of us, under the heavens.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They were who they were and they were who they had to be.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Those times and their times are past, but our time is now.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We each must learn to be bold enough to live out who we are and dare to challenge who we could be.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We need only be the best of ourselves, seizing the most of our times, steering our country our way.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And if we are scared, then let the words of Mr Chiam See Tong, Singapore's longest-serving Opposition Member, give us courage.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In a sense, this is not surprising – good ideas are the product of long reflection and examination, but they are also, sometimes, the result of an urgent felt need, some local knowledge from ground experience or even strong emotional response.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As we have seen in the past few days, bold ideas are not in short supply.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But sieving them through the good from the not so practical or reckless ones, the strong from the popular and perhaps, even more difficult: implementing these ideas, if not flawlessly, then at least successfully, is far more difficult.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is far easier to write a policy paper than to actually make the policy happen.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I say this not to belittle the role of bold ideas but to argue their limitations.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We ought not to let ideas be our masters but think more deeply about their weight and impact.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: That is, we should worry less about what we do than why we do them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Today, Mr Speaker, Sir, I argue one simple idea, which is to rethink the way we evaluate ideas.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to rethink the role of the market and of economic reasoning.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For a long time, the economic reasoning that our Government applied to public policies have stood us in good stead.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Whether in healthcare, housing or the management of much of our social policy, such reasoning has allowed us to make good use of our resources.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The magic words in any policy was whether it was "sustainable", that is, whether it would "pay for itself".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A long-term reliance on Government funding is sometimes the kiss of death for a good idea.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For, if the idea was good, surely, money can be found from the market.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But economic reasoning is empty without a moral foundation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Such foundations cannot and do not exist without a conversation about values – not just what is cheap, but what is right; not just about generating income, but about giving meaning.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For too long, we have made decisions based more on an economic compass, as if the use of $1 has the moral equivalence of the loss of another.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need regulations on responsible use of funds, on fiscal prudence, good procurement but, equally, we ought to be having a conversation about reciprocity, trust and relationships.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They know the magic of little gestures of a sticker with a thumbs-up stuck on an untidy worksheet for encouragement for a little child who handed in his homework despite family difficulties; a treat of a small snack; a lift to school to a pupil who otherwise would not want to come.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Teachers who have all these years paid for all forms of Children's Day treats and surprises for our children, all these things which cost them no small amount of money, and yet, whose value transcends price.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Teachers who have bought their own red pens to mark the test papers of all our children, they do not think that "the Ministry of Education (MOE) does not pay for red pens".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They do not think "I should means-test the kids and give treats only to those who cannot afford it".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is laughable and an insult to think that they do this in exchange for free parking.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, of course, the withdrawal of free parking would not make teachers any less likely to do the many incredible, unpriced things they do.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Rather, it is a reciprocity and a give and take which I feel we have lost by insisting on this strict calculus of benefits.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Using a clean wage argument implies that all the years of free parking had tarred teachers with an "unclean" wage.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Teachers, I think, have accepted this and have moved on.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But something still sits uncomfortably on this matter for me.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And I want to address this squarely: not all Government policies have a complete recourse to dollars and cents.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need, within our current structures, to make more room from the lexicon of morality, duty, relationships and trust.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Rather, it is an appeal to the ideas of justice and community that have informed Singapore public policymaking at the start of our journey 53 years ago.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Thinking about the issue using a pure economic lens is, I argue, a mistake, as is the reduction of "clean wage" – surely a moral idea – to a mere tableau of taxable benefits.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Without this lexicon, we will not be able to address the greatest problems that have arisen in our time.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The current debate has framed it as a problem of inequality but that risks mere description without a thesis.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We might better frame it as a problem of an overweening dominance of economic magical thinking, a problem which, again, could be addressed by recalibrating the balance between the economics and the morality of our public actions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I have said before in this House that this compensates for such matters as luck in birth and circumstances and I still hold that view even more strongly today.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the past, it used to be that a degree was a tried and tested way to climb up the ladder.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Today, more and more of us, Ministers included, have said that a degree is not the only way.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the United States (US), the higher education premium has not increased for the past 10 years.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: When the premium on higher education falls, it is replaced by more varied paths, and decision-making always levies a higher cognitive tax on the poor.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We must make sure that the transition to the new economic structure benefits the least advantaged in our society.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, I know that we need to be sensitive to the accusations of unfairness, that it is unfair that the people who pay taxes get the least out of the system, that Singapore ought to be a country for all, rather than always take from one side and giving to the other.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And yet this is the truth of a nation – those who have more bear a larger burden.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is how we tie to one another as Singaporeans, confident that whoever falls upon hard times, rich or poor, they will have a helping hand.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is our only safety net against fate and bad luck, whether in bad health or accidents.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Incidentally, this also includes many external events outside our control.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: All in the recognition that in the veil of ignorance, luck and chance attend to all men and women, and all Singaporeans need to stick together through thick and thin.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I do not mean this to say that we need a minimum wage, or universal welfare.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need a partnership of all Singaporeans, for a deeper engagement with Singaporeans with different needs, to negotiate paths through the complexity of our interests.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And within the past few months alone, I think we have seen unusually cool and unusually warm days.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is a significant problem and not one that we can solve alone.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For example, in changing the way we live, and spend resources, in making changes to our diet, for one, and our energy consumption for another.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to make sure that the capital that we rely on today still remains for the needs of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, Mr Speaker, Sir, mine is a simple idea.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to make what is cheap, efficient and quick to what is fair, just and right.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It may be that there is no one policy, no matter how bold, that will address the most pressing problems of our times.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It may be that Singapore today is a problem for the foxes rather than hedgehogs, but we need first to recognise that foxes speak the multi-tonal language of values, rather than the universal language of money.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We must, therefore, make language of morality our vernacular in policy matters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: He could not speak English, and apparently the staff at the counter did not understand him and told him to stand aside while they served others.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Eventually, he said, they told him to leave.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Over and over, the resident described to me his encounter.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: How he felt the counter staff looked down on him, how others in the queue became aware of his inability to speak English.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I explained to my resident that I would write an appeal for him with regard to his licence application.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But over and over, he continued to describe his encounter to me.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Every look he thought he saw, every tone he heard, every slight he felt, his dignity, Mr Speaker, had been hurt.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have programmes to build a fair and just society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
